This is based primarily on qualitative focus group data; the paper does not report a separate quantitative metacognition measure.
finding.measure: Focus group interview themes about comprehension support, personalization, and learner autonomy

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing EFL Speaking Skills through AI-Supported Literary Works: A Quantitative Study on Drama, Poetry, and Short Stories
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an AI-assisted literary intervention can improve EFL learners’ speaking skills. The authors respond to a persistent instructional problem in EFL contexts: learners often have limited speaking practice, low confidence, and little immediate feedback, especially in input-poor environments where English is rarely used outside class.

The intervention combined drama, poetry, and short stories with AI-supported activities over 12 weeks. The AI platform provided speech recognition, pronunciation and fluency feedback, language analysis, adaptive support, and interactive practice with literary materials. The study used a pretest/post-test quantitative design plus semi-structured interviews to capture learner perceptions. Although the manuscript describes both quantitative and qualitative components, the intervention was pre-experimental and lacked a control group, so causal attribution to AI is limited.

Participants were undergraduate EFL learners at an Indonesian university. Speaking was assessed with a standardized rubric covering pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, fluency, and interaction. Results showed large gains from pretest to post-test (mean 12.86 to 24.07; t(27)=42.47, p<.001, d=1.55), with large subscale effects especially for vocabulary (d=1.72) and interaction (d=1.64). Interview data suggested that learners valued vocabulary enrichment, increased confidence, immediate feedback, motivation, and personalization. The authors conclude that AI-supported literary works are promising for speaking development, but they recommend larger randomized controlled trials to verify effectiveness and rule out bias or ceiling effects.

finding.finding_summary: Speaking performance improved substantially after the 12-week AI-supported literary intervention. Mean overall speaking scores increased from 12.86 (SD=2.14) at pretest to 24.07 (SD=1.03) at post-test, a gain of 11.21 points; the paired-samples test was significant, t(27)=42.47, p<.001, with a large effect size (d=1.55). Subscales also improved significantly, including pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, fluency, and interaction.
finding.measure: Standardized speaking rubric assessing pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, fluency, and interaction

finding.finding_summary: Learners reported improved confidence, motivation, and reduced speaking anxiety after using the AI-supported literary activities. Qualitative interviews highlighted that the private, non-judgmental AI environment made students more willing to speak, and survey ratings were high for confidence (M=4.57/5) and motivation (M=4.46/5).
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews and closed-ended learner perception ratings on confidence, motivation, and anxiety-related comfort
finding.std_deviation: Confidence item SD=0.57; motivation item SD=0.69

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests gains in personalized learning engagement and self-monitoring through immediate feedback, though durable skills were not the primary outcome. Learners described using the AI feedback to notice errors, practice repeatedly, and tailor study to their own needs, indicating metacognitive support within the speaking tasks.
finding.measure: Learner perceptions from interviews and questionnaire items about instant feedback and personalized learning
finding.std_deviation: Instant feedback item SD=0.39; personalization item SD=0.63

finding.finding_summary: Vocabulary development was a major documented benefit of the intervention. The vocabulary subscale increased from 2.61 (SD=0.50) to 4.89 (SD=0.32), with a very large effect size (d=1.72), and participants consistently reported learning and using new words from the literary texts with AI support.
finding.measure: Vocabulary subscale of the speaking rubric

paper_profiles.title: The AI generation gap: Are Gen Z students more interested in adopting generative AI such as ChatGPT in teaching and learning than their Gen X and millennial generation teachers?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how Generation Z undergraduate students and Gen X/Gen Y teachers perceive, understand, and intend to use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education. The authors were motivated by the rapid spread of GenAI in 2023 and the need to understand whether younger students and older teachers differ in their openness, concerns, and readiness for classroom integration.

The study used an online mixed-methods survey with closed-ended items and open-ended responses. A total of 583 participants were included: 399 students and 184 teachers, mostly based in Hong Kong, with additional respondents from Mainland China and other regions. Quantitative analysis compared student and teacher responses on use frequency, perceived benefits, knowledge of risks/limitations, and concerns; qualitative thematic coding examined intended uses and worries about GenAI in teaching and learning.

Findings suggest that Gen Z students were generally more optimistic and more frequent users of GenAI than teachers, seeing it as useful for saving time, improving writing, supporting learning, and providing anonymous help. Teachers also recognized benefits, but were more cautious about overreliance, misinformation, bias, and the need for fact-checking, policies, and responsible-use guidelines. Across both groups, respondents emphasized that GenAI should complement rather than replace human teaching, and that institutions need clear governance, AI literacy, and updated assessment practices to manage academic integrity and pedagogical change.

finding.finding_summary: Participants commonly reported that GenAI could support writing tasks, including essay structure, proofreading, grammar checking, and improving writing quality. In the quantitative survey, students rated GenAI as more helpful for becoming a better writer than teachers did (MS=3.29, SD=1.16; MT=3.06, SD=1.23; t=2.07, p=0.039), and open-ended responses frequently described using it for writing support and literature reviews.
finding.measure: Perceptions and intended uses related to writing support, proofreading, essay drafting, and writing improvement

finding.finding_summary: A major finding was that respondents viewed GenAI as a productivity tool that could save time and streamline repetitive tasks. Students agreed more strongly than teachers that GenAI could help save time (MS=4.16, SD=0.83; MT=3.90, SD=0.88; t=3.38, p<0.001), and both groups described using it for summarising information, drafting emails, generating summaries/quizzes, and supporting administrative work.
finding.measure: Perceptions of time-saving/productivity and intended use for repetitive or administrative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI may support some durable skills, especially by helping users brainstorm, consolidate information, and receive feedback, but it also raised concerns that overreliance could undermine critical thinking and evaluative ability. Teachers were more concerned than students that GenAI could encourage dependence and reduce students’ own thinking, while qualitative data stressed the need to use GenAI to foster critical reflection rather than replace it.
finding.measure: Perceptions of critical thinking, evaluative skills, originality/creativity, and overreliance

finding.finding_summary: The study strongly emphasized the need for institutional policy, governance, and assessment redesign in response to GenAI. Both students and teachers agreed that higher education institutions should have a plan for managing GenAI risks (students M=4.47, SD=0.83; teachers M=4.53, SD=0.86), and qualitative findings repeatedly called for clear guidelines, responsible-use protocols, and updated assessment practices.
finding.measure: Agreement with institutional planning/policy items and qualitative themes about governance, guidelines, and assessment redesign

paper_profiles.title: Education reform and change driven by digital technology: a bibliometric study from a global perspective
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (bibliometric review of education research literature; no direct human participant population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a bibliometric review of global research on digital technology in education from 2000 to 2022. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, it maps the field’s development using Web of Science records, PRISMA screening, and visualization tools (CiteSpace, VOSviewer, Charticulator) to identify publication trends, leading authors, countries, institutions, journals, and thematic hotspots.

The review argues that digital technology has become a major driver of educational reform, expanding learning across time and space and supporting teaching and learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. It divides the field into developmental phases and shows a shift from early computer-focused work to later emphases on social media, mobile learning, blended learning, digital literacy, digital transformation, and teacher professional development. The authors conclude that technology adoption in education is shaped by both technological change and historical context, and they highlight professional development and digital transformation as current frontiers.

Because this is a bibliometric synthesis, the paper does not evaluate a specific AI tool’s effects on students or teachers in a single study. Its relevance to K-12 implementation mechanisms is conceptual and field-mapping in nature: it suggests that digital technology adoption in schools is driven by infrastructure, digital skills, leadership, professional development, and pandemic-related pressures, but it does not provide direct empirical estimates of teacher morale or classroom engagement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that digital technology adoption in education is shaped by institutional, technological, and historical factors, with the COVID-19 pandemic accelerating digital transformation across schools and higher education. It identifies digital transformation and professional development as major current hotspots, but also notes barriers such as infrastructure gaps and psychological resistance among teachers and students. No single effect size is reported because this is a bibliometric synthesis of 588 articles rather than an outcome study.
finding.measure: Bibliometric indicators, keyword burst analysis, publication trends, and thematic mapping of education research

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses engagement-related themes in the literature, especially the emerging keywords 'engagement,' 'participation,' and 'digital skill,' and notes that digital technology can support learner motivation and self-efficacy. However, it also reports concerns that technology may distract learners or disrupt learning and memory, so the direction of the field’s findings is mixed rather than uniformly positive. No effect size is available because the paper synthesizes research trends rather than reporting a primary intervention study.
finding.measure: Keyword bursts and thematic evolution in the literature on learner engagement, participation, and digital literacy

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that a major stream of the literature frames digital technology as improving teaching and learning effectiveness, extending education across time and space, and supporting teacher professional development and emergency remote teaching. It also identifies professional development as a key hotspot, suggesting that technology can improve the organization and execution of teaching work, although the paper does not quantify workload reduction or productivity gains. No effect size is reported because the study is bibliometric and descriptive.
finding.measure: Literature themes on teaching effectiveness, professional development, and implementation of digital tools in educational practice

paper_profiles.title: Interventions to Reduce Stigma Related to Mental Illnesses in Educational Institutes: a Systematic Review
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines whether anti-stigma interventions delivered in educational institutes reduce stigma related to mental illness and improve related knowledge, attitudes, help-seeking intentions, and social distance. The authors searched eight databases and identified 44 randomized controlled trials conducted in schools, colleges, universities, medical schools, and adult educational settings, with studies spanning 1998–2018.

The interventions included psychoeducation, contact-based approaches, role-play, case vignettes, videos, online modules, Mental Health First Aid, and mixed-format classroom programs. Most studies targeted students, especially adolescents and undergraduates, and many focused on depression, schizophrenia/psychosis, autism, or mental health problems in general. Across outcomes, the review found that many studies reported improvements in stigma, attitudes, help-seeking, knowledge, and social distance, but effects were heterogeneous and often limited by high risk of bias and short follow-up.

Overall, the review concludes that educational-institute-based anti-stigma interventions are promising, especially when they combine education with contact or other active components. The authors also note that many interventions were short-term, concentrated in high-income countries, and focused more on public stigma than self-stigma, indicating a need for stronger trials, longer follow-up, and culturally tailored programs in low- and middle-income settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 11 studies measuring attitudes and 11 studies measuring help-seeking, most reported favorable changes after anti-stigma interventions. For stigma-related outcomes, 19/25 studies showed significant improvement, and the review reports that interventions such as psychoeducation, contact-based learning, role-play, and video/case-vignette approaches generally improved attitudes toward people with mental illness and intentions to seek help.
finding.measure: Stigma scales, attitude scales, and help-seeking intention/attitude measures
finding.study_size: n=44 studies (with 25 stigma studies; 11 attitude studies; 11 help-seeking studies)

finding.finding_summary: The review includes several interventions that used classroom discussion, case vignettes, and contact-based activities intended to shift beliefs and reasoning about mental illness, which are related to perspective-taking and critical evaluation. These interventions were generally associated with improved understanding and reduced stigma, but the paper does not isolate durable-skill outcomes as a primary endpoint, so this assignment is modest-confidence.
finding.measure: Knowledge/attitude outcomes from classroom-based stigma-reduction activities

finding.finding_summary: The review notes one intervention focused on engagement in psychotherapy treatment and several studies that improved help-seeking intentions, but it does not directly measure teacher workload or productivity. Because the paper includes interventions delivered by teachers/instructors in school settings and discusses improved willingness to seek help, the operational-efficiency link is indirect and weakly substantiated.
finding.measure: Help-seeking intentions and related engagement outcomes
finding.study_size: n=11 help-seeking studies; one study on engagement in psychotherapy treatment

paper_profiles.title: SEARCH: A Meta-Framework and Review of the Field of Positive Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Applied Positive Psychology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in positive education: the field has expanded rapidly, but schools and researchers lack a coherent, evidence-based framework for deciding which wellbeing interventions to use and how they map onto student outcomes. The authors propose the SEARCH meta-framework, which organizes positive education into six pathways: strengths, emotional management, attention and awareness, relationships, coping, and habits and goals.

The framework was developed in two stages. First, the authors synthesized a very large positive psychology literature using bibliometric and natural language processing methods, then road-tested the resulting pathways through action research with ten schools. Second, they conducted a systematic review of 75 peer-reviewed school-based intervention studies (total student N=35,888) to evaluate whether the six pathways are supported by evidence in educational settings.

The review concludes that SEARCH is a useful and practical organizing framework for positive education research and implementation. Across the reviewed studies, single-focus interventions generally showed pathway-consistent benefits for student wellbeing and, in many cases, for school-based outcomes such as engagement, grades, confidence, and academic aspirations. The evidence was strongest for some positive outcomes, while reductions in negative wellbeing indicators were less consistent, and the authors emphasize both the utility of SEARCH and the need for further research on additivity and generalizability.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review finds that single-focus positive education interventions often improved student social-emotional outcomes across the six SEARCH pathways, including higher strengths use/knowledge, emotional intelligence, gratitude, engagement, hope, life satisfaction, self-esteem, and some reductions in anxiety, depression, and aggression. Effects were reported across 75 studies (total student N=35,888), with several pathway-specific studies showing significant gains, though not all studies found benefits and some effects were moderated by baseline levels or faded over time.
finding.measure: Strengths knowledge/use, hope, emotional intelligence, gratitude, life satisfaction, positive affect, self-esteem, engagement, anxiety, depression, aggression, peer relations
finding.study_size: n=35,888 (75 studies total); pathway-specific samples varied

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that interventions targeting SEARCH pathways were associated with improvements in durable skills such as self-regulation, attention, awareness, and coping-related competencies, especially through mindfulness/meditation, coping, and self-regulation programs. These interventions were linked to better emotional control and student abilities to focus, monitor themselves, and manage stress, although the review does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, attention, awareness, coping skills, mindfulness, meditation, emotional regulation
finding.study_size: n=35,888 (75 studies total); pathway-specific samples varied

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that many interventions improved school-based and academic outcomes, including academic expectations, academic motivation, academic confidence, academic performance scores, GPA, school enjoyment, classroom engagement, and scholastic confidence. Reported examples include a strengths program that increased academic expectations and motivation, and a multi-year strengths-based program with moderate effects and an average 7% gain in standardized academic performance scores.
finding.measure: Academic expectations, academic motivation, academic ability perceptions, GPA, standardized academic performance, school engagement, scholastic confidence, school transition readiness
finding.study_size: n=35,888 (75 studies total); pathway-specific samples varied
finding.effect_size: d=not_reported; moderate effects reported in one study; 7% gain in standardized academic performance scores

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Scotland’s Future: Report of a review of teacher education in Scotland
paper_profiles.population: Educators (K-12 teachers and prospective teachers in Scotland)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report is a national review of teacher education in Scotland, commissioned by the Scottish Government and led by Graham Donaldson. It asks what kinds of teachers and leaders Scotland needs for the future, how teacher education should be structured across initial teacher education, induction, and career-long professional learning, and how the system can better support Curriculum for Excellence.

The report is based on a literature review, a call for evidence, surveys of serving teachers, and consultations with universities, schools, local authorities, and other stakeholders. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, it synthesizes evidence and proposes a reform agenda: stronger school-university partnerships, more rigorous selection, better alignment of theory and practice, improved use of ICT, and more coherent career-long professional learning.

Its main conclusion is that Scottish education should move toward a model of extended teacher professionalism in which teachers are reflective, enquiring, collaborative, and engaged in leadership from the start of their careers. The report argues that teacher education should be more coherent, more relevant to classroom realities, and better connected to system-level improvement, with the ultimate aim of improving learning for children and young people.

finding.finding_summary: The review proposes a broad system-level reform of teacher education in Scotland, arguing that greater coherence across selection, initial teacher education, induction, and career-long professional learning would strengthen the profession and improve learning. It recommends new partnership structures, more consistent standards, stronger quality assurance, and improved workforce planning, but does not report experimental effects or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional arrangements for teacher education, partnership, standards, and workforce planning

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that current teacher education and CPD are often fragmented, haphazard, and inefficient, and proposes more integrated pathways, better use of time, and stronger alignment between university and school learning. It also calls for improved information flow and workforce planning to better match teacher supply with demand, but provides no quantitative efficiency estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher education coherence, time use, CPD organization, and workforce planning processes

finding.finding_summary: A substantial theme of the review is that effective teachers should be reflective, committed, collaborative, and able to support motivation and engagement in learners. The report links these attributes to Curriculum for Excellence and to teacher professionalism, but the evidence is qualitative and policy-oriented rather than outcome-testing.
finding.measure: Teacher and student perceptions of teacher qualities including engagement, motivation, reflection, and interpersonal skill

finding.finding_summary: The report emphasizes critical thinking, reflection, inquiry, collaboration, and networking as core skills for twenty-first-century teaching and leadership. It draws on stakeholder views and international literature to argue that these durable skills should be developed from entry into the profession, but it does not quantify their effects on measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Stakeholder views and literature on reflective, enquiring, collaborative, and leadership-related teacher capabilities

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies literacy as a key area needing stronger preparation and support, noting that some newly qualified teachers have difficulties with literacy and that all teachers need sound understanding of how children acquire literacy skills. It recommends better attention to literacy in teacher education, but does not report direct intervention effects or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher preparedness and understanding of literacy acquisition; references to literacy skills in teacher education

finding.finding_summary: The report similarly identifies numeracy as a foundational area that teacher education must address more explicitly, including how children develop numeracy skills over time. The document is a policy review and offers recommendations rather than empirical estimates of impact.
finding.measure: Teacher preparedness and understanding of numeracy acquisition; references to numeracy in teacher education

paper_profiles.title: Factors influencing academic staff satisfaction and continuous usage of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines what factors shape academic staff satisfaction and continued use of generative AI tools in higher education. The authors argue that, although GenAI is increasingly used for teaching, research, and administrative tasks, less is known about what drives educators to keep using it after initial adoption. To address this gap, they combine the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM), and add ethical considerations and security/privacy as additional predictors.

The study used an online survey of 127 faculty members at Allama Iqbal Open University in Pakistan, a distance-learning institution, and analyzed the data with PLS-SEM. Respondents reported using GenAI for teaching activities such as lesson planning, content creation, and assessment support, with many using tools like ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, and Copilot. The model found that effort expectancy, ethical consideration, and expectation confirmation were positively related to satisfaction/confirmation pathways, while performance expectancy predicted continuous intention to use GenAI but not satisfaction. Social influence was not significant.

Overall, the paper concludes that sustained GenAI use in higher education depends less on social pressure and more on whether the tools are easy to use, ethically acceptable, secure, and consistent with user expectations. Satisfaction itself was a strong predictor of continued intention to use GenAI. The authors recommend institutional training, technical support, clear ethical guidelines, and better infrastructure to support responsible and effective GenAI integration in academic work.

finding.finding_summary: The study primarily shows that GenAI supports academic staff’s work processes and continued use when it is easy to use, supported by infrastructure, and perceived as useful for job performance. Performance expectancy predicted continuous intention to use GenAI (β=0.149, p=0.021), and facilitation conditions also predicted continuous intention (β=0.289, p=0.006) in a sample of n=127 faculty members.
finding.measure: Continuous intention to use GenAI; survey constructs assessing performance expectancy and facilitation conditions

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses strongly on institutional conditions for responsible GenAI implementation, including ethics, security/privacy, and support structures. Ethical consideration predicted expectation confirmation (β=0.198, p=0.009), security and privacy predicted academic staff satisfaction (β=0.225, p=0.007), and the authors propose policy and institutional guidelines to support sustainable GenAI adoption.
finding.measure: Ethical consideration, security/privacy, expectation confirmation, and academic staff satisfaction surveys

paper_profiles.title: Examining Teaching Competencies and Challenges While Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how instructors integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education teaching and learning, focusing on the competencies needed and the challenges they encounter. Guided by an intelligent TPACK framework, the authors reviewed 23 empirical studies published from 2019 to 2023 and coded them for AI integration competencies, pedagogical strategies, and implementation limitations.

The review identifies four main competency areas: AI literacy/readiness, AI-supported innovative pedagogy, AI as intelligent learning partners to increase student engagement, and AI-driven learning experience design and delivery. Across the included studies, AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, automated feedback systems, adaptive learning systems, robots, and GenAI were associated with improved engagement, personalized feedback, workload reduction, and support for self-regulated learning and higher-order thinking. The review also highlights four recurring challenges: short-term novelty effects, digital divides, technical deficiencies, and ethical concerns such as privacy, fairness, transparency, and accessibility.

Overall, the paper argues that successful AI integration depends on instructor preparation, purposeful course design, ethical awareness, and human supervision. It emphasizes that AI can supplement but not replace instructor social presence and that sustainable implementation requires coordinated attention to pedagogy, learner readiness, and institutional support. The study is focused on higher education rather than K-12, but it offers implementation mechanisms that are conceptually relevant to daily teaching work and teacher support roles.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI tools were repeatedly associated with increased student engagement, motivation, self-efficacy, and positive affect in learning contexts. The review synthesizes evidence from 23 studies (2019-2023), reporting that chatbots, robots, and adaptive systems could support self-regulated learning and engagement, though some effects were short-term and novelty-driven rather than sustained.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-efficacy, and self-regulated learning measures reported in the included primary studies
finding.study_size: n=23 studies (review synthesis); primary-study sample sizes varied and are not fully reported in the review

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported learning environments were linked to gains in higher-order thinking skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and collaboration. These benefits were especially associated with AI tools used as learning partners, including chatbots, GenAI, and adaptive systems that prompted students to analyze outputs, reflect, and engage in algorithmic thinking.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognitive skills, and collaborative learning outcomes reported in the included studies
finding.study_size: n=23 studies (review synthesis); primary-study sample sizes varied and are not fully reported in the review

finding.finding_summary: A consistent finding across the reviewed literature is that AI tools can reduce instructor workload and improve task efficiency, especially through automated grading, instant feedback, and administrative support. The review notes that these tools help instructors save time on routine tasks and supplement instructor availability, although technical and ethical limitations remain.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, grading efficiency, feedback timeliness, and task automation outcomes reported in the included studies
finding.study_size: n=23 studies (review synthesis); primary-study sample sizes varied and are not fully reported in the review

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI integration improved learning outcomes across subject-specific contexts, with English language learning the most frequently represented area and additional studies in computing programming, medical education, and international relations. The summarized studies suggest benefits for personalized support, feedback, and content mastery, but the review does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Subject-specific learning outcomes such as language learning performance, programming learning, and medical concept understanding
finding.study_size: n=23 studies (review synthesis); primary-study sample sizes varied and are not fully reported in the review

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies focused on English language learning and found that AI tools such as chatbots and automated writing support improved writing, ideation, communication, and language practice. The review indicates that AI often provided immediate and personalized feedback in language-learning contexts, though some systems had limited depth or did not improve syntactic complexity.
finding.measure: Writing, ideation, communication, and language-learning outcomes in English learning contexts
finding.study_size: n=7 English language learning studies within the 23-study review

paper_profiles.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into public health education and healthcare: insights from the COVID-19 and monkeypox crises for future pandemic readiness
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines how the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted education and healthcare systems and argues that these disruptions created an opportunity to rethink how artificial intelligence (AI) could support public health education, workforce training, and healthcare delivery. Although the paper discusses higher education broadly, its main emphasis is on preparing public health and healthcare professionals for future outbreaks, using COVID-19 and monkeypox (Mpox) as motivating cases.

The article synthesizes experiences from multiple countries and settings to describe how institutions shifted to remote, hybrid, synchronous, and asynchronous teaching, and how these shifts affected learning continuity, assessments, student engagement, and educator workloads. It also reviews the expansion of telemedicine, videoconferencing, and AI-enabled tools such as chatbots, epidemiological modeling, and machine translation during the pandemic. The authors propose that AI can strengthen outbreak prediction, remote service delivery, and educational continuity, but emphasize that successful adoption requires infrastructure, ethical safeguards, data access, training, and coordinated institutional policy.

The paper concludes with recommendations for integrating AI into public health education and healthcare systems, especially in developing contexts where internet access, funding, and digital capacity are limited. Its central contribution is conceptual and policy-oriented rather than empirical: it frames AI as a strategic tool for preparedness, workforce support, and scalable remote learning and care, while warning that equity, privacy, and governance challenges must be addressed.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI, remote learning platforms, telemedicine, and hybrid education models can strengthen institutional readiness for future health crises by improving continuity of instruction, outbreak preparedness, and healthcare delivery. It does not report a single evaluated effect size; instead it synthesizes examples such as widespread adoption of Zoom/WebEx/Teams, AI chatbots, and epidemiological modeling as mechanisms for institutional adaptation.
finding.measure: Institutional practices, preparedness, and adoption of AI-enabled and remote-delivery systems

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI-powered tools and digital platforms can make educational and healthcare tasks more efficient, including remote teaching, appointment scheduling, symptom assessment, medication reminders, and telehealth interactions. It also notes that during COVID-19, institutions used videoconferencing and AI tools to reduce barriers to service delivery, but no quantitative efficiency estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Task efficiency, service delivery efficiency, and workflow support in education and healthcare

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed COVID-19 education literature, the paper reports increased anxiety, stress, reduced motivation, and feelings of isolation among students and educators in remote learning contexts, while also noting that flexible learning and improved access could support engagement and continuity. These are descriptive findings drawn from cited studies rather than a new empirical analysis, and no pooled effect sizes are provided.
finding.measure: Student and teacher motivation, anxiety, stress, isolation, and engagement in remote learning contexts

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that blended learning, asynchronous learning, and AI-supported tools can foster self-regulation, personalized learning, and collaboration, especially through recorded sessions, flexible access, and project continuation across settings. However, these claims are supported by narrative synthesis and examples rather than direct measurement in this paper.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, collaboration, flexibility in learning, and problem-solving in remote/blended settings

finding.finding_summary: The review specifically highlights AI-driven epidemiological modeling, outbreak prediction, and analysis of immune responses as promising supports for scientific and public health reasoning. It also cites a Morocco case in which Google Classroom was reported to support scientific thinking skills in a fluid mechanics course, but the paper itself does not present new experimental estimates.
finding.measure: Epidemiological modeling, outbreak prediction, and scientific thinking skills

paper_profiles.title: Prospective Artificial Intelligence (AI) Applications in the University Education Level: Enhancing Learning, Teaching and Administration through a PRISMA Base Review Systematic Review
paper_profiles.venue: Pakistan Journal of Life and Social Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews prospective applications of artificial intelligence in university education, focusing on how AI can improve teaching, learning, and administration. Using a PRISMA-based systematic review, the authors screened 292 publications from 2019–2024 and finalized 84 studies drawn from academic journal articles, conference papers, and institutional reports.

The review emphasizes AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated grading, predictive analytics, learning management systems, and administrative automation. It argues that AI can increase efficiency, personalize instruction, and support decision-making, while also identifying major risks including data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, unequal access, and potential depersonalization of educational services.

Although the paper is framed around university education rather than K-12, it is directly relevant to implementation pathways for AI in daily teaching work because it discusses automation of routine tasks, lesson planning support, real-time analytics, and teacher time savings. The main conclusion is that AI offers meaningful benefits but must be implemented with strong governance, fairness checks, and equitable access strategies to avoid worsening inequality or reducing human interaction in education.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI streamlines administrative and teaching tasks such as attendance tracking, grading, lesson planning, scheduling, and routine student monitoring, freeing staff time for more student-centered work. It does not report a single pooled effect size, but repeatedly characterizes these efficiencies as a major benefit across the 84 included studies.
finding.measure: Administrative task automation, grading efficiency, attendance tracking, scheduling, lesson planning, and teacher workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools can improve student engagement through personalized learning, real-time feedback, and adaptive content, but also warns that over-automation can depersonalize services and reduce classroom engagement if human interaction is diminished. No quantitative effect size is reported; the paper presents these as synthesized conclusions from the reviewed literature.
finding.measure: Student engagement, classroom participation, and perceived personalization of learning experiences

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI-supported learning can foster problem solving and critical thinking through adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, simulations, and difficult problem prompts, although these claims are based on the reviewed literature rather than a meta-analytic estimate. It also notes that technology may support creative solutions and self-paced learning, but no effect size or confidence interval is provided.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem solving, self-paced learning, and creative solution generation

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI can improve institutional decision-making, resource allocation, and operational management through predictive analytics and administrative automation, but it also raises major governance concerns around privacy, bias, digital divide, and equitable access. The paper does not provide a quantitative institutional effect size; instead, it synthesizes ethical and implementation pathways across the literature.
finding.measure: Institutional efficiency, governance practices, data privacy, algorithmic fairness, and equitable access

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Educational Transformation: Trends and Future Directions
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Systems and Informatics
paper_profiles.population: K-12, Higher Education, and Vocational Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence is transforming education, with a particular focus on AI-enabled personalized learning, assessment, tutoring, administrative automation, and smart campus functions. The authors ask what trends characterize current AI-in-education work and what future directions and implementation challenges should guide the field, using a PRISMA-based systematic review.

The review synthesizes 175 articles drawn from major databases and related sources. Across the reviewed literature, AI is presented as improving learning efficiency, personalization, feedback, grading, prediction of student risk, and operational productivity, while also introducing concerns about privacy, bias, infrastructure, training, and the digital divide. The paper emphasizes that successful implementation depends on teacher/administrator training, equitable access, and responsible governance rather than technology alone.

Although the paper discusses K-12 education explicitly, it is not an empirical study of a single K-12 intervention or sample; instead, it is a broad review spanning K-12, higher education, and vocational contexts. Its main conclusion is that AI has substantial promise for educational transformation, but current evidence is uneven and long-term, theory-driven, and ethically grounded research is still needed, especially regarding student outcomes and implementation conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI applications such as personalized learning, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, and automated feedback were associated with improved learning efficiency, academic achievement, and more tailored instruction. The review also notes that benefits were context-dependent and that evidence remained uneven across settings, with the authors emphasizing the need for more longitudinal and theory-driven studies rather than reporting a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency, academic achievement, personalized learning outcomes, feedback quality

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly links AI-supported personalized learning and adaptive instruction with higher student engagement and motivation, noting that learner-centered systems can make lessons more relevant and accessible. However, the paper also cautions that over-reliance on AI and unresolved ethical concerns may limit sustained benefits for student engagement and experience.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, learner participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can support collaboration, peer-to-peer communication, and adaptive problem solving through intelligent tutoring systems, guided inquiry, and personalized pathways. These claims are synthesised from the reviewed literature rather than measured in a single experiment, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Collaboration, peer-to-peer communication, problem-solving, critical thinking related outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion is that AI can reduce teacher workload and improve operational efficiency through automated grading, assessment, administrative automation, predictive analytics, and real-time feedback. The review states that AI can save teachers time and effort, improve productivity, and streamline institutional processes, but the evidence is summarized qualitatively across the 175 reviewed studies rather than quantified with a pooled estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading efficiency, administrative efficiency, task automation

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI can improve institutional efficiency, resource allocation, smart-campus functionality, and broader access to education, suggesting meaningful system-level benefits. At the same time, it highlights institutional barriers and risks including privacy, algorithmic bias, infrastructure gaps, training deficits, and digital divide issues, so the overall institutional impact is presented as both positive and constrained.
finding.measure: Institutional efficiency, resource allocation, smart campus operations, access and equity considerations

paper_profiles.title: The impact of AI literacy on work–life balance and job satisfaction among university faculty: a self-determination theory perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether university faculty members’ AI literacy is associated with their work–life balance and job satisfaction, and whether those relationships operate through Self-Determination Theory (SDT) basic psychological needs. The authors argue that AI literacy is not only a technical capability but also a psychological resource that may shape autonomy, competence, relatedness, and ultimately faculty well-being in AI-mediated academic work.

Using an online survey of 511 university faculty members in China, the study measured AI literacy, perceived autonomy, perceived competence, perceived relatedness, work–life balance, job satisfaction, and technology acceptance. Structural equation modeling showed that AI literacy positively predicted all three psychological needs, and those needs all positively predicted work–life balance. However, only perceived autonomy directly predicted job satisfaction; perceived competence and relatedness were not significant direct predictors of job satisfaction. Work–life balance positively predicted job satisfaction, indicating an indirect route from AI literacy to satisfaction through improved balance.

The study also found that technology acceptance strengthened the links between AI literacy and all three psychological needs, suggesting that favorable attitudes toward AI help translate literacy into positive psychological experiences. Overall, the paper concludes that AI literacy can support faculty well-being, especially when institutions pair AI skill development with support for technology acceptance and psychologically supportive AI integration.

finding.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of n=511 university faculty, AI literacy significantly increased perceived autonomy (β=0.404, p<0.001), perceived competence (β=0.468, p<0.001), and perceived relatedness (β=0.432, p<0.001). These psychological need satisfactions were associated with better work–life balance, but only autonomy had a direct positive association with job satisfaction (β=0.221, p<0.001); competence and relatedness were not significant direct predictors of job satisfaction.
finding.measure: AI literacy; perceived autonomy, perceived competence, perceived relatedness; job satisfaction; work–life balance

finding.finding_summary: AI literacy was theorized and empirically linked to more efficient AI use in academic work, and higher AI literacy significantly improved perceived competence and autonomy in using AI, which in turn improved work–life balance. Work–life balance was positively predicted by autonomy (β=0.278, p<0.001), competence (β=0.259, p<0.001), and relatedness (β=0.251, p<0.001), consistent with reduced role strain and better management of workload through AI use.
finding.measure: Work–life balance; perceived autonomy/competence/relatedness in using AI

finding.finding_summary: The study proposes and tests a faculty-level pathway in which AI literacy and technology acceptance shape psychological need fulfillment and well-being, with implications for institutional support and AI literacy initiatives. Technology acceptance significantly moderated the effects of AI literacy on autonomy (β=0.116, p=0.007), competence (β=0.114, p=0.004), and relatedness (β=0.199, p<0.001), indicating that institutional efforts to improve acceptance may strengthen the benefits of AI literacy.
finding.measure: Moderation effects of technology acceptance on AI literacy → psychological needs

paper_profiles.title: Teaching in the AI Era: Sustainable Digital Education through Ethical Integration and Teacher Empowerment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how AI integration in education affects educators’ daily work, professional autonomy, and well-being, using a Marxian theory of alienation as the conceptual lens. The authors argue that AI is often implemented as a form of algorithmic management that can reshape teaching into a data-monitored, standardized activity, potentially reducing educators’ sense of ownership, agency, meaning, and collegial connection.

Empirically, the study uses a cross-sectional survey of 395 educators in Northern Cyprus, including university faculty and some secondary/primary/vocational educators. The survey measured four dimensions of alienation—product of labour, labour process, professional identity, and interpersonal relations—along with overall perceptions of AI. Results showed moderate to high alienation across all dimensions, with the strongest alienation tied to the product of labour. Positive perceptions of AI were significantly associated with lower alienation on all dimensions, but the authors emphasize that optimism alone does not fully offset structural constraints imposed by AI systems.

The paper concludes that sustainable AI adoption requires ethical and participatory governance: human oversight, transparency, co-design with educators, accountability mechanisms, and professional standards that preserve teacher autonomy. Rather than rejecting AI, the authors advocate for implementation practices that frame AI as augmentative and relationship-preserving, so that technological innovation does not undermine teacher morale, engagement, or the broader human mission of education.

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on how AI changes educators’ day-to-day work through automation, scripted lesson paths, and algorithmic oversight. In the survey of 395 educators, positive perceptions of AI were associated with lower alienation from the labour process (β ≈ -0.51, p < .001), suggesting some perceived usability benefits, but teachers still reported substantial constraints on autonomy and workflow standardization (mean 3.7/5, SD=0.7).
finding.measure: Survey-based alienation from the labour process; perceptions of AI's effect on lesson planning, pacing, and teaching workflow

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on how AI adoption functions as a governance and institutional change issue, not just a classroom tool issue. Across the 395 educators surveyed, AI integration was linked to significant alienation from professional identity and interpersonal relations, and the authors argue that top-down implementation, surveillance, and weak teacher participation threaten sustainable educational governance.
finding.measure: Survey-based alienation dimensions and interpretive analysis of AI governance, oversight, and institutional decision-making

paper_profiles.title: Cracking the code of teacher burnout: the chain mediation of GPT integration degree through behavioral engagement and classroom atmosphere in a cross-level chain mediation model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether and how the degree of GPT/ChatGPT integration in teaching is related to teacher burnout, with a special focus on two proposed mechanisms: students’ behavioral engagement and classroom atmosphere. The authors argue that AI tools may not directly reduce burnout, but could do so indirectly by improving students’ engagement and the overall classroom environment, thereby making teaching more rewarding and less stressful.

The study used cross-level survey data from 47 teachers and 506 students across 10 Chinese universities. Teachers reported teacher burnout and GPT integration degree, while students reported behavioral engagement and classroom atmosphere; the authors analyzed the nested teacher-student data using multilevel structural equation modeling and chain mediation tests. Results showed no significant direct effect of GPT integration on teacher burnout, but significant negative indirect effects through behavioral engagement, classroom atmosphere, and the chain path behavioral engagement → classroom atmosphere. The paper concludes that GPT’s value in education is mediated by classroom social processes rather than acting as a standalone burnout reducer, and that implementation requires strong technical support and attention to teacher autonomy.

finding.finding_summary: GPT integration degree was associated with better student behavioral engagement, and behavioral engagement was in turn negatively associated with teacher burnout. The paper reports significant positive paths from GPT integration degree to behavioral engagement (β=0.471, p<0.05) and from behavioral engagement to teacher burnout (β=-0.455, p<0.05), indicating that higher engagement corresponded to lower burnout.
finding.measure: Student behavioral engagement (school engagement scale, adapted 5-item questionnaire)
finding.effect_size: β=0.471 for GPTID→BP; β=-0.455 for BP→TB

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that GPT integration degree did not have a statistically significant direct effect on teacher burnout (β=-0.042, p=0.712), but it did have significant indirect negative effects via behavioral engagement and classroom atmosphere. The authors interpret this as GPT reducing burnout primarily by easing classroom processes and improving teaching efficiency rather than by directly changing teacher well-being.
finding.measure: Teacher burnout (MBI-ES-derived 8-item scale) and GPT integration degree
finding.effect_size: β=-0.042 for direct GPTID→TB; indirect effects β=-0.214 (via BP), β=-0.181 (via CA), β=-0.103 (via BP→CA)

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional/classroom-system level, classroom atmosphere significantly mediated the relationship between GPT integration degree and teacher burnout. GPT integration degree positively predicted classroom atmosphere (β=0.382, p<0.05), and classroom atmosphere negatively predicted teacher burnout (β=-0.472, p<0.05), supporting the view that GPT affects burnout through classroom-level organizational conditions.
finding.measure: Classroom atmosphere (4-item adapted scale) and teacher burnout
finding.effect_size: β=0.382 for GPTID→CA; β=-0.472 for CA→TB; indirect β=-0.181 for GPTID→CA→TB
finding.confidence_interval: [0.104, 0.660] for GPTID→CA; [-0.772, -0.172] for CA→TB; [-0.298, -0.063] for indirect path

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in Education: Investigating Students Online Learning Behaviors
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Information and Education Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what factors shape high school students’ intentions to use ChatGPT and their actual use of it for learning. The authors adapt the UTAUT2 acceptance model to a K-12 context, focusing on performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, behavioral intention, and ChatGPT use.

The study was conducted in four public high schools in Pasuruan City, Indonesia. Data came from a survey of 385 students (with 358 reported in the demographic table), analyzed using SEM-PLS, and supplemented by student interviews. The paper also describes school-level implementation supports such as training, counseling, device access, internet connectivity, usage guidelines, and monitoring.

The main findings are that social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit significantly increase behavioral intention to use ChatGPT, and that habit, facilitating conditions, and behavioral intention significantly predict actual ChatGPT use. Performance expectancy and effort expectancy did not significantly predict intention, while facilitating conditions did not significantly predict intention but did predict actual use. The authors conclude that adoption in schools depends less on expected performance or ease of use than on supportive social environments, repeated use habits, and institutional access supports, and they recommend clearer policies, training, and infrastructure improvements for responsible classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT helped them complete assignments more efficiently and improve the quality of their work. In the SEM-PLS results, performance expectancy did not significantly predict behavioral intention (O=0.035, t=0.802, p=0.423), but the descriptive/interview evidence still indicated perceived academic support for homework and school tasks among high school users.
finding.measure: Self-reported assignment completion efficiency and assignment quality; perceived usefulness for learning tasks

finding.finding_summary: Social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit significantly predicted students’ behavioral intention to use ChatGPT. Path coefficients were SI→BI O=0.189 (t=3.475, p=0.001), HM→BI O=0.174 (t=2.807, p=0.005), and H→BI O=0.507 (t=7.745, p=0.000), indicating that peer/teacher encouragement, enjoyment, and repeated use were major drivers of adoption intent.
finding.measure: Behavioral intention to use ChatGPT; social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit scales

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can support learning, but some students reported over-dependence on the tool and reduced critical thinking/independent thinking. This is based on interview evidence rather than a quantified cognitive outcome measure, so the finding is best characterized as mixed: beneficial for support and speed, but with potential tradeoffs for critical thinking.
finding.measure: Interview-reported critical thinking/independence concerns; perceptions of support for learning

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was associated with improved efficiency in completing assignments and became a key driver of actual use when students had access and formed habitual use patterns. In the structural model, habit had a strong positive effect on GPTU (O=0.353, t=7.064, p=0.000), behavioral intention predicted GPTU (O=0.456, t=9.634, p=0.000), and facilitating conditions predicted GPTU (O=0.118, t=3.004, p=0.003).
finding.measure: ChatGPT use frequency and self-reported efficiency in completing school assignments

finding.finding_summary: The study emphasizes that school policies, infrastructure, and training shape ChatGPT implementation in daily learning. Interviews and discussion sections describe the importance of stable internet, adequate devices, parental consent, usage guidelines, monitoring, and teacher-led counseling/training; facilitating conditions also predicted actual use (O=0.118, t=3.004, p=0.003), though not intention.
finding.measure: School infrastructure/support conditions; policy and training practices; facilitated actual use
finding.study_size: n=358; school context across 4 public high schools

paper_profiles.title: Digital Learning Design: Designing Effective Online and Blended Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This SpringerBrief is a practitioner-oriented handbook on designing effective online and blended learning environments. It addresses the shift from traditional teaching to digital learning and argues that effectiveness depends less on the tools themselves than on the quality of instructional design, cognitive alignment, and motivational support.

The book presents a systematic design process, including needs analysis, target group analysis, learning outcomes, content structuring, learning organization, teaching strategies, learning activities, and reflection. It also discusses how cognitive science principles such as working memory limits, multimedia learning, and motivation (e.g., ARCS) should guide design decisions, and how authentic tasks can support transfer to real-world contexts.

The context is broad educational practice rather than a single empirical sample: the intended audience is teachers, trainers, and digital learning professionals working in blended or online settings. The book additionally describes the myScripting tool and notes that AI tools can streamline context analysis, content creation, personalization, assessment, and feedback, reducing educator workload while preserving the educator’s strategic and ethical role.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that AI can streamline time-consuming educational design tasks such as context analysis, content creation, interactive activity development, assessment, and feedback. It states that by automating repetitive and standardized work, AI can significantly reduce teacher and educational designer workload, freeing time for strategic planning and direct learner interaction; however, no empirical effect size or sample is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time-consuming educational design tasks

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Impacts of Implementing Block Mode of Teaching in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what impacts block mode of teaching (BMT) has after implementation in higher education institutions. The authors note that BMT is increasingly used as a condensed teaching format, but prior research on its consequences is limited and fragmented, especially across institutions and student groups.

To address this gap, the study uses a multiple-case study approach across five higher-education institutions that have adopted BMT: Victoria University, Salford University, Colorado College, Heriot-Watt University, and Quest University. The authors collected secondary data from university websites, media reports, blogs, academic publications, forums, and related sources, then applied thematic analysis to identify recurring positive and negative impacts.

The paper proposes a taxonomy of 21 impacts grouped into eight categories. Reported positives include greater flexibility in course design, improved support for disadvantaged students, better student engagement and interaction, stronger motivation, and more adaptable institutional operations during disruptions such as COVID-19. Reported negatives include increased pressure on lecturers, difficulties securing staff support, and some academic concerns such as heavier self-study demands and a shift toward more group work. Overall, the authors conclude that BMT can improve student outcomes and institutional flexibility, but it also creates workload and implementation challenges for staff and some students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports multiple engagement-related effects of block mode of teaching. Positive findings include increased student motivation, higher satisfaction for some student groups due to greater care, and improved interaction with lecturers and classmates; however, it also reports a marginal decrease in satisfaction with subject design. These findings are synthesized qualitatively from multiple institutional cases rather than estimated with a single effect size.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction, motivation, and interaction as reported in secondary sources across case studies

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that BMT can increase students’ collaboration and time-management related behaviors. In particular, it reports more interaction with classmates and lecturers, the ability for students to self-select a pace that fits their circumstances, and quicker realization of whether a chosen course is suitable for them. These are qualitative findings drawn from the thematic analysis of five institutional cases.
finding.measure: Reported collaboration, interaction, course pacing, and time-management flexibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies both efficiency gains and workload burdens associated with implementing BMT. Positive effects include greater institutional flexibility in course redesign and the ability to respond more quickly to disruptions and government regulations, while negative effects include more pressure on lecturers, challenges in securing staff support, and the need to alert students about workload and assessment timing. The evidence is descriptive and based on secondary case data rather than quantitative estimation.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, staff support, institutional flexibility, and operational responsiveness

finding.finding_summary: BMT is portrayed as producing broader institutional benefits, including improved pass rates at Victoria University, greater flexibility for universities to redesign teaching structures, and safer operation during the COVID-19 pandemic through smaller classes and hybrid/online delivery. The study also suggests that BMT can help universities attract students and better align provision with learner needs, though these conclusions are drawn from qualitative case evidence rather than causal estimation.
finding.measure: Institutional outcomes such as pass rates, teaching flexibility, and pandemic-related operational adaptation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that BMT can improve academic performance in general, especially for disadvantaged students, with examples including higher grades and pass rates in some institutions. It also notes negative academic consequences such as heavier self-study demands, simplified content, increased group assessments, and concerns from high-achieving students, indicating that academic effects are not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Grades, pass rates, and reported academic performance/assessment patterns

paper_profiles.title: Innovating Assessment for Education for Sustainable Development
paper_profiles.venue: Perspectives and Practices of Education for Sustainable Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter examines how assessment design in higher education can be used to advance Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), with a particular emphasis on authentic, interdisciplinary, learner-centered, and future-oriented assessment. The chapter argues that assessment is not merely a final measurement tool, but a central part of pedagogy that shapes learning objectives, student engagement, feedback practices, and the development of sustainability competencies. It also explicitly situates these discussions within contemporary pressures on assessors, including workload, student mental health, and the growing challenge of artificial intelligence in assessment contexts.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the chapter synthesizes established assessment literature and illustrates ideas through practice-based examples and case studies from UK higher education, including the University of Manchester Living Lab, Environmental Law and Management Systems at the University of Southampton, Keele University consultancy projects, and work placement modules. It discusses formative and summative assessment, flipped classrooms, learner co-production, group work, authentic assessment, and other formats as mechanisms for deeper learning and sustainability-relevant skill building. The chapter’s main conclusion is that diverse, authentic, and carefully supported assessment approaches can strengthen learning, student agency, and employability while also improving the relevance of higher education to real-world sustainability challenges.

Because the chapter is conceptual and practice-oriented rather than a primary empirical study, it does not present experimental or correlational evidence with effect sizes. Its contribution is instead a structured framework of assessment principles and examples intended to guide educators and institutions in redesigning assessment for ESD, while being attentive to inclusivity, student wellbeing, and staff workload.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that formative, authentic, and reflective assessment can support student motivation, engagement, self-regulation, and confidence, especially when learners are given safe spaces to experiment and receive feedback without grade consequences. It cites practitioner examples such as flipped learning and SDG-focused collaborative exercises, but does not report original quantitative effect sizes or sample-based outcome estimates.
finding.measure: student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, reflective learning

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the chapter is the development of durable skills through assessment, including critical thinking, collaboration, communication, systems thinking, and self-evaluation. The chapter presents this as a consistent conclusion across its discussion of authentic assessment, group projects, interdisciplinary tasks, reflective writing, and work-integrated learning, but it does not provide new quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: critical thinking, collaboration, communication, systems thinking, self-evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter repeatedly notes that innovative assessment can increase educator workload because formative work requires more feedback and some assessment formats are time-consuming to design, mark, and support. At the same time, it suggests that well-designed assessment, clearer rubrics, and digital or collaborative models may improve manageability and make feedback more purposeful, but no quantitative workload data are reported.
finding.measure: educator workload, marking time, assessment manageability

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that assessment reform can influence institutional practice by embedding sustainability across curricula, strengthening partnerships with external organizations, and aligning teaching with institutional commitments to ESD. Examples such as the University Living Lab and assessment tied to real clients are used to show how assessment can produce broader organizational and community impacts, but these are illustrative rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: curriculum integration, partnership building, institutional sustainability engagement

paper_profiles.title: Comparative International Research in the Area of Educational Platforms and MOOCs: An Opinion of IT Students Using Data Mining Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how undergraduate computer science students in Poland, Kazakhstan, and Ukraine use educational platforms and MOOCs, and whether usage patterns vary by country, gender, age, and level of study. The authors are interested in identifying patterns in students’ attitudes toward self-learning platforms, the types of courses they seek, and their use of complementary coding resources such as Git systems and Stack Overflow.

The study uses an anonymous questionnaire administered online in June 2023 to 158 students from three universities. The authors analyze responses with data mining methods, including visualization, decision trees, Naïve Bayes, and generalized linear models, using RapidMiner and Orange. Most machine-learning attempts did not produce strong classification, suggesting few meaningful group differences in platform use across countries, genders, or study levels.

The main findings are that educational platforms are widely used, usually at least weekly, with Udemy rated as the most useful platform across countries. Engineering students tend to use platforms more frequently than master’s students, and students in Ukraine use them somewhat less frequently than those in Poland and Kazakhstan. Course-topic preferences were relatively evenly distributed, and the only clear correlation reported was between use of Git systems and Stack Overflow. The paper concludes that these tools supplement formal study and may strengthen student confidence and competencies, but it does not test impacts on grades or other academic outcomes directly.

finding.finding_summary: The study found no strong or consistent differences in educational-platform use across gender, country, or level of study, and it did not identify a dominant course-topic preference. The authors report that machine-learning classifiers performed poorly (best accuracy 36.9%, classification error 63.1%), suggesting weak separability of student groups on these variables.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency and perceived usefulness of educational platforms; course-topic preferences; use of Git systems and Stack Overflow

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that using educational platforms helps students supplement university learning and may enhance confidence and readiness for exams, although this was not directly measured. Survey responses showed that most students used platforms at least once a week and rated Udemy as the most useful platform, indicating substantial learner engagement with self-directed learning resources.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of platform use and usefulness ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that educational platforms are used to deepen programming/IT knowledge beyond formal coursework. Students commonly use these platforms to expand knowledge in computer science, and the authors note that the knowledge and practical skills gained can better prepare students for exams, though exam-score effects were not tested.
finding.measure: Self-reported use of educational platforms for programming/IT topics; course-topic selections

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the use of educational platforms does not differ significantly across the analyzed groups and does not produce institutional credit or exam exemptions at the University of Silesia. The paper does not find evidence of system-level differences in platform adoption, but it does recommend future work on educational impacts across additional countries and contexts.
finding.measure: Institutional context description; cross-country survey comparisons

paper_profiles.title: The University in Transition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length scholarly work examines how universities are changing in response to Open Science, internationalization, funding pressures, bureaucratization, and shifting expectations about teaching, research, and public engagement. It asks what the university is for, how it has developed historically, and how it should evolve to remain legitimate and socially valuable in the future.

The authors argue that the modern university has become too research-dominant, too metrics-driven, and too separated from society, with negative consequences for teaching, staff autonomy, workload, and morale. They propose Open Science as a broad pathway for restoring the connection between universities and society by expanding Open Access, FAIR data, Public Engagement, team science, and new recognition-and-reward systems that value teaching and collaboration more highly.

The context is the contemporary European/Dutch research university, especially Utrecht University, but the arguments are framed as broadly relevant to higher education internationally. The work is primarily conceptual and historical rather than empirical, drawing on literature, policy developments, and institutional examples rather than original data collection. Its main conclusion is that a transition to Open Science is both necessary and irreversible, and that organizational, cultural, and incentive changes are required to support it.

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe the university system as increasingly burdened by bureaucracy, rules, procedures, accountability obligations, efficiency pressures, and workload growth. They argue that underfunding, performance metrics, and a separation of teaching from research have made teaching a 'burden' and have contributed to dissatisfaction among teachers and reduced autonomy, but they provide no original effect sizes or quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: University workload, bureaucratization, accountability obligations, and teaching burden as described in the institutional system

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that universities are undergoing a system-level transition driven by Open Science, internationalization, funding regimes, and changing accountability structures. It claims these forces have produced both positive changes (greater openness, societal relevance, international collaboration) and negative ones (metrics dominance, loss of autonomy, weakened teaching-research integration), but it does not present empirical tests.
finding.measure: Institutional change in university governance, recognition and reward systems, openness, and societal engagement

paper_profiles.title: Design of the Bottom-up Innovation project - a participatory, primary preventive, organizational level intervention on work-related stress and well-being for workers in Dutch vocational education
paper_profiles.population: Adult vocational education workers in Dutch vocational schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a study protocol describing a workplace intervention aimed at reducing work-related stress and improving well-being among employees in Dutch vocational education. The authors argue that stress management efforts in education have often focused on helping individuals cope, while leaving organizational sources of stress unchanged. The project therefore tests whether a participatory, organizational-level approach can improve teachers’ and staff members’ need for recovery and vitality.

The intervention, called the Heuristic Method, uses participatory action research. In phase 1, an ‘Engine of Development’ group conducts interviews, an open-ended questionnaire, and group sessions to identify stressors and generate work-oriented solutions; in phase 2, management implements tailored solutions with support from facilitators as needed. The study is conducted in two vocational education institutions in the Netherlands and uses a controlled, non-randomized mixed-methods design with baseline, 6-month, and 18-month follow-ups.
