Because this is a protocol, the paper reports intended measures and analytic plans rather than results. The primary outcomes are need for recovery and vitality; secondary measures include job demands/resources, work ability, job satisfaction, commitment, work engagement, burnout, sickness absence, productivity, and related organizational indicators. The paper concludes that the study is designed to provide evidence on whether participatory organizational change can improve employee well-being and illuminate how and why such an intervention does or does not work.

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported because this is a study protocol rather than a results paper. The study is designed to test whether the intervention improves vitality and reduces need for recovery, but no outcome data are presented in the article.
finding.measure: Vitality (UWES-9 vigor subscale) and need for recovery (VBBA subscale)

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported in this protocol. The planned evaluation includes job satisfaction, commitment, work ability, sickness absence, in-role performance, and productivity, but the paper does not report results for these measures.
finding.measure: Job satisfaction, commitment, sickness absence, in-role performance, productivity, and work ability

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported because the article is a protocol. The intervention is explicitly organizational and includes process evaluation of implementation, participation, and context, but the paper provides no outcome results for institutional change.
finding.measure: Process evaluation indicators; organizational efficacy; implementation/fidelity/context measures

paper_profiles.title: Effects of cooperative learning on students’ learning outcomes in physical education: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.population: Primary school through university students in physical education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether cooperative learning (CL) improves student learning outcomes in physical education (PE) compared with traditional, teacher-centered instruction. The authors argue that prior reviews were too narrow, often focusing on only one affective outcome, and that a broader quantitative synthesis was needed to evaluate CL across multiple learning domains.

The intervention studied is direct CL in PE, including structured approaches such as Jigsaw, Learning Teams, and Student Teams-Achievement Divisions (STAD). The review searched 12 databases in English, Spanish, and Turkish and included true experimental and quasi-experimental studies with students from primary school through university. In total, 40 studies (56 effect sizes) with 3,985 participants were retained after outlier removal.

The meta-analysis found a moderate positive overall effect of CL on learning outcomes (Hedges’s g = 0.459, 95% CI [0.324, 0.595]), with positive effects in affective, cognitive, physical, and social domains. The largest effect was in social learning (g = 0.612), followed by cognitive (g = 0.589), physical (g = 0.471), and affective learning (g = 0.304). Moderator and meta-regression analyses found no significant moderation by publication source, country, grade level, research design, sport content, teaching structure, intervention duration, publication year, sample size, or study quality score, but heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 82.7%).

finding.finding_summary: Cooperative learning had a significant moderate positive effect on social learning outcomes in physical education. Across 10 independent effect sizes and 1,127 participants, the pooled effect was Hedges’s g = 0.612, indicating improved social outcomes such as peer relations, empathy, and related social-affective measures.
finding.measure: Social learning outcomes in physical education (e.g., empathy, peer relations, social-affective learning)

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis also found a significant moderate positive effect of cooperative learning on cognitive learning outcomes that included skills such as critical thinking and problem solving. Based on 8 independent effect sizes and 962 participants, the pooled effect was Hedges’s g = 0.589.
finding.measure: Cognitive learning outcomes in physical education (e.g., critical thinking, problem solving)

finding.finding_summary: Cooperative learning produced a significant moderate positive effect on physical learning outcomes in PE. Across 24 independent effect sizes and 1,859 participants, the pooled effect was Hedges’s g = 0.471, suggesting improved physical/performance-related outcomes in the PE setting.
finding.measure: Physical learning outcomes in physical education

finding.finding_summary: Affective learning outcomes were significantly improved by cooperative learning, though the effect was smaller than for the other domains. Across 18 independent effect sizes and 1,919 participants, the pooled effect was Hedges’s g = 0.304, indicating a small positive effect on motivation- and attitude-related outcomes.
finding.measure: Affective learning outcomes in physical education (e.g., motivation, attitudes)

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of AI-Generated, Context-Specific Case Studies in Improving Critical Thinking Skills in ODL
paper_profiles.venue: American Journal of Advanced Technology and Engineering Solutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether AI-generated, context-specific case studies improve critical thinking in open and distance learning (ODL) settings. The paper frames the problem as a limitation of static, instructor-created cases in ODL, which may lack authenticity, personalization, and timely feedback for geographically dispersed learners.

Using a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group design, the author compared an experimental group receiving AI-generated, culturally and disciplinarily tailored case studies with adaptive feedback to a control group using traditional static cases. Participants were 200 learners from Bangladesh Open University and selected private universities offering ODL or blended programs, drawn from education, business, and health sciences. Critical thinking was measured primarily with the California Critical Thinking Skills Test (CCTST), alongside engagement and authenticity measures. The intervention lasted six weeks and was delivered through Moodle-based learning management systems.

The paper reports that the AI-generated case condition produced substantially larger gains in critical thinking than the control condition. The experimental group improved by 7.3 points on the CCTST (18.4 to 25.7) versus 1.8 points in the control group (18.6 to 20.4), with a large effect size for the experimental group (d = 0.85). Regression and structural equation modeling indicate that personalization, engagement, authenticity, and adaptive feedback were all positively associated with critical thinking, with the combined model explaining a substantial proportion of variance. The study concludes that AI-generated case studies can strengthen higher-order thinking and learner engagement in ODL, especially where contextualization and feedback are otherwise limited.

finding.finding_summary: AI-generated, context-specific case studies substantially improved critical thinking among ODL learners. The experimental group’s CCTST scores increased from 18.4 to 25.7 (gain = 7.3) over six weeks, compared with 18.6 to 20.4 in the control group (gain = 1.8); the experimental-group pre/post gain was large (d = 0.85, p < .001).
finding.measure: California Critical Thinking Skills Test (CCTST)

finding.finding_summary: Learner engagement increased in the AI-generated case condition relative to the control group. The experimental group’s mean engagement score was 4.2/5 versus 3.1/5 for controls, with higher skills engagement (4.4) and emotional engagement (4.3); engagement was positively associated with critical thinking (β = .39, p < .001).
finding.measure: Online Student Engagement Scale (OSE); LMS analytics (hours spent, forum contributions)

paper_profiles.title: Innovating transfusion training: a BOPPPS-based blended learning model to enhance nursing interns’ specialized competency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This quasi-experimental mixed-methods study examined whether a BOPPPS-based blended learning model could improve transfusion nursing training for undergraduate nursing interns. The problem addressed was that traditional rotational clinical internships often provide fragmented, unstructured exposure to specialized procedures such as blood transfusion, leaving interns with limited theoretical mastery, weak self-directed learning (SDL), and inconsistent practice opportunities.

The intervention combined online asynchronous learning, synchronous discussion, simulation practice, and a supervised real-world transfusion procedure within a structured BOPPPS framework (bridge-in, objective, pre-test, participatory learning, post-test, summary). Participants were 78 nursing interns at a tertiary teaching hospital in China, with 40 in the experimental group and 38 in the control group receiving traditional training. Quantitatively, the intervention significantly improved theoretical knowledge scores and SDL scores, but did not produce a statistically significant difference in operational skills scores. Qualitative interviews with 13 experimental-group interns suggested high acceptability, better engagement, clearer learning goals, and perceived gains in confidence and competence.

Overall, the paper concludes that the BOPPPS-based blended model is effective for strengthening theoretical learning and SDL in transfusion nursing education, while its effect on procedural performance was not clearly demonstrated with the current assessment and practice intensity. The authors note that the model may be especially useful as a structured supplement to conventional clinical internships, but that future studies should use larger, multicenter samples and more sensitive skill assessments.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group showed significantly higher self-directed learning (SDL) scores than the control group after training, indicating improved motivation/engagement and learning initiative. Post-test total SDL score was 105.88±7.30 in the experimental group versus 94.84±8.17 in the control group (n=78; p<0.001).
finding.measure: Nursing College Students’ Independent Learning Ability Scale (SDL total score; also subscales for self-management, information seeking, collaborative learning)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved a durable-skill–adjacent learning outcome related to independent learning and metacognitive self-management. The experimental group’s SDL subscale scores and total SDL score increased more than the control group’s, with between-group differences favoring the BOPPPS-based blended model (e.g., total SDL 105.88±7.30 vs 94.84±8.17, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Self-directed learning scale subscales and total score
finding.std_deviation: Experimental total SDL SD=7.30; Control total SDL SD=8.17

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group achieved significantly higher theoretical transfusion knowledge scores than the control group. Scores were 68.91±10.53 for the BOPPPS-based blended group versus 60.47±17.04 for traditional training (n=78; p=0.010), indicating improved domain-specific learning in transfusion nursing.
finding.measure: Proctored written transfusion nursing theoretical knowledge exam (0–100)

finding.finding_summary: Operational skills performance did not differ significantly between groups after the intervention. The experimental group scored 90.35±2.02 versus 89.71±1.94 in the control group, and the between-group difference was not statistically significant (p=0.160; n=78).
finding.measure: Standardized transfusion operational skills checklist / hospital operational procedures evaluation (0–100)

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence Competence of K-12 Students Shapes Their AI Risk Perception: A Co-occurrence Network Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Finnish upper secondary students perceive risks related to artificial intelligence in schoolwork, and whether those risk perceptions differ by self-reported AI competence. The authors ask two main questions: which AI-related concerns students identify as risks, and how AI competence shapes the structure of those concerns.

The study used a questionnaire with 163 students in one Finnish general upper secondary school that was participating in an AI education development project. Students rated their AI competence on a 4-item Likert scale and selected from 14 binary AI-risk concerns spanning systemic, institutional, and personal domains. The authors then used co-occurrence network analysis with regression-adjusted edge weights to compare how lower- and higher-competence students associated different concerns.

Findings show that students most often worried about AI being inaccurate or biased, AI-enabled cheating, and personal learning harms such as reduced critical thinking and creativity. Lower-competence students reported more concerns overall and focused more on personal and learning-related risks, misuse, and addictive use, whereas higher-competence students emphasized systemic and institutional risks such as bias, inaccuracy, and school rules. The paper concludes that AI competence is linked to the type and structure of perceived risks, supporting the need for AI literacy, teacher guidance, and clearer institutional policies for equitable and responsible AI integration in K-12 education.

finding.finding_summary: Students' AI competence was associated with different perceived risks to durable skills, especially critical thinking and creativity. Lower-competence students more often endorsed concerns that AI use may reduce critical thinking and creativity, and these concerns were central in the low-competence network (Less_creative EC = -0.53; Less_critical EC = -0.49), while higher-competence students were less centered on these personal-skill risks.
finding.measure: Binary self-reported concern items about reduced critical thinking and reduced creativity; co-occurrence network centrality and regression-adjusted edge weights

finding.finding_summary: The paper also captured broader personal and affective concerns, including fear of misuse and fear that AI would be too addictive, which are relevant to student well-being and self-regulation. Lower-competence students reported these concerns more often overall, and fear-based risks were more central in the low-competence network than in the high-competence network.
finding.measure: Binary self-reported concern items about fear of misuse and addictive use; co-occurrence network centrality and regression-adjusted edge weights

finding.finding_summary: Students with higher self-reported AI competence were more likely to connect AI risks to systemic and institutional issues such as bias, inaccuracy, cheating, teachers' rules, and school policy. The strongest competence-positive edges included AI_cheating—Biased (β=0.022), Biased—Inaccurate (β=0.017), and AI_cheating—Teachers_rules (β=0.015), indicating a stronger institutional framing among higher-competence students.
finding.measure: Binary concern items covering cheating, bias, inaccuracy, teacher rules, and school policy; regression-adjusted co-occurrence network edges and eigenvector centrality

finding.finding_summary: The study directly addresses AI-related concerns in schoolwork rather than academic achievement, with findings centered on how AI may affect learning processes. Students frequently endorsed concerns that AI use may reduce learning, and lower-competence students more often linked AI to reduced learning, while higher-competence students linked cheating and accuracy concerns more strongly.
finding.measure: Binary self-reported concern item about reduced learning; co-occurrence network analysis of AI-related concerns in school assignments

paper_profiles.title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: a Survey
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (AI survey; no human participant population studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of two related AI subfields: statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). Rather than evaluating an educational intervention or conducting an empirical study with participants, it organizes the literature around shared dimensions such as inference style, logic syntax, semantics, learning, representations, paradigms, and learning tasks.

The paper explains how StarAI uses logic to build probabilistic graphical models and how NeSy uses logic either to template neural architectures or to define loss functions. It compares proof-based and model-based approaches, discusses propositional, relational, and first-order logic, and reviews fuzzy, probabilistic, and mixed semantics. The survey’s main conclusion is conceptual: these fields share common foundations and techniques, and understanding their parallels can support cross-fertilization in future research.

Because the paper is a broad methodological survey, it does not study K-12 schools, teachers, classrooms, or educational outcomes empirically. It provides no comparative evidence on teacher morale, classroom engagement, or other school-level impacts of AI tools. Its relevance to education research is indirect, as it may inform future AI system design rather than evaluate any educational use case.

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artificial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface for the third International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI’2021). Its purpose is to frame the relationship between conceptual modeling and artificial intelligence, emphasizing how each field can complement the other while also addressing the limitations of AI’s black-box outputs and the scalability limits of conceptual models.

The paper does not report an empirical study of K-12 education, a student intervention, or teacher practice. Instead, it introduces a research framework with four categories of CMAI work: exaptation, CM-driven, AI-driven, and CM- & AI-driven research. It then briefly summarizes the invited workshop papers and situates them within this framework, highlighting applications such as improving machine learning with conceptual models and using AI techniques for model search and predictive business process management.

Overall, the paper is conceptual and agenda-setting rather than empirical. It offers no study population, no quantitative outcomes, and no evidence about teacher morale, classroom engagement, or school-level educational impacts.

paper_profiles.title: Augmented Computational Design
paper_profiles.venue: Artificial Intelligence in Performance-Driven Design: Theories, Methods, and Tools Towards Sustainability (book chapter)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter proposes a conceptual and mathematical framework called Augmented Computational Design (ACD) for using artificial intelligence in generative design. The paper argues that many design problems can be reformulated as discrete decision-making tasks, where AI can help in two dual ways: mapping many input decisions to a few performance outcomes, and navigating backward from desired outcomes to feasible design decisions.

The chapter is primarily methodological and theoretical rather than an empirical evaluation of AI in education or K-12 settings. It develops a formal representation of design spaces, discusses Jacobian and pseudo-inverse approximations, and situates AI methods within a spectrum from rule-based to statistical/probabilistic approaches. As an illustrative case, it describes a Bayesian Belief Network meta-model trained to approximate the Dutch NTA 8800 building energy model using 20,000 Sobol-sampled simulations and sensitivity analysis that reduced 269 inputs to 15 influential parameters. The paper reports that these 15 parameters explain about 90.45% to 92.30% of the final energy performance score, and that the resulting shallow BBN can be cross-validated with NRMSE and MAPE for robustness. The chapter’s conclusions focus on explainability, reversibility, and scalability in computational design, not on classroom or teacher outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Modular Belief Updates and Confusion about Measures of Certainty in Artificial Intelligence Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines conceptual confusion in artificial intelligence research about how to represent uncertainty, specifically the distinction between absolute belief and belief updates. The authors define and analyze a property they call modularity for belief updates, showing how modular update quantities can be derived probabilistically and why they are useful in reasoning under uncertainty.

The paper focuses on expert systems rather than educational settings, using MYCIN and INTERNIST-I as illustrative cases. It argues that both systems implicitly treated elicited quantities such as certainty factors and evoking strengths as modular belief updates when they were in fact often absolute measures of belief, leading to inconsistencies and problematic assumptions such as conditional or marginal independence.

The main conclusion is methodological: AI systems should distinguish clearly between belief and belief change, and measures used in expert systems should be aligned with their mathematical properties and elicitation meaning. The paper does not report an empirical study, K-12 population, or educational intervention, and it contains no evidence about teacher morale or classroom engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Bias Amplification in Artificial Intelligence Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual/position piece arguing that a major risk of contemporary AI systems is bias amplification, especially when training data are incomplete, non-representative, or otherwise discriminatory. Rather than studying a specific educational intervention, it surveys examples from hiring, advertising, facial recognition, chatbots, criminal justice, healthcare, and public-sector data use to illustrate how machine learning can reproduce and scale inequities.

The author argues that bias can arise through dataset bias, association bias, automation bias, interaction bias, and confirmation bias, and that these forms of bias can produce both representative harm and allocative harm. The paper emphasizes that the public sector should create data standards, transparency requirements, and accountability mechanisms, and should support discrimination-aware machine learning and broader data-sharing standards to reduce harmful bias.

The paper is not an empirical K-12 education study and does not evaluate AI tools in schools, teacher morale, classroom engagement, or student outcomes. Its relevance to education research is indirect: it highlights governance and equity risks that could affect any AI deployment, including in educational contexts, but it provides no quantitative evidence of impact in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that biased AI systems can amplify discrimination and produce representative and allocative harms at scale, creating negative institutional consequences if not addressed through data standards and oversight. However, this is a conceptual argument supported by examples from other domains rather than an empirical study of policy or institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how AI education can be made more accessible in K-12 classrooms by integrating AI concepts into existing core subjects rather than teaching AI only as a standalone computing topic. The authors argue that teachers need curriculum scaffolds, practical supports, and clearer ways to connect AI to what they already teach.

To investigate this, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 teachers from diverse subject areas and grade bands. Teachers were introduced to AI concepts and tools, then worked in small groups with researchers to design integrated lesson plans for social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and an exemplar physics curriculum. Data sources included workshop audio, pre/post questionnaires, and participant artifacts; the analysis was thematic/qualitative. The workshop surfaced four recurring teacher priorities—evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration—and three main integration points for AI in core curriculum: data, reflection, and ethics.

The main conclusion is that teachers were enthusiastic about embedding AI into non-CS subjects, but they need more scaffolding around AI objectives, classroom implementation, and especially ethics discussions. The paper does not test student learning outcomes or teacher morale with an intervention; instead, it provides design guidance for co-developing integrated AI curricula and reflects on the opportunities and constraints of remote co-design with teachers.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that integrated AI lessons could support student engagement, and engagement emerged as one of the four major design priorities in the workshop. Participants described using real-world anchors, student-driven topics, competition, and gamification to increase engagement, but this was design feedback rather than a measured student outcome.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported perceptions of student engagement in co-designed curricula

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on collaboration and reflection as central features of integrated AI curricula. Teachers emphasized group work, peer discussion, and reflection on data, bias, and real-world implications as ways to develop collaboration and deeper thinking, but no student-level outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Teacher design discussions and curriculum artifacts emphasizing collaboration and reflection

finding.finding_summary: One co-designed curriculum targeted ESL and was explicitly built around pronunciation practice and an AI-powered pronunciation app. The paper reports the curriculum design, not student performance, so the evidence is limited to teachers’ successful integration of AI with language practice activities.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL pronunciation curriculum and teacher discussion of language practice activities

finding.finding_summary: A literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities was co-designed to integrate AI with vocabulary learning and image-based classification. The paper reports that teachers successfully produced an implementable draft and discussed using vocabulary words and images as training data, but it does not measure literacy gains.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum for vocabulary learning

finding.finding_summary: The exemplar physics curriculum embedded AI into a paper-airplane design task, using dimensions and time-of-flight data to train a model and prompting reflection on model improvement and bias. This indicates a positive design pathway for scientific reasoning, but the paper does not report student science outcomes.
finding.measure: Co-designed physics curriculum using experimental data and model-reflection tasks

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced integrated curricula in social studies and history-related contexts, including a lesson on data and government policy and another on hairstyle/professionalism ethics tied to the CROWN Act. The paper reports successful curriculum design and teacher enthusiasm for these non-CS integrations, but no learner outcome measures.
finding.measure: Co-designed social studies/history curriculum artifacts

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, scalable feedback on their classroom discourse practices, especially their use of "talk moves" that support student participation and mathematical reasoning. The authors argue that human observation and transcript coding are too slow and resource-intensive to scale, so they build an AI-supported system that can automatically detect talk moves from classroom speech and present teachers with personalized feedback.

The core intervention is the TalkMoves application, which combines automated speech recognition with NLP classifiers, including BiLSTM and transformer models, to label teacher utterances in classroom transcripts. The paper reports model development and evaluation on 501 K-12 math lesson transcripts (176,757 sentences total) manually annotated for six talk moves plus a none class. The best model, RoBERTa-Large, achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the held-out test set, outperforming the earlier BiLSTM baseline (F1 = 65%).

The application was piloted with 21 teachers in two Midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019-2020 academic year. Teachers recorded lessons, reviewed the dashboard feedback, completed surveys, and participated in interviews, but the paper primarily reports system development, model performance, and implementation details rather than causal effects on teacher morale, classroom engagement, or student outcomes. The authors conclude that the system shows promise for supporting teacher professional learning and can approximate expert coding reasonably well, while also noting limitations such as noisy classroom speech, skewed label distributions, and under-recognition of child speech by the ASR system.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that automated NLP can substantially reduce the manual labor required to identify accountable talk moves in K-12 math lessons. The best transformer model (RoBERTa-Large) achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set, improving over the prior baseline (F1 = 65%), suggesting the system can scale feedback generation more efficiently than human transcript coding.
finding.measure: Model classification performance for six talk moves plus None on held-out test transcripts
finding.study_size: n=501 transcripts; 176,757 sentences (115,418 teacher sentences, 61,339 student sentences)

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test whether the tool improved teacher morale, motivation, or student engagement; it only motivates the system in terms of supporting engagement and professional learning. The pilot with 21 teachers collected surveys and interviews, but no quantitative outcome results on morale or engagement are reported, so there is no empirical evidence of effect on this outcome in the text provided.
finding.measure: Teacher surveys/interviews and dashboard use, without reported outcome analysis

finding.finding_summary: The application is designed to support instructional reflection and better classroom discourse, which are plausibly related to metacognitive and communication-oriented teaching practices. However, the paper does not directly measure teacher or student collaboration, critical thinking, or metacognition as outcomes; it only reports that the system detects talk moves that are intended to broaden and deepen mathematical discussion.
finding.measure: Automated detection of discourse strategies intended to support reasoning and discussion

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI Fall Symposium Series (AAAI FSS-21): Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review/proposal about how to certify artificial intelligence and machine learning systems for trustworthy deployment. Rather than studying an educational intervention, it surveys certification concepts from systems engineering, verification and validation, model cards, and uncertainty analysis, and organizes them into a proposed Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) for evaluating AI systems.

The paper argues that AI systems should be certified through a staged process: conceptual idea, design, implementation test, and managed deployment. It emphasizes the need to document data sources, quantify uncertainty, assess explainability/interpretability/transparency, and define intended use and limitations, so that performance bounds can be established and users can have calibrated trust in AI outputs.

A worked example focuses on image data fusion for automatic target recognition using an ATR benchmark database, comparing anisotropic diffusion and CNN-based fusion methods across distances and views. The example reports performance tradeoffs, especially speed versus accuracy, and uses those results to illustrate how certifiable bounds might be set for AI image fusion methods. The paper does not study K-12 schools, teachers, morale, or classroom engagement; its contribution is methodological and largely domain-general.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (including educators teaching elementary, middle, and high school subjects)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers can be supported to design artificial intelligence curriculum that is integrated into non-computing core subjects. The authors argue that AI education is often isolated from regular classroom practice and is therefore inaccessible to many teachers and students, especially those outside computer science classrooms.

To explore this problem, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse grade levels, subjects, and countries. The workshop included introductory presentations on AI, tool demonstrations, card sorting, pre-work using AI learning tools, and collaborative curriculum design with researchers. Teachers co-created draft lesson plans that embedded AI into social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and an exemplar physics curriculum.

The main findings are qualitative and focus on what teachers need to feel able to teach integrated AI lessons. Teachers emphasized four recurring needs: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Across the drafts, AI was integrated through three main pathways: using subject-area data to train models, prompting reflection on subject content and AI behavior, and incorporating ethics discussions. The paper concludes that teacher co-design can reveal practical supports needed for broader AI adoption in K-12 classrooms and suggests that integrated AI curricula may help expand access beyond traditional computing settings.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the co-design workshop increased their familiarity with AI from an average of 4.8/7 to 5.8/7 and their confidence in integrating AI into their curriculum to 5.6/7. Participants also described the experience as expanding their understanding of AI teaching possibilities and making AI feel more accessible, which suggests improved teacher morale/self-efficacy rather than student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher self-ratings of AI familiarity and confidence to integrate AI into curriculum; workshop reflections

finding.finding_summary: The co-designed curricula explicitly supported engagement, collaboration, and reflection as central design goals. Teachers described group work, peer discussion, and reflective questions as important for helping students contribute ideas, understand ethics, and make sense of AI-related decisions, but the paper does not report quantitative student outcomes.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of co-designed lesson plans and workshop discussions about engagement, collaboration, and reflection

finding.finding_summary: One of the three curriculum drafts targeted ESL and was designed around an AI-powered pronunciation application. Teachers proposed using students' pronunciation recordings as data to train a classification model, with the app then used to support pronunciation practice; however, the paper reports no student outcome data for language fluency.
finding.measure: Qualitative curriculum design for ESL pronunciation practice

finding.finding_summary: Another curriculum draft focused on literacy for students with learning disabilities, using vocabulary words and image classification to integrate AI concepts into literacy instruction. The intended outcome was to support vocabulary learning and related literacy skills, but no implementation or achievement data are reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative curriculum design for vocabulary/literacy instruction

finding.finding_summary: An exemplar physics curriculum embedded AI into a paper-airplane activity, where students would use design data and time-of-flight measurements to train a model predicting airplane effectiveness. The paper presents this as a feasible integration point for scientific reasoning and model-based inquiry, but it does not report experimental effects on learning.
finding.measure: Qualitative co-designed physics curriculum using paper-airplane design and prediction tasks

finding.finding_summary: Teachers successfully co-designed integrated curricula in social studies, ESL, and literacy, showing that AI can be embedded in non-CS core subjects such as government, history, and vocationally relevant language learning. The evidence is qualitative and demonstrates feasibility and design pathways rather than measured academic gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of integrated curricula drafts and workshop discussions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that co-designing with teachers can increase the accessibility and potential adoption of AI education across K-12 settings by aligning AI curriculum with teachers' values, classroom constraints, and subject standards. Teachers identified practical barriers and supports related to evaluation, logistics, collaboration, and ethics scaffolding, suggesting institutional design requirements for broader implementation, but no policy-level outcomes are measured.
finding.measure: Qualitative findings from co-design workshop, teacher reflections, and curriculum artifacts

paper_profiles.title: A Pilot Study on Teacher-Facing Real-Time Classroom Game Dashboards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a teacher-facing, real-time dashboard for an educational game can help teachers better monitor and facilitate student gameplay in K-12 classrooms. The motivation is that teachers often need to understand what students are doing in a game while class is in progress, but checking individual screens is slow and may not reveal higher-level patterns or struggling students.

The authors used a participatory design approach grounded in the LATUX workflow. In phase one, twelve teachers and teaching mentors participated in a workshop where they created prompt cards and dashboard mockups describing the game data they wanted to see. In phase two, the team built a prototype dashboard for the educational game Lakeland and piloted it with four teachers across several classroom sessions; three of the four teachers tested multiple classes, and the classrooms ranged from grades 6-12, mostly online because of COVID-19 shutdowns.

The study found that teacher input clearly shaped the prototype and that teachers generally viewed the dashboard as usable and helpful for classroom facilitation. Survey responses were positive for co-design, feasibility, and effectiveness, and interviews suggested the dashboard helped teachers identify student progress, inactivity, and strategy use, which in some cases supported timely feedback. However, the pilot also surfaced limitations: bugs, missing class-level overviews, and some visualizations that were hard to interpret quickly. The authors conclude that teacher-facing dashboards for classroom game sessions are promising, but need further development and larger-scale evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the dashboard made it easier to monitor students during gameplay, reducing the need to inspect each student screen individually. Survey ratings were favorable for usability and workflow support (e.g., 'If I were to play Lakeland again, I would use this tool' = 5/5; 'I will recommend my colleagues use this tool' = 5/5), though the pilot was small and some bugs reduced smoothness of use.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and interview feedback on ease of use, setup, and facilitation support

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was intended to help teachers notice student disengagement, frustration, indecision, and whether students were making progress, which are all closely tied to engagement and persistence. Teachers described using the interface to identify inactive or struggling students and to better understand whether students were engaged with the game, but the paper did not report standardized student engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement, frustration, inactivity, and progress during gameplay

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard included strategy-related models, such as a diagonal field strategy detector, and teachers said these visual cues helped them understand students' gameplay strategies. Evidence is qualitative and teacher-reported rather than a direct measurement of student durable-skill gains, so the finding is about facilitation and visibility of strategic thinking rather than an outcome effect.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback on visibility of student strategy and decision-making during gameplay

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a common challenge in exploratory and open-ended K-12 science classrooms: teachers often cannot quickly see how students are reasoning from brief, open-ended assessment responses. The authors argue that this limits teachers’ ability to make timely instructional adjustments, especially in learning environments where student thinking is distributed across many small groups or digital submissions.

To address this, they designed LearnLens, a generative AI-enhanced, teacher-facing dashboard that summarizes student responses and surfaces common misconceptions, alongside visualizations such as student-response tables, filters, word clouds, and bar charts. The system was developed for a 15-lesson middle school Earth science curriculum and was informed by teacher feedback during professional development. The GenAI component used GPT-4o with iterative prompt engineering and human validation, and the authors note that early prompts sometimes hallucinated or overreached beyond the data.

The study itself is a qualitative evaluation based on a single 1-hour semi-structured interview with two 6th-grade science teachers in an urban public school. Teachers reviewed the dashboard in a guided walkthrough and discussed how they would use it, what they trusted, and how it might affect instruction. They expressed positive reactions to the visualizations and especially the AI-generated summaries of student misconceptions, while being cautious about AI-generated prescriptive recommendations that went beyond the data.

Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI-supported teacher dashboards may help teachers make sense of open-ended student work, support instructional adaptation, and potentially make open-ended curricula more approachable. However, the evidence is preliminary and limited to perceived usefulness and trust in a small qualitative sample, with no causal test of effects on teacher morale, student engagement, or learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the dashboard helped them review student responses more efficiently and provided summaries/insights that their existing tools did not generate. In a 1-hour interview with two 6th-grade science teachers, they valued the word clouds, filtering, verbatim responses, and especially the AI-generated summaries of misconceptions as a way to quickly make sense of open-ended data.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of dashboard usefulness and efficiency for interpreting student responses

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was described as supporting teacher sense-making, interpretation of student thinking, and planning instructional adaptations, which are durable skills related to analysis and metacognition in teaching practice. Teachers said the AI-generated insights helped them connect response patterns to classroom discussion and think about future instructional changes, but the evidence is qualitative and based on self-report.
finding.measure: Teacher sense-making, interpretation, and planned instructional adaptation during dashboard walkthrough interviews

finding.finding_summary: Teachers suggested the dashboard could support broader use of open-ended curricula by making student thinking more visible and the pedagogy more approachable. The authors frame LearnLens as a possible catalyst for curricular change, but this is speculative and based on interview feedback rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reflections on potential curricular adoption and broader instructional use

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was designed to help teachers interpret students’ open-ended Earth science responses about concepts such as absorption, runoff, rainfall, and related misconceptions. Teachers found the AI-generated insights useful for identifying gaps and misconceptions in students’ understanding of these scientific ideas, but the study did not measure student learning gains.
finding.measure: Teacher interpretation of students’ open-ended science responses and misconceptions
finding.study_size: n=2 teachers; student responses from one check-in (student N not reported)

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge high school teachers face in teaching collaborative argumentation and in making sense of student discussion without a reliable record. The authors developed Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP classifiers to identify argument moves, specificity, and collaboration in transcripts of classroom dialogue and then presents those codes through visual analytics and planning supports.

The study evaluated a desktop version of DT with 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools. Teachers led and discussed recorded literature discussions, then used DT in cognitive interviews and completed usability surveys. The evaluation used human-coded transcripts to generate analytics and separately assessed the automated classifiers against those same annotations.

The main findings were that teachers judged DT to be helpful for learning about and facilitating collaborative argumentation, with high mean usefulness ratings across most features and an overall helpfulness rating of 4.72/5. The NLP models showed moderate-to-substantial agreement with human annotations, with kappa values of 0.574 for argument moves, 0.727 for specificity, and 0.566 for collaboration. However, the paper does not report student learning gains or teacher morale outcomes; its evidence is primarily about usability and classifier performance rather than educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was helpful for analyzing classroom discussion and supporting their facilitation work. In a usability survey with 18 high school ELA teachers, most items received very favorable ratings (e.g., overall helpfulness mean = 4.72/5; annotated transcript helpfulness mean = 4.89; pie charts helpfulness mean = 4.78), suggesting the tool reduced the burden of reviewing discussion evidence manually.
finding.measure: Teacher usability/perceived usefulness survey of DT features and overall helpfulness

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support teachers’ instructional attention to collaborative argumentation, including claim/evidence/explanation moves, specificity, and collaboration. Teachers agreed that DT helped them recognize student strengths and weaknesses during discussion (both means = 4.72) and gave them more insight into student learning than they usually get from reflecting on discussion alone (mean = 4.67), indicating positive support for collaborative reasoning-related practice.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings about recognizing strengths/weaknesses and insight into student collaborative argumentation

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student engagement directly, but it does report teacher perceptions that DT encouraged changes in facilitation of discussion (mean = 4.28) and was helpful for teaching literature discussions overall. This is indirect evidence of support for classroom discussion engagement, but it is not a direct outcome measure of morale or student engagement.
finding.measure: Teacher survey item on whether the system encouraged changes to discussion facilitation; overall helpfulness ratings

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers and AI tutoring systems can be designed to work together more effectively in K-12 classrooms. The core question is whether giving teachers real-time AI-generated analytics about students’ learning and behavior can improve classroom orchestration and student outcomes, rather than leaving teachers to monitor AI-supported classrooms without such support.

The authors describe an iterative, human-centered design process that produced Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses for teachers. Before the main evaluation, the team conducted participatory design work with teachers and pilot studies to refine the tool, using classroom observations and causal alignment analysis to shape the design. Lumilo presents real-time indicators and detailed student information from an AI tutor so teachers can decide whom to help and when, while still keeping attention on the classroom.

The main field experiment involved 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/school districts. Classrooms were randomly assigned within teacher to one of three conditions: no glasses, glasses without analytics, or glasses with analytics. Students completed pre- and post-tests on linear equation solving while working with the AI tutor Lynnette. The study found that Lumilo improved student learning, especially for students with lower pre-test scores, and that the analytics condition outperformed the reduced-glasses condition, indicating that the real-time analytics—not just the wearable form factor—contributed to the benefit. The paper also reports that teachers used Lumilo to shift attention toward students needing help, which reduced the usual “rich get richer” pattern in AI-supported classrooms. The study focuses on student learning and teacher attention allocation; it does not directly measure teacher morale or engagement as outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: In a field experiment with 286 analyzed middle school students (343 enrolled; 57 absent/excluded) across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed greater learning gains on a linear equation solving pre/post test than students in the No Glasses (business-as-usual) condition, and also outperformed the Glasses-only condition. The paper reports that the real-time analytics component contributed above and beyond the monitoring-only glasses, but does not provide a numeric effect size in the text provided.
finding.measure: 15-minute pre-test and post-test on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teacher use of Lumilo changed classroom attention patterns in ways that likely benefited students’ engagement with support, but this outcome is not directly measured with a survey or validated engagement scale. Teachers were observed spending more time with students who entered with lower prior knowledge, and the authors describe this as reducing the usual unequal attention pattern in AI-supported classrooms; however, the evidence is indirect and centered on teacher behavior rather than a direct engagement measure.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation / classroom observation of time spent with students by prior knowledge
finding.study_size: n=286 students in the main field study; 14 teachers, 15 classrooms across pilot studies

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that Lumilo supported teachers’ in-the-moment judgment and metacognitive orchestration by helping them interpret AI alerts alongside classroom cues, but this was not tested with a direct durable-skills assessment. Observational evidence indicates teachers used the tool to make richer inferences about student needs and to decide when to intervene, complementing the AI tutor with brief prompts and encouragement.
finding.measure: Classroom observation of teacher decision-making and attention allocation
finding.study_size: n=286 students in the main field study; 14 teachers in pilot studies

finding.finding_summary: Lumilo appears to improve the efficiency of teacher orchestration in AI-supported classrooms by helping teachers identify which students needed attention and where to spend time. The paper reports that teachers spent an average of about 24 seconds per student visit while using Lumilo, and that the tool helped direct attention where it was most needed, but no formal workload or productivity metric is reported.
finding.measure: Observed teacher time allocation / visit duration in the classroom
finding.study_size: 14 teachers, 15 classrooms, 304 students in pilot studies; 8 teachers, 18 classrooms, 286 students analyzed in the field study

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates learning in the context of an AI tutor for linear equation solving, which is a mathematics task already captured above; there is no separate non-mathematics academic outcome. The main academic contribution beyond test gains is the demonstration that real-time teacher support can reduce unequal learning patterns by shifting attention to lower-performing students, but this is still within mathematics learning rather than another academic domain.
finding.measure: Not applicable beyond the mathematics outcome

paper_profiles.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Schools: Unveiling Factors Influencing Teachers’ Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference of Artificial Intelligence in Education 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses why AI-based adaptive learning platforms, despite evidence of positive effects on student learning, are adopted slowly in schools and what factors predict teachers’ real-world engagement with such tools. The authors argue that adoption depends on more than perceived usefulness or ease of use, and that school-level, human, and ethical factors may matter as much as platform features.

To study this, the authors developed and validated a survey instrument intended to capture holistic adoption factors at the school level. After literature review, expert input, teacher pilot testing, and exploratory factor analysis, they fielded the instrument with 792 public school teachers from Grades 5-12 in a country-wide K-12 context. The final instrument yielded seven factors: workload, teacher ownership, perceived support, perceived knowledge and confidence, classroom orchestration, product quality, and ethics. They then correlated survey responses with teachers’ log-data-based engagement on the adaptive learning platform and built a predictive model (catboost) to estimate real-world engagement.

The main findings were that teacher engagement was positively associated with perceptions of useful professional development, belief in the platform’s success, satisfaction with the platform, helpful feedback, trust, being part of a community, content alignment, ease of use, guidance, access to help, leadership support, self-efficacy, and opportunities to share. The model explained 24.4% of variance in engagement (R2 = 0.244), suggesting promise but also substantial unexplained variability. The paper concludes that reducing additional workload, increasing ownership and trust, providing support mechanisms, and minimizing ethical/privacy concerns are important for adoption; however, teacher engagement remains a complex phenomenon that is only partially predictable from survey measures.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher engagement with the adaptive learning platform was positively associated with perceptions that the system did not add workload and with efficiency-related beliefs about the platform. The workload factor itself had a mean of 3.09, suggesting teachers neither strongly agreed nor disagreed that the tool changed workload, while items such as platform efficiency and no additional lesson-planning load correlated significantly with real-world engagement (e.g. r=0.1805 for efficiency; r=0.1128 for no extra lesson planning).
finding.measure: Teacher workload perceptions; efficiency-related survey items; real-world platform engagement (active days from log data)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers who reported higher self-efficacy, greater confidence, and stronger perceptions of support and ownership were more engaged with the platform. Several engagement-correlated items reflected motivational and affective dispositions, including self-efficacy (r=0.1086), trust in the platform (r=0.1788), belief in success (r=0.2258), and satisfaction with the platform (r=0.2002).
finding.measure: Teacher self-efficacy, confidence, trust, satisfaction, ownership, and engagement-related survey responses; platform active days

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined classroom orchestration, collaboration, and support behaviors that map onto durable skills such as time management, classroom coordination, and collaboration. Teachers who felt they could find balance between platform use and other teaching tasks, and who perceived opportunities to share and receive guidance, showed higher engagement; for example, can find balance correlated with engagement at r=0.1316 and opportunity to share at r=0.1063.
finding.measure: Classroom orchestration, opportunity to share, community participation, guidance/support perceptions; platform active days

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that adoption depends on school-level and institutional factors beyond the tool itself, including leadership support, shared vision, help structures, and privacy/ethics. Leadership’s belief in the platform correlated significantly with engagement (r=0.1397), and ethics/privacy concerns were identified as a meaningful barrier, with the ethics factor averaging 2.25 and a negative loading on the no-privacy-concerns item.
finding.measure: School leadership belief, governance/support structures, teacher ownership/community, privacy and ethics perceptions, and platform engagement

finding.finding_summary: Although student academic outcomes were not directly measured, the paper did examine curriculum alignment, content quality, and learning platform satisfaction as predictors of teacher engagement. Content alignment with national curricula was significantly associated with engagement (r=0.1530), and teachers who rated content as high quality or the platform as efficient were more engaged.
finding.measure: Content alignment and product quality perceptions; teacher engagement with adaptive learning platform

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI tools can be integrated into secondary classrooms as a teaching partner rather than a replacement for teachers. The central question is how teachers design, frame, and implement AI-supported activities, and how teacher judgment, prior AI experience, and subject/grade-level context shape student engagement and instructional usefulness. The study is framed as an early-stage classroom co-design pilot rather than a controlled impact evaluation.

Over seven weeks in spring 2025, 21 in-service teachers from five Washington State schools and districts used four Colleague AI Classroom features: Teaching Aide, AI-assisted assessment and grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. Teachers designed AI-supported lessons, used the tools with more than 600 students in grades 6-12, and provided weekly reflections, surveys, meetings, and interviews. The report combines teacher self-report, platform usage logs, and qualitative reflections to describe implementation patterns, engagement, and perceived value.

The main conclusion is that AI added the most value when teachers tightly structured its use with clear goals, prompts, and monitoring. Teachers generally viewed the tools as useful for formative feedback, lesson support, and reducing workload, but they also emphasized that AI scores were often unreliable and required teacher oversight. Engagement and learning benefits varied by grade level and subject, with stronger results in more structured, goal-oriented uses and more mixed results in math and some STEM contexts where domain precision mattered more. Overall, the report suggests promise for AI as a classroom support tool, but not as an autonomous instructional actor.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported conversations often increased student engagement and confidence, especially when they used clear scaffolds and framed the AI as a thought partner. In Teaching Aide implementations, 35% of teachers said the tool helped most students learn and 62% said some students learned from it; only 3% reported no benefit. Teachers also noted that multilingual learners and hesitant students became more willing to participate after practicing with the AI.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement and perceived learning in AI-supported conversations
finding.study_size: N=18 teachers (Teaching Aide exit tickets/feedback); up to 600 students participated

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports clear workload and efficiency benefits from AI-assisted grading and Student Growth Insights. Teachers said AI-generated narrative feedback saved time, AI grading covered a median of 92.2% of submitted work, and SGI reduced the burden of scanning student conversations by surfacing common questions and misconceptions. These features were repeatedly described as streamlining feedback cycles and reducing teacher oversight burden, though teachers still retained final grading authority.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of workload reduction; platform logs for AI grading coverage and assessment processing
finding.study_size: N=19 teachers in assessment phase; 58 assessment records; 936 student submissions across 33 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math subjects, teachers reported that AI-supported activities helped with writing, prewriting, brainstorming, language practice, and disciplinary inquiry. In English/ELA and Spanish, teachers described AI feedback as useful for revising student work and supporting proficiency development, while science teachers reported gains in inquiry and culturally relevant content exploration. Results were mixed in math and earth science because the tool struggled with diagrams and technical reasoning.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported instructional usefulness and student learning in subject-specific classroom tasks
finding.study_size: N=21 teachers; subject-specific implementations across grades 6-12

finding.finding_summary: Math implementations showed promise for concept talk but more mixed results than other subjects. Teachers reported that middle school math had some thoughtful engagement, but high school math was less engaging, and math/earth science were described as having more difficulty with accurate diagrams and flexible problem-solving reasoning. The tool was seen as usable for mathematical discussion, but trust and accuracy concerns limited stronger gains.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement and learning in math classroom implementations
finding.study_size: Included within N=21 teachers; math classes were part of the pilot across grades 6-12

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI helped with writing-related tasks such as brainstorming, prewriting, and revision, and that narrative feedback was especially valuable for improving student work. In assessment uses, 57% of teachers said AI feedback was helpful, and many described using it as a first-draft scaffold to support students in revising written work. However, AI-generated scores were often viewed as inconsistent, so the strongest benefits were in formative writing support rather than grading.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness of AI feedback for writing and revision; assessment feedback survey responses
finding.study_size: N=13 teacher feedback survey respondents in assessment phase; broader implementation by N=19 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The report describes positive effects for language-learning and oral participation, especially in Spanish and multilingual settings. Teachers reported that AI conversations helped multilingual learners find their voice and that Spanish teachers used AI for real-time ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback, shifting attention from task completion toward individualized skill development. Evidence is qualitative and teacher-reported rather than measured with standardized speaking or listening outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported classroom language practice and proficiency feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that AI-supported activities promoted deeper thinking when teachers framed tasks around goals, evidence, and revision. Teachers reported that structured prompts, seminar preparation, proof sketches, and feedback/revision cycles supported student reasoning, reflection, and self-improvement behavior. However, these gains depended heavily on teacher mediation and were weaker when interactions became superficial or aimless.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported depth of inquiry, reasoning, revision, and metacognitive behavior in AI-supported tasks
finding.study_size: N=21 teachers; classroom reflections across 114 Teaching Aide conversations and assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The report indicates that AI sometimes increased student confidence and reduced anxiety by providing immediate, low-pressure feedback before peer or teacher review. Teachers noted that some students were more willing to revise and participate after interacting with AI, and that the tool could create a less intimidating environment for hesitant learners. These are qualitative observations, not measured changes in motivation scales.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of student confidence, anxiety reduction, and willingness to participate

paper_profiles.title: Inverted Classroom an der Hochschule Karlsruhe - ein nicht quantisierter Flip
paper_profiles.venue: Das Inverted Classroom Model: Begleitband zur ersten deutschen ICM-Konferenz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the rationale for using the Inverted Classroom Model (ICM) in higher education, especially in engineering and mathematics courses at Hochschule Karlsruhe. The authors frame the problem as one of heterogeneous student preparation, limited semester-long study habits, and high instructor workload in traditional lecture-based teaching, and argue that ICM may better support active learning and student engagement while also potentially making courses more attractive to a broader range of students.

The paper is primarily a practice-oriented discussion and implementation report from the SKATING project, which supported faculty in designing, producing, and evaluating flipped teaching formats. It outlines several variants of inversion, from minimally flipped recorded summaries to partially or fully inverted topics, and describes one pilot implementation in Higher Mathematics 3 with about 20 motivated third-semester engineering students. The implementation used videos hosted via YouTube/ILIAS, in-class problem solving, observation of sessions, online surveys, and follow-up evaluation to examine acceptance, process quality, and possible effects.

The main conclusion is cautiously positive but not quantitative: the authors report good student acceptance, some evidence that students prepared the videos and engaged in class, and a strong perceived fit with goals such as motivating students and creating a more interactive classroom. At the same time, they emphasize that ICM requires substantial preparation, careful process monitoring, and attention to unintended risks such as increased student time demands and instructor workload. Rather than claiming proven learning gains, the paper argues that successful use depends on adapting the model to local needs and evaluating it with multiple measures over time.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes a pilot inverted-classroom implementation in Higher Mathematics 3 with about 20 third-semester engineering students, but it does not report quantitative achievement gains. The authors instead note that students were able to correctly reproduce relevant points from the videos and participated in guided self- and partner-solving during class; later exams and comparison with the previous year were planned to assess learning outcomes, but results are not reported here.
finding.measure: math course understanding / video content recall / planned exam performance

finding.finding_summary: A central goal and observed outcome of the pilot was increased student motivation and engagement. The authors report that the teacher wanted a two-sided 'flow' experience and to spark curiosity, and that student feedback was mostly positive; the in-class sessions featured active participation, with many students having watched the videos in advance and engaging in problem solving and discussion.
finding.measure: student motivation, curiosity, satisfaction, participation in class, acceptance of the ICM

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes collaborative and self-directed learning during the in-class phase. Students worked in guided self-study and partner-reasoning segments, and the authors argue that ICM increases room for direct interaction between students and with the instructor, supporting collaboration and active problem solving. No quantitative estimate is provided.
finding.measure: collaboration, interactive participation, problem solving in class

finding.finding_summary: Operationally, the paper reports both added implementation burdens and potential longer-term efficiencies. Creating and producing one video session took about 1 hour of total work, with roughly 30 minutes extra teacher setup time plus 30 minutes for organization per recording session; the authors also note that the method may reduce future effort after initial material creation and that recording summaries can still create noticeable overhead.
finding.measure: teacher workload / preparation time / production time for learning videos

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that, if pilot evaluations remain positive, the SKATING project could serve as a multiplier for wider institutional adoption of the Inverted Classroom Model at Hochschule Karlsruhe. It presents the initiative as a way to improve study conditions and teaching quality institutionally, but no measured policy or system-level outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: institutional implementation / dissemination potential / project-based teaching reform

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Multi-Agent AI Supporting Teachers in Scaling Differentiated Learning for Diverse Students
paper_profiles.population: K–12 teachers and school principals; worksheet evaluation focused on in-service K–12 teachers (with examples aligned to grade 7 mathematics)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting differentiated instruction in increasingly heterogeneous K–12 classrooms, where teachers must account for variation in performance, motivation, language proficiency, and learning differences such as dyslexia and ADHD. The authors argue that existing AI educational tools are largely student-facing and performance-centric, leaving a gap for teacher-facing systems that can support inclusive differentiation while preserving teacher autonomy.

To address this gap, the paper introduces FACET, a teacher-facing multi-agent AI framework with four agents: learner simulation, diagnostic assessment, worksheet generation, and evaluation. Teachers specify learner profiles, upload or select materials, and retain full review control over generated outputs. The system is designed to produce curriculum-aligned and accessibility-aware differentiated worksheets, including adaptations for neurodivergent learners. The framework was evaluated through two stakeholder studies: workshops with German school principals (N=30) about workflow integration and a survey of in-service K–12 teachers (N=70) who rated five generated worksheets for grade 7 mathematics.

Findings suggest strong perceived value for the tool in supporting inclusive differentiation and reducing teacher workload. Principals emphasized the need for curriculum alignment, accessibility, and teacher-in-the-loop control as prerequisites for adoption. Teachers rated scaffolded worksheets favorably, especially for low-performance or low-motivation profiles, with didactic structure and clarity scoring above the midpoint. However, enrichment materials for highly motivated/high-performing learners were weaker, and the dyslexia-adapted worksheet showed mixed results, especially on font readability and overall suitability for reading difficulties.

Overall, the paper concludes that multi-agent AI can support differentiated instruction in principle, but current outputs are better at scaffolded support than enrichment and still require refinement for accessibility and real classroom deployment. The authors frame the work as formative and preliminary, with ongoing longitudinal school partnerships planned to examine teacher trust, workflow integration, and student feedback under authentic conditions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides qualitative and descriptive evidence that FACET could reduce teacher workload by scaling differentiated material creation and simplifying prompt use through reusable learner profiles. In workshops with school principals (N=30), participants emphasized that differentiation is difficult to sustain without AI support given large class sizes and teacher shortages; however, this is perceived value rather than a measured time-saving effect.
finding.measure: Workshop themes and stakeholder perceptions of workload reduction and workflow integration

finding.finding_summary: Teachers rated scaffolded worksheets for low-motivation and mixed-performance profiles favorably on didactic structure and clarity, suggesting the system may better support engagement-oriented design than generic materials. In the survey (N=70), worksheets for low-motivation learners received the highest ratings on didactic structure (M=4.41-4.50/6) and clarity (M=4.23-4.46/6), while a high-performance/high-motivation worksheet scored lower overall, indicating weaker support for more engaging enrichment.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of didactic structure, clarity, format/design, and creativity; perceived support for motivation/engagement
finding.std_deviation: Worksheet SDs reported in table (e.g., didactic structure SD=1.02-1.20; clarity SD=1.05-1.20)

finding.finding_summary: FACET was evaluated using grade 7 mathematics worksheets on area calculation, and teachers generally rated the scaffolded math materials as pedagogically suitable. In the survey (N=70), worksheets for low-motivation profiles received the strongest ratings for didactic structure and clarity, but the high-performance/high-motivation worksheet was rated lower across all dimensions, suggesting the system currently performs better for scaffolded numeracy support than for enrichment.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of grade 7 mathematics worksheet quality (area calculation)
finding.std_deviation: Worksheet SDs reported in table (e.g., didactic structure SD=1.02-1.20; clarity SD=1.05-1.20)

finding.finding_summary: The dyslexia-adapted worksheet was designed to improve reading accessibility through typographic and layout changes, and teachers rated language simplification and spacing/layout positively. However, font readability and overall suitability for reading difficulties were only near the midpoint, indicating incomplete success on literacy-accessibility adaptation rather than a clearly positive effect.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of dyslexia-adapted worksheet readability, language simplification, and spacing/layout
finding.std_deviation: Font readability SD=1.61; language simplification SD=1.40; spacing/layout SD=1.39; suitability for reading difficulties SD=1.47

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of scaling high-quality feedback on classroom discourse in K-12 mathematics, a task that traditionally requires expert observers to manually code lesson transcripts. The authors present TalkMoves, an AI-enabled application that automatically analyzes classroom recordings and identifies teachers’ use of six “Accountable Talk” discourse moves, then turns those detections into teacher-facing feedback dashboards.

Methodologically, the paper combines natural language processing and speech processing with supervised sequence classification. The team trained and compared several model families, including BiLSTM variants and transformer-based models (BERT, RoBERTa, XLNet, ALBERT, and distilled versions), using 501 transcript files totaling 176,757 sentences from K-12 math lessons. Human annotators labeled sentences for six talk-move categories plus a none class, with high inter-rater reliability (Cohen’s kappa above .90 for each talk move). The best-performing model was RoBERTa-LARGE, reaching F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set.

The application was piloted with 21 teachers in two midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019-2020 academic year. Teachers used the system to view feedback, completed surveys, and participated in interviews, and the interface provides lesson-level analytics such as counts of teacher and student talk, talk-move frequencies, wait time, and student response patterns. The paper’s main conclusion is that transformer-based NLP can produce feedback that is roughly on par with expert coding reliability for this task, suggesting promise for supporting teachers’ professional learning. However, the paper also emphasizes limitations, especially errors introduced by automatic speech recognition and the under-detection of student talk in noisy classroom audio.
