finding.finding_summary: The system substantially improves the efficiency and scalability of generating classroom-discourse feedback by automating sentence-level coding that would otherwise require expert human observers. The best model (RoBERTa-LARGE) achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set, compared with a prior baseline of 65% F1, indicating more reliable automated classification for producing teacher feedback at scale.
finding.measure: Model classification performance for identifying teacher talk moves in classroom transcripts (F1, MCC) as a proxy for automated feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the TalkMoves pipeline can scale discourse-based instructional feedback across teachers and districts, reducing dependence on scarce expert coders and potentially changing how districts support teacher professional learning. In the pilot deployment, 21 teachers across two midwestern school districts used the application over the 2019-2020 year, suggesting feasibility for institutional use, though the paper does not report district-level outcome effects.
finding.measure: Pilot implementation/uptake of the TalkMoves application in schools; teacher use and feedback delivery at district scale

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence should be integrated into K-12 STEM education while addressing ethical risks such as algorithmic bias, privacy invasion, surveillance, and inequitable access. It is framed around the tension between AI’s potential to support personalization, feedback, and operational efficiency and its potential to reinforce systemic inequities and diminish human judgment in teaching and learning.

Methodologically, the article is a critical conceptual review and synthesis of literature published between 2016 and 2025, rather than a study that collects new empirical data. It reviews AI applications in STEM classrooms, focusing on intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, and surveillance-oriented tools, and discusses both reported benefits and risks. The paper also proposes a three-phased implementation roadmap and a four-phase professional development model grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI can support K-12 STEM education only if implementation is paired with strong ethical safeguards, bias audits, privacy protections, equity-centered design, and sustained teacher professional development. It emphasizes low-resource and culturally responsive adaptations so that AI does not widen the digital divide. The article is primarily a framework and policy-oriented synthesis, not an empirical comparison of AI effects on teacher morale or classroom engagement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems and automated assessments can reduce teacher workload by automating feedback, scoring, and diagnostic analysis. It cites literature suggesting these tools improve assessment scalability and free educators to focus on higher-order instruction, but it does not report original effect sizes or a direct empirical test in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher workload and assessment efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional implications of AI adoption, including policy alignment, mandatory ethics and equity audits, data governance, and professional development structures. It concludes that AI integration could support more equitable and sustainable systems if carefully governed, but could also deepen surveillance, bias, and access inequities without oversight; no original empirical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Policy alignment, governance, equity audits, institutional implementation capacity

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses student engagement, teacher confidence, and buy-in as relevant to AI implementation, but these are presented as anticipated or cited outcomes rather than directly measured in new data. It notes that one implementation scenario would assess student engagement surveys and that teacher professional development is intended to improve confidence and trust in AI, but no empirical results are reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Student engagement surveys; teacher confidence/trust (discussed conceptually)

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can act as an automated teacher coach by scoring classroom instruction and generating feedback that is useful for improving teaching. The authors frame three coaching tasks for generative AI: predicting scores on classroom-observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and offering actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses transcripts from the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) dataset of 4th- and 5th-grade elementary mathematics classrooms in four U.S. school districts. The authors evaluate zero-shot GPT-3.5/ChatGPT outputs against expert human rubric scores and human teacher ratings of model-generated feedback. For scoring tasks, they compare model predictions with human scores using Spearman correlations; for qualitative feedback tasks, two experienced math teachers rate outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Overall, ChatGPT performs poorly as a scoring tool, with low or near-zero correlations with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items, and added rubric descriptions or reasoning do not reliably improve performance. For feedback generation, teachers judge many responses as relevant or actionable, but often not insightful; for MQI especially, performance is weaker. A major risk is redundancy and limited novelty: 82% of suggestions repeat what the teacher already does in the transcript. The paper concludes that generative AI may eventually support teacher coaching, but current off-the-shelf systems are not yet reliable enough to replace expert coaching and should be used cautiously with human oversight.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can reduce the effort of teacher coaching by automatically scoring classroom transcripts and generating instructional feedback. It finds that the model can produce relevant and sometimes actionable feedback, but its score predictions correlate poorly with human ratings (e.g., Spearman values near 0 across many CLASS/MQI items), and 82% of suggestions are redundant, limiting practical usefulness as a coaching aid.
finding.measure: Human-rated usefulness of automated feedback; Spearman correlation between model-predicted and human rubric scores; teacher ratings of relevance/faithfulness/insightfulness/actionability/novelty
finding.study_size: Task A: n=100 transcript segments; Task B: 216 CLASS examples and 288 MQI examples; Task C: 36 suggestions; 2 human teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies elementary mathematics instructional quality through MQI-based transcript scoring and feedback generation. ChatGPT shows low correlation with human MQI scores across EXPL, REMED, LANGIMP, and SMQR (e.g., DA correlations of 0.02, 0.05, 0.00, and 0.17, respectively), and teachers rate MQI-related highlights/missed opportunities as especially weak in relevance and insightfulness.
finding.measure: MQI rubric scores (EXPL, REMED, LANGIMP, SMQR) and teacher ratings of generated feedback for math instruction
finding.study_size: Task A: n=100 transcript segments; Task B: 288 MQI examples; Task C: 36 suggestions

paper_profiles.title: School Virus Infection Simulator for Customizing School Schedules During COVID-19
paper_profiles.population: K-12 schools (self-contained and departmentalized classrooms; elementary through high school contexts modeled)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how schools can customize schedules during the COVID-19 pandemic to reduce within-school transmission while preserving a meaningful amount of face-to-face instruction. The authors note that schools and policymakers must choose among many scheduling options under uncertainty, and they argue that existing guidance does not fully capture how internal school factors such as classroom type, ventilation, and cohorting interact with schedule design.

To study this, the paper introduces the School-Virus-Infection-Simulator (SVIS), an agent-based infection simulator built on an extended SEIR/Wells-Riley framework. The simulator models students moving through lesson schedules in either self-contained or departmentalized classrooms, with parameters for classroom volume, ventilation, masking, disease progression, and different cohorting/scheduling patterns. The authors compare a range of schedule types, including UNESCO-style hybrid schedules and custom week/day-based patterns, over 12-week simulations.

The study does not evaluate an AI tool for teacher morale or classroom engagement directly; rather, it is a simulation study focused on infection control and schedule planning. The main conclusions are that increasing ventilation reduces simultaneous infections, but schedule design is often more influential and less stable in its effects. The impact of a given schedule depends strongly on classroom type, and some schedules can reduce peak simultaneous infections while maintaining face-to-face learning. The authors conclude that teachers and education policymakers should consider schedule design jointly with classroom structure rather than relying only on the percentage of in-person instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The SVIS is presented as a planning tool that helps teachers and education policymakers customize school schedules to reduce the maximum number of simultaneously infected students while maintaining a certain percentage of face-to-face lessons. The paper argues this can support practical decision-making under constraints such as limited ventilation upgrades and classroom availability, but it does not report a direct effect size for workload or productivity.
finding.measure: Simulation-based schedule planning utility; maximum number of students infected simultaneously; percentage of face-to-face lessons

finding.finding_summary: The central contribution is a school-level decision-support simulator for teachers and education policymakers to evaluate reopening and hybrid scheduling policies during COVID-19. Across simulations, ventilation and schedule customization changed peak infection outcomes, and the paper concludes that institutional scheduling choices should be tailored to classroom type and risk constraints.
finding.measure: Simulated school scheduling outcomes under different classroom types and ventilation/schedule policies

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter is a broad conceptual survey of generative AI for information access (IA) systems. It explains how modern generative models, especially large language models, change the design space for search, retrieval, and response generation by enabling both information generation and information synthesis.

The paper is not an empirical study of schools or teachers. Instead, it reviews foundational techniques such as Transformers, scaling laws, training stages (pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF), prompt optimization, multimodal applications, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling. Across these topics, it argues that generative AI can improve user experience, support grounded responses when paired with external knowledge, and open up new composite information tasks, while also introducing risks such as hallucination, high inference cost, maintenance difficulty, and unclear performance tradeoffs.

Because the chapter focuses on general AI and information-retrieval research rather than K-12 education, it does not report teacher, classroom, or student outcome data. Its conclusions are theoretical and forward-looking: generative AI is promising for information access, but many open questions remain about scaling, reliability, retrieval planning, and system control.

paper_profiles.title: All Together Now: Teachers as Research Partners in the Design of Search Technology for the Classroom
paper_profiles.venue: KidRec’21 (ACM Interaction Design and Children workshop proceedings)
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) and secondary school students in classroom contexts; teachers as research partners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that teachers should be treated as core research partners, not merely facilitators or study participants, in the design and evaluation of search technologies for classroom use. The authors motivate this position by describing recurring barriers in educational technology adoption, including gaps between design assumptions and classroom practice, limited attention to teacher expertise, and the need for tools that support authentic student learning activities.

The paper is grounded in the authors’ multi-year research experience designing and evaluating classroom search tools for children, including work in primary school settings across Italy, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States. Rather than testing a specific AI intervention, the article is a reflective, practice-based discussion of how teacher involvement improves research relevance, usability, and interpretability of findings, and how it can make search tasks and technologies better aligned with classroom realities.

The main conclusions are conceptual rather than experimental: involving teachers helps determine research priorities, ensures that practical classroom constraints shape the design, improves the usability and adoption potential of outcomes, and helps researchers interpret results more accurately. The paper also argues that teacher collaboration benefits teachers themselves by giving them a voice in technology design and professional learning opportunities. However, it does not report comparative empirical evidence about measurable effects on teacher morale, classroom engagement, or student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT and related systems, for education. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors synthesize early research, plausible use cases, and known risks to argue for responsible, human-centered adoption in learning and teaching.

The paper discusses how LLMs may support students through personalized practice, feedback, tutoring, quiz generation, language support, and conversational scaffolding, and how they may assist teachers with lesson planning, assessment, content creation, and professional development. It also reviews technical and educational challenges including bias, copyright, privacy, sustainability, overreliance, verification, and the difficulty of distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work.

The context is broad K-12, higher education, and professional learning rather than a single population or field trial. The main conclusion is cautiously optimistic: LLMs could improve learning and teaching workflows if they are integrated with strong oversight, clear pedagogical purpose, and safeguards for equity, accuracy, and integrity, but the paper does not present direct comparative outcome evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can reduce teacher workload by supporting lesson planning, generating quizzes and exercises, creating personalized feedback, and semi-automating assessment. These claims are illustrative and supported by references to prior work in the article, but the paper itself reports no original effect estimates, sample sizes, or controlled comparisons.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that LLM-based tools may improve student engagement and participation, especially in group and remote learning, and may help reduce foreign-language learning anxiety or low willingness to communicate. These are presented as potential benefits drawn from cited examples rather than as findings from a new empirical study in this paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement, participation, language-learning anxiety, willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames LLMs as tools that can support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact checking, but it also warns that overreliance may weaken those same skills. No new empirical test is reported; the paper’s conclusion is that benefits depend on careful integration and active human guidance.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, fact-checking

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is institutional governance around copyright, privacy, bias, sustainability, fairness, and school-level access to LLMs. The authors argue that responsible adoption requires policies, human oversight, training, and infrastructure, while also warning that unequal access could widen educational divides.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, sustainability, access

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no original study; discussion of students across cited studies, including undergraduate, vocational education, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/review-style discussion of the promise and risks of artificial intelligence in education. It asks whether AI tools improve learning by personalizing instruction and reducing cognitive load, or whether they undermine deep learning by encouraging cognitive offloading, lower retention, weaker critical thinking, reduced creativity, and diminished motivation.

The article does not report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples from AI-enabled learning tools such as ChatGPT, adaptive learning systems, and intelligent tutoring systems, framing them through Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory. The authors argue that AI can support lower-order tasks and personalization, but overuse or poorly designed integration may reduce active engagement, autonomy, and higher-order thinking.

The discussion cites a mix of studies across higher education, vocational education, and language learning, including findings that AI-supported students may improve procedural performance or specific aspects of idea generation while also showing risks such as memory decline, lower conceptual understanding, and reduced creative confidence. The main conclusion is that AI should complement rather than replace human instruction, with teacher guidance, reflection, AI-free practice, and fairness safeguards used to prevent dependency and preserve cognitive development.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI has mixed effects on durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and creativity. It cites prior studies suggesting AI can help with certain performance aspects, but overreliance may reduce critical scrutiny, increase cognitive fixation, lower creative confidence, and weaken independent problem-solving; no new effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, cognitive engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that AI may improve motivation-related competence through personalized learning, but excessive dependence can reduce autonomy, relatedness, and intrinsic motivation. It cites prior work on AI and motivation rather than reporting new data, and provides no effect size or sample size for its own claims.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI-supported learning outcomes across non-core academic areas such as vocational education and language learning. It cites prior studies reporting improved communicative competence and fluency in language learning, but also warns that AI can reduce retention and concept formation if used excessively; no original quantitative estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Language learning performance, vocational education learning, retention

paper_profiles.title: AI in the Classroom: A Boon or a Threat to Pedagogical Practices?
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school students; sixth-grade students; teachers from schools in Almaty
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI tools in school settings help or harm pedagogy, with a focus on student engagement, independence, critical thinking, and retention. The authors frame AI as a dual-edged technology that can personalize learning and support content creation, but may also encourage over-reliance and weaken traditional learning processes.

The study combines a brief literature review, a teacher survey from schools in Almaty, and an experiment with sixth-grade students. In the experiment, students used AI tools to write short stories, then one week later retold them so the authors could assess retention and engagement. Teachers reported mixed views: some saw AI as increasing engagement and supporting motivation, while others worried it reduced student independence and fostered dependency.

Results from the student activity suggested that AI could create initial interest, but engagement was generally low, customization of AI-generated stories was minimal, and retention after one week was only moderate, with about half of students able to retell the story accurately. The paper concludes that AI should supplement, not replace, traditional instruction, and that younger learners may need structured guidance to avoid passive use and over-reliance.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported mixed perceptions of AI’s effect on student engagement and motivation. In the survey, 41.7% rated engagement with AI-assisted assignments at level 3, 33.3% at level 4, 16.7% at level 2, and 8.3% at level 5, suggesting moderate but inconsistent engagement gains rather than a clear positive effect.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement with AI-assisted assignments and overall motivation/academic progress
finding.study_size: n=12 teachers for Figure 1; n=12 teachers overall survey figures

finding.finding_summary: The study found mixed evidence for AI’s influence on independent work, critical thinking, and creativity. Teachers were evenly split on whether AI helped or hindered independence (25% at the most negative and 25% at the most positive end), and the authors observed minimal student customization of AI-generated stories, indicating potential over-reliance. No formal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of independence; observation of student customization and brief interviews about AI-assisted storytelling
finding.study_size: n=12 teachers; sixth-grade students (exact n not reported)

finding.finding_summary: In the sixth-grade storytelling task, students used AI tools to create short stories and were asked to retell them one week later to assess retention. Approximately half of the students could recall and retell the story with reasonable accuracy, indicating moderate retention rather than a strong learning benefit; students also showed only minimal customization of the written stories.
finding.measure: Story retell after one week; comprehension/retention of AI-generated written content

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines concerns about using ChatGPT in education, focusing on early adopters and the broader public discourse around the chatbot’s educational use. The authors ask what risks and issues arise when ChatGPT is used in educational settings, rather than testing whether it improves learning outcomes. The study is framed as an instrumental qualitative case study of ChatGPT as a representative advanced chatbot.

finding.finding_summary: Participants often described ChatGPT as useful for reducing instructional workload, generating teaching materials, creating quizzes, and providing immediate feedback. However, the paper also reports that output quality, structure, and accuracy were inconsistent, sometimes making teachers’ duties more complicated rather than easier.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of teacher workload, resource creation, and task efficiency from interviews and educator scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The study found that users, including educators and students, experienced excitement and enjoyment when interacting with ChatGPT, and some described emotional attachment. At the same time, users reported disappointment, lack of emotional value, and concerns that the system is not humanized and cannot reflect emotions or genuine empathy.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of emotions, attachment, satisfaction, and perceived engagement during ChatGPT interactions

finding.finding_summary: A central theme was that ChatGPT may support learning and stimulate understanding, but it can also weaken critical thinking, promote laziness, and facilitate cheating if used uncritically. The paper repeatedly emphasizes the need for prompt skill, critical thinking, and user competence to obtain useful outputs and avoid overreliance.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of critical thinking, cheating, prompt skill, and user competence in interviews, tweets, and educator scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies institutional concerns including cheating, privacy, data security, fairness, misinformation, and the possibility that schools may respond with bans or restrictive policies. It argues that adoption should be guided by guidelines, governance, and responsible-AI principles rather than simple prohibition.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence from tweets, interviews, and use scenarios about policy, ethics, privacy, fairness, and institutional response

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016 through 2022. The authors ask what the trends are in AI-in-education research in higher education, where the studies were conducted, who authored them, what populations and domains were studied, and how AI was being used across the literature.

Using PRISMA procedures, the authors screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the review maps the field: it finds rapid growth in publications in 2021–2022, a geographic shift toward China as the leading publication source, and a strong concentration of studies in undergraduate settings, especially language learning, computer science, and engineering. Education departments were the most common first-author affiliation, suggesting increasing educator involvement in the field.

Grounded coding identified five main uses of AI in higher education: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review concludes that AI in higher education is still mostly being used to automate or augment existing practices—such as assessment, prediction, feedback, and learning analytics—rather than to transform pedagogy. It also highlights gaps, including limited research in developing countries, limited work with graduate students, and relatively little focus on how AI supports instructors and managers.

finding.finding_summary: This review does not test a single instructional intervention, but it synthesizes how AI was used across 138 higher-education studies. AI applications were most commonly used for assessment/evaluation, predicting student outcomes, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning; the review reports counts such as 26 studies for automatic assessment, 21 for predicting, 18 for ITS, and 19 for managing student learning. The paper is descriptive and field-mapping rather than impact-estimating, so no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of AI use categories across included studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to support student emotions, persistence, engagement, and self-regulation, but the review itself only summarizes these patterns rather than estimating effects. Examples include AI systems that assessed student emotions, provided personalized feedback, and supported goal initiation, planning, action control, and emotion control. The evidence is qualitative/descriptive at the review level, with no aggregate effect size reported.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of studies involving emotions, engagement, persistence, and self-regulation support
finding.study_size: n=138 studies reviewed; specific primary-study counts not pooled

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that AI is frequently used to increase efficiency in higher education, especially through automatic assessment, feedback generation, test creation, learning analytics, and instructional design support. The review notes that automatic assessment was the most common assessment use and that AI can reduce instructor grading time and help manage large student data sets, but it does not report a combined effect size for workload reduction. The findings are descriptive and based on counts of study purposes rather than direct outcome comparisons.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of efficiency-related uses such as grading, feedback, learning analytics, and curriculum/instruction design

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies institutional-level uses of AI such as managing student learning, enrollment/admissions prediction, quality assurance, and large-scale data analysis for decision-making. It argues that AI has potential to help managers and administrators use big data for actionable insight, though the paper also notes that this is an underexplored area and only a small number of studies addressed it directly. No effect size or comparative institutional outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of management, admissions, and institutional analytics uses
finding.study_size: n=138 studies reviewed; management-related studies noted as 19

finding.finding_summary: Some included studies addressed higher-order thinking, problem solving, and collaboration-related activities, especially in the assessment/evaluation code where AI was used to evaluate reflections, community identity, and higher-order thinking. The review also notes AI support for group work assessment and student interaction analysis, but it does not estimate causal effects on durable skills. Evidence is descriptive and secondary, not an outcome evaluation.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of studies involving higher-order thinking, reflections, and group work

finding.finding_summary: Literacy-related uses of AI were common, especially in language learning contexts involving writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. The review highlights automatic assessment and feedback for writing, including systems used to improve academic writing skills and provide personalized feedback. Because the paper is a systematic review, it reports patterns of use and study counts rather than pooled literacy gains; no effect size is given.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of language-learning studies involving writing, reading, and vocabulary

paper_profiles.title: Flipped classroom improves student learning in health professions education: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether flipped classroom instruction improves learner outcomes compared with traditional classroom teaching in health professions education. The authors focused on comparative studies in which students received pre-class video-based instruction and then attended face-to-face classes with active learning, and they synthesized results from 28 eligible studies published in peer-reviewed journals.

The review included medical, nursing, pharmacy, public health, dental, chiropractic, and related health-professions learners, mostly in undergraduate or graduate professional programs. Across 2,295 students in flipped classrooms and 2,420 in traditional classrooms, the meta-analysis found a statistically significant advantage for flipped instruction on achievement outcomes (SMD=0.33, 95% CI 0.21-0.46), with substantial heterogeneity (I2=75.6%) but no evidence of publication bias.

Moderator analyses suggested that the effect was robust across study designs and student/instructor equivalence checks, and that the presence of pre-class readings or exercises did not clearly change the result. The one subgroup finding was that flipped classrooms were more effective when instructors used quizzes at the start of in-class sessions. The paper also reports that most surveyed students preferred flipped over traditional classes, though some students disliked the additional time required for pre-class video work.

finding.finding_summary: Across 28 comparative studies with 2,295 students in flipped classrooms and 2,420 in traditional classrooms, flipped instruction produced a significant improvement in learner achievement. The pooled standardized mean difference was 0.33 (95% CI 0.21-0.46, p<0.001), indicating a small-to-moderate positive effect on objective course performance measures such as exams and post-tests.
finding.measure: Objective student achievement/performance (exam scores, post-test scores, objective assessments)

finding.finding_summary: The review also examined student preference/satisfaction with the flipped classroom format, based on five survey-based studies. Overall, 228 of 320 respondents (71%) preferred flipped classrooms over traditional classrooms, suggesting generally favorable student attitudes toward the intervention.
finding.measure: Student preference/satisfaction surveys

finding.finding_summary: The authors discussed that flipped classrooms may enhance active learning processes such as engagement, interaction, and application of knowledge, but these were not the primary pooled outcomes. Evidence from the included studies was indirect and mostly reflected learner preference and in-class participation rather than a direct quantitative measure of durable skills.
finding.measure: Indirect references to engagement, interaction, and application during active learning

paper_profiles.title: Ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether there is a global consensus on ethical artificial intelligence in education (AIED) and maps the principles found across international policy and guideline documents. Rather than studying an AI tool or instructional intervention, it conducts a thematic analysis of ethics-oriented reports and frameworks from organizations such as UNESCO, OECD, and the European Commission.

The authors synthesize these documents into seven ethical principles for AIED: governance and stewardship, transparency and accountability, sustainability and proportionality, privacy, security and safety, inclusiveness, and human-centered AIED. The paper argues that existing guidelines overlap on many themes but differ in emphasis and terminology, and that education-specific ethical frameworks are needed because generic AI ethics guidance does not fully capture educational contexts.

The intended context is broad educational governance and decision-making, including students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional leaders. The main conclusion is prescriptive: the authors propose a framework to guide ethical design, deployment, and regulation of AIED, while acknowledging that future work should test and refine these principles in implementation settings and impact studies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate a field intervention; instead it identifies and synthesizes recurring ethical and governance themes across six international AIED policy/guideline documents. It concludes that there is substantial overlap on core principles such as governance, transparency, privacy, safety, inclusiveness, and human-centeredness, but no single universal consensus or standard framework specifically tailored to education.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of international policies and guidelines on AIED

paper_profiles.title: A review of the use of virtual reality head-mounted displays in education and training
paper_profiles.population: Mixed K-12, higher education, and training populations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of experimental and quasi-experimental studies on head-mounted display (HMD) virtual reality in education and training, motivated by the post-2013 emergence of lower-cost, higher-quality consumer VR hardware. The authors searched eight databases and screened 8,177 references, ultimately including 21 studies published since 2013 that used HMDs with sufficiently wide fields of view and reported original empirical data.

The review focuses on two broad questions: how HMD-based VR affects learner experience and whether it improves learning outcomes. Across the included studies, the authors examined immersion/presence, physical discomfort (including cybersickness), learner attitudes, and cognitive, psychomotor, and affective skill acquisition. The included evidence spans students, teachers, and professionals in settings such as engineering, history, medicine, science, and vocational training; most studies were small, non-randomized, and single-institution.

The main conclusion is that HMDs do not automatically improve learning and often show no advantage over desktops or traditional instruction. The clearest benefits appear in narrow cases: spatial/visual understanding, some head-movement-related psychomotor tasks, and some affective or stress-related simulations. However, the review also identifies important risks and limitations, including cybersickness, distraction from the learning task, technological barriers, and inconsistent transfer from simulation to real-world performance. Overall, the evidence base is limited and of modest quality, so the authors call for more rigorous and authentic-context research.

finding.finding_summary: This review found that HMD-based VR can improve some non-core academic skills, especially spatial and visual understanding, but it often showed no advantage over traditional instruction or less immersive technologies. Across the included studies, results varied by task and context: some studies favored HMDs for spatial awareness or particular learning tasks, while others found no difference or even worse knowledge acquisition (e.g., HMD leading to the lowest acquisition in one comparison study).
finding.measure: Learning outcomes in history, engineering, anatomy/pathology, museum learning, and other non-core subject areas

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that HMDs often increased learner engagement, interest, enthusiasm, and perceived usefulness, but these benefits were not uniform and were sometimes offset by discomfort, distraction, or no difference in motivation. For example, one study found more engaged behavior with HMDs than desktops (n=57 high school students), while another found no motivation difference between groups; cybersickness also negatively affected attitudes and could reduce outcomes.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, interest, enthusiasm, attitudes toward VR, and related learner experience measures

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a small number of studies touching durable skills such as problem solving, understanding connections between phenomena, and observational/visual-scanning skills. Evidence was mixed: one study suggested dialogue in VR fostered deeper conceptual understanding than narration, while another showed improved adherence to a visual-scanning technique in the simulator; however, the review emphasizes that these findings are task-specific and limited in generalizability.
finding.measure: Problem-solving-related understanding, visual scanning technique, and conceptual understanding measures

finding.finding_summary: A few included studies reported improved task efficiency or performance speed with HMD-based VR, but the review concludes that these gains were inconsistent and often did not transfer to real-world performance. For example, one comparative study found the HMD group performed a task faster, while another found assembly or other task improvements inside the simulation without corresponding real-world transfer; the review therefore treats efficiency benefits as limited and context-dependent.
finding.measure: Task performance speed, efficiency, and simulator task completion measures

finding.finding_summary: The review does not provide evidence of broader institutional or policy-level effects; it explicitly notes that no included studies examined behavior or organizational change outcomes. Its discussion of classroom adoption focuses on barriers such as content availability, hardware management, and equity, but these are not measured as institutional impacts in the reviewed studies.
finding.measure: Organizational change, behavior, policy, or institutional outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach for classroom instruction. The authors frame three zero-shot coaching tasks for the model: (A) scoring classroom transcript segments using established observation rubrics, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (C) giving actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset of 4th- and 5th-grade elementary mathematics classrooms from 317 teachers across four U.S. school districts. For Task A, the authors compare ChatGPT’s predicted scores with human observer scores on selected CLASS and MQI items. For Tasks B and C, experienced math teachers evaluate the model’s generated feedback for relevance, faithfulness to the transcript, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Overall, the paper finds that ChatGPT has substantial room for improvement as a teacher coach. Score predictions correlate poorly with human ratings across all items, and added rubric descriptions or reasoning prompts do not materially help. For feedback generation, teachers often rate the outputs as not insightful or not relevant, though many suggestions are still actionable and faithful; a major limitation is redundancy, with 82% of suggestions describing what the teacher already does. The authors conclude that generative AI may complement, but cannot replace, expert coaching in its current form, and they emphasize hallucination risk, privacy concerns, and the need for human-in-the-loop safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning outcomes, but it directly evaluates ChatGPT on elementary mathematics classroom instructional quality using MQI rubric items. On the quantitative scoring task, correlations with human ratings were uniformly low across MQI dimensions (e.g., DA: EXPL 0.02, REMED 0.05, LANGIMP 0.00, SMQR 0.17; DA+ and RA were similarly low or worse), indicating weak alignment with expert judgment of math instruction quality. In qualitative feedback tasks, teachers often judged the outputs as not insightful or relevant, especially on MQI items, suggesting limited current usefulness for improving math instruction.
finding.measure: MQI observation scores (EXPL, REMED, LANGIMP, SMQR) and teacher ratings of generated highlights/missed opportunities and suggestions
finding.study_size: Task A: n=100 transcript segments; Task B: n=288 MQI-annotated items from 18 segments; Task C: n=36 suggestions

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates whether ChatGPT can reduce teacher coaching burden by automatically scoring classroom instruction and generating feedback. Results suggest some promise for scalability, but the model’s poor score calibration and frequent redundancy limit its practical efficiency gains: 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did, and qualitative ratings showed many responses were not insightful or relevant. The authors conclude that the tool could complement human coaching, but current output quality is insufficient for stand-alone use.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty; redundancy of suggestions
finding.study_size: Task B: n=504 annotated feedback examples total across CLASS and MQI; Task C: n=36 suggestions

paper_profiles.title: All Together Now: Teachers as Research Partners in the Design of Search Technology for the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that teachers should be treated as full research partners in the design of classroom search technologies, rather than being used only as informants, facilitators, or study subjects. The authors motivate this position from several years of collaboration on search and recommender systems intended for children in primary and secondary classrooms.

The paper is not an intervention study; it is a reflective, experience-based position piece grounded in the authors’ prior classroom research across Italy, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States. It describes how involving teachers from the beginning helps define research priorities, align designs with classroom practice, improve usability and adoption, and interpret results in ways that fit educational realities.

The main conclusion is that teachers add indispensable expertise about pedagogy, curriculum, classroom workflow, and children’s technology use, and that research on educational search tools benefits from sustained teacher partnership. The paper also notes that such collaboration can make classroom studies less intrusive and more authentic, but it does not present comparative outcome data on student learning, engagement, teacher morale, or efficiency.

paper_profiles.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Schools: Unveiling Factors Influencing Teachers’ Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference of Artificial Intelligence in Education 2023
paper_profiles.population: K-12 public school teachers (Grade 5 to Grade 12 context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses why AI-based adaptive learning platforms, despite evidence of benefits for student learning, are adopted slowly in schools. The authors argue that research and implementation efforts have often focused too narrowly on individual teacher acceptance or platform features, while overlooking broader school-level factors such as workload, support, governance, ownership, and ethical concerns.

To study this, the authors developed and validated a survey instrument for school-level adoption factors and administered it to 792 public school teachers in a country-level K-12 setting. They used exploratory factor analysis to identify seven dimensions of adoption-related perceptions: workload, ownership, perceived support, knowledge/confidence, classroom orchestration, product quality, and ethics, then correlated these factors with teachers’ real-world engagement with an adaptive learning platform using platform log data.

The main findings were that teachers’ engagement was positively associated with perceived professional development/support, belief in the platform’s success, satisfaction with the platform, helpful feedback, trust, content quality, and related factors. A predictive model using survey factors explained 24.4% of the variance in engagement (R2=0.244), suggesting these non-technical and human factors are meaningful predictors of adoption. The paper also reports that teachers did not perceive major workload increases on average, but classroom orchestration was more difficult and privacy/security concerns were present. Overall, the study concludes that successful AI adoption in schools depends not only on technical quality but also on teacher support, ownership, trust, and minimizing extra workload and ethical risks.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that operational factors mattered strongly for teachers’ engagement with the AI platform. Teachers generally did not report additional workload on average (mean workload factor = 3.09), but items related to no additional analytics work, switching tools, classroom behavior management, and balancing learning were among the factors linked to engagement; classroom orchestration was harder (mean = 2.74).
finding.measure: Teacher survey factors on workload and orchestration; correlations with platform engagement

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ engagement with the adaptive platform was positively associated with support-related and confidence-related perceptions, including helpful professional development, access to help, sufficient guidance, self-efficacy, trust, and belief in the platform’s success. These items showed statistically significant positive correlations with real-world engagement, with coefficients ranging up to r=0.246 for helpful CPD.
finding.measure: Teacher engagement with adaptive learning platform logs, correlated with survey items on self-efficacy, trust, support, and ownership

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines school-level adoption conditions rather than student outcomes. It identifies governance-adjacent and institutional factors such as leadership belief, community support, teacher ownership, ethical concerns, and whole-school support mechanisms as important predictors of engagement, and reports that a multivariate model using these factors explained 24.4% of the variance in teachers’ real-world engagement (R2=0.244).
finding.measure: Survey-derived school-level adoption factors and predictive model of teachers’ real-world engagement with the platform

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (mixed grade levels; elementary through high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how K-12 teachers can be engaged in co-designing AI curriculum that is integrated into core subjects rather than taught only as standalone computer science content. The authors motivate the work by noting that AI education is increasingly relevant, but many teachers lack scaffolding, confidence, and classroom-ready materials to incorporate it into existing instruction.

To study this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 educators from diverse grade levels and subject areas, including English language arts, science, history, ESL, STEM, library science, and computer science. Participants received short presentations on AI concepts and tools, completed pre-work exploring tools such as Teachable Machine and Machine Learning for Kids, and then worked in small groups with researcher support to design integrated lesson plans.

The main contribution is descriptive and design-oriented rather than evaluative: the paper identifies teacher-valued supports and four recurring design considerations—evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration—when creating AI curriculum. The workshop produced draft curricula for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities, showing three integration pathways: using data from subject activities, prompting reflection, and embedding ethics discussions. Participants reported higher familiarity with AI and confidence integrating it after the workshop, but the study does not test student learning outcomes or compare the approach against ordinary instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified practical scaffolds and classroom logistics as central to making AI curriculum usable, including clearer tool guidance, explicit evaluation frameworks, and supports for lesson structure. The workshop did not measure time savings or workload directly, but the qualitative findings suggest the co-design process helped surface implementation needs that could improve classroom usability.
finding.measure: Teacher interview/discussion themes about logistics, tools, evaluation, and implementability

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized learner engagement as a key design goal and proposed hooks such as real-world contexts, student-driven topics, gamification, and competition. The paper reports that participants also rated their confidence in integrating AI into their own curriculum at 5.6/7 after the workshop, and their familiarity with AI increased from 4.8/7 to 5.8/7, indicating improved educator readiness rather than direct student engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher discussion themes; pre/post self-ratings of AI familiarity and confidence integrating AI

finding.finding_summary: The co-design process repeatedly highlighted collaboration, reflection, and conceptual evaluation as important classroom supports. Teachers designed activities requiring peer work, reflective discussion, and explanation of reasoning, suggesting the integrated curricula were intended to foster collaboration and metacognitive thinking, though these skills were not directly assessed in students.
finding.measure: Teacher-designed curriculum features and discussion themes on collaboration/reflection

finding.finding_summary: Teachers successfully co-created draft integrated AI lesson plans for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The paper describes concrete curriculum artifacts such as a social studies lesson on data and government policy, an ESL pronunciation app, and a vocabulary lesson for literacy, demonstrating feasible integration of AI concepts into non-CS subjects.
finding.measure: Completed co-designed curriculum drafts and workshop artifacts

finding.finding_summary: One of the co-designed curricula targeted ESL and embedded AI into pronunciation practice through an AI-powered app. The paper presents this as a workable curriculum draft in which students record pronunciations to train a classifier, but it does not report student language-learning outcomes or compare against ordinary ESL instruction.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL pronunciation curriculum artifact

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities that integrated AI through vocabulary practice and image classification. This is presented as a viable lesson-plan draft rather than an evaluated intervention, so the paper provides design evidence but no measured literacy gains.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum artifact for vocabulary/image classification

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that integrated AI curriculum may broaden access to AI beyond computing classes and make it more accessible to non-CS and non-technical learners. The paper argues that teacher buy-in and co-design are important for adoption, but it does not evaluate policy or institutional change directly.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on accessibility, adoption, and relevance of integrated AI curriculum

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping high school teachers notice and interpret the quality of students’ collaborative argumentation during classroom discussions. The authors argue that this is an advanced teaching skill that many teachers struggle to develop, partly because classroom talk is hard to monitor in real time and difficult to review afterward without a record.

To support this work, the paper introduces Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP models to automatically code discussion transcripts for argument moves, specificity, and collaboration. DT then presents multiple visualizations and transcript-based analytics intended to help teachers identify strengths, weaknesses, and next instructional steps. The system was evaluated with 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools who used a desktop version of DT with manually coded transcripts and then participated in surveys and cognitive interviews.

The main findings are that teachers generally perceived DT as useful, easy to use, and helpful for learning about and planning for collaborative argumentation. However, this is a usability and feasibility study rather than a comparative efficacy trial: it does not compare DT to ordinary instruction or other supports on student or teacher outcome gains. The paper also reports moderate to substantial agreement between automated classifiers and human annotations, with weaker performance for some collaboration labels such as agree and challenge/probe.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was helpful for their teaching workflow and for analyzing student discussion, suggesting reduced effort in interpreting classroom talk. On a 13-item usability survey completed by 18 high school ELA teachers, all teachers agreed or strongly agreed with most items (9 of 13 items had a mean of 4.5), and the overall item "Overall, Discussion Tracker is helpful for my teaching of literature discussions" had a mean of 4.72.
finding.measure: Teacher usability survey ratings of helpfulness, ease of use, and support for planning/analysis

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed specifically to help teachers support collaborative argumentation, a core durable skill. Teachers rated the analytics as helpful for recognizing students’ strengths and weaknesses during discussion and for making changes to facilitation, with means such as 4.72 for strengths/weaknesses recognition and 4.28 for encouraging more facilitation changes.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of utility for understanding and supporting students’ collaborative argumentation

finding.finding_summary: The study reports teacher-perceived support for making discussion facilitation changes and more insight into student learning, but it does not directly measure student motivation, engagement, or self-regulation. Any relevance to social-emotional skills is indirect and based on teachers’ perceptions rather than outcome measures.
finding.measure: Indirect teacher perceptions related to student discussion engagement and facilitation

paper_profiles.title: Can AI support student engagement in classroom activities in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether conversational AI, specifically ChatGPT, can improve student engagement in in-class learning activities compared with peer discussion without AI. The motivation is the challenge of low engagement in large, often hybrid computer science classes, where instructors have limited ability to sustain interaction and students may be reluctant to speak up.

The authors conducted a within-subject study in an undergraduate computer science course at a U.S. public university. Across two 50-minute Friday class sessions, students completed similar reading-and-discussion activities under two conditions: one with ChatGPT prompting questions and giving feedback, and one with peer discussion only. The analysis included 101 paired participants for quantitative outcomes and 85 ChatGPT conversations plus 54 peer conversations for qualitative analysis.

Results showed that the ChatGPT condition produced significantly higher self-reported engagement, higher perceived usefulness for learning, and higher post-activity quiz scores than the peer-only condition. The paper also reports that ChatGPT interactions were more verbose, more feedback-rich, and had more follow-up discussion, while peer discussions were shorter and more likely to go off topic. The authors conclude that instructor-supervised conversational AI may support engagement and learning in large classes, but they caution that findings are limited to a computer science setting, an online/hybrid context, and a short two-session intervention.

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT during the in-class activity significantly increased students’ engagement compared with peer discussion without AI. On the student engagement as a factor scale, the AI condition scored higher (mean=2.89, SD=0.43) than the no-AI condition (mean=2.76, SD=0.45), with Wilcoxon z=-3.45, p<.001; subscales including interest, enjoyment, excitement, improved understanding, challenge, and feeling in control were also significantly higher.
finding.measure: Student engagement as a factor scale; student perspective of engagement in class scale (ASPECT)
finding.std_deviation: AI SD=0.43; no-AI SD=0.45 (student engagement as a factor scale); AI SD=1.08; no-AI SD=1.06 (ASPECT)

finding.finding_summary: The AI condition also improved engagement-related durable skills tied to the activity, especially interaction quality and perceived control. Students in the ChatGPT condition reported significantly higher engagement on ASPECT (mean=4.73, SD=1.08 vs. 4.33, SD=1.06; z=-2.47, p=.014), and conversation analysis showed more feedback comments and follow-up exchanges with AI than with peers, indicating deeper questioning and iterative dialogue.
finding.measure: ASPECT scale; qualitative conversation metrics (questions, feedback comments, follow-ups, off-topic turns)
finding.study_size: n=101 paired participants; qualitative analysis of 85 AI chats and 54 peer conversations
finding.std_deviation: AI SD=1.08; no-AI SD=1.06 for ASPECT

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that the ChatGPT-supported discussion improved immediate learning of the specific course content relative to peer discussion. Students rated the AI activity as more useful for learning (mean=3.24, SD=0.93) than the no-AI activity (mean=2.72, SD=0.69; z=-4.59, p<.001), and post-activity quiz scores were significantly higher in the AI condition (mean=4.11, SD=1.11) than in the peer condition (mean=3.72, SD=1.28; p=.015).
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of activity for learning; 5-item post-activity quiz on the reading/topic
finding.std_deviation: AI SD=0.93; no-AI SD=0.69 (usefulness); AI SD=1.11; no-AI SD=1.28 (quiz scores)

finding.finding_summary: Although not a broad science-content study, the intervention required students to read a research article and discuss it using AI prompts, then answer content questions. Performance on the topic quiz was significantly better in the ChatGPT condition (mean=4.11/5, SD=1.11) than in the peer discussion condition (mean=3.72/5, SD=1.28), suggesting improved reasoning/understanding about the technical material in the activity.
finding.measure: 5-item MCQ quiz on the article/topic

paper_profiles.title: Sticky Help, Bounded Effects: Session-by-Session Analytics of Teacher Interventions in K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2026 (International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers decide whom to help during technology-supported K-12 math classwork, and whether those help visits have effects that persist beyond the current session. The authors combine teacher interviews with log analysis from an intelligent tutoring system (MATHia), focusing on whether prior help history and in-the-moment engagement states such as idle or struggle predict teacher intervention, and whether help influences later engagement or learning.

The study includes nine middle-school math teachers in interviews and log data from 339 students across 14 classes in ten U.S. K-12 schools during the 2022–23 school year. The quantitative analysis uses mixed-effects logistic regression, cross-lagged panel models, and additive factor modeling over 1.4 million student-system interactions and 9,565 inferred classwork sessions. Teachers reported aiming for equitable coverage, engagement, and learning support, but the log analyses found that help was “sticky”: students helped once were more likely to be helped again (OR=1.32), and help recurred across sessions. Idle behavior predicted less subsequent help, and prior help did not predict later skill acquisition; help was positively related to immediate within-session learning but not to sustained gains in later sessions.

Overall, the paper concludes that teacher attention in ITS-supported classrooms is temporally concentrated and often revisits the same students, while measurable learning benefits appear largely session-bound. The authors argue that dashboards should better surface coverage gaps and under-visited students to support more equitable allocation of teacher attention. They also caution that the data are observational and limited by incomplete help logging, so the findings should be interpreted as directional associations rather than causal effects.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher help in session t−1 did not significantly predict the number of new knowledge components acquired in session t (b_K = 0.04, z = 0.64, p = .52). Within sessions, help and learning were positively correlated (r ≈ .13, p < .001), but the cross-session analysis found no sustained learning benefit from help beyond the current session.
finding.measure: New skill acquisition / first mastery of knowledge components estimated from AFM-predicted mastery probabilities; cross-lagged panel model of help and later KC acquisition
finding.study_size: n=339 students; 9,565 classwork sessions; AFM fit on 425,285 first attempts across 827 KCs

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that their interventions aimed to sustain student engagement and reduce idle/struggle states, but the quantitative results were mixed. Prior idle behavior strongly predicted teacher help in the descriptive model (OR = 2.74, 95% CI [1.83, 4.11]), yet in the cross-lagged model prior idle behavior predicted less subsequent teacher help (b1 = -0.10, z = -2.62, p = .009) and prior help did not significantly predict later idle (d1 = -0.05, p = .147).
finding.measure: Idle engagement state; cross-lagged panel model and mixed-effects logistic regression
finding.effect_size: OR=2.74 for idle predicting help; b1=-0.10; d1=-0.05
finding.confidence_interval: OR [1.83, 4.11] for the mixed-effects model; not_reported for cross-lagged paths

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test a productivity intervention per se, but it substantively analyzes how teacher attention is allocated in real time and how help is distributed across students. Help was highly concentrated: in the average session, about 50% of students received all the help, and prior help history increased the odds of another help visit (OR = 1.32, 95% CI [1.19, 1.46]). The authors frame this as a coverage/allocation problem for teacher orchestration and dashboard design rather than a direct efficiency gain.
finding.measure: Teacher help allocation and concentration across students; Lorenz curve / Gini coefficient; logistic regression of intervention likelihood

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-student relationship and teaching styles in primary education. A model of analysis
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Professional Capital and Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ perceptions of teacher-student relationships are associated with perceived teaching styles in primary education, and whether those perceptions vary by student characteristics. The authors frame teaching style along a directive-versus-participative continuum and teacher-student relationship along emotional-versus-educational dimensions, arguing that both are important for understanding classroom experience and student engagement.

Using census data from 21,126 sixth-grade students in the Canary Islands (Spain), the study constructs latent variables from a student questionnaire and estimates a structural equation model, followed by mean-comparison tests. The results show that participative teaching style is more strongly associated with both emotional and educational relationship perceptions than directive style, and that girls and students from lower parental education backgrounds generally perceive these constructs differently. The paper concludes that classroom perceptions are heterogeneous and shaped by gender and family cultural capital, suggesting that contextualized student feedback can help inform teaching practice and policy.

This is not an AI-instruction study; it provides contextual evidence on classroom relationships and teaching style rather than evaluating an artificial intelligence tool.

finding.finding_summary: In a census of 21,126 sixth-grade students, participative teaching style was more strongly associated with students’ perceived emotional relationship and educational relationship with teachers than directive style. The SEM fit was acceptable and all estimated coefficients were significant at 1%; the authors report that participative teaching correlated much more with both relationship types, with standardized coefficient comparisons supporting Hypotheses 1 and 2.
finding.measure: Student-perceived teacher-student relationship (EmotionalR, EducationalR) and student-perceived teaching style (DirectiveTS, ParticipativeTS) from questionnaire items

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that periodic diagnostic assessments can be used to construct latent indicators of teaching style and teacher-student relationship for educational monitoring and policy feedback. It does not test a policy intervention, but it suggests that the model could inform context-specific educational policy and teacher development by capturing student feedback at scale.
finding.measure: Feasibility/use of diagnostic assessment questionnaires and latent-variable model for educational monitoring and feedback

paper_profiles.title: Multimodal Engagement Analysis from Facial Videos in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper addresses the problem of automatically estimating student engagement from classroom video in real secondary-school lessons. The authors argue that most prior engagement work relied on computer-based learning settings or very small classroom samples, and they aim to build and evaluate a scalable computer-vision approach that can work with unconstrained classroom footage. Their focus is not on changing instruction, but on measuring visible engagement from teacher-centered classroom video.

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that student engagement can be predicted from classroom facial video better than chance, with the best person-independent models reaching AUROC = 0.620 in Grade 8 and AUROC = 0.719 in Grade 12 using attention-based features. Personalization with about 60 seconds of student-specific data improved AUROC by an average of +0.084, with gains up to +0.124, indicating that engagement detection can be meaningfully improved with limited individualized calibration.
finding.measure: Continuous observer-rated engagement discretized into low/medium/high classes; AUROC for engagement classification
finding.study_size: n=15 focal students (75 labeled samples total; 128 students recorded overall)

paper_profiles.title: Individual and Group-wise Classroom Seating Experience: Effects on Student Engagement in Different Courses
paper_profiles.venue: Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether where students sit in flexible high-school classrooms is associated with how engaged they feel and how physiologically synchronized they are with peers. The authors argue that prior seating studies relied heavily on self-report and coarse seating categories, so they instead combine precise floor-plan-based seating locations with wearable electrodermal activity (EDA) data and repeated engagement surveys.

The study was conducted over four weeks in a Year 10 high school setting with 23 students and 6 teachers across 10 courses. Students reported their class engagement after lessons, and some also wore Empatica E4 wristbands to capture EDA signals. Seating locations were clustered into three groups (left, right, back) to reflect the flexible, non-traditional classroom layouts used at the school.

The main findings are correlational rather than causal. Students sitting closer together tended to report more similar engagement (overall corr = -0.30, p < 0.05), and proximity was also associated with higher physiological synchrony in some analyses, especially using mixed or tonic EDA and in certain courses such as Language and Maths. However, the physiological synchrony result was not robust after Bonferroni correction in the pooled analysis, and the paper emphasizes heterogeneity across students and courses. The authors conclude that seating arrangement may matter for engagement, but effects vary by context and are not consistently significant across all physiological measures.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly examined student engagement in high school classes as a function of seating proximity and seating group patterns. Across 1,123 student-pair observations, students sitting closer together reported more similar engagement (corr = -0.30, p < 0.05), but the effect was heterogeneous: 18 of 23 students showed significant negative correlations, 2 showed marginal effects, and 3 showed no clear relationship. The engagement measure was a 5-item self-report scale adapted from ISEQ; sample size was 23 students across 10 courses, with 488 survey responses.
finding.measure: Self-reported class engagement (5-item adapted ISEQ; behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement components)
finding.study_size: n=23 students; 488 survey responses; 1,123 student-pair instances

finding.finding_summary: The paper also touches on engagement-related collaborative/social learning dynamics by examining whether seating proximity corresponds to similarity in engagement and physiological synchrony among peers. It found that students sitting near each other were more likely to have similar engagement and synchrony, but this was not uniform across contexts and did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction in the pooled physiological analysis. This suggests possible peer-related coordination effects, but evidence is limited and indirect for collaboration or other durable skills.
finding.measure: Physiological synchrony derived from EDA; pairwise similarity in engagement

paper_profiles.title: AI-Driven Interface Design for Intelligent Tutoring System Improves Student Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Symposium on Neural Gaze Detection (as cited in paper; proceedings listed as Woodstock ’18)
paper_profiles.population: K-12 students using an English test-preparation intelligent tutoring system (new incoming users; TOEIC-focused mobile self-study app)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether making an intelligent tutoring system’s diagnostic results more AI-rich, transparent, and human-like can increase student engagement. The authors argue that although ITSs can personalize instruction, their interfaces often underuse AI outputs in ways that motivate continued study. They therefore design two diagnostic-page interfaces for Santa, a mobile AI tutoring system, that differ in the amount and presentation of AI-generated feedback and explanations.

The intervention is tested in two controlled A/B experiments with new Santa users. In the first experiment, the authors compare a page design with and without a radar-chart component summarizing AI analysis of students’ performance; in the second, they compare page design A versus a more detailed and explainable page design B. The sample sizes are large (over 20,000 users overall across experiments), and the engagement outcomes are conversion rate, ARPU, total profit, and the average number of free questions consumed. Across both experiments, the AI-enhanced designs outperform the comparison conditions on all measured engagement metrics, with the radar chart associated with up to a 25.13% increase in total profit and design B producing higher engagement than design A. The paper concludes that more informative and explainable AI-driven interface design can improve student engagement in an ITS context.

finding.finding_summary: Controlled A/B tests found that AI-driven interface designs increased student engagement. With the radar chart added to page design A (n=1,391 vs n=1,486), conversion rate rose from 5.25% to 6.26%, ARPU from $5.92 to $6.94, total profit from $8,236.01 to $10,305.58, and the average number of free questions consumed from 14.77 to 16.51; the authors report up to a 25.13% increase in total profit. In the later A/B test comparing page design A (n=9,442) and page design B (n=9,722), design B similarly improved engagement across all four measures.
finding.measure: Conversion rate, Average Revenue Per User (ARPU), total profit, average number of free questions consumed
finding.study_size: n=2,877 in radar-chart test; n=19,164 in A vs B test

paper_profiles.title: SCB-Dataset: A Dataset for Detecting Student and Teacher Classroom Behavior
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th); Middle School; High School; Undergraduate; Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of publicly available, high-quality classroom behavior datasets in education, particularly datasets that include both student and teacher behaviors in real classroom environments. The authors argue that such data are necessary for applying computer vision and large vision-language models (LVLMs) to education research and classroom analysis.

To address this gap, the paper introduces SCB-Dataset, a public dataset built from classroom videos collected from open websites and then converted into object detection and image classification datasets. The dataset contains 19 classroom behavior classes spanning student and teacher actions, with separate formulations for object detection and classification. The authors benchmark the dataset using YOLO series detectors and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-instruct fine-tuned with LLaMA Factory, reporting strong detection/classification performance on many classes.

The study is not an intervention study in schools and does not test whether AI improves instruction, teacher morale, or student engagement relative to ordinary instruction. Its main contribution is infrastructure: a labeled dataset and baseline model results meant to support future AI applications in education. The paper also highlights practical challenges such as class imbalance, occlusion, dense classrooms, and similar behaviors that make classroom behavior recognition difficult.
