finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that automated classroom behavior detection can support classroom analysis and reduce manual effort, but it does not test teacher workload in a school implementation. The strongest evidence is benchmark performance on the dataset: YOLOv7 achieved mAP@0.5 of 94.0% on the teacher-behavior object-detection subset, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-instruct reached overall F1 of 83.8% on image classification, indicating the technical feasibility of automating this kind of analysis (n=13,330 object-detection images; n=21,019 classification images).
finding.measure: Object detection mAP and image-classification F1 for classroom behavior recognition tasks
finding.study_size: n=13,330 object-detection images; n=21,019 image-classification images

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SCB-Dataset fills a gap in publicly available educational datasets and can support future applications of AI in education. However, this is an infrastructure contribution rather than an evaluation of policy, institutional change, or downstream educational outcomes, so the finding is limited to dataset availability and benchmark utility.
finding.measure: Creation of a public classroom behavior dataset and benchmark evaluation
finding.study_size: n=13,330 object-detection images; n=21,019 image-classification images

paper_profiles.title: Assessment of Personalized Learning in Immersive and Intelligent Virtual Classroom on Student Engagement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether personalized learning in an immersive, intelligent virtual classroom can be assessed using eye-tracking and whether such an environment is associated with higher student engagement. The authors frame the work around AI-enabled personalization in virtual learning environments, arguing that adaptive content and intelligent feedback can better match learners’ pace, interests, and needs than traditional instruction.

Methodologically, the paper combines a literature review with a small case study using a VR classroom application built on Unity and deployed on a PICO VR 4 Pro headset with eye-tracking. Eight participants completed a questionnaire covering cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement, and the system also recorded gaze metrics such as gaze offset, fixation, and saccadic reaction time. The study’s main conclusion is that 3D eye-tracking paradigms can be used to assess engagement in virtual classrooms, and that personalized learning in VR was perceived as beneficial by most participants.

The empirical evidence is limited by the very small sample size and the absence of a comparison group or causal design. The paper reports generally positive engagement responses and suggests that saccadic reaction time may be a useful indicator of attention and cognitive processing, but it does not provide robust effect estimates or direct evidence that AI tools outperform ordinary instruction. Its contribution is primarily methodological and exploratory rather than confirmatory.

finding.finding_summary: In a case study with eight participants (n=8), personalized learning in the VR classroom was reported to support higher engagement across cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions. Table 1 shows generally high mean engagement scores for most participants (e.g., Participant 2 scored 5.00 across all three dimensions), but the paper does not report inferential statistics, effect sizes, or a comparison against ordinary instruction.
finding.measure: 11-item Likert questionnaire assessing cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement; eye-tracking indicators of engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that eye-tracking metrics, especially saccadic reaction time, can help assess students’ attentional processing and interaction with learning materials in a VR classroom. However, this is presented as an exploratory measurement finding rather than a tested improvement in durable skills such as metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Eye-tracking metrics including gaze patterns, fixation duration, and saccadic reaction time

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Perspectives and Experiences After Deployment of AI Literacy Curriculum in Middle-School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school teachers experienced implementing modules from MIT’s Responsible AI for Computational Action (RAICA) curriculum. The study addresses a practical question in K-12 AI education: how teachers understand, adapt, and feel about teaching AI literacy when they receive ongoing professional development and curriculum materials for a novel, project-based unit.

The intervention consisted of three RAICA modules taught by seven teachers with interdisciplinary backgrounds in art, business, and computer science. Using eight semi-structured remote interviews plus thematic analysis, the authors explored teachers’ instructional strategies, changing beliefs about AI, and recommendations for improving the curriculum and support materials. The study found that teachers generally increased their understanding of AI concepts and ethical implications, used flexible and interdisciplinary teaching strategies to engage students, and appreciated peer support and the curriculum’s open-ended design.

At the same time, teachers reported substantial implementation challenges, including technical difficulties with AI tools, limited time for preparation, need for clearer guidance, and uneven student readiness. They requested stronger technical support, more explicit instructions, additional examples, and accommodations for diverse learners. Overall, the paper concludes that AI literacy curricula can be engaging and meaningful in middle school, but successful deployment depends heavily on professional development, flexibility, and practical classroom supports.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that implementing the RAICA modules increased classroom engagement, playful learning, and student interest in AI. They described students as more engaged when lessons used tangible examples, interdisciplinary connections, and creative project formats, and teachers themselves became more enthusiastic and confident about teaching AI-related content.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of student engagement, interest, and classroom participation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described growth in students' critical thinking, empathy, and collaboration while working through AI ethics, design thinking, and peer feedback activities. The curriculum was said to help students reason about bias, stakeholders, and unintended impacts, although these claims are qualitative and not tied to standardized measures.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of critical thinking, empathy, collaboration, and design thinking

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the RAICA curriculum and associated PD improved their understanding of AI and helped them adapt materials for the classroom, but also increased preparation burden because the content was novel, open-ended, and technically demanding. They requested more time, clearer guides, walkthroughs, and technical support, indicating both productivity gains and workflow strain.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of preparation time, need for support, and curriculum usability

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued for integrating AI literacy into the school curriculum and for providing broader teacher professional development and support structures. The paper suggests the curriculum may strengthen institutional capacity for AI education, but these are recommendations and perceptions rather than measured policy outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of curriculum integration and professional development needs

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing peer assessment with artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence can enhance peer assessment in higher education. It proposes a theoretical framework with six areas in which AI may assist peer assessment: assigning peer assessors, enhancing individual reviews, deriving peer grades/feedback, analyzing student feedback, facilitating instructor oversight, and supporting broader peer assessment systems.

To ground the framework, the authors conduct a rapid scoping review of 79 AI-related peer assessment papers and also present a case study of the RiPPLE system. The review indicates that most studies reported AI improvements to peer assessment processes, especially in grading/feedback, feedback analysis, and related automation tasks, but that evidence is uneven across subtopics and many areas remain under-studied. The RiPPLE case study illustrates AI-supported learner sourcing, peer review, personalized practice, and instructor monitoring, showing how AI can scale peer assessment while preserving human oversight.

The paper is primarily a synthesis and conceptual review rather than a single empirical evaluation. It highlights both benefits and risks, including potential gains in feedback quality, reliability, and efficiency, but also concerns about strategic reporting, rogue reviews, inconsistent reliability, and the need for instructor intervention. Because the work focuses on higher education peer assessment rather than K-12 classrooms, it is only indirectly relevant to teacher morale or classroom engagement in school settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI was repeatedly reported to reduce instructor workload and make peer assessment more scalable by automating grading, feedback analysis, reviewer assignment, and spot-checking. The paper also reports that RiPPLE supports instructors by directing attention to resources that need expert review, and that one of the main benefits of peer assessment systems is workload reduction for teachers.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, automation of grading/feedback/oversight processes

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies reported improved student attitudes, motivation, or emotional experience when AI-supported peer assessment was used, but other studies found negative or more complex effects. For example, one study reported that when students knew peer assessment responses were considered by the system, they had more positive attitudes, while another found that more negative feedback or reinforcement without guidance worsened emotional experience and self-learning behavior.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, motivation, emotional exhaustion, self-learning behavior, appreciation of teamwork aspects

finding.finding_summary: The paper frequently frames AI-supported peer assessment as improving durable skills such as evaluative judgment, writing quality, collaboration, and feedback-giving. For example, several reviewed studies found better review quality, improved writing quality, stronger teamwork understanding, or more effective collaboration when AI or AI-assisted peer assessment tools were used.
finding.measure: Writing quality, review quality, teamwork effectiveness, evaluative judgment, collaboration behaviors

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the review concerns peer assessment in writing and text-based feedback, and multiple studies reported improvements in writing quality or peer feedback quality with AI support. For example, SWoRD was reported as effective in improving writing quality, and several text-analysis tools were found to generate feedback or classifications comparable to teacher analysis.
finding.measure: Writing quality, elaborated feedback quality, text-based peer comments

finding.finding_summary: The review covers peer assessment across programming, design, dance, general coursework, and other higher-education tasks rather than a single academic domain. Many included studies found that AI-supported peer assessment improved attainment, aligned more closely with human/teacher assessments, or produced comparable learning outcomes across these varied subjects.
finding.measure: Attainment, scores, task performance across programming/design/dance/general coursework

paper_profiles.title: A Feasibility and Implementation Integrity Study of the Community Builder (CoBi): An AI-based Collaboration Support System in K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Community Builder (CoBi), a classroom-wide AI system designed to support students’ collaboration skill development by detecting and visualizing instances of uplifting discourse during small-group work. The authors frame CoBi as a reflection-support tool rather than an assessment system, emphasizing privacy-preserving, class-level feedback and teacher-guided reflection routines before, during, and after collaborative activities.

The study reports three design-based research investigations in middle school STEM classrooms in the western United States: an interview study with three teachers and 12 students, a technical feasibility/initial implementation study with 24 fully consented students across three classrooms, and an implementation integrity study with 37 fully consented students across three classrooms. Across these studies, students and teachers generally viewed the idea positively and saw potential for supporting collaboration and classroom reflection, with a strong preference for qualitative visualizations such as a growing tree over more quantitative displays like a radar chart.

The paper’s main conclusions are that CoBi is technically feasible in real classrooms and can be integrated into middle school instruction, but its effective use requires substantial teacher professional learning and careful orchestration. The authors also identify implementation risks and heterogeneity: teachers sometimes interpreted CoBi as a monitoring or grading tool, students raised privacy concerns, real-time feedback could distract or invite gaming of the system, and the revisiting/reflection phase was often short or repurposed in ways that only partly aligned with the system’s design goals. The paper is explicitly not an efficacy study and does not claim learning gains; instead, it focuses on buy-in, feasibility, and implementation integrity.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines collaboration skill support and reflection around collaboration, but it is not an efficacy trial and reports no outcome gains. Students and teachers generally valued the idea of using CoBi to improve collaboration, yet the paper reports significant implementation variability, privacy concerns, and risks of gaming or misinterpretation; for example, in Study 2 at least six students intentionally tried to manipulate the speech-processing pipeline by repeating phrases like “please and thank you” to see whether they could influence the visualization. No effect size or pre/post learning outcome was reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher attitudes, classroom engagement with collaboration routines, and observed collaborative behaviors during CoBi-supported activities
finding.study_size: n=15 interview participants; n=24 fully consented students in Study 2; n=37 fully consented students in Study 3

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on students’ engagement, buy-in, privacy comfort, and classroom experience rather than direct affective outcomes. In interviews, students and teachers reacted positively to the idea of an AI system that could provide positive reinforcement, but some students worried about surveillance and being a “snitch,” and teachers worried real-time feedback could disrupt teaching and put them on the spot. No standardized social-emotional measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview themes about buy-in, privacy, perceived surveillance, and classroom experience; observed reactions during classroom use
finding.study_size: n=15 interview participants; n=61 students across six classrooms across Studies 2 and 3 (24 and 37 fully consented, respectively)

finding.finding_summary: Operationally, CoBi was technically feasible and the browser interfaces loaded properly, with visualizations updating every 10 seconds as intended, but the study also identified workflow problems. Time constraints often cut the revisiting phase short, the time slider caused confusion between teacher and student views, and teachers needed professional learning and researcher support to integrate the system smoothly.
finding.measure: Technical feasibility observations, implementation integrity notes, and classroom workflow observations
finding.study_size: n=24 fully consented students in Study 2; n=37 fully consented students in Study 3

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence Improving Student Learning Achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether students’ use of artificial intelligence tools is associated with better learning achievement in a university civics education program. The authors frame AI as a way to address the challenge of abstract or complex course material and argue that tools such as ChatGPT, Bard/Gemini, and Perplexity may provide personalized support, faster feedback, and greater motivation.

The study uses a quantitative survey design with random sampling and multiple linear regression. The sample consisted of 61 active students in the Pancasila and Citizenship Education program at STKIP Pasundan Cimahi, Indonesia. Students reported their AI usage and completed questionnaire items on learning achievement; the analysis also included descriptive statistics, normality and homogeneity checks, t-tests, and ANOVA. ChatGPT was the most commonly used tool (62.3%).

The paper reports a positive and statistically significant association between AI use and learning achievement (B=0.842, t=9.233, p<.001; F=85.245, p<.001). The authors conclude that AI explains 59.1% of the variance in learning outcomes, while 40.9% is due to other factors not included in the model. The paper also claims AI improves motivation, material absorption, and innovation in learning, but it does not compare AI against a non-AI classroom condition experimentally, so the evidence is correlational rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: AI use was positively associated with student learning achievement in the Pancasila and Citizenship Education course. In the regression model with n=61, artificial intelligence use significantly predicted achievement (B=0.842, t=9.233, p<.001), and the overall model was significant (F=85.245, p<.001). The authors report that AI explained 59.1% of the variance in learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Learning achievement in Pancasila and Citizenship Education, measured via questionnaire/academic assessment scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI enhanced student motivation, which is treated as part of the learning process and a contributor to achievement. However, this was not reported as a separate analyzed outcome with its own inferential test or effect size, so the evidence is descriptive and secondary to the main achievement analysis.
finding.measure: Student motivation (self-reported perception in questionnaire)

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim AI improved material absorption and innovation in learning, and they also mention improved analytical and critical thinking skills as intended outcomes. These claims are presented as general conclusions rather than as separately modeled outcomes, so no independent effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived material absorption, innovation in learning, analytical/critical thinking (self-reported or discussed as intended outcomes)

paper_profiles.title: Language Learning Through Games: A Computational Linguistics Perspective
paper_profiles.venue: Euro-Global Journal of Linguistics and Language Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines whether NLP-enhanced digital games can improve second-language learning outcomes compared with traditional instruction. The paper is framed as an interdisciplinary exploration of game-based learning, computational linguistics, and AI-driven language pedagogy, with a focus on engagement, motivation, and language practice in multilingual ESL contexts.

The intervention is LinguaQuest, a story-driven ESL learning game that uses speech recognition, dialogue management, adaptive feedback, and vocabulary/grammar mini-games. The paper describes the game architecture in detail and then presents a simulated quasi-experimental evaluation with N=40 adult international university students split into a game-based group and a traditional instruction group over four weeks. The traditional group completed parallel content through textbook exercises, worksheets, and instructor-led activities.

The reported results favor the game condition on vocabulary retention, speaking proficiency, and engagement/motivation, while grammar gains were roughly equivalent across groups. The game group also showed higher retention on a delayed vocabulary test and lower reported anxiety. Because the study is explicitly simulated rather than a real empirical trial, the findings should be treated cautiously; nevertheless, the paper argues that NLP-enabled games can complement conventional instruction and may be especially valuable for communicative practice and learner engagement.

finding.finding_summary: The simulated game-based group outperformed the traditional instruction group on speaking outcomes. Oral test ratings increased from about 6 to 8 in the game group versus about 6 to 7.2 in the control group; objective speaking rate rose from roughly 90 to 110 words per minute, and errors decreased from 8 to 4 per 100 words, compared with a smaller change in the traditional group.
finding.measure: Oral speaking test ratings, speaking rate (words per minute), grammatical error count per 100 words

finding.finding_summary: Engagement, motivation, and anxiety outcomes favored the game condition. On a 5-point survey, the game group rated enjoyment at 4.6 vs 3.4 in the control group, motivation at 4.4 vs 3.5, and speaking anxiety lower (2.0 vs 3.0), indicating higher engagement and lower nervousness during practice.
finding.measure: Engagement/motivation/anxiety survey items; in-game playtime and homework time logs

finding.finding_summary: Vocabulary learning and retention were higher in the game condition than in traditional instruction. Immediate post-test performance was about 85% correct for the game group versus 75% for the control group, and the delayed retention test 4 weeks later was about 80% versus 70%, suggesting better longer-term vocabulary retention in the game group.
finding.measure: 50-item vocabulary test, immediate post-test and delayed retention test

finding.finding_summary: Grammar gains were similar across the two conditions. Both groups improved by about 15 percentage points on the grammar post-test (approximately 60 to 75 out of 100), and the paper reports no significant difference between game-based and traditional instruction on this measure.
finding.measure: Grammar accuracy test (multiple-choice and sentence correction items)

paper_profiles.title: Beyond the lesson plan: Reflective practice as a catalyst for teacher professional growth
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can function as a reflective partner in teacher professional development. The authors argue that AI is increasingly positioned not as a replacement for teachers but as a tool that can reduce routine work, provide feedback, and support reflective pedagogy, while also noting that empirical evidence for AI-supported reflective practice remains limited, especially for in-service teachers in primary and secondary education.

Using a systematic literature review (SLR) approach, the authors searched SpringerLink and screened 9,083 records down to 26 included articles. The review synthesizes studies on reflective practice, teacher learning, and AI-enabled supports, then organizes the findings into five components: reflective awareness, critical analysis of teaching practice, reflection-based decision making, pedagogical innovation and experimentation, and collaborative/continuous professional learning. Across these themes, AI is portrayed as helping teachers notice strengths and gaps, compare instructional approaches, personalize practice, reduce workload, and support professional learning communities.

The paper is primarily conceptual and synthesis-oriented rather than an evaluation of a single intervention. Its main conclusion is that AI may strengthen teacher professional growth by supporting data-driven reflection and evidence-based pedagogy, but it also explicitly acknowledges a key limitation: the proposed taxonomy has not been directly validated in classroom practice. The review also emphasizes ethical concerns, implementation conditions, and the need for future empirical testing of the AI-reflective practice framework in real educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI can reduce teachers’ digital workload and administrative burden, freeing time for planning and reflective decision-making. Across the included literature, AI-supported tools (e.g., learning analytics, adaptive systems, ChatGPT) are described as speeding up personalization and providing data-driven feedback, but the paper does not report a single pooled effect size or direct experimental estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, digital burden, planning time, and perceived efficiency in reflective/administrative tasks
finding.study_size: n=26 included articles (systematic review); primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI can support teacher professional development, collaborative learning communities, and evidence-based pedagogy within supportive policy ecosystems. It also emphasizes governance issues such as ethics, AI literacy, curriculum alignment, and professional standards, but these are synthesized claims from prior studies rather than direct causal effects measured in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher professional development, collaborative professional learning communities, ethics/policy alignment, and institutional support for AI use
finding.study_size: n=26 included articles (systematic review); primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports that AI supports teacher noticing, critical analysis, reflection-based decision making, and pedagogical innovation—capacities closely aligned with metacognition and reflective judgment. The paper does not provide a quantitative estimate, but repeatedly characterizes AI as improving teachers’ ability to compare approaches, interpret feedback, and make evidence-informed decisions.
finding.measure: Teacher reflective awareness, critical analysis, decision-making, and metacognitive reflection
finding.study_size: n=26 included articles (systematic review); primary-study sample sizes not reported

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Computer-Assisted Learning and AI-guided Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the evidence on computer-assisted learning (CAL) and AI-guided tutoring in education, with a focus on whether these technologies can improve student learning and reduce educational inequalities. The authors synthesize prior causal studies and then add new evidence from Italy on generative AI adoption using Google Trends data, framing the discussion around both effectiveness and the structural conditions needed for successful implementation.

The paper first summarizes a set of randomized evaluations of CAL programs in K-12 and related settings, emphasizing that learning gains are strongest in mathematics and depend heavily on implementation quality, teacher support, and curriculum alignment. It then reviews newer studies of generative AI tutors and hybrid AI-human tutoring models, including classroom-based experiments in Turkey, Ghana, the United States, and Nigeria. Across these studies, the strongest positive effects come from well-designed tools that scaffold student reasoning rather than giving direct answers, and from models that combine AI with human instructional support.

The paper’s own empirical contribution uses weekly region-level Google Trends data from Italy to examine ChatGPT adoption in education and employment searches across regions. It finds that early adoption was concentrated in higher-income regions but diffused over time as digital infrastructure improved, suggesting partial convergence while still revealing persistent digital divides. Overall, the paper concludes that AI in education can improve learning, especially in disadvantaged contexts, but only when paired with strong pedagogical design, teacher training, and institutional support; otherwise it may reinforce existing inequities.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes multiple randomized evaluations showing that CAL and AI-guided tutoring generally improve mathematics outcomes, often by meaningful margins. Reported effects include 0.21-0.24 SD gains in math for CAL with supervision in El Salvador (n≈6,400), 0.56 SD short-term gains in Brazil (n≈870), 0.12-0.22 SD gains in U.S. district RCTs (n=224 teachers, 10,979 students), 0.23 SD math gains in a hybrid tutoring model (n=3,906 students), and 0.36 SD gains from an AI conversational tutor in Ghana (n=477 with complete data).
finding.measure: Math achievement / standardized math test scores / algebra and arithmetic test scores / STAAR math / math failure rates

finding.finding_summary: The review reports some positive evidence for language-related outcomes, but the evidence is weaker and less consistent than for mathematics. The paper cites a review average effect of about 0.15 SD for language arts/reading/spelling interventions and notes a Nigerian generative AI tutoring study with a 0.23 SD gain in English (n=414 complete data), suggesting potential benefits when the intervention is well supervised and contextually grounded.
finding.measure: Language arts / reading comprehension / spelling / English achievement
finding.study_size: multiple studies; review-level and one RCT (n=414 complete data)
finding.effect_size: 0.15 SD review average; 0.23 SD in English in Nigeria

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes evidence that some AI-enabled tutoring models improve engagement alongside achievement. In the quasi-experimental hybrid tutoring studies in U.S. urban schools, students receiving AI-informed human tutoring showed significant gains in both achievement and engagement, with larger benefits for lower-performing students; however, the exact engagement effect size is not reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement
finding.study_size: approximately 500 students in three urban schools

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that pedagogical design shapes whether AI supports or undermines durable skills such as reasoning, metacognition, and autonomous learning. In the Turkish RCT, GPT-Tutor improved practice and avoided post-test harm, while GPT-Base improved practice but reduced subsequent unaided performance (−0.054 points, a 17% drop), with especially negative effects among lower-performing students; the paper interprets this as cognitive offloading and reduced autonomous learning.
finding.measure: Unaided post-test performance; autonomous learning / cognitive offloading / metacognitive strategy use

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that AI and CAL can improve instructional efficiency and reduce staffing or cost burdens, especially in hybrid tutoring models. Examples include a 30% reduction in cost per student and 50% fewer tutors needed in the 4-to-1 tutoring model (n=3,906 students), about $20 per tutor per year for Tutor CoPilot, and $48 per student for the Rori conversational tutor, suggesting substantial operational advantages when AI augments human tutoring.
finding.measure: Cost per student, tutor staffing requirements, teacher/tutor support efficiency
finding.study_size: multiple studies; including 3,906 students and 900 tutors/1,800 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s Italy analysis shows that AI adoption in education is shaped by regional inequality and digital infrastructure. Using weekly region-level Google Trends data, it finds that early ChatGPT adoption was concentrated in higher-income regions but gradually diffused as infrastructure improved, indicating partial convergence alongside persistent divides. The broader review argues that without policy attention to training, infrastructure, and implementation, AI can widen existing inequalities even when it improves learning in pilot studies.
finding.measure: Regional ChatGPT search intensity / adoption proxy; digital divide patterns
finding.study_size: all Italian regions, weekly region-level data

paper_profiles.title: Revealing Networks: Understanding Effective Teacher Practices in AI-Supported Classrooms using Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how teacher practices in AI-supported mathematics classrooms relate to student learning differences, using multimodal classroom data and quantitative ethnography. The authors ask whether adding out-of-tutor teacher data improves inference of student learning rates, how teacher-student behavioral connections differ for students with low versus high learning rates, and whether those patterns change before versus after teacher visits.

The study combines log data from an AI tutor for linear equation solving with classroom observation notes and spatial teacher-position data from a single 7th-grade math classroom in a U.S. public school. The analytic approach uses Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis (T/ONA) to model temporal co-occurrence among in-tutor actions (e.g., hints, correct attempts) and out-of-tutor teacher behaviors (e.g., screen alignment, talking). The authors report that models including teacher practices fit better than tutor-log-only models, and that low- and high-learning-rate students show different behavioral networks: low-learning-rate students were more likely to request hints after teacher monitoring/talking, whereas high-learning-rate students were more likely to produce correct attempts after those same teacher behaviors.

The paper also examines teacher visits and finds that, for low-learning-rate students, post-visit behavior shifts toward more consecutive correct attempts in the tutor, while high-learning-rate students show comparatively little change. Qualitative replay of observation notes suggests a possible explanation: low-learning-rate students often received more procedural help and were associated with hint misuse or disengagement, while teacher visits sometimes provided more conceptual, self-explanation-oriented support that aligned with better in-tutor performance. Overall, the paper is best understood as a single-site observational case study that offers methodological evidence and hypothesis-generating findings about effective teacher support in AI-supported classrooms, not as a causal test of an AI intervention.

finding.finding_summary: In a 7th-grade linear equation-solving classroom (n=85 students), adding teacher practice data to tutor-log models improved learning-rate inference (AIC 150.60 vs 158.30; t=12.76, 95% CI [7.06, 9.63], p<.001), indicating teacher behaviors were meaningfully associated with in-tutor math performance. Students with low learning rates showed more hint requests after teacher monitoring/talking, whereas students with high learning rates showed more correct attempts after those same teacher behaviors; after teacher visits, low-learning-rate students increased consecutive correct attempts.
finding.measure: Linear equation-solving tutor performance, first-correct-attempt and correct-attempt patterns, learning-rate inference from iAFM/T/ONA models
finding.confidence_interval: [7.06, 9.63] for AIC difference; other CIs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The study indirectly examined student engagement/disengagement through detector codes and teacher interactions in the tutor classroom. Low-learning-rate students were more associated with hint abuse, idling, and teacher visits prompted by disengagement, while teacher support after visits was linked to more productive in-tutor behavior; however, the paper does not report a direct causal effect of AI or teacher support on engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Detector codes for idling, struggle, tutor misuse; observation notes on disengagement/hint abuse and teacher visits
finding.effect_size: IRR=1.71 for prompt frequency per observation note in low vs high learning-rate group (from qualitative count model); other effect sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative component suggests differences in the type of teacher support mattered: high-learning-rate students more often received conceptual prompts and self-explanation questions, while low-learning-rate students more often received procedural guidance. The paper frames these patterns as relating to students' ability to reflect and self-explain, but it does not directly measure metacognition or critical thinking with a validated instrument.
finding.measure: Observation notes on teacher talk during screen alignment and visits; qualitative coding of conceptual vs procedural support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that multimodal teacher-data features improve the efficiency of inferring which students are learning quickly or slowly in the AI tutor, which could support more targeted classroom orchestration. The main quantified result was improved model fit when adding teacher practice codes (AIC 150.60 vs 158.30), but the study does not measure teacher workload directly or report time-savings in classroom management.
finding.measure: Model fit / AIC for learning-rate inference using tutor-only versus multimodal T/ONA features

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (serving elementary through high school classrooms)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of making AI education accessible in K-12 settings, especially outside of computer science classes. The authors ask how K-12 teachers’ values and classroom considerations should shape AI curriculum design, and how AI can be integrated into core subjects such as social studies, ESL, and literacy.

To study this, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse subjects and grade levels. Participants received introductory presentations on AI and AI tools, completed pre-work, and then worked in small groups with researchers to create draft integrated lesson plans. The resulting curricula embedded AI concepts into subject lessons through three main integration points: data, reflection, and ethics.

The study is primarily qualitative and descriptive, focusing on teacher perspectives, design processes, and the feasibility of integrated AI curricula. The main conclusions are that teachers strongly valued supports for evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that they needed scaffolding to teach AI ethics and data-related concepts confidently. The workshop increased participants’ reported familiarity with AI and confidence in integrating AI into their curriculum, but the paper does not provide a controlled comparison or causal evidence of student outcomes. Its main contribution is a set of design insights and example lesson drafts for broader AI-in-education curriculum development.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the workshop and co-design process increased their comfort and confidence with AI integration, and participants valued supports for learner engagement. Reported confidence about integrating AI into their own curriculum averaged 5.6/7 after the workshop, and participants described the workshop as expanding their sense of AI teaching possibilities.
finding.measure: Teacher self-reported familiarity with AI; teacher self-reported confidence about integrating AI into their curriculum; workshop feedback on engagement-related supports

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies collaboration, reflection, and evaluation as design priorities in integrated AI curricula. Teachers repeatedly emphasized group work, student reflection, and discussion as important supports; the co-designed curricula were explicitly built to foster collaboration and reflective thinking around AI, data, and ethics.
finding.measure: Teacher-designated curriculum features and workshop discussion themes related to collaboration and reflection

finding.finding_summary: One of the co-designed curricula targeted ESL instruction through an AI-powered pronunciation application. The paper describes this as an implementable curriculum draft, but it does not test learner outcomes, so evidence is limited to design-level support rather than measured gains in speaking or listening.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL curriculum focused on pronunciation practice and AI classification
finding.study_size: n=15 teachers in co-design; student outcomes not tested

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities that embedded AI in vocabulary learning and image classification. This is evidence of curriculum design feasibility rather than an evaluated literacy effect; the paper does not report student reading or writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum for vocabulary learning and image classification
finding.study_size: n=15 teachers in co-design; student outcomes not tested

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on integrated AI curriculum development in non-computing subjects, including social studies, ESL, literacy, and physics exemplars. Teachers successfully produced first-draft curricula that connected AI to core content via data, reflection, and ethics, but the work does not evaluate student academic achievement in these subjects.
finding.measure: Co-designed integrated curricula across social studies, ESL, literacy, and physics exemplars

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified logistics and tool selection as important classroom implementation concerns, and the workshop provided resources, scaffolding, and researcher support intended to make AI curriculum easier to implement. The paper suggests these supports may reduce friction, but it does not measure teacher workload or implementation time directly.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported logistics considerations and implementation support needs

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge teachers face in exploratory, open-ended learning environments: students’ thinking is often hidden in digital work products, making it difficult to interpret understanding, misconceptions, and next instructional steps in real time. The authors propose LearnLens, a teacher-facing dashboard that combines conventional visual analytics (student response tables, filtering, word clouds, bar charts) with a generative AI component that summarizes class understanding and identifies common misconceptions.

LearnLens was implemented as a high-fidelity prototype within a 15-lesson middle school Earth science curriculum focused on runoff, absorption, and related scientific concepts. The study involved two 6th-grade science teachers from an urban public school, and the evaluation consisted of semi-structured interviews as the researchers walked them through the dashboard. Teachers generally valued the dashboard’s modular visualizations and especially the AI-generated summaries for making student thinking visible and supporting instructional adjustment, but they were cautious about prescriptive recommendations that went beyond the data.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated, data-grounded summaries can support teacher sense-making in open-ended classrooms and may reduce the effort needed to interpret student responses. However, the evidence is limited to a small qualitative usability/interview study, so the paper provides preliminary design-oriented support rather than causal evidence that the tool improves teacher morale, classroom engagement, or student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the dashboard’s visualizations and AI-generated summaries made it easier to review open-ended student responses and identify misconceptions, reducing the need to manually interpret raw data. In the single 1-hour interview analyzed, both 6th-grade teachers said existing tools mainly organize responses without giving feedback, while LearnLens provided timely, actionable summaries grounded in student data.
finding.measure: Semi-structured teacher interview feedback on dashboard usability, sense-making, and perceived support for instructional decision-making

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LearnLens could support broader adoption of open-ended curricula by making student thinking more visible and reducing the instructional burden on teachers. This claim is based on teacher interview reactions and author interpretation rather than measured institutional outcomes, so the evidence is preliminary and indirect.
finding.measure: Teacher interview statements about potential curriculum adoption and instructional support

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging learning analytics to enhance immersive teacher simulations: Challenges and opportunities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how learning analytics can be used to strengthen immersive teacher simulations, especially generative AI-enhanced virtual classroom environments. The central problem is not whether AI improves K-12 student outcomes, but how multimodal analytics can make preservice teachers’ pedagogical reasoning, discourse patterns, behavioral sequences, and visual attention visible so that simulation-based teacher education can support reflection and improvement.

The chapter uses TeacherGen@i, a web-based VR simulation with AI-driven student agents, as a case study. It describes a cohort of 33 preservice teachers at a university in South Korea who completed 33 recorded simulation sessions in a Digital Education course. The authors analyze verbal interaction data with a BERT-based Bloom’s taxonomy classifier, temporal interaction patterns with lag sequential analysis, and gaze data with heatmaps and attention dispersion measures. The paper is primarily descriptive and design-oriented: it presents multimodal analytics methods, a prototype dashboard, and example findings showing that preservice teachers mostly used lower-order remembering/understanding discourse, while sequential patterns and gaze visualizations revealed structured scaffolding, student-driven reasoning chains, and selective attention.

Main conclusions are that AI-enhanced immersive simulations can generate rich data for formative reflection, but the chapter does not provide causal evidence that the tool improves teacher morale, classroom engagement, or K-12 student learning relative to ordinary instruction or other supports. Its contribution is methodological and conceptual, arguing that analytics dashboards may help teachers see and revise their practice, and that future work should validate these indicators and ensure ethical, equitable deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter analyzes preservice teachers’ spoken discourse in a simulated classroom, classifying 1,269 interaction turns across 33 sessions with BERT and Bloom’s taxonomy. It reports that the dominant discourse was remembering and understanding, but it does not test whether the AI simulation improved language fluency outcomes or compare them against ordinary instruction.
finding.measure: Preservice teachers’ verbal interaction turns coded by cognitive level/Bloom’s taxonomy
finding.study_size: n=33 preservice teachers; 33 sessions; 1,269 interaction turns

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports descriptive evidence that the AI-enhanced simulation surfaced structured pedagogical reasoning, scaffolding chains, and sequential interaction patterns that reflect instructional thinking. However, the evidence is not a causal test of improvement; it shows how multimodal analytics made these skills visible in 33 simulation sessions rather than demonstrating an estimated effect size.
finding.measure: Discourse-coded pedagogical reasoning, sequential interaction patterns, and gaze-based attention indicators

finding.finding_summary: The chapter states that automated analytics and dashboards can reduce instructor workload and support scalable feedback in teacher simulations, citing prior work and illustrating a prototype dashboard. This paper itself does not quantify the workload reduction, but it argues that AI-augmented logging, transcription, and scoring can make teacher training more efficient.
finding.measure: Instructor workload / automation of logging, transcription, scoring, and dashboard feedback

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach for K-12 instruction. The authors focus on three teacher-coaching tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments using established observation rubrics, identifying instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning.

The study uses transcripts from the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) dataset, consisting of 1,660 recorded 4th- and 5th-grade elementary mathematics observations from 317 teachers across four school districts. The authors evaluate zero-shot GPT-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT) outputs against expert human scores and human teacher judgments, using CLASS and MQI observation items and qualitative rating criteria such as relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Mainly, the paper finds that ChatGPT has clear limitations as a teacher coach in this setting. Its quantitative rubric scores correlate weakly with human ratings, and added rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought-style prompting do not materially improve performance. For qualitative feedback, teachers often judged responses as uninsightful or irrelevant, though many outputs were still considered actionable and faithful; the model’s largest weakness was redundancy, with 82% of suggestions repeating something the teacher already did. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may complement, but cannot replace, human coaching, and they emphasize risks such as hallucination, misinterpretation, and privacy concerns when applying LLMs to classroom data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates ChatGPT on elementary mathematics instructional quality using CLASS and MQI rubric scores plus qualitative feedback on math instruction. Quantitatively, model-human Spearman correlations were low across items (e.g., CLBM up to 0.35, CLPC -0.06 to 0.04; MQI items mostly 0.00-0.17), indicating weak alignment with expert ratings. Qualitatively, teachers often found the model’s math-feedback responses uninsightful or irrelevant, though some suggestions were actionable; 82% of suggestions were redundant and merely restated what the teacher already did.
finding.measure: CLASS and MQI observation rubric scores; teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty for feedback on elementary math transcripts
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for Task A; n=18 transcript segments for Task B; n=18 transcript segments / 36 suggestions for Task C; 317 teachers in source dataset

paper_profiles.title: Sticky Help, Bounded Effects: Session-by-Session Analytics of Teacher Interventions in K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers decide whom to help in technology-supported K-12 mathematics classrooms, and whether teacher help has effects that persist beyond the current class session. The authors combine qualitative interviews with nine middle-school math teachers and large-scale log analysis from MATHia classroom use to study two linked questions: what factors drive in-the-moment help decisions, and whether those help visits predict later engagement or learning.

The quantitative dataset includes 1,437,055 student-system transactions from 339 students across 14 classes in 10 U.S. schools. Using mixed-effects logistic regression, cross-lagged panel models, and additive factors modeling, the study finds that prior help history strongly predicts additional help later (OR = 1.32, 95% CI [1.19, 1.46]), indicating a “sticky” pattern of repeated teacher attention. Idle behavior also predicts being helped in the moment, but the cross-session effects are weaker and asymmetric: prior idle does not lead to more later help, and prior help does not reduce later idle. For learning, help is positively associated with immediate within-session learning, but help in one session does not predict more new skills in later sessions, suggesting that the measurable benefits are largely session-bound.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher help was associated with immediate within-session learning, but there was no evidence that help in one session improved later skill acquisition. In the AFM-based learning analysis, help and learning were positively correlated within sessions (r≈.13, p<.001), yet prior teacher help did not significantly predict the number of new KCs learned in the next session (bK = 0.04, z = 0.64, p = .52) across 425,285 first attempts and 827 KCs.
finding.measure: AFM-estimated new knowledge component (KC) acquisition / mastery, plus within-session help-learning correlation
finding.study_size: n=339 students; 1,437,055 transactions; AFM fit on 425,285 first attempts across 827 KCs
finding.std_deviation: AFM variance components: student σ² = 0.29, skill σ² = 1.26

finding.finding_summary: The study directly modeled student disengagement states as outcomes and predictors of teacher intervention, focusing on idle behavior as an engagement indicator. Prior help did not meaningfully reduce later idle behavior (d1 = -0.05, z = -1.45, p = .147), while prior idle behavior predicted reduced subsequent teacher help (b1 = -0.10, z = -2.62, p = .009), suggesting engagement effects were fleeting and asymmetric.
finding.measure: Idle engagement state; cross-lagged panel model of idle/help across sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies how teacher attention is allocated in real time and whether help history affects intervention patterns, which has direct implications for orchestration efficiency. Prior help significantly increased the odds of receiving additional help (OR = 1.32, 95% CI [1.19, 1.46]), and help was highly concentrated across students (Gini = 0.641), indicating that teacher attention clustered rather than being evenly distributed.
finding.measure: Likelihood of teacher intervention; distribution/concentration of help across students

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a case study of designing and evaluating Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses intended to help teachers support students more effectively in AI-supported K-12 classrooms. The authors argue that successful human–AI partnerships require participatory design with practitioners, iterative testing in real classroom settings, and a theory of complementarity between teacher and AI capabilities.

The paper describes multiple formative design activities with K-12 teachers, including classroom observations, storytelling, card sorting, speed-dating, and replay enactments, which informed the design of real-time teacher awareness tools. Lumilo provides at-a-glance indicators and detail views about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior while teachers use an AI tutor. In pilot studies with 14 teachers, 15 classrooms, and 304 students, the system was iteratively refined to better steer teacher attention toward students needing help.

The main empirical evaluation was an in-the-wild field experiment with 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts. Students in classes where teachers used Lumilo, especially the analytics-enabled version, showed greater pre/post learning gains on linear equation solving than students in a business-as-usual condition or a minimal-glasses condition without analytics. The study also found that Lumilo shifted teacher attention toward lower-performing students and reduced the typical tendency for higher-pretest students to benefit more, suggesting that real-time teacher augmentation can improve both individual learning and equity in AI-supported classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: In a field experiment with 343 middle school students (286 analyzed), classes where teachers used Lumilo showed greater pre/post gains on a linear equation solving test than classes in business-as-usual and minimal-glasses conditions. The paper reports that the analytics-enabled version improved learning beyond the effects of the glasses alone, indicating that real-time teacher analytics contributed to higher mathematics achievement.
finding.measure: Pre/post linear equation solving test scores

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines student engagement/attention-related classroom functioning through teacher behavior and student support patterns, but it does not report a direct standardized engagement or motivation outcome. Observational and process evidence suggests teachers used Lumilo to intervene more often with students needing help and to provide encouragement, which the authors interpret as supporting more effective in-class engagement with the AI tutor.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation and classroom interaction patterns

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly discusses teacher-supported metacognitive prompting as part of the Lumilo intervention, and the analytics highlighted students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior. While no separate metacognition test is reported, classroom observations indicate teachers used the system to prompt students to reflect on their work and persist through unproductive ruts, implying improved metacognitive support during problem solving.
finding.measure: Observed teacher prompting and support for student metacognition during AI-tutored work

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to improve teacher orchestration efficiency by making it easier to monitor students and decide whom to help. Process data showed teachers using Lumilo spent about 24 seconds per student visit on average and redirected attention toward students with lower incoming knowledge, suggesting more targeted teacher time use rather than reduced workload per se.
finding.measure: Teacher time allocation / classroom attention allocation

paper_profiles.title: On the development of an AI performance and behavioural measures for teaching and classroom management
paper_profiles.venue: CHI 2025 Workshop on Augmented Educators and AI: Shaping the Future of Human and AI Cooperation in Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a two-year project to build AI-driven measures for analyzing teaching and classroom management behaviors from multimodal classroom sensor data. The core problem is that traditional teacher observation is subjective, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale, so the authors propose automated analysis of audio, video, and sensor streams to create objective indicators of teacher actions and speaking style.

The system was developed using recordings from regular classroom lessons at the National Institute of Education in Singapore. The dataset contains 45 usable recordings from 12 teachers and about 69 hours of video, with 10 training videos manually annotated to support model development. The paper reports computer vision and speech-processing pipelines for detecting actions such as writing on the board, gesturing, moving around the room, and extracting acoustic features like loudness and speaking rate.

The main product is a proof-of-concept Teacher Trainer dashboard that visualizes teaching behaviors, spatial movement, and vocal features for self-review. An informal evaluation with eight NIE researchers found the dashboard clear, usable, and non-judgmental, and participants appreciated the reduction in manual workload. The paper does not test student learning outcomes or compare the AI system against ordinary instruction in a controlled way; instead, it argues that the tool may support teacher reflection and professional development in an Asian educational context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the AI-based dashboard reduced manual workload and supported more efficient review of classroom recordings. In an informal evaluation with eight NIE researchers, participants specifically praised the automated audio-video analysis and event detection compared with current manual workflows, but no quantitative productivity effect was reported.
finding.measure: Informal usability and workflow feedback on automated classroom-analysis dashboard

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was described as non-judgmental and as encouraging constructive reflection, which the authors frame as supporting teacher self-review and professional growth. However, this was based on informal evaluator feedback rather than a measured change in morale, engagement, or self-efficacy, so the evidence is qualitative and indirect.
finding.measure: Evaluator perceptions of self-review, reflection, and usability

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual and design problem in AI literacy: how to help learners recognize and mitigate human cognitive biases when using generative AI, rather than treating AI outputs as neutral or authoritative. The paper argues that current AI literacy efforts focus too heavily on technical prompt skills and algorithmic bias, while under-addressing metacognitive skills such as bias awareness, self-monitoring, and reflective decision-making in human-AI interaction.

The paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AI literacy intervention built around two core design ideas: deliberate friction and bi-directional human-AI interaction. Deliberate friction is used to slow users down at both prompt formulation and output interpretation, while a prompt refinement tool and a bias visualization map aim to make bias explicit and actionable. The paper is primarily a design/position contribution, illustrating the framework with work-in-progress prototypes and referencing initial mixed-methods user research with university students that identified needs around bias awareness, AI understanding, and critical thinking.

The context is university student use of LLM-based tools in academic work, especially for tasks like summarization, argument development, and research synthesis. The paper does not report a controlled evaluation of learning outcomes; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and early prototype work to motivate future research on evaluation methods, scaffolding, trust dynamics, and bias measurement.

Overall, the main conclusion is that effective AI literacy tools should move beyond automation-oriented assistance and explicitly cultivate metacognition, reflection, and agency. The paper emphasizes possible risks of over-reliance, confirmation bias, and anchoring bias in human-AI workflows, but these are presented as design concerns and theoretical motivations rather than empirical findings from this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that metacognitive AI literacy interventions may improve critical thinking, bias awareness, and self-regulation during AI use, but it does not present outcome data from a controlled study. Its only empirical basis is an initial mixed-methods user study with university students that identified three support needs: bias awareness, AI understanding, and critical thinking; no effect sizes or comparative results are reported.
finding.measure: Survey and interview responses about metacognitive support needs; prototype usability and expert review observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses productivity-oriented AI use and suggests that deliberate friction may reduce over-automation and prompt users to think more carefully, but it provides no empirical evidence that the proposed tool improves efficiency. No task-time, workload, or productivity outcomes are reported in the paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge high school English Language Arts teachers face in supporting students’ collaborative argumentation during classroom discussions. The authors developed Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that automatically codes discussion transcripts for argument moves, specificity, and collaboration using NLP models, then presents teachers with visual analytics, coded transcripts, collaboration maps, and goal-setting supports.

The evaluation involved 18 high school ELA teachers from 4 schools. Teachers used a desktop version of DT after their own recorded class discussions; transcripts were manually coded and then used to generate analytics for a usability study, while the underlying NLP classifiers were separately evaluated against human annotations. Teachers rated DT as helpful for understanding student discussion and reported that it gave them more insight into student learning and ideas for changing facilitation, although ease of use was the lowest-rated item. The automated classifiers showed moderate-to-substantial agreement with human coders for argument moves and specificity, but weaker performance for collaboration, especially for agree and challenge/probe labels.

Overall, the paper concludes that discussion analytics can support teacher learning about collaborative argumentation, but it is an early-stage system study rather than an outcome-impact study on student achievement or a comparison against ordinary instruction. The evidence is based on teacher perceptions and classifier validity rather than direct causal effects on classroom engagement or teacher morale.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that DT was helpful for understanding and supporting collaborative argumentation, a durable skill involving collaboration, reasoning, and use of evidence. In the usability survey with 18 high school ELA teachers, the overall item "Discussion Tracker is helpful for my teaching of literature discussions" had a mean of 4.72/5, and items on recognizing strengths and weaknesses in student discussion both averaged 4.72/5.
finding.measure: Teacher usability survey ratings of discussion analytics for collaborative argumentation

paper_profiles.title: Need of AI in Modern Education: in the Eyes of Explainable AI (xAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper argues that AI can support modern education, but its complexity and opacity create challenges for trust, transparency, and fairness. The central substantive question is not whether AI improves instruction directly, but whether explainable-AI methods can reveal feature importance and bias in a predictive model relevant to educational opportunity, especially the relationship between parental income and access to education.

The authors train an XGBoost classifier on the Adult Census Income dataset and then compare multiple post-hoc explanation and fairness tools, including permutation importance, SHAP, LIME, decision-tree surrogates, and FairML. Their analysis focuses on whether different explanation methods surface consistent drivers of the income prediction and whether sensitive attributes are implicated in the model’s decisions. They report that permutation importance, SHAP, and surrogate models highlight features such as marital status, education, capital gains, and age, while FairML exposes dependence on sensitive variables such as race, nationality, and sex that other methods may not make salient.

The broader conclusion is that explanation methods are not interchangeable and can disagree in meaningful ways, especially regarding bias detection. The paper emphasizes that LIME can be unstable across runs, SHAP may miss some fairness issues, and FairML can reveal discriminatory patterns that matter for educational equity. The work is primarily a methodological/illustrative chapter using an adult income prediction task as a proxy for parental-income-related educational access, rather than a K-12 intervention study or a direct test of classroom outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Communication of Prospective Teachers with Students in Mathematics Learning at Senior High School (SMA)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how prospective mathematics teachers communicate with students during mathematics instruction at a senior high school in Indonesia. The stated focus is on teacher communication skills—such as using appropriate language, explaining procedures, guiding board work, and facilitating discussion and question-and-answer activities—rather than on any AI tool or technology intervention.

The study was conducted at SMAN 1 Madura with a prospective teacher from the Mathematics Education Study Program at Madura University doing field practice (PLP). Data were collected through interviews, field notes, documentation, and video recordings in a descriptive qualitative design. The paper describes observed teaching behaviors in calculus topics (limits and derivatives) and argues that effective teacher communication helps students understand mathematical symbols, procedures, and strategies.

The main conclusion is that prospective teachers need to master communication in mathematics learning because it supports accurate calculation, student participation, and classroom discussion. The paper recommends strengthening prospective teachers’ communication skills so they can better guide students and support learning in other contexts. It does not provide comparative empirical evidence, experimental outcomes, or findings about AI tools, teacher morale, or engagement beyond descriptive observations of classroom interaction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that prospective teachers were able to use formulas, rules, and methods simultaneously to make accurate calculations in calculus lessons on limits and derivatives. The study is descriptive and qualitative, so no effect size or statistical comparison is reported; the finding is based on observed classroom practice at SMAN 1 Madura.
finding.measure: Observed teacher use of formulas, rules, and methods in calculus problem-solving (limits and derivatives)
finding.study_size: n=1 prospective teacher / one classroom setting

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes prospective teachers as using language appropriate to students’ level of understanding and communicating explanations orally and in writing while working through problems on the board. This is presented as supporting students’ comprehension of symbols, procedures, and strategies, but the paper offers no quantitative outcome data.
finding.measure: Observed oral and written teacher-student communication during mathematics instruction
finding.study_size: n=1 prospective teacher / one classroom setting

finding.finding_summary: The study describes classroom discussion and question-and-answer activities as ways the prospective teacher stimulated student participation and cooperation. The paper treats these as desirable communication practices that help students engage in discussion and think through mathematical ideas, but it does not measure durable skills directly with an instrument or comparison group.
finding.measure: Observed discussion, questioning, and student cooperation in mathematics class
finding.study_size: n=1 prospective teacher / one classroom setting

paper_profiles.title: Towards The Ultimate Brain: Exploring Scientific Discovery with ChatGPT AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a meta-experiment and demonstration of ChatGPT’s generative capabilities rather than a conventional empirical study. The author constructs a gamified text-adventure environment in which ChatGPT acts as a researcher exploring generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs), proposing hypothetical theories, evaluating them against custom criteria, and generating content such as limericks, mathematical expressions, and proof-like arguments.

The core question is whether a language model can help co-create scientific-style content and remain coherent across nested prompts and roleplay settings. The paper emphasizes that the outputs are speculative and not scientifically validated; the “GPT4” theory is a fictional construct created within the game. The author concludes that ChatGPT can generate creative, contextually consistent text and some plausible-looking mathematical prose, but cannot independently conduct rigorous science or produce verifiable discoveries.

The paper is not about K-12 education, instructional interventions, or student outcomes. It does not study teachers, classrooms, school systems, or any educational population; the only human participant context is the adult author interacting with ChatGPT while crafting the manuscript. As such, it provides no direct empirical evidence about AI improving teacher morale, classroom engagement, or instructional effectiveness in schools.

paper_profiles.title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '24 International Workshop on GenAI-LA / arXiv
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), where missing quiz-score and attempt data can weaken learner modeling and knowledge tracing. The authors propose 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation), a framework that first imputes missing values via tensor factorization and then augments data using generative models.

The empirical work uses a real AutoTutor reading-comprehension dataset from the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL), involving 118 adult learners in a "Cause and Effect" lesson. The paper compares GAN- and GPT-4-based simulation strategies for generating additional learner-performance samples, with K-means++ clustering and power-law learning-curve fitting used to characterize individual learning patterns.

Results show that tensor completion can effectively densify sparse performance tensors and that GAN-produced simulations are more reliable than GPT-4 outputs for this numerical data-simulation task. GPT-4 produced broader, less stable parameter distributions, while GAN better preserved the original range and consistency of learner parameters. The study concludes that generative AI can support data augmentation for ITS research, but that GPT-4 is currently less suitable than GAN for precise numerical simulation of learner performance data.

finding.finding_summary: The framework improved handling of sparse learner-performance data for reading-comprehension tutoring data by imputing missing values with tensor completion and augmenting simulated samples with generative models. In the dataset of 118 adult AutoTutor learners, original sparsity was 81.25%–85.45% across lesson conditions, and the authors report that tensor completion efficiently imputed missing question-attempt entries.
finding.measure: Sparse learner performance data imputation / tensor completion quality in an AutoTutor reading-comprehension dataset

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main contribution is methodological efficiency for educational data processing: it proposes a scalable framework for densifying and augmenting sparse learner-performance data to support downstream modeling in ITSs. The authors report that the method can generate scalable, personalized simulations and that tensor completion efficiently recovers missing entries, but they do not provide a formal efficiency effect size.
finding.measure: Scalable simulation / data imputation for ITS learner modeling

paper_profiles.title: Exploring utilization of generative AI for research and education in data-driven materials science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early uses of generative AI in materials-science research and education, based on the authors’ AIMHack2024 hackathon. The authors ask how tools like ChatGPT and MyGPT can support practical software learning, AI-assisted documentation, and GUI development for a Bayesian optimization package (PHYSBO) and related materials-science workflows.

The paper presents three demonstrations: using ChatGPT to help participants learn ImageJ for object counting, using MyGPT to generate tutorials and documentation for PHYSBO from source materials, and using ChatGPT to convert Python scripts into a Windows executable and GUI for PHYSBO. The context is a small interdisciplinary hackathon with about 30 participants, mostly researchers and students in materials science and related fields. The paper is primarily a descriptive report rather than a controlled evaluation, but it argues that generative AI reduced the effort needed to learn unfamiliar software and to produce usable tutorials and interfaces.

A key conclusion is that generative AI can be helpful for education and research workflows when paired with human verification. The authors note that URL-only prompting produced inaccurate outputs in MyGPT, while uploading structured PDFs improved accuracy, and they emphasize that AI-generated outputs still require testing and validation. Because the paper focuses on demonstrations rather than comparative outcome measurement, it does not provide K-12 evidence on teacher morale, classroom engagement, or student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that generative AI reduced the time and effort required to learn unfamiliar software, generate tutorials, and convert Python scripts into a Windows executable and GUI. In the hackathon context (approximately n=30 participants), ChatGPT/MyGPT were used to produce step-by-step software instructions, a PHYSBO tutorial, and a GUI/manual workflow, with the authors concluding that these tasks were substantially streamlined compared with manual documentation or trial-and-error learning.
finding.measure: Observed feasibility, tutorial generation accuracy, and author-reported reduction in effort/time for software learning and packaging tasks
