finding.study_size: n=approximately 30 hackathon participants (contextual demonstration; not a controlled sample)

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how secondary teachers in Washington State used a generative AI platform, Colleague AI Classroom, in real classrooms during a seven-week co-design pilot. The central question is not whether AI autonomously improves student outcomes, but how teachers integrate AI-supported features into instruction, grading, feedback, and student inquiry, and what conditions make that integration useful or problematic.

The pilot involved 21 in-service teachers across five Washington districts and one independent school, spanning grades 6-12 and a range of subjects including math, science, ELA, Spanish, engineering, and other elective areas. Teachers used four features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, AI-assisted assessment/grading for rubric generation and formative feedback, AI Tutor for student-directed support, and Student Growth Insights for teacher-facing summaries of student needs. Data came from surveys, planning and reflection forms, group meetings, interviews, and platform logs.

The main conclusions are that AI can support classroom instruction when teachers provide strong framing, clear goals, and ongoing monitoring. Teachers generally found the platform most useful as a formative tool: it could increase engagement in structured conversations, accelerate feedback cycles, surface misconceptions, and reduce teacher workload. However, the report also emphasizes substantial heterogeneity by grade band and subject, with stronger results in some contexts (e.g., humanities, some science and Spanish uses) and more mixed or weaker results in math, earth science, and less structured implementations. The study is exploratory and descriptive, with no randomized comparison against ordinary instruction, so its findings speak to implementation conditions, benefits, and risks rather than causal impact.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported conversations and feedback could help multilingual and English learners participate more actively, build confidence, and improve writing-related tasks such as prewriting and brainstorming. For example, high school English and Spanish implementations were described as supporting individualized language practice and ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback, but these are qualitative observations rather than controlled effects.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses, exit tickets, reflections on student participation and language-related classroom tasks
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; up to 600 students across Teaching Aide implementations

finding.finding_summary: Math implementations showed both promise and limitations. Teachers reported that middle school math sometimes produced thoughtful engagement and concept talk, but high school math was more mixed, with trust and accuracy concerns, especially around flexible non-linear reasoning and the AI’s difficulty with diagrams. No quantitative achievement gains were reported, and the evidence is based on teacher-reported classroom experiences.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement and learning in math classes using Teaching Aide and assessment tools
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; math classes were a subset of the pilot

finding.finding_summary: Science classrooms were among the strongest contexts for the platform, with teachers reporting that AI-facilitated conversations supported inquiry, expanded opportunities for culturally relevant content, and helped students work through misconceptions. The report also notes that science implementations often benefited from structured prompts and formative feedback, though earth science and some technical science tasks were more variable because of diagram and technical-reasoning limits.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement, perceived learning, and formative feedback use in science classes
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; science classes were a subset of the pilot

finding.finding_summary: Across non-core subjects, teachers reported useful applications in Spanish, engineering, programming, business law, and related courses. The clearest examples were Spanish and other humanities/interdisciplinary STEM settings, where AI supported real-time feedback, brainstorming, and individualized skill development; however, outcomes varied by subject and task, and the report does not provide controlled achievement metrics.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported learning, engagement, and feedback utility across non-core subjects
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; multiple non-core subject classes

finding.finding_summary: The paper consistently reports improved student engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate when AI use was structured and teacher-mediated. Teachers described students as more willing to revise, more willing to speak through the AI in class, and more confident after receiving immediate feedback, though engagement varied widely by implementation quality and student age. Reported engagement patterns were largely descriptive (e.g., 28% of conversations had most students engaged thoughtfully; 62% showed mixed engagement; 3% showed no benefit).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement and reports of student confidence/participation in AI-supported activities
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide exit tickets; n=21 teachers overall

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI supported deeper thinking, inquiry, revision, and reasoning when prompts were well structured and tied to clear goals. The report highlights improved seminar preparation, proof sketches, brainstorming, and revision cycles, but also notes that without scaffolding the tool could lead to shallow exchanges or overreliance. Evidence is qualitative and implementation-focused rather than outcome-measure-based.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on student inquiry, revision, reasoning, and conversation quality

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is a central focus of the paper, with teachers reporting reduced workload from AI-assisted grading, rubric generation, conversation summaries, and Student Growth Insights. The report states that AI grading covered a median of 92.2% of submitted work, mean submission rate was 54.8% (SD = 27.9), and teachers viewed the system as saving hours of scanning and speeding formative feedback, although AI scores were often reviewed or corrected by teachers.
finding.measure: Platform logs of grading coverage, teacher survey responses, and reflections on time saved and feedback workflow
finding.study_size: 58 classroom-level assessment records across 33 classrooms; n=19 teachers in assessment phase; n=21 teachers overall

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests potential institutional value from AI adoption through teacher co-design, privacy agreements, and classroom workflow redesign, but it does not evaluate policy or district-level outcomes directly. The main institutional implication is that sustainable implementation depends on teacher AI competency, clear governance, and alignment with district routines; this is an inferred organizational takeaway rather than a measured institutional effect.
finding.measure: Teacher/district implementation context, MOU-based participation, and reflections on adoption conditions
finding.study_size: n=5 districts; 1 independent school; n=21 teachers

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (grades 7-10; students aged 12-18 in UAE context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can function as a teacher assistant to reduce workload and help prevent burnout. The authors frame teacher burnout as a major issue driven in part by time-consuming non-teaching tasks such as lesson planning and content development, and they focus on whether ChatGPT can generate useful lesson plans and supporting materials for secondary-school teaching.

Methodologically, the study uses an explanatory research approach and tests ChatGPT with scripted prompts for lesson planning and material development in English (Grade 7 creative writing), mathematics (Grade 8 square roots and cube roots), and science/chemistry (Grade 10 decomposition reactions). The setting is the UAE, and the authors evaluate the outputs against the 5Es instructional model, with two researchers qualitatively judging the generated lesson plans and revisions. There was no student outcome measurement, no teacher sample, and no comparator condition; the evidence is therefore based on the perceived utility and quality of ChatGPT outputs rather than on causal effects on actual workload, burnout, or retention.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can produce lesson plans and related materials that are potentially useful for teachers, especially when prompts are specific and iterative. However, the first-pass outputs were often incomplete or insufficiently aligned with pedagogical expectations, and the authors argue that human oversight and prompt refinement are necessary to improve quality. The study’s main contribution is a proof-of-concept argument that ChatGPT may help streamline planning and support teacher well-being indirectly, but it does not provide direct empirical evidence that teacher workload or burnout actually decreases in practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can relieve teacher workload by generating lesson plans and supplementary materials for secondary-school classes, but this is based on qualitative evaluation of AI outputs rather than measured time savings or burnout reduction. Across Grade 7 English, Grade 8 math, and Grade 10 science prompts, the authors found that ChatGPT could produce usable lesson-plan elements after prompt refinement, suggesting potential to streamline planning and free teacher time, but no actual workload outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans and content using the 5Es instructional model

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames ChatGPT as potentially relevant to UAE education policy and school-level AI integration, especially for reducing burnout and improving teacher job satisfaction and well-being. This is a conceptual and practice-oriented claim supported by the authors’ analysis of generated lesson plans, not by direct institutional data or policy evaluation.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of implications for UAE educational reform and AI integration

paper_profiles.title: Attitudes towards and expectations on the role of artificial intelligence in the classroom among digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers
paper_profiles.venue: LUMAT: International Journal on Math, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics teachers in Finland (primary, lower secondary, upper secondary)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers view artificial intelligence in school, with emphasis on their expectations, perceived opportunities, and perceived risks. The authors frame AI through the Will-Skill-Tool model and study teachers’ current digital-tool use as a proxy for likely AI adoption, noting that most respondents had little direct classroom experience with AI tools at the time of data collection.

The study used a web-based survey of 85 Swedish- and Finnish-speaking mathematics teachers collected in spring and autumn 2020, before ChatGPT-3. The survey combined closed-response items, Likert attitude statements, and open-ended questions about current digital resources, possible AI uses, risks, and attitudes toward AI. Teachers reported broad use of digital tools, saw AI as potentially useful for individualized learning, homework support, and assessment follow-up, but also raised concerns about privacy, overreliance on algorithms, social effects, and the possibility that tools could distract from mathematical reasoning.

Overall, the paper concludes that these teachers are generally open to AI and likely early adopters, but their views are balanced rather than uncritically positive. The findings are primarily descriptive and perception-based; they do not test an intervention or measure student outcomes. The study is therefore useful for understanding teacher-facing AI attitudes and expected usefulness, but it does not provide causal evidence about workload reduction, morale, well-being, or retention.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived AI as potentially helpful for reducing teacher effort in follow-up and assessment tasks, and many saw AI-based tools as useful for making student progress easier to monitor. In the survey, 56/85 teachers (66%) selected 'make it easier for teacher to follow-up and assess students,' and open responses described AI-like tools as aiding assessment, analytics, and automatic exercise generation, but these were expectations rather than measured workload effects.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on perceived AI usefulness for follow-up and assessment; open-ended responses about added value of digital/AI tools

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected AI to increase motivation and interest for students in mathematics, but they also worried that AI and digital tools could reduce concentration, persistence, collaboration, and social interaction. For the AI-specific item, 56/85 (66%) endorsed increased motivation/interest, while open responses and risk items highlighted possible negative emotional and social consequences.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on AI/digital tools increasing motivation and interest; open-ended risk comments about social and emotional effects

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI and digital tools could support higher-order mathematical thinking through individualized pathways and differentiation, but they also worried that heavy tool use could shift attention away from conceptual learning, reasoning, and problem solving. The paper reports these as perceived effects on student thinking and classroom practice, not as measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items and open-ended responses about differentiation, conceptual understanding, reasoning, and problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on mathematics teaching and teachers’ expectations that AI could support individualized learning, challenges for advanced students, and adaptive learning materials, but could also distract from mathematical skill development. In the survey, 66/85 teachers (78%) endorsed creating individual learning paths and 69/85 (81%) endorsed offering challenges for interested students; however, these are perceived benefits, not achievement effects.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on AI functions in mathematics learning and classroom use; open-ended comments on mathematical learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expressed concern that AI could raise privacy, data security, and trust issues and could affect classroom relationships and equity. They also reported that AI discussions were already taking place in schools, suggesting emerging institutional interest, but the paper does not evaluate policy or implementation outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher responses about AI risks, school discussions, and concerns about data handling, privacy, inequality, and trust

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in-the-loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The authors focus on a key practical question for K-12 AI tools: whether teacher-assisted AI task generation is time-efficient, what prompting strategies teachers use, and how students respond to the personalized problems.

Seven middle school math teachers used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems in ASSISTments across two units: proportional relationships/percentages (Unit 4) and expressions/equations/inequalities (Unit 6). The study combined log analysis of teacher-ChatGPT interactions, coded teacher speech, student survey ratings, and open-ended student feedback. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 personalized problems for 521 seventh-grade students. The paper reports that teachers spent about 4 minutes per problem on average, that time did not become clearly more efficient over time, and that using 3–5 prompts was associated with better student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests. Students generally preferred finer-grained specific cultural references over broad categories, while teachers often had to spend substantial time revising AI outputs for realism, age appropriateness, and numerical accuracy.

Overall, the study concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support reflective instructional design and improve the quality of AI-generated tasks, but it is not especially time-efficient and may not scale well for highly individualized personalization. The authors argue that teacher oversight remains important for depth, realism, and appropriateness, yet also note a tension between teacher mediation and students’ desire for more fine-grained personalization.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-consuming and did not appear to become clearly more efficient with experience. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), with Unit 4 averaging 204 seconds and Unit 6 averaging 286 seconds; the increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6 was statistically significant (B=70.4 seconds, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher time per personalized problem; number of prompts used per problem; mixed-effects regression on time and prompts
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds per problem (Unit 6 vs Unit 4); B=1.26 prompts per problem; B=0.240 for 3–5 prompts vs other prompt counts
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds overall; SD=153 Unit 4; SD=169 Unit 6; SD=2.6 prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured students’ interest and perceived closeness of personalized math problems to their own interests. Student ratings were modest overall (interestingness M=2.46/5, closeness M=2.53/5), and problems created with 3–5 prompts received significantly higher ratings by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale. Ratings improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6 as teachers revised their approaches (interestingness B=0.33, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended student feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected on 52-53 problems; open-ended feedback from 446-454 responses
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 points on 5-point scale for 3–5 prompts; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs Unit 4
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 interestingness; SD=1.28 closeness; Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20; Unit 6 closeness SD=1.29

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and their teachers perceived a generative-AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors were motivated by the idea that young learners often struggle to begin and elaborate on math story writing, and that GenAI might provide scaffolding for story generation, mathematical language use, and classroom engagement.

The intervention was a classroom implementation of an in-house GenAI-powered learning technology built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. Students in six elementary classrooms (79 fifth graders across two U.S. schools) completed a structured three-step activity: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In this process, students analyzed math stories, visually represented ideas, and then co-created culturally relevant math stories with AI; teachers also participated in interviews after the implementation.

Data came from semi-structured focus-group interviews with 10 students, one-on-one interviews with all six teachers, open-ended student survey responses, and classroom observations. The study used inductive and deductive thematic analysis to identify perceived benefits and challenges. The main conclusions are that participants perceived GenAI as supporting creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest, curiosity, and ownership, while also surfacing concerns about overreliance, limited feedback, lack of autonomy, weak social connection, and accessibility/communication limitations. Because the paper is qualitative and perception-based, it does not provide causal effects on teacher outcomes such as workload, morale, well-being, or retention.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students perceived the GenAI-supported math-story activity as helping students understand mathematical problems, represent mathematical knowledge, and uncover misconceptions. The evidence is based on thematic analysis of interviews, survey responses, and observations from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, knowledge representation, and misconception detection in story-based math writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the GenAI activity as increasing interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. Teachers and students described math as more enjoyable and engaging, with students showing enthusiasm for continuing the activity and feeling more responsible for their work as authors of math stories. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The study reports perceived gains in creativity, flexible/divergent thinking, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. Students and teachers described the activity as helping students refine prompts, compare AI strengths and weaknesses, and generate original stories; however, the evidence is qualitative and no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content

finding.finding_summary: The paper also frames the activity as supporting academic writing in mathematics, specifically creative mathematical writing/story composition. Participants perceived that GenAI helped students draft, expand, and improve stories, but the study does not report quantitative writing-skill outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived quality and development of creative mathematical writing

paper_profiles.title: Quadratic Forms and Automorphic Forms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a set of graduate-level lecture notes surveying the classical theory of quadratic forms over number fields and their connection to modular and automorphic forms. It develops foundational definitions and results on quadratic spaces and lattices, local-global principles, theta functions, modular forms, and related arithmetic constructions such as the neighbor method.

The paper is not an empirical study and does not evaluate an educational intervention, AI tool, or any K-12 teacher-facing outcome. Instead, it is a mathematical exposition aimed at readers in advanced mathematics, especially graduate students, and serves as a survey of theory rather than a research report with measured outcomes.

Because the text contains no education setting, no teachers, no AI system, and no outcome measures related to workload, usefulness, morale, well-being, or retention, it is excluded from the requested K-12 AI evidence sub-question. There are also no empirical findings to extract for the knowledge graph beyond the bibliographic metadata and the fact that it is a theoretical notes-style document.

paper_profiles.title: Creative Problem Solving in Intelligent Agents: A Framework and Survey
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (non-human / AI systems; no K-12 human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys research on creative problem solving (CPS) in artificial intelligence, with an emphasis on how agents handle tasks that cannot be solved using their initial knowledge or action space. The authors define CPS as the process by which an agent expands its conceptual space to discover new concepts that enable it to solve an otherwise unachievable goal.

The paper proposes a framework for CPS organized around four components: problem formulation, knowledge representation, knowledge manipulation, and evaluation. It reviews prior work across planning and reinforcement learning, as well as symbolic, non-symbolic, and hybrid representations, illustrating how AI systems can discover new actions, substitute objects, adapt motion, or generate new morphologies to solve novel tasks.

This is a broad survey of computational creativity and robotics-oriented AI methods rather than an empirical study of teachers, students, or schools. No K-12 educational implementation, teacher-facing AI tool, or teacher outcome is directly studied. The paper’s main contribution is conceptual and taxonomic: it clarifies CPS definitions, categorizes the literature, and identifies open research questions for future AI systems.

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Signal Processing and Machine Learning: Math Learning Equity for Elementary and Middle School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a perspective/policy-style piece arguing that strong early mathematics foundations are essential for later success in signal processing and machine learning, and that many students do not get adequate math support early enough. The authors describe systemic barriers to early math learning and argue for more robust homework, in-school practice, family communication, and summer catch-up opportunities.

The paper’s main concrete examples are descriptions of three university- or foundation-run out-of-school math support programs: CyMath at Iowa State, Algebra by 7th Grade at Purdue, and Math Motivators. These programs serve elementary and middle school students, often from underrepresented or disadvantaged backgrounds, and use a mix of in-person, hybrid, and online tutoring/mentoring plus adaptive software such as ALEKS. The article reports anecdotal or program-level observations such as improved standardized-test percentiles for some CyMath students and a cited relationship between ALEKS progress and state test proficiency in Ab7G, but it does not present a formal empirical study of AI use in K-12 teacher-facing contexts.

For the research sub-question focused on direct K-12 teacher-facing AI evidence about teacher perceived usefulness, workload, morale, well-being, or retention, this paper is not a match. It does not study teachers as the primary users of an AI tool, does not directly measure any focal teacher outcome, and the AI-related element is limited to student-facing adaptive math software (ALEKS) within broader tutoring programs. The article is best characterized as a qualitative/essay-like overview with illustrative program descriptions rather than evaluative evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring utilization of generative AI for research and education in data-driven materials science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes three demonstrations from the AIMHack2024 hackathon showing how generative AI can support research and education in data-driven materials science. The authors focus on using ChatGPT-like tools to help with software trial-and-error learning, to build an AI tutor for the PHYSBO Bayesian optimization package, and to convert Python scripts into a Windows GUI executable for easier use in teaching and practice settings.

The study context is a hackathon with about 30 participants from materials science, information science, bioinformatics, and related fields. The evidence is primarily descriptive and tutorial-based rather than experimental: the authors show that ChatGPT could generate step-by-step instructions for using ImageJ, that MyGPT responses became more accurate when full documentation PDFs were provided, and that ChatGPT could help generate a usable GUI/manual for PHYSBO.exe. The paper concludes that generative AI can reduce workload and improve accessibility for software learning and documentation, but outputs still require human verification because inaccuracies can occur.

This paper is not K-12 teacher-facing and does not directly measure any of the focal outcomes in K-12 teachers (such as perceived usefulness, workload, morale, well-being, or retention). It is therefore outside the requested evidence scope for direct K-12 teacher AI evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceived a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in an authentic sixth-grade mathematics classroom. The study asks what roles students assign to the TA, what benefits they perceive from learning with it, and what challenges they encounter. The authors situate the work in the growing interest in generative AI for education and in the long-standing learning-by-teaching literature on teachable agents.

The intervention was a custom GenAI-powered TA built with GPT-4-Turbo and deployed in two class periods in a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States. A total of 108 sixth-grade students in six classes used the system during a rate-and-ratio unit, interacting with the agent through text-based conversations around eight math problems. The system included personalized topic and difficulty selection, gamification, and retrieval-augmented generation over math Q&A data. Data came from classroom observations, open-ended surveys, and semi-structured focus-group interviews with a subset of 14 students, and the authors used thematic analysis.

Findings are entirely perceptual and qualitative: students described the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver, and they reported benefits such as a more student-centered climate, greater autonomy, improved mathematical understanding, stronger self-efficacy and motivation, and more positive attitudes toward AI. They also identified barriers including poor problem presentation, shallow questions, mismatch with learning styles, technical problems, and a need for more teacher facilitation. Because the study does not measure teacher-facing outcomes such as workload, morale, or retention, it does not directly answer the teacher-focused sub-question, but it does provide K-12 evidence about student perceptions of a GenAI math tool.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that learning with the GenAI-powered teachable agent improved their mathematical understanding and ability to apply knowledge in a sixth-grade rates-and-ratio unit. In qualitative reports from 108 sixth-graders, they said teaching the agent helped them clarify concepts such as ratio, revisit misconceptions, and use knowledge in new scenarios; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Students’ perceived improvement in math understanding and application of knowledge (open-ended surveys, focus-group interviews, classroom observations)

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the experience as increasing enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and positive attitudes toward AI. Across the 108 sixth-grade participants, the TA was described as fun, confidence-building, and motivating, but the evidence is qualitative and no standardized scale or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived joy of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and attitude toward AI

finding.finding_summary: Students said the TA prompted deeper reasoning, elaboration, communication, perspective-taking, and collaborative problem-solving. In the sixth-grade classroom study (n=108), students described having to explain their thinking, respond to follow-up prompts, and work with the agent as a partner; the study is qualitative and reports no quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Perceived cognitive, social, and collaborative capacities (reasoning, explanation, perspective-taking, collaboration)

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school students perceive and want AI to function as a peer collaborator in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS). The authors argue that most prior AI-in-education work centers on tutor-like roles, while far less is known about student expectations for AI peers inside group work. To address this gap, they use a participatory design camp to study students’ lived experiences with human-only CPS and with two AI peers embedded in mathematics tasks.

The study was conducted during a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students in the United States. Students completed grade-aligned middle school mathematics CPS tasks, first in human-only groups and then with an AI peer technology probe built around GPT-4o, text-based interaction, and a multi-agent collaborative script. The camp included surveys, reflections, interviews, and design artifacts. Quantitatively, the study found that AI peers reduced perceived temporal demand and that students perceived better task efficiency, but also increased physical demand and reduced social cohesion and task integration. Qualitatively, students wanted AI peers to be scaffold-first, controllable, conversationally responsive, socially attuned, and emotionally supportive rather than overly teachy or answer-giving.

Overall, the paper concludes that middle school students do not simply want more powerful AI help; they want a peer-like collaborator that supports co-agency, preserves productive struggle, and aligns with classroom social norms. The work contributes design guidance for future AI peers in K-12 mathematics, emphasizing hints and checks, user control over timing and amount of help, peer-like tone, and emotional scaffolding.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on middle-school mathematics collaborative problem solving and reports that students experienced AI peers as helpful for progressing through grade-aligned math tasks, especially through hints, checks, and procedural scaffolding. However, the study is primarily design-oriented; it does not report direct learning gains on math achievement, so the mathematical outcome is best characterized as task-level support rather than demonstrated academic improvement.
finding.measure: Grade-aligned middle-school mathematics collaborative problem-solving tasks; qualitative judgments of math-helpfulness and dialogue artifacts

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI peers could reduce temporal pressure and sometimes felt helpful, but they also described frustration, self-blame, and reduced social warmth when the AI failed to respond empathetically or appropriately to uncertainty. On the NASA-TLX, temporal demand was lower with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than with human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), but qualitative accounts showed that emotional attunement was missing and that frustration could be redirected inward.
finding.measure: NASA Task Load Index temporal demand; interview and reflection themes about frustration, trust, and emotional scaffolding
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=18 interviews; n=5 whole-class reflection sessions
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 for lower temporal demand with AI peers; qualitative emotional findings not quantified
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 (AI peers) vs SD=4.13 (human-only) for temporal demand

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines collaboration, co-agency, turn-taking, and group coordination in middle-school CPS. Compared with human-only collaboration, AI peers lowered perceived group integration-task (GIT) and attractions to group-social (ATGS), indicating weaker collaboration quality even while speeding the task; students also repeatedly asked for an AI that would work with them rather than do the work for them.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ), especially Group Integration-Task (GIT) and Attractions to Group-Social (ATGS); qualitative reflections/interviews on collaboration and co-agency
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=18 interviews; n=5 whole-class reflection sessions
finding.effect_size: d=0.81 for lower GIT; d=0.94 for lower ATGS
finding.std_deviation: GIT SD=1.58 (AI peers) vs SD=1.52 (human-only); ATGS SD=1.81 (AI peers) vs SD=2.05 (human-only)

finding.finding_summary: AI peers improved perceived efficiency on one dimension but increased operational burden on another. In paired comparisons, temporal demand was significantly lower with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than in pure human CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13; d=1.15), suggesting less time pressure, but physical demand was higher with AI peers (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41; d=1.14), reflecting typing, navigation, and interface overhead.
finding.measure: NASA Task Load Index temporal demand and physical demand subscales
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 (temporal demand, lower with AI peers); d=1.14 (physical demand, higher with AI peers)
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 (AI peers) vs SD=4.13 (human-only); physical demand SD=4.65 (AI peers) vs SD=2.41 (human-only)

finding.finding_summary: Students wanted AI peers to support collaborative reasoning by asking questions, negotiating methods, and providing examples rather than enforcing a fixed procedure. The qualitative evidence shows that students valued co-agency and shared sensemaking as central to good collaboration, but they perceived the AI as sometimes 'teachery,' distracting, or not listening, which undermined collaboration.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews, whole-class reflections, and participatory design artifacts describing desired collaboration behaviors

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Healthcare: Why, How, and When?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic/scoping review of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in healthcare published between 2012 and early 2022. Its central question is why explainability matters for trustworthy AI, how XAI methods are implemented, and when different explanation types are appropriate in medical applications.

The review synthesizes XAI methods such as dimension reduction, rule extraction/knowledge distillation, feature importance, attention mechanisms, and surrogate models across healthcare use cases including diagnosis, prognosis, and medical image analysis. It does not study teachers, students, or schools, and it does not evaluate any K-12 education intervention, AI tool, or teacher outcome directly. The paper concludes that XAI is important for trust, but that evidence for practical utility remains limited and that explainability must be paired with validation, data-quality reporting, and governance.

Because the paper is a literature review focused on healthcare, it provides only conceptual discussion of explainability and trustworthiness rather than direct empirical evidence about K-12 education. There are no teacher-facing measures of workload, perceived usefulness, morale, well-being, or retention-related outcomes, and no grade-band or subject-area education context is reported.

paper_profiles.title: Numerical analysis techniques for non-linear dynamics
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2018 CERN–Accelerator–School course on Numerical Methods for Analysis, Design and Modelling of Particle Accelerators, Thessaloniki, Greece
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a lecture-style proceedings contribution on numerical methods for analyzing nonlinear dynamics in particle accelerators. It introduces phase-space analysis, fixed points, Poincaré maps, resonance behavior, chaos onset, dynamic aperture, Lyapunov exponents, and frequency map analysis, using accelerator examples such as sextupole and octupole maps, the LHC, SNS, and CLIC pre-damping rings.

The paper is not an empirical education study and does not concern K-12 teachers or students. It is a technical review/tutorial aimed at accelerator-physics practitioners, explaining how nonlinear dynamics and chaotic behavior are detected and mitigated in accelerator systems. The conclusions are methodological: frequency-map and diffusion analyses are useful for diagnosing resonances and optimizing machine working points, but the paper contains no teacher-facing AI intervention, no K-12 context, and no educational outcomes.

Because the requested K-12 teacher-facing AI focal outcomes are absent, no outcome assignments are reported.

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the design, iterative prototyping, and field evaluation of Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses intended to help K-12 teachers better support students using AI tutoring software during class. The central question is how to create an effective human–AI partnership in real classrooms, where teachers can use real-time AI-generated analytics to decide whom to help and when, while still leveraging their own contextual knowledge of students.

The authors describe a participatory design process with K-12 teachers, including field observations, storytelling, card sorting, speed-dating exercises, and replay enactments, followed by pilot studies in live and simulated classrooms. The resulting tool, Lumilo, overlays at-a-glance indicators and drill-down details about students' learning, metacognition, and behavior. Across four pilot studies, the tool was refined using causal alignment analysis and classroom observations, with the goal of improving teacher attention allocation in AI-supported classrooms.

The paper's main empirical evaluation is a field experiment in middle school math classrooms with 343 students, 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts. Classrooms were randomly assigned to business-as-usual, a reduced glasses-only condition, or full Lumilo with analytics; results show that the full tool improved student learning and shifted teachers' attention toward lower-knowledge students. Although the paper is fundamentally about teacher-facing AI augmentation, it does not directly measure teacher workload, morale, well-being, or retention; instead it focuses on teacher attention allocation as a mechanism and on student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measured teacher attention allocation as an in-class process outcome. In the pilot and field studies, teachers using Lumilo spent more time with students who entered with lower initial knowledge, and in the classroom pilots teachers spent an average of about 24 seconds per visit with each student while using the tool. The evidence suggests the tool improved the targeting of teacher time, although it did not directly measure total workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation / time spent with students during class sessions
finding.study_size: pilot studies: 14 teachers, 15 classrooms, 304 students; field experiment: 8 teachers, 18 classrooms, 343 students (286 analyzed)

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual and design problem in AI literacy: how to help learners recognize and mitigate cognitive biases when interacting with generative AI systems. The author argues that current AI literacy tools overemphasize technical and fairness concerns while under-addressing human biases such as anchoring and confirmation bias, which can distort how people formulate prompts and interpret AI output.

The paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AIED intervention designed for human-AI bias mitigation. The tool concept includes two core interface components: a prompt refinement tool that flags potentially biased prompts before submission, and a bias visualization map that highlights possible biases in AI-generated responses after output is received. The paper is primarily conceptual and design-oriented, informed by prior mixed-methods user research with university students and by evaluation of an earlier prototype using usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews.

The intended population is university students, not K-12 teachers or students. No causal effects, quantitative outcomes, or teacher-facing workload/well-being measures are directly reported in this paper. The main conclusion is that metacognitive friction, bidirectional prompt-and-output interventions, and adaptive scaffolding may help users become more critical and reflective AI collaborators, but empirical validation is left for future work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that DeBiasMe is intended to support metacognitive skills and critical engagement with AI by making bias awareness explicit at both the prompt and response stages. However, this is presented as a design claim and future direction rather than a reported empirical effect; the only evidence mentioned is earlier prototype evaluation with usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews, without quantitative outcomes.
finding.measure: Usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, expert reviews; metacognitive skill support is discussed conceptually

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (mixed grade band; elementary, middle, and high school educators)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers can be supported to design AI curriculum that is integrated into core subjects rather than taught only as standalone computer science content. The authors argue that AI education is often inaccessible to many learners and that teacher co-design may reveal practical needs and classroom-context constraints that designers should address.

To investigate this, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 teachers and education professionals. Participants first learned about AI concepts and tools, then used pre-work, group discussions, and facilitated design activities to create integrated AI lesson plans in social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and physics. The paper analyzes audio transcripts, questionnaires, and participant deliverables to identify recurring teacher values and design considerations.

The main findings are that teachers valued four supports when designing AI-integrated curricula: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Teachers also connected AI to subject content through data, reflection, and ethics. The workshop increased reported familiarity with AI and confidence in integrating AI into curricula, but the study is primarily descriptive and qualitative rather than causal. It does not evaluate classroom implementation or student outcomes; instead, it shows how teacher co-design can surface design requirements for more accessible K-12 AI education.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the workshop increased their confidence about integrating AI into their own curriculum, with an average post-workshop rating of 5.6/7, and they valued supports that would make implementation smoother, including clearer tools, scaffolding, and logistical guidance. The paper also reports a slight increase in familiarity with AI from an average of 4.8/7 to 5.8/7, suggesting perceived efficiency and readiness gains rather than measured workload reduction.
finding.measure: Self-reported familiarity with AI; self-reported confidence about integrating AI into curriculum; perceived helpfulness of workshop components

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described the workshop and integrated AI curriculum work as engaging and rewarding, and the post-workshop discussion suggests increased enthusiasm and a more positive attitude toward teaching AI. This is based on qualitative feedback and perceived helpfulness ratings rather than a validated morale or well-being scale.
finding.measure: Participant reflections on workshop helpfulness and whether the workshop changed their opinion about teaching AI

finding.finding_summary: The workshop emphasized collaboration as a core design consideration and used teacher co-design to support curriculum development across multiple subjects. Teachers repeatedly highlighted collaborative work as important for student learning and for the curriculum design process itself, but the evidence is descriptive and based on workshop discourse rather than an outcome test.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of co-design workshop discussions and curriculum drafts

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on integrating AI into non-computing K-12 subjects, including social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and physics. The main finding is that teachers successfully co-designed draft lessons that linked AI to subject matter through data, reflection, and ethics, but the study does not measure student academic achievement in these subjects.
finding.measure: Co-designed curriculum drafts and thematic analysis of integrated subject connections

paper_profiles.title: BERT4beam: Large AI Model Enabled Generalized Beamforming Optimization
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (wireless communications simulation study; no human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of optimizing downlink multi-user MISO beamforming with AI models that can generalize across tasks, system scales, and utility functions. The authors argue that conventional convex optimization is accurate but too slow for dynamic wireless settings, and that existing deep learning approaches are too task-specific to scale to the diversity of 6G communication scenarios.

To address this, the paper proposes BERT4beam, a framework that reformulates beamforming as a token-level sequence learning problem and adapts BERT-style transformer architectures to wireless channel state information. Two models are introduced: BERT for single-task beamforming and UBERT for multi-task beamforming. Both are trained and evaluated entirely in simulation against classical optimization baselines and other neural models (MLP, CNN, GCN, GAT, GPT), using sum-rate, minimum-rate, and energy-efficiency objectives across varying numbers of users, antennas, and power budgets.

The results show that the proposed transformer-based methods achieve performance close to conventional optimization, with BERT and especially UBERT outperforming several neural baselines and showing strong generalization to unseen user counts and power settings. UBERT is positioned as the more flexible multi-task approach, while BERT is noted for strong generalization under dynamic user counts. The study is methodologically a simulation/algorithm paper and does not involve K-12 teachers, students, or educational settings.

paper_profiles.title: Expansive Participatory AI: Supporting Dreaming within Inequitable Institutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that participatory AI efforts should do more than solicit feedback on existing technologies; they should help communities imagine socially just futures and question inequitable institutional norms. The authors frame this as a challenge of “desettling” institutions, emphasizing that co-design should not be constrained by immediate technical feasibility or by taken-for-granted practices within settings such as schools.

The paper presents a set of design principles for expansive co-design with youth and illustrates them through a Learning Futures Workshop. In the workshop, high-school-aged youth were brought to a non-school collaborative setting, asked to build fantastical collaborative spaces from materials, and then invited to imagine how AI could support those ideal spaces and how such ideas might translate into classroom contexts.

The paper is a conceptual and reflective qualitative case study rather than an empirical evaluation of a K-12 AI intervention with measured teacher or student outcomes. Its main contribution is a framework for participatory AI design with youth, along with observations that the workshop encouraged youth to reimagine classroom goals beyond work alone and to think expansively about possible AI futures. It does not directly measure teacher usefulness, workload, morale, well-being, or retention-related outcomes, and it does not provide causal or correlational evidence on those focal outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2024 Workshop on Generative AI for Learning Analytics / arXiv
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), which can limit accurate learner modeling, knowledge tracing, and simulation of learning processes. The authors propose a framework called 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation) that combines tensor factorization for data imputation with generative models for data augmentation.

The approach is evaluated on an AutoTutor reading comprehension dataset from the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL), specifically a 'Cause and Effect' lesson involving 118 participants. The method first densifies sparse learner-question-attempt tensors using tensor completion, then uses GAN and GPT-4 based simulation to generate additional learning-performance samples tailored to clustered learning patterns. The paper compares GAN and GPT-4 simulations and reports that GAN produces more reliable and consistent synthetic parameter distributions than GPT-4 in this numerical simulation task.

The main conclusion is that generative models, especially GANs, may be useful for augmenting sparse educational performance data in ITS contexts, and that tensor completion can help impute missing learner-performance entries. The work is methodological and simulation-focused; it does not study K-12 teachers, teacher-facing AI tools, workload, morale, well-being, retention, or perceived usefulness outcomes directly.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper arguing that research on generative AI and critical thinking often conflates two different constructs: performed critical thinking, which refers to independent cognitive work done without AI assistance, and demonstrated critical thinking, which is the critical thinking that appears in outputs produced with AI help. The authors argue that many current evaluations of GenAI systems only assess the quality of the final AI-assisted product, which may overstate whether users’ own underlying critical thinking ability has improved.

The paper synthesizes prior work from education, psychology, and human-computer interaction to propose a conceptual distinction and to clarify how critical thinking should be measured in AI studies. It discusses implications for both research design and AI system design, emphasizing that systems may improve the visible output of reasoning without strengthening unaided reasoning skills. The paper is not an empirical study with K-12 teachers or students; instead, it is a conceptual framework and call for future studies that directly measure performed critical thinking over time.

Because the paper is theoretical and does not report original data, there is no sample, intervention, comparator, or effect size to extract. Its main contribution is conceptual: it urges future researchers to distinguish between AI-augmented performance and independent skill development when evaluating GenAI in education and other domains.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual position paper rather than an empirical study, so it does not report original results on critical thinking outcomes. It argues that many GenAI studies measure only demonstrated critical thinking in AI-assisted outputs rather than performed critical thinking without AI, and therefore cannot support claims about actual gains in independent critical thinking ability.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: How Do Teachers Create Pedagogical Chatbots?: Current Practices and Challenges
paper_profiles.venue: CHI 2025 Workshop on Augmented Educators and AI: Shaping the Future of Human and AI Cooperation in Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers create, adapt, test, and deploy LLM-based pedagogical chatbots for classroom use. The authors focus on understanding teacher practices and challenges across the chatbot creation lifecycle, including design, implementation, and deployment, rather than evaluating student learning outcomes or comparing chatbot tools experimentally.

The study is based on hour-long semi-structured interviews with seven Korean K-12 teachers. Three participants were experienced chatbot creators, and four were novice teachers who used the commercial platform Mizou to build a chatbot during the study. The paper reports that teachers prefer task-specific chatbots aligned to existing lesson plans, intentionally constrain chatbot behavior, and rely on prompt templates and iterative testing for safety and pedagogical validity.

A major finding is that teachers experience substantial time burden during prompt engineering, debugging, and reviewing chatbot conversations after class. Teachers also face cognitive burden when monitoring live interactions and difficulty conducting systematic post-deployment review. The authors conclude that future systems should better support teacher chatbot creation through contextual design references, role-separated collaboration with developers or interface agents, and tools for monitoring and analyzing student-chatbot interactions.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that prompt engineering, debugging, real-time monitoring, and post-class conversation review all required substantial time and effort. The paper describes these as major workflow burdens for K-12 teachers, with one novice teacher noting the process would be difficult to sustain during the semester.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports of time burden, workload, and effort during chatbot design, testing, deployment, and review

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized challenges and practices related to pedagogical judgment, testing, and adapting chatbots to lesson-specific goals, including deciding appropriate chatbot roles, testing for validity, and reviewing student interaction patterns. These findings speak to teachers' planning, troubleshooting, and reflective evaluation work, but the study does not quantify changes in durable skills.
finding.measure: Interview themes about pedagogical design, testing, debugging, and reflective review practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher-created chatbots require institutional support structures such as contextual lesson-plan references, collaboration between teachers and developers, and interface-agent support for testing and analytics. These are proposed design and organizational implications rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Interview-derived design implications about support systems and workflows

paper_profiles.title: A Performance Study of GA and LSH in Multiprocessor Job Scheduling
paper_profiles.venue: IJCSI International Journal of Computer Science Issues
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a classic computer-science scheduling problem: how to assign dependent tasks to multiple processors so that total completion time (makespan) is minimized. The authors compare two heuristic approaches—genetic algorithms (GA) and list scheduling heuristic (LSH)—using simulated task graphs and MATLAB-based experiments.

The study varies the number of tasks and processors, then compares the finishing time produced by each algorithm across multiple synthetic scenarios. Results suggest that LSH can perform as well as or better than GA for small task sets, but GA tends to produce shorter makespans as task counts and processor counts increase. The authors conclude that GA is the stronger performer overall, though LSH may be preferable when problem size is small or when scheduling time itself must be kept low.

This is not a K-12 teacher-facing AI study and does not measure teacher outcomes such as perceived usefulness, workload, morale, well-being, or retention. It is a technical optimization paper about multiprocessor scheduling in computing systems, not an education study.

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic literature review of tutoring systems in education, focusing on intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), robot tutoring systems (RTS), and multimodal hybrids. The authors reviewed 86 representative studies from 1972–2024 and organized them using a framework spanning artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances.

The review’s main goal is to map the evolution of tutoring systems and summarize how different AI approaches, such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and large language models, support adaptive instruction, feedback, and engagement. The paper argues that software-based ITS are strongest in cognitive adaptability and scalability, while robot-based systems are stronger in social and emotional engagement. It also highlights persistent challenges around data privacy, scalability, and ethical deployment.

This paper is not a direct study of K-12 teacher-facing AI outcomes such as teacher perceived usefulness, workload, morale, well-being, or retention. Instead, it synthesizes prior research on tutoring systems mainly from the student-learning perspective and uses secondary coding of system features and reported findings. As a result, it is primarily relevant as a background review of AI tutoring systems rather than as direct evidence for teacher-facing outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Findings on Teaching Machine Learning in High School: A Ten-Year Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what has been learned from a decade of work on teaching machine learning (ML) in high school, with a particular focus on content, pedagogical strategies, and technology. The authors conduct a systematic literature review of English-language publications from 2011–2021, searching multiple academic databases and repositories and ultimately retaining 30 relevant studies after applying inclusion, exclusion, and quality criteria.

The review synthesizes findings from workshops, courses, hackathons, summer camps, and curriculum pilots that introduced ML and broader AI concepts to high school students. Across the reviewed studies, students generally learned basic ML concepts and algorithms, with many activities emphasizing hands-on, problem/project-based, collaborative, and use-modify-create learning. The paper concludes that active and student-centered approaches tend to support engagement and learning, that visual tools and block-based environments can help novices build ML applications, and that more rigorous evaluations are still needed in this area.

Although the review is not an intervention study itself, it reports that teaching strategies such as hands-on work, project-based learning, and collaborative activities were associated with higher student engagement, motivation, confidence, and interest in ML. It also notes practical challenges, including time demands, uneven group composition, and the need to better adapt materials to student skill levels. Overall, the paper positions high school ML education as a growing K-12 research area with promising but still methodologically limited evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that active, hands-on, problem/project-based learning was repeatedly associated with stronger student engagement, motivation, confidence, and enjoyment in ML learning activities. Several included studies describe students as actively engaged, eager to continue tasks beyond requirements, and more motivated to reflect on and discuss their projects, but the review does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Student feedback, observations of engagement/participation, motivation and enjoyment reports across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that collaborative, peer-to-peer, and inquiry-based approaches helped students develop discussion, problem-solving, and higher-order thinking around ML concepts. Included studies report students working in groups, explaining ideas to one another, and drawing conclusions from ML models, suggesting gains in collaboration and critical thinking rather than a single quantified effect.
finding.measure: Observed collaboration, peer discussion, inquiry/higher-order thinking tasks, and related student reflections

paper_profiles.title: Medical artificial intelligence readiness scale for medical students (MAIRS-MS) – development, validity and reliability study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops and validates a psychometric scale to measure perceived medical artificial intelligence readiness among medical students. The authors argue that future physicians will need foundational knowledge of AI, data science, and related ethical/legal issues, and that medical education needs a way to assess students’ preparedness for these topics.

Using a sequential exploratory mixed-method approach, the researchers generated items from expert input and literature review, then administered the resulting survey to undergraduate medical students at two public universities in Turkey. The study used exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis to refine the instrument from 27 to 22 items and to test its structure, reliability, and measurement invariance by gender.

The final MAIRS-MS showed a four-factor structure (cognition, ability, vision, ethics) with acceptable model fit and strong internal consistency overall (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.877). The authors conclude that the scale is a valid and reliable tool for assessing perceived AI readiness in medical students and may be useful for curriculum development and needs assessment in medical education. The paper does not evaluate an AI intervention or student learning/behavior outcome; it is an instrument development study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test an intervention or report changes in durable skills; instead, it develops a self-report readiness scale that includes cognitive/competency domains such as understanding AI concepts and using AI appropriately. The study only provides psychometric evidence for the instrument, not an outcome effect on metacognition, critical thinking, or related skills.
finding.measure: Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (MAIRS-MS) self-report survey items
finding.study_size: n=865 total (EFA n=544 valid, CFA n=321 valid)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the MAIRS-MS may be useful for curriculum development, learner needs assessment, and monitoring perceived readiness for AI-related training in medical schools. This is a proposed institutional use of the instrument rather than a measured institutional effect, so no causal impact estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived readiness scale intended for curriculum development / needs assessment

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating AI in foreign language education: An investigation into ChatGPT’s effect on foreign language learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how ChatGPT affected foreign language learning experiences in a university English program in Turkey. The authors focus on whether and how a teacher used ChatGPT in online classes to support reading, writing, grammar, vocabulary, and creative language activities, addressing a perceived gap in research on practical classroom use of generative AI in language education.

The study involved 13 preparatory-class university students aged 18–20 at a foundation university in Ankara. Over four weeks, the course instructor integrated ChatGPT into online English lessons delivered via Microsoft Teams, including reading, writing, grammar, vocabulary, and group discussion activities. Data came from semi-structured interviews and were analyzed thematically.

The paper concludes, based on student perceptions, that ChatGPT was associated with improved writing, grammar, vocabulary learning, motivation, and engagement, especially in interactive and creative tasks. Students also noted limitations such as limited speaking impact, no listening impact, occasional technical issues, and concerns about over-reliance, shortcuts, and misuse. Because the evidence is qualitative and based on student perceptions rather than measured pre/post outcomes, the study provides suggestive but not causal evidence of classroom engagement effects.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT as improving writing skills, including idea generation, sentence construction, and essay feedback. The finding is based on thematic analysis of interviews with 13 preparatory-class students after four weeks of ChatGPT-integrated online English instruction; no numeric effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of writing improvement; ChatGPT-assisted writing tasks and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported limited impact on speaking and no impact on listening, while noting that ChatGPT was useful for language practice in general. This was inferred from post-intervention interviews after a four-week implementation with 13 students; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of speaking and listening impact

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported increased motivation and engagement during ChatGPT-assisted online classes. The qualitative evidence comes from interviews with 13 preparatory-class students after four weeks of use, but the study did not report measured engagement scores or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of motivation and engagement

finding.finding_summary: Students described ChatGPT as supporting creative writing, interactive learning, and exploration of different cultures, which the authors interpret as fostering broader learning skills. These are interview-based perceptions from 13 students in a four-week classroom implementation; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of creativity, interaction, and cultural exploration

finding.finding_summary: Students said ChatGPT saved time and made research and task completion more efficient, especially by giving quick access to information and feedback. The result is qualitative and perception-based, derived from interviews with 13 university preparatory students after four weeks of use; no quantitative estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of time-saving and efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether four learning-related perception dimensions—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—are structured similarly when students learn with AI tools, and whether those relationships differ between middle and high school students. The authors frame the work as a response to the limited K-12 evidence on how students perceive AI-mediated learning, especially in computer science education.

The study was conducted in authentic extracurricular computer science classrooms with 53 students total: 25 middle school students aged 10–13 and 28 high school students aged 15–20 (11th–12th grade). Middle school students used Teachable Machine in an introductory AI course, while high school students used LLMs such as Gemini and Claude in vibe coding/Python activities. Students completed a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale items and open-ended responses about their AI experiences; the authors analyzed the data using correlations, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining.

The main finding is that student perceptions were generally positive, but the structure of those perceptions differed by age group. Middle school students showed strong positive correlations across the four dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluation of AI-supported learning, while high school students showed weaker and more differentiated correlations, indicating that they assessed usability, clarity, comfort, and motivation more independently. The paper concludes that AI integration in K-12 computer science should be developmentally responsive, with more scaffolding and clarity-oriented design for younger learners and more autonomy/technical sophistication for older learners.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive experiences with AI tools, and the aggregated perception dimensions of experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation were positively related. In the middle-school group, correlations among dimensions were strong (e.g., Experience–Clarity ρ=0.79; Clarity–Motivation ρ=0.60), while high-school students showed weaker, more differentiated associations (e.g., Experience–Motivation ρ=0.02), suggesting that AI use was positively perceived but interpreted differently by age group.
finding.measure: 17-item student perception questionnaire covering experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation; plus open-ended reflections

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how tinkering can be integrated into primary-school classroom practice through a model the authors call TIDE (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration). The broader problem addressed is how to preserve the open-ended, exploratory character of tinkering while still making it viable in formal schooling, especially in science/physics education. The authors argue that teachers often appreciate tinkering but struggle to connect it to curriculum and to handle the spontaneous scientific questions that arise.

The project described was carried out in Bologna, Italy, from September 2021 to September 2022 and involved 13 primary-school classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students. Teachers received professional development, access to a resource library, and documentation tools; the central classroom activity was a light-focused tinkering workshop (“Light Play”) implemented multiple times per class. Data came from teacher questionnaires and fishbowl documentation/protocol analysis, with some qualitative classroom documentation and teacher reflections.

The findings suggest that tinkering can increase student engagement, participation, collaboration, and agency, particularly among students teachers viewed as less school-oriented or disengaged. At the same time, the study shows that some high-achieving students experienced frustration in open-ended tasks, and that teachers often felt unprepared to pursue the scientific questions generated by the activity. Overall, the chapter concludes that tinkering can reveal student capabilities and support classroom re-engagement, but that stronger disciplinary support for teachers is needed if such practices are to be sustained and connected to science learning objectives.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that tinkering sessions surfaced authentic scientific questions about light and color, including why overlapping filters did not produce white light and how additive versus subtractive mixing work. However, teachers often felt unable to answer or extend these questions, indicating that the activity revealed scientific reasoning opportunities without fully translating them into sustained disciplinary investigation.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire and fishbowl protocol analysis of student-generated research questions and teacher responses

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported unexpectedly high engagement, participation, sustained attention, creativity, and willingness to participate during tinkering, especially among students typically seen as non-aligned or disengaged. In the questionnaire, 70% of teachers said tinkering revealed unexpected or partially expected student behavior, and responses described students as enthusiastic, active, and more willing to collaborate; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement, participation, attention, and enthusiasm in questionnaire and post-workshop reflections
finding.study_size: 20 teachers responding to the final questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: The chapter suggests positive effects on collaboration, self-reflection, mutual assistance, and problem-solving in the tinkering workshops. Teachers repeatedly noted that students worked well in pairs and groups, became protagonists in the activity, and learned to manage frustration and focus on process rather than immediate success, but these results are based on teacher perceptions rather than standardized measures.
finding.measure: Teacher descriptions of collaboration, self-reflection, mutual help, and persistence during tinkering tasks

finding.finding_summary: At the classroom and school level, the project aimed to integrate tinkering into everyday school life and found that most teachers did not isolate it as an extracurricular episode but incorporated it into classroom routines in varying ways. The chapter concludes that documentation practices and co-design can support institutional uptake, but that more disciplinary preparation is needed for broader and more durable integration.
finding.measure: Teacher reporting on integration of tinkering into classroom/disciplinary practice and final project reflections

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Healthcare: Why, How, and When?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
