This paper is a PRISMA-style scoping/systematic review of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in healthcare, focusing on why XAI is needed, how XAI methods work, and when they should be applied. The review surveys literature published from 2012 through early 2022 and synthesizes common XAI approaches such as dimension reduction, feature importance/selection, attention mechanisms, knowledge distillation, and surrogate models.

The paper is not an empirical study of a new intervention; instead, it organizes the healthcare XAI literature and discusses technical and governance issues including interpretability, fidelity, trust, validation, and limitations of post-hoc explanations. It concludes that while XAI may improve trustworthiness and practical adoption of AI in healthcare, stronger evidence, better evaluation methods, and more rigorous validation are still needed. No K-12 educational setting, student population, or teacher-facing AI tool is studied in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: High School Class for Gifted Pupils in Physics and Sciences and Pupils’ Skills Measured by Standard and Pisa Test
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates a specialized Serbian high school track for students with special abilities in physics, comparing their achievement in physics and science with students in standard grammar school and mathematics-track classes. The authors describe the program as a broadened curriculum that included physics, mathematics, computer science, chemistry, biology, laboratory equipment, PCs, university collaboration, and guest teaching. The main question is whether this specialized curriculum is associated with stronger pupil achievement and higher-order scientific competencies over time.

The study reports repeated achievement testing across cohorts from 2003–2008, including physics tests administered to special-class students and comparison groups in Nis and other Serbian cities. It also uses OECD/PISA 2006 science competency tasks to compare gifted physics pupils with grammar-school pupils and national samples. The paper finds that the special-class pupils generally outperform standard classes in physics and show higher proportions of top-level performance on PISA-style science tasks, especially among the older and more selected cohorts.

The evidence is descriptive and comparative rather than causal: there is no random assignment, and the paper notes small samples, cohort differences, and selection effects. Conclusions emphasize that carefully designed curricula and well-trained teachers may help gifted students maintain and extend their scientific reasoning, but the paper does not directly measure teacher-facing AI tools or classroom engagement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Gifted physics-class students scored higher than comparison groups on physics achievement and PISA science competency tasks. In one 4th-grade comparison, the special physics class scored 85.68% total on an external physics test versus 74.26% for the mathematics class and 34.47% for the standard class (n=9, 8, and 25 respectively). On PISA-style science tasks, the gifted 1st-grade physics class showed much higher top-level performance (about 80%) than grammar-school peers (0.3%), though the authors note age and selection differences.
finding.measure: Physics achievement tests; OECD/PISA 2006 science competency tasks; percentage correct and percentage in highest proficiency levels
finding.study_size: n=9-32 per comparison group; PISA sample included 11, 10, 14, 11, and 32 pupils across groups

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the specialized curriculum supports higher-order thinking, critical reasoning, and problem solving, as reflected in performance on complex physics and science tasks. For example, the special physics class outperformed standard classes on higher-complexity physics items and reached the highest PISA proficiency levels more often than comparison groups, suggesting stronger transfer of reasoning skills beyond routine content recall.
finding.measure: Complex-item physics test performance; PISA science proficiency levels; complex problem-solving and reasoning tasks

finding.finding_summary: Across multiple test administrations, the specialized 'physicists' class generally achieved better results than the standard class and, in some cases, comparable or better results than mathematics-track classes. For the first-generation 4th-grade cohort, the physics-specialized class reached 85.68% total on one external physics exam and 37.93% on another internal exam, compared with 34.47% and 14.32% for the standard class.
finding.measure: Standardized and custom physics achievement tests
finding.study_size: n=7-25 per group depending on test

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure engagement, motivation, or on-task behavior, but it repeatedly frames the program as designed to increase intrinsic and instrumental motivation for physics and sciences. Conclusions also state that the attractive curriculum, guest lecturers, laboratory work, excursions, book support, and awards helped attract better pupils and increase enrollment over generations.
finding.measure: Author interpretation of program attractiveness, student enrollment growth, and stated motivation goals

paper_profiles.title: Creative Problem Solving in Intelligent Agents: A Framework and Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys creative problem solving (CPS) in artificial intelligence, focusing on how agents can solve previously unachievable tasks by expanding their conceptual space. The authors propose a framework that organizes CPS research around problem formulation, knowledge representation, knowledge manipulation, and evaluation, and they connect these ideas to broader concepts in computational creativity.

The review covers planning-based, reinforcement-learning-based, and hybrid CPS approaches for autonomous agents, especially robots operating in novel or unstructured environments. It discusses symbolic, non-symbolic, and hybrid representations, as well as methods for discovering new actions, tools, structures, and policies. The paper’s main contribution is conceptual synthesis rather than new empirical evidence.

This paper does not study K-12 classrooms, teacher-facing AI tools, or student engagement outcomes. It is a domain survey in AI/robotics, and no educational intervention, grade band, subject area, or classroom implementation is reported. As a result, it provides no direct evidence relevant to student classroom engagement in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of High School Programme for Gifted Pupils in Physics and Sciences in Serbia - Experience in Regional Cooperation - SEENET-MTP Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates a specialized high school physics/science program for gifted students in Serbia, comparing students in the special class with students in standard grammar school classes and special mathematics classes. The authors are interested in whether the broadened curriculum, extra laboratory work, university collaboration, and related enrichment activities are associated with stronger student achievement and better perceptions of teaching and learning.

The evaluation uses repeated test data collected across multiple cohorts from 2003 to 2010, including physics tests, PISA science competency tasks, and an external science knowledge test administered by the Serbian Ministry of Education. The sample includes high school students in Nis and comparison groups from other Serbian schools/classes. Results consistently show higher science and physics achievement for the special physics class than for control groups, especially on problem solving and higher-order science tasks.

The paper also reports student and teacher perceptions from the external evaluation, with special-class students rating their program and teacher-student relationships more positively and reporting more opportunities for research, project work, and experimental activities. The evidence is largely observational and descriptive rather than causal, and it does not study teacher-facing AI tools or direct classroom engagement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the special physics class outperformed comparison groups on physics and science assessments, especially on higher-complexity and problem-solving items. Across several cohorts and test administrations, the paper reports substantially higher totals for the special class (e.g., 85.68% vs. 74.26% vs. 34.47% on the spring 2007 physics test; 22% higher results on the external science knowledge test for physics tasks), indicating stronger scientific reasoning and application skills.
finding.measure: Physics tests, PISA 2006 science competency tasks, and external science knowledge test
finding.study_size: multiple cohorts; exact pooled n not_reported (examples include n=9, 7, 20, 11, 10, 36, 38, 47 across subgroup tests)

finding.finding_summary: The external evaluation found that students in the special physics class rated their program and teacher-student relationships more positively than comparison students. They reported greater opportunities for research, project design, and experimental work, and gave significantly higher ratings for teacher support of independence, active participation, respect, and creativity (reported means around 4.7-4.8/5.0 versus 3.0-3.8/5.0 in other classes).
finding.measure: Student and teacher questionnaires on curriculum, teaching, extracurricular activities, and teacher-student relationship
finding.study_size: special physics class students n=36; comparison groups n=38 and n=47; teachers n=12; school management n=5

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the special program supports higher-order thinking and problem solving, and reports better performance on tasks requiring complex reasoning. The authors also note that students perceived stronger support for independence and creativity, which aligns with durable-skill development, though the paper does not report a standardized durable-skills measure.
finding.measure: Higher-order physics/science test items and PISA science proficiency levels; student perception items about independence and creativity

paper_profiles.title: AI-Fuzzy Markup Language with Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a descriptive report on the 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning, including related elementary-school participation. The event aimed to introduce students and teachers to computational intelligence concepts such as fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation, and to provide hands-on AIoT/FML learning experiences.

The approach combined lectures, workshops, and co-learning activities using AI-FML tools, NUWA Lab, AI-FML learning platforms, and robots such as Kebbi Air. The program was delivered in both physical and virtual formats in Taiwan, with participants also attending from Japan, Indonesia, and other countries. The paper describes the workshop tasks and learning framework, but it does not evaluate a teacher-facing AI intervention with a control group or experimental comparison.

Evidence presented is based on attendance, short reports, and feedback surveys from participants. The authors conclude that participants appeared to understand core CI concepts better than in prior schools and that the event may help stimulate student interest in future research and AI-related fields. However, the paper is primarily a qualitative program report with perceived outcomes rather than a causal study of student engagement or classroom behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants found the summer school engaging and that the event helped stimulate interest in computational intelligence and future research. This conclusion is based on short reports and feedback surveys from 80 attendees, but no standardized engagement measure or causal comparison is provided.
finding.measure: participant feedback surveys and short reports

finding.finding_summary: The workshop tasks emphasized problem solving, collaborative group work, and presenting short reports, suggesting gains in collaboration and applied thinking. The paper states that participants understood CI principles to a higher degree than in previous schools, but it does not report quantitative learning or collaboration outcomes.
finding.measure: short reports, workshop participation, and participant feedback
finding.study_size: n=78 attended at least two-thirds of lectures/workshops; n=80 submitted reports/feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the summer school as a successful outreach effort that broadened participation in computational intelligence education across elementary, junior high, senior high, university students, and teachers from multiple countries. Evidence is descriptive, based on attendance, certificates issued, and feedback comments rather than institutional outcome measures.
finding.measure: attendance, certificate completion, and feedback comments
finding.study_size: n=214 registered; n=78 attended at least two-thirds of activities

paper_profiles.title: Cyberbullying of High School Students in Bangladesh: An Exploratory Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines cyberbullying experiences, online activities, and cyber-safety awareness among high school students in Bangladesh. The authors frame the problem as a growing safety issue for adolescents in a context with limited prior local research, and they aim to identify which online behaviors are associated with victimization, how often cyberbullying occurs, and how students respond when it happens.

The study uses a survey administered in May 2018 to 21 students in classes 8–10 from urban and rural areas of Bangladesh. The questionnaire collected demographics, cyberbullying victim/perpetrator experiences, bystander responses, help-seeking behavior, and opinions about prevention. Findings are descriptive: most students reported using the internet at home, common activities included talking with friends and searching for information, and many students viewed cyberbullying as upsetting and lacking adequate school-based support.

The paper concludes that cyberbullying awareness is low and that schools and teachers should do more to teach cyber-safety strategies and integrate cyberbullying into the curriculum. It proposes school ICT policies, discussion-based prevention, and parent involvement, but it does not test any AI tool, teacher-facing intervention, or student engagement outcome. Because it is a small cross-sectional survey with no intervention and no causal comparison, the evidence is descriptive and correlational rather than experimental.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students perceive limited school support for cyberbullying and recommends school-level policy and curriculum changes, but it does not evaluate any implemented policy, program, or institutional intervention. The evidence is descriptive only (n=21) and contains no causal estimate of institutional impact.
finding.measure: Survey responses about help-seeking, school staff support, and opinions on cyber-safety curriculum/policy

paper_profiles.title: High School Computer Science Participation: A 6-Year Enrollment Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This research brief examines long-run participation in high school computer science (CS) courses across seven public high schools in large suburban districts in the Northeastern United States. The motivating question is whether access to CS has translated into sustained student enrollment, and whether participation patterns differ by sex and race over time.

Using de-identified administrative course-enrollment data from the 2018-2019 through 2023-2024 academic years, the authors analyzed 329,961 course enrollments from 15,861 unique students in grades 9-12. They classified courses as CS or non-CS using SCED codes, and separately examined foundational CS and advanced CS participation. The study does not evaluate an AI intervention or any teacher-facing AI tool; it is an enrollment-trend analysis of CS participation.

Results show that overall CS participation was relatively stable, rising from 10% of students enrolling in at least one CS course in 2018-2019 to 15% in 2022-2023, then declining to 13% in 2023-2024. Participation differed by sex: males increased from 13% to 18% over the study period, while female participation remained at 7% in the first and last years and generally declined in between. Racial participation patterns varied, with Asian students participating at the highest rates and other groups showing smaller or less consistent changes. The authors conclude that access has expanded, but participation remains limited and uneven, indicating a need for continued work on enrollment barriers and student engagement in CS pathways.

finding.finding_summary: Across seven public high schools, overall participation in CS courses was relatively stable over six academic years, increasing from 10% of students enrolled in at least one CS course in 2018-2019 (636 of 6,256) to 15% in 2022-2023, then falling to 13% in 2023-2024. The study reports substantial subgroup differences by sex and race, but no causal intervention effect because this is an observational enrollment trend analysis rather than an AI study.
finding.measure: Percentage of students enrolled in at least one high school CS course; enrollment trends by sex and race

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses student engagement conceptually, but it does not directly measure classroom engagement, attention, participation, on-task behavior, or related affective outcomes. The only directly observed outcome is course enrollment/participation in CS, which is an institutional participation metric rather than a student engagement measure.
finding.measure: Course enrollment/participation in CS

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers can design AI education that is more accessible by embedding AI concepts into core subjects rather than treating AI as a standalone computing topic. The motivation is that many teachers lack AI expertise and many existing AI curricula are difficult to adopt in regular classrooms, especially outside computer science.

The authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse grade bands and subject areas. Teachers were introduced to AI concepts and tools, then worked in small groups with researchers to draft integrated AI lesson plans for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The workshop also included prompts around ethics, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and participants completed pre/post questionnaires plus submitted design artifacts.

The study is not an intervention study with student outcomes; instead, it qualitatively analyzes teacher discussions, workshop artifacts, and survey responses to identify design considerations for integrated AI curriculum. The main conclusion is that teachers value scaffolds for evaluation and ethics, want student engagement supports such as real-world anchors and gamification, and see promising entry points for integrating AI through data, reflection, and ethics in non-CS subjects. The paper argues that teacher co-design can improve the accessibility and classroom fit of AI curriculum, but it does not test effects on student engagement or learning in actual K-12 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that integrated AI curriculum would need clear logistical supports and explicit tool guidance to be implementable in classrooms. The workshop analysis suggests the co-design process helped surface practical requirements for lesson structure, technology choice, and scaffolding, but this was based on teacher perceptions rather than classroom implementation outcomes (n=15).
finding.measure: Teacher workshop discussions, pre/post questionnaires, and curriculum artifacts about feasibility/logistics

finding.finding_summary: Engagement was a central design consideration, with teachers proposing real-world anchors, student-driven topics, competition, and gamification to increase student interest in AI-integrated lessons. The evidence is purely perceived/design-oriented: teachers discussed how these features could support engagement, collaboration, and reflection, but no student engagement outcomes were measured (n=15).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement and engagement-oriented curriculum design features

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes collaboration, reflection, and critical thinking as intended outcomes of the co-designed curricula. Teachers described group work, peer discussion, and reflection on data, bias, and real-world implications as ways to support these skills, but these are proposed curriculum features rather than measured student effects (n=15).
finding.measure: Teacher-generated curriculum designs and qualitative discussion of collaboration/reflection/critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: One co-designed curriculum targeted ESL and focused on pronunciation practice, vocabulary, and language learning through an AI-powered pronunciation application. This is substantively about language instruction, but the paper reports only the design of the curriculum and teacher rationale, not student language outcomes or classroom implementation results (n=15 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher-designed ESL curriculum concepts and lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: Another co-designed curriculum targeted literacy for students with learning disabilities, using vocabulary words and image classification to support literacy instruction. The finding is limited to the existence and content of the designed curriculum; no student reading/writing outcomes were measured (n=15 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher-designed literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities

finding.finding_summary: The paper produced integrated AI lesson concepts for social studies and other non-CS subjects, showing that teachers could connect AI concepts to core curriculum such as government, ethics, and subject-specific data. This is a design/feasibility finding from teacher co-design rather than a measured student academic outcome (n=15).
finding.measure: Teacher co-designed integrated curriculum artifacts and discussion of subject integration

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether core learning-perception dimensions—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—remain interrelated when students learn with AI, and whether those relationships differ between middle school and high school students. The motivation is to understand how student perceptions of AI-mediated learning are structured across developmental stages, particularly in K-12 computer science contexts where AI tools are increasingly being introduced.

The study was conducted in extracurricular computer science classes in authentic classroom settings. A total of 53 students participated: 25 middle school students (ages 10–13) and 28 high school students (grades 11–12, ages 15–20). Middle school students used Teachable Machine in an introductory AI module, while high school students used generative AI tools such as Gemini and Claude during Python programming activities with prompting instruction. Students completed a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale and open-ended questions, and the authors analyzed correlations, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text-mining outputs.

Findings show generally positive perceptions of AI use in both groups, but with distinct developmental patterns. Middle school students exhibited strong positive correlations across the four learning dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluative pattern in which positive experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation tend to move together. High school students showed weaker and more differentiated relationships among dimensions, indicating a more critical appraisal in which usability, clarity, and motivation are judged more independently. The paper concludes that AI implementation in K-12 CS should be age-sensitive, with more structured scaffolding for younger students and more nuanced support for older learners.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive perceptions of the AI-supported learning experience, including comfort, motivation, and overall experience. In the middle school group, the four dimensions were strongly intercorrelated (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.79; Clarity-Motivation ρ=0.60), suggesting that positive perceptions in one area generalized to the others (n=25 middle school; n=28 high school; total n=53).
finding.measure: Questionnaire measures of experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation (Likert-scale survey items and open-ended responses)
finding.std_deviation: 0.85 (overall sample Cronbach's alpha? no, SD not reported for the construct-level finding)

finding.finding_summary: The study touches durable-skill-like evaluative processes such as comprehension and critical differentiation of AI output, but the central evidence is about perceptions rather than performance. High school students showed weaker or near-zero correlations between experience and motivation (ρ=0.02) and between experience and comfort (ρ=0.16), indicating more differentiated judgments of the AI tool and its learning value (n=28 high school).
finding.measure: Correlation patterns among survey dimensions and text-mined open-ended reflections about AI's influence on learning

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school  Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a new German-language benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on middle-school curriculum content. The authors assemble 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, with questions grounded in real textbooks and some adversarial items designed to be unanswerable from the image alone. They then evaluate 13 open-weight VLMs using automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring.

The paper is not an intervention study in classrooms and does not examine teacher-facing AI tools or student engagement outcomes. Instead, it focuses on model benchmark performance across domains such as math, history, biology, music, religion, sports, and arts, reporting that even the strongest systems achieve under 45% overall accuracy. The main conclusion is that middle-school-level multimodal tasks in German remain challenging for current VLMs and that performance on public benchmarks does not reliably predict performance on this dataset.

finding.finding_summary: This benchmark study evaluates VLM accuracy on middle-school curriculum questions across nine subjects, not student learning. Across 2,038 questions on 486 images, the best model achieved 43.26% overall accuracy (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with domain peaks around 54% in history and religion and especially low performance in music and math. The result indicates substantial limitations in current VLMs on K-12 subject-content understanding.
finding.measure: Open-ended benchmark answer accuracy on middle-school curriculum questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper also assesses model performance on adversarial questions intended to test whether systems can avoid unsupported inferences and say when an answer is not present in the image. Overall adversarial accuracy was much lower than regular accuracy, with the best models reaching 29.62%-32.83% overall and many models far lower, showing that current VLMs often fail on uncertainty recognition and robust reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial, unanswerable image-question items
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions; adversarial subset within benchmark

finding.finding_summary: Math was one of the studied school subjects and was relatively weak for the models. Best math accuracy was 34.09% for Qwen2.5VL 32B, while other models ranged much lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%), showing that even basic geometry and calculation questions were frequently missed.
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle-school math questions

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical conceptual review and synthesis of literature on the integration of AI in K-12 STEM education, with a strong focus on ethical concerns such as bias, privacy, surveillance, equity, and transparency. Rather than presenting new empirical data, it surveys recent scholarship and policy-oriented sources to frame how AI tools like intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies may affect teaching and learning in schools.

The paper proposes a three-phased implementation roadmap and a four-phase professional development model for educators, grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy. It argues that responsible AI adoption in K-12 STEM should be equity-centered, supported by teacher PD, and accompanied by governance safeguards, bias audits, and student data protections.

Although the paper references student engagement surveys and other outcomes in illustrative implementation scenarios, it does not report original empirical findings from a specific K-12 study. Its main contribution is a normative and framework-oriented synthesis aimed at guiding future implementation and research rather than evaluating a discrete AI intervention in schools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI integration in K-12 STEM can support personalized learning and operational efficiency, but only if institutions address significant risks related to algorithmic bias, privacy, surveillance, and governance. It proposes a phased implementation roadmap, teacher PD model, and mandatory ethics/equity audits, but these are framework recommendations rather than outcomes from an evaluated intervention.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of ethical, policy, and implementation considerations

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-powered tools such as automated assessment and intelligent tutoring systems may reduce teacher workload by automating scoring, delivering real-time feedback, and supporting scalable personalization. However, these claims are discussed at a conceptual level and are not supported by original effect estimates in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / assessment automation / implementation efficiency (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses student engagement, agency, and critical engagement with AI as intended benefits of ethically designed AI integration and AI literacy activities. In one implementation scenario, student engagement surveys are mentioned as a planned evaluation measure, but no results are reported, so the evidence is aspirational rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Student engagement surveys (mentioned in proposed pilot scenario)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and critical algorithmic literacy as key student outcomes of AI ethics instruction in K-12 STEM. It cites prior work and proposes project-based and role-playing activities, but does not present original data demonstrating gains in these skills.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / AI ethics literacy / ethical reasoning (conceptual and cited literature)

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames AI as potentially supporting STEM learning through adaptive feedback and assessment, while also warning that over-reliance may constrain scientific curiosity and higher-order reasoning. These claims are synthesized from prior literature and examples, not tested empirically in this paper.
finding.measure: STEM learning / scientific reasoning / knowledge integration (conceptual synthesis)

paper_profiles.title: Who is Helping Whom? Student Concerns about AI-Teacher Collaboration in Higher Education Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive AI-assisted classroom analysis and intervention systems in higher education, with particular attention to AI tools that observe students and notify teachers so they can provide targeted help. The authors motivate the work as a response to growing deployment of classroom sensing and learning analytics systems, and they ask how students understand the implications of AI-teacher collaboration for classroom dynamics, fairness, privacy, and teaching practice.

The study uses the Story Completion Method with 65 higher-education participants from China and Australia. Participants responded to speculative classroom scenarios involving facial recognition, emotion recognition, gaze tracking, real-time behavior analysis, early warning, and adaptive recommendations. The paper is not a direct intervention study; instead, it elicits perceived consequences of AI-mediated classroom observation and teacher intervention.

Findings center on students’ concerns that AI can decontextualize learning, oversimplify behavior, and create unfair evaluations, especially for quieter, introverted, or otherwise atypical students. Participants also described tensions in human-AI cooperation, including bias, power imbalances, and the risk that teachers may over-rely on AI outputs. A major theme is that surveillance-like AI monitoring may prompt students to change behavior strategically—pretending, performing, gaming the system, or resisting—which could undermine the accuracy and effectiveness of the AI itself. The paper also reports some positive perceptions, such as AI potentially helping teachers notice struggling students and distribute attention more evenly, but these are speculative and perceived rather than measured outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily elicits perceived effects of teacher-facing AI on student engagement-related behavior. Participants anticipated that AI monitoring could cause students to become more cautious, pretend engagement, avoid mistakes, force participation, or otherwise alter behavior to manage how they are seen; at the same time, some imagined AI helping introverted or struggling students receive attention and support. These are speculative perceptions from 65 higher-education participants, not observed behavioral effects.
finding.measure: Story completion narratives about perceived engagement, participation, attention, and behavior under AI monitoring/intervention

finding.finding_summary: Participants thought AI could increase teachers’ efficiency by helping identify students needing support, distributing teacher attention, and providing real-time analytic cues for intervention. However, they also worried that student gaming, performativity, and distorted data would reduce the effectiveness of the system and make AI-driven evaluation less trustworthy. No quantitative efficiency outcome was measured; the evidence is wholly perceived and speculative.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher attention allocation, intervention targeting, and evaluation efficiency in story scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies perceived institutional and governance consequences of AI-teacher collaboration, especially fairness, bias, authority, and surveillance in educational decision-making. Participants argued that AI may reproduce or amplify bias, shift authority from teachers to systems, and create power imbalances, while also being viewed by some as a potentially fair third party. These are qualitative perceptions from 65 participants rather than causal institutional effects.
finding.measure: Perceived fairness, bias, authority, and governance implications of AI-assisted classroom analysis

paper_profiles.title: Can AI support student engagement in classroom activities in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a conversational AI tool, specifically ChatGPT, can support student engagement in in-class activities in a large undergraduate computer science course. The authors frame the problem as low engagement in large classes, especially in hybrid or online settings where peer discussion and instructor interaction can be limited.

The study used a within-subject classroom design in an undergraduate core software engineering/computer science course at a U.S. public university. Students completed two 50-minute Friday activity sessions one week apart: one in which they discussed a reading with ChatGPT and one in which they discussed a different reading with peers. Engagement was measured using self-report scales (student engagement as a factor scale and ASPECT), perceived usefulness, a short knowledge self-report sequence, a post-activity quiz, and qualitative coding of chat transcripts for questions, feedback comments, follow-ups, and off-topic behavior.

Results suggested that the AI condition was rated higher on self-reported engagement, perceived usefulness, and quiz performance than the peer-discussion condition. The AI conversations were also more verbose and contained more feedback and follow-up, while off-topic responses were rare. The authors conclude that instructor-supervised ChatGPT use may help support cognitive engagement and learning in large higher-education classrooms, but note limitations including the short duration, non-counterbalanced within-subject design, and reliance on self-reported engagement measures.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject classroom study with 101 paired undergraduate participants, the ChatGPT condition produced significantly higher self-reported engagement than the peer-discussion condition. On the student engagement as a factor scale, the AI activity had a mean of 2.89 (SD=0.43) versus 2.76 (SD=0.45) without AI, z=-3.45, p<.001; on ASPECT, the AI activity scored 4.73 (SD=1.08) versus 4.33 (SD=1.06), z=-2.47, p=.014.
finding.measure: Self-reported student engagement as a factor scale; ASPECT (Assessing Student Perspective of Engagement in Class)

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines early implementation lessons from a seven-week classroom pilot of Colleague AI, a generative AI platform designed for teacher-directed use in secondary classrooms. The study asks how teachers design and implement AI-assisted instructional tools, how teacher judgment and AI competency shape student-AI interactions, and what supports are needed for effective integration.

Twenty-one in-service teachers from five Washington State school settings used four features of the platform: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. Across more than 600 students in grades 6-12, the study collected teacher surveys, weekly reflections, planning forms, interviews, group meetings, and platform logs. The report is explicitly a co-design/pilot study rather than a controlled efficacy trial, and it emphasizes implementation patterns, teacher perceptions, and descriptive usage evidence.

The main conclusion is that teacher framing, scaffolding, and AI fluency are central to whether the tools produce meaningful classroom value. The strongest reported benefits were in structured student-AI conversations and formative feedback cycles, where AI acted as a teacher-mediated "third agent" supporting inquiry, revision, and personalized feedback. However, the evidence is largely descriptive and self-reported, with no direct causal estimate of student learning or engagement outcomes from the AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the Teaching Aide supported student conversation, inquiry, and participation in secondary classrooms, with particularly notable benefits for multilingual learners who became more willing to contribute after practicing with the AI. However, engagement and learning were uneven across grade bands and subjects, and some classrooms experienced surface-level or off-task interaction rather than sustained academic dialogue.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement in AI-assisted conversations; qualitative observations of student participation and classroom discourse
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers reporting on 114 Teaching Aide conversations across up to 600 students

finding.finding_summary: The AI tools were used across ELA, Spanish, history/civics, and interdisciplinary subjects to support writing, prewriting, brainstorming, and proficiency-oriented feedback. Teachers especially noted that AI-supported conversations and narrative feedback helped students improve essay quality and language-production tasks, though outcomes varied by subject and implementation quality.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported instructional use and perceived student learning in ELA, Spanish, and other non-STEM subjects

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that student engagement increased when teachers framed AI use clearly, modeled participation norms, and tied activities to meaningful class products. Teachers reported that AI conversations and feedback sometimes helped anxious or hesitant students participate, and that students showed visible self-improvement behavior in response to feedback. The report does not provide causal estimates, but it consistently describes improved engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate when the teacher-mediated design was strong.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated engagement, participation, and student response to AI feedback; exit tickets and reflection forms
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide; n=13 teachers for assessment feedback; platform logs from 33 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests that AI-supported activities promoted deeper inquiry, evidence-based reasoning, revision, and metacognitive reflection when teachers provided clear prompts and follow-up structures. Teachers described AI as helping students generate drafts, receive feedback, and revise work, and they used the platform to surface misconceptions and next steps. These findings are descriptive and based on teacher reports rather than direct student performance measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported inquiry quality, revision cycles, and evidence-based reasoning in AI-supported activities

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI grading and Student Growth Insights features reduced workload by accelerating rubric creation, feedback generation, and review of student patterns. In platform logs, AI graded a median of 92.2% of submitted work, and teachers described the narrative feedback as a useful first draft that saved time and supported faster turnaround for formative assessment.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, rubric-generation and feedback efficiency; platform log metrics on AI grading coverage
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers; 58 assessment records; 936 student submissions across 33 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: The study frames AI integration as a teacher-student-AI collaborative model and reports that school and district partnerships, privacy policies, and teacher co-design were important implementation conditions. The evidence is institutional and implementation-focused rather than outcome-based, but it suggests that adoption depends on governance, teacher oversight, and workflow alignment.
finding.measure: Implementation conditions, district partnership structure, and teacher co-design process
finding.study_size: n=5 Washington State districts and 1 independent school

paper_profiles.title: Assessment of Personalized Learning in Immersive and Intelligent Virtual Classroom on Student Engagement
paper_profiles.population: Not clearly K-12; mixed/unspecified participants (n=8) in a virtual classroom case study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether immersive, intelligent virtual classrooms can be used to assess personalized learning and student engagement, with a particular emphasis on eye-tracking as an engagement-measurement method. The authors motivate the work by arguing that conventional self-report and platform-log data may be too limited to capture real engagement, and they propose a VR-based classroom application that collects gaze and eye-movement data while students interact with learning content.

The study develops a Unity-based VR application on a PICO VR 4 Pro headset and uses embedded eye-tracking to generate static-gaze, dynamic-gaze, and saccadic metrics. The paper reports a small case study with eight participants who completed an 11-item questionnaire covering cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement. Results are presented as participant-level mean scores and descriptive analysis; the paper does not report a controlled comparison, random assignment, or inferential effect sizes.

The main conclusion is that 3D eye-tracking paradigms may be useful for assessing engagement in virtual classrooms, and that metrics such as gaze patterns, fixation duration, and saccadic reaction time could indicate attentiveness and cognitive processing. The paper also argues that personalized learning in VR was perceived positively by most participants, but it remains primarily a prototype/case-study paper rather than direct evidence of K-12 student outcomes. It does not provide clear K-12 classroom evidence, nor does it isolate a teacher-facing AI tool used by teachers or schools to change student engagement.

finding.finding_summary: In an eight-participant case study, participants reported generally high perceived behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement in the VR personalized-learning environment. The paper describes higher participation in discussion and positive subjective responses to personalized learning, but it does not report a causal comparison, effect size, or statistical test.
finding.measure: 11-item Likert questionnaire covering cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement; descriptive eye-tracking metrics

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that eye-tracking metrics such as gaze patterns, fixation duration, and saccadic reaction time can reflect attentional processing and engagement-related self-regulation in a virtual classroom. Evidence is descriptive and based on a small case study, so the paper supports measurement feasibility more than demonstrated student-skill gains.
finding.measure: Eye-tracking metrics (gaze patterns, fixation duration, saccadic reaction time)

paper_profiles.title: Competing Visions of Ethical AI: A Case Study of OpenAI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how OpenAI publicly frames “ethical AI” over time, asking how the company’s web articles and publications deploy terms such as ethics, safety, alignment, responsibility, and related concepts. The authors treat AI ethics as a discursive field and analyze a longitudinal corpus of OpenAI-authored public communications from 2015 through July 2025.

Methodologically, the study combines qualitative content analysis with computational text analysis, including keyword frequency tracking, n-gram clustering, and PCA-based topic visualization. The corpus includes 424 OpenAI website articles and 30 OpenAI-authored or co-authored publications, with separate attention to open web communications versus academic-register outputs.

The paper finds that OpenAI’s public discourse overwhelmingly foregrounds safety, risk, compliance, and alignment, while explicit ethics language is rare and often superficial when it appears. The authors argue that this pattern signals an ethics-washing tendency: ethics is not absent entirely, but is displaced into peripheral references, tagging conventions, and narrow technical or reputational framings rather than sustained normative engagement. The paper does not study K-12 education, student engagement, or teacher-facing AI tools, so it is not directly relevant to the requested sub-question.

finding.finding_summary: The study provides descriptive evidence that OpenAI’s public-facing discourse shifted toward safety, risk, governance, and alignment while explicit ethics language remained rare. Across 424 web articles, only 16 (3.8%) contained an ethics-related term; among 30 publications, 31 of 180 reviewed texts (17.2%) used such language, usually only a few times and often in peripheral contexts. This is a discourse-analysis finding about institutional framing, not an intervention effect.
finding.measure: Qualitative content analysis and computational text analysis of OpenAI public communications; keyword frequencies, thematic clustering, and manual audit
finding.study_size: n=454 documents (424 web articles; 30 publications used for publication corpus analysis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure operational efficiency outcomes, but it does describe how OpenAI’s discourse emphasizes compliance, evaluation, and procedural safety over ethics. No quantitative productivity or workload outcomes are reported, so any operational implication is interpretive rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Discourse patterns around safety, policy, governance, and responsibility

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how teachers can use generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4o, to personalize middle school mathematics tasks for students’ interests. The central question is not about student achievement, but about the practical process of teacher-in-the-loop personalization: what prompting moves teachers use, how much time the process takes, and how students respond to the personalized problems.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated in training and then used ChatGPT to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems for two units (proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities). Teachers created 143 personalized problems for 521 students in ASSISTments. Data came from chat logs, teacher video/audio, and student interest/closeness ratings plus open-ended feedback. The study found that teachers often needed multiple prompts to get acceptable outputs, spent about 4 minutes per problem on average, and focused heavily on realism and matching popular-culture interests. Students generally preferred finer-grained, specific references over broad topics, and their ratings were highest when teachers used about 3–5 prompts per problem. Teachers did not become clearly more efficient over time; instead, they used more prompts and more time in the second unit, though student ratings also improved.

The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop generative AI can support personalized math task design, but broad-grain personalization is time-consuming and may not align with students’ preferences for highly specific personalization. It also argues that teacher judgment remains important for checking realism, appropriateness, and mathematical clarity, even if doing so limits scalability.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure math achievement directly, but it does examine teacher-created mathematics problem quality and how students rated personalized math tasks. Using 3–5 prompts per problem was associated with higher student ratings of interestingness and closeness to students’ interests by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073), suggesting a modest improvement in the quality of personalized math task design.
finding.measure: Student ratings of personalized mathematics problems for interestingness and closeness to interests; teacher prompting/time in creating math problems
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 143 personalized math problems; 7 teachers
finding.std_deviation: problem creation time SD=165.7 seconds; prompts per problem SD=2.6

finding.finding_summary: Student reactions indicated that the personalized tasks were often perceived as more interesting when they matched students’ interests, especially specific popular-culture references. Across 454 responses to the interest question, 163 responses implied the problem was interesting and 243 implied it was not; average interestingness ratings were 2.46/5 overall, rising from 2.27/5 in Unit 4 to 2.56/5 in Unit 6 (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student self-reported interestingness ratings and open-ended feedback about personalized math problems
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 responses to interest question
finding.std_deviation: overall interestingness SD=1.24; Unit 4 SD=1.17; Unit 6 SD=1.26

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing AI personalization was time-consuming rather than clearly efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems (3.2 prompts/problem) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (about 4 minutes; SD=165.7), with no clear evidence of becoming faster over time; in fact, Unit 6 required more prompts and more time than Unit 4. The Unit 6 increase was statistically significant for both prompts (B=1.26, SE=0.41, t=3.08, p=0.0025) and time (B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher prompt counts and time spent interacting with ChatGPT while creating personalized math problems
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 prompts; B=70.4 seconds; 3.2 prompts/problem; 246 seconds/problem
finding.std_deviation: prompts per problem SD=2.6; time per problem SD=165.7 seconds

finding.finding_summary: The study has implications for classroom and curriculum implementation of teacher-facing generative AI, but it does not evaluate policy or institutional change directly. It suggests that teacher-in-the-loop personalization may be feasible only at broad grain sizes and requires significant planning time and teacher judgment, which constrains scalability for classroom and school adoption.
finding.measure: Implementation feasibility and teacher/student reactions in a school-based ASSISTments context

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating AI-Powered Learning Assistants in Engineering Higher Education: Student Engagement, Ethical Challenges, and Policy Implications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how undergraduate engineering students used and perceived an AI-powered learning assistant, the Educational AI Hub, in two civil and environmental engineering courses at a large R1 public university. The paper asks whether students found the tool useful, how they compared it with human support, what ethical concerns shaped use, and how engagement related to trust, comfort, and perceived usefulness.

The intervention was a course-integrated AI assistant offering notes generation, chatbot support, flashcards, quiz generation/grading, coding help, and syllabus support. The study used a mixed-methods explanatory sequential design with pre/post surveys, system usage logs, and qualitative coding of student prompts. Across 65 survey participants (48 active users), students reported that the tool was convenient and comfortable to use, especially for homework and conceptual understanding, but they were less convinced it improved grades and remained concerned about academic integrity and policy ambiguity. Engagement was positively associated with comfort and perceived helpfulness, and negatively associated with distrust.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI assistants can support student engagement in higher education when they are task-aligned, accessible, and clearly governed, but that trust and ethical clarity are key barriers. The findings are descriptive and correlational rather than causal, and they concern undergraduate engineering rather than K-12 settings. Because the paper is outside the requested K-12 teacher-facing AI scope, it does not provide direct evidence for the sub-question about classroom engagement outcomes in K-12 teacher-use contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable engagement-related perceptions of the Educational AI Hub, especially convenience and comfort, but also notable apprehension and ethical concern. In post-survey responses, 68% rated the tool as more convenient than human help, 47% felt more comfortable using it, and 49% reported apprehension about AI use in the course, indicating simultaneously positive and hesitant engagement.
finding.measure: Post-usage survey ratings of convenience, comfort, apprehension, and trust related to the AI Hub
finding.study_size: n=45-47 (item-level survey samples); 48 active users total

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the AI Hub supported students’ conceptual understanding and task-specific problem solving, which are related to durable skills such as metacognition and independent learning. Students said the tool helped them learn course concepts (61%) and complete homework (63%), and chatbot queries were often about conceptual/theory help (30.4%) and assignment/class help (19.5%).
finding.measure: Post-survey usefulness ratings and qualitative coding of chatbot questions
finding.study_size: n=46 for usefulness items; 494+ coded query topics across 581 chatbot messages

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the AI assistant as improving access to help and reducing friction in getting course support. Compared with human assistance, 68% found it more convenient, and usage logs showed heavy reliance on the chatbot (555 messages, used by 46 of 48 active users), suggesting the tool functioned as an efficient support channel rather than a replacement for instruction.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of convenience and system usage logs (message counts, feature use)
finding.study_size: n=48 active users; survey item Ns around 45-47
finding.std_deviation: SD=11.81 for total AI interactions; SD=9.437 for chatbot messages

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed strong interest in future AI integration but also significant concern about unclear policy and academic integrity boundaries. Eighty-three percent agreed using AI as an academic aid is ethical, 80% wanted similar tools in other courses, and 58% worried about being accused of misconduct, indicating that policy clarity and institutional guidance are central to adoption.
finding.measure: Post-survey attitudes toward ethics, policy restrictiveness, misconduct concerns, and future AI use

paper_profiles.title: Recognising the importance of preference change: A call for a coordinated multidisciplinary research effort in the age of AI
paper_profiles.venue: The AAAI-22 Workshop on AI For Behavior Change held at the Thirty-Sixth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual position article arguing that AI systems can change human preferences and that this phenomenon deserves a dedicated multidisciplinary research agenda, which the authors call ‘Preference Science.’ The central problem is not an educational intervention or empirical evaluation, but rather the ethical and scientific challenge of understanding how AI-powered systems, behavioral design, and choice architecture can shape people’s preferences over time.

The article synthesizes ideas from psychology, behavioral science, economics, philosophy, law, and machine learning to define preference broadly, distinguish first-order preferences from meta-preferences and preference-change preferences, and propose a causal framework linking behavior, capability, choice architecture, and preference. It discusses how recommender systems and behavior-change techniques can create feedback loops that alter preferences, and it argues that ethical and legal safeguards are needed to distinguish acceptable from manipulative influence.

This paper does not study a K-12 sample, a school-based intervention, or any student classroom outcome. It is a theoretical and normative paper focused on AI/behavior change generally, with examples drawn from consumer platforms and public policy rather than education research. No empirical evidence, implementation setting, comparator, or follow-up duration is reported because the paper is not an empirical study.

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (grades 3-12; mathematics teachers and their students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents TalkMoves, an AI-enabled application that automatically analyzes classroom recordings and gives K-12 mathematics teachers personalized feedback on their use of discourse practices known as accountable talk moves. The system combines automated speech recognition and transformer-based natural language processing to label teacher utterances in classroom transcripts, with the goal of helping teachers reflect on and improve discussion-based instruction.

The paper is primarily a technical systems and model-development study. It reports training and evaluating several sequence-classification models on 501 transcripts of K-12 math lessons, finding that transformer models substantially outperform a prior BiLSTM baseline for talk-move detection (best F1 = 79.33%, MCC = 0.7779 on the test set). The deployed application was piloted with 21 teachers in two midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019-2020 school year, but the reported evidence focuses on model performance and teacher use/feedback rather than causal impacts on student outcomes.

For the sub-question on student classroom engagement outcomes, the paper does not directly measure student engagement, attention, participation, on-task behavior, or related classroom behavior outcomes. It discusses engagement conceptually and references prior literature, and the system outputs feedback intended to improve discourse, but no student engagement outcome data, comparator analysis, or follow-up impact evaluation are reported. As a result, it does not provide direct K-12 evidence of teacher-facing AI affecting student engagement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not evaluate student mathematics achievement directly; instead, it evaluates model performance for detecting accountable talk moves in K-12 math lesson transcripts. The best transformer model (ROBERTA-LARGE) achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set for classifying six talk-move labels plus 'none' across 501 transcripts (176,757 sentences).
finding.measure: Talk-move classification performance on annotated K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames accountable talk as a means to support student engagement and equitable participation, but it does not directly measure any student engagement outcome. The only empirical results are on NLP model accuracy (e.g., F1 = 79.33%), not on student attention, participation, on-task behavior, or classroom engagement after teachers used the tool.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; engagement is only discussed as a theoretical rationale
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers piloting the application; no student engagement outcome sample reported

paper_profiles.title: AI & Data Competencies: Scaffolding holistic AI literacy in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter presents the AI & Data Acumen Learning Outcomes Framework, a structured curriculum and assessment framework intended to scaffold holistic AI literacy in higher education. The paper argues that AI literacy should extend beyond technical skills to include ethics, self-efficacy, collaboration, sociocultural awareness, innovation and creativity, cognitive skills, and technical competency, organized across four proficiency levels.

The chapter is not an empirical evaluation of a classroom intervention. Instead, it synthesizes literature and describes a task-force-driven framework development process at the University of Arizona, drawing on expert input, job-posting analysis, workforce surveys, and iterative review. The intended users are academic leaders, curriculum designers, instructors, and assessment specialists who want to embed AI literacy across university curricula, benchmark programs, and support faculty development.

The paper’s main conclusion is that higher education needs a flexible, transdisciplinary, and ethically grounded approach to AI education. It proposes the framework as a practical roadmap for curriculum design, learning activities, and assessment, but it does not report direct student outcome data, K-12 settings, or teacher-facing AI tools affecting classroom engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered learning environment for creative mathematical writing. The authors are interested in whether GenAI can support students in understanding math concepts, creating original math stories, and experiencing more interest and ownership in learning, while also identifying challenges such as overreliance on AI, lack of feedback, and reduced social interaction.

The study was conducted in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. Students used a custom GenAI platform built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 during four class periods in one setting and eight sessions in another, following an Ask–Represent–Transform workflow to read math stories, model ideas visually, and co-create culturally relevant math stories with AI. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

The paper reports perceived benefits in creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement, including increased interest, curiosity, focus, and ownership. However, it is not a causal study and does not report direct quantitative measures of student engagement outcomes. Instead, it provides qualitative evidence that teachers and students perceived the AI-supported activities as engaging and motivating, while also highlighting implementation challenges such as the AI being too perfect, limited room for revision, and insufficient social and pedagogical support.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity improved mathematical understanding, including breaking down problems, representing knowledge visually, and uncovering misconceptions. The evidence is qualitative and based on thematic analysis of interviews, surveys, and observations from 79 fifth-grade students across six classrooms; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem comprehension, and mathematical knowledge representation during story-based math writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the GenAI activity as increasing students’ interest, curiosity, focus, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. Teachers specifically noted that culturally relevant story creation with AI increased attention and engagement in class, but the study provides only qualitative perceptions rather than direct behavioral engagement measures.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, attention/focus, enjoyment, and ownership in math learning

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that working with GenAI supported divergent/convergent thinking, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and problem formulation. These were reported as perceived learning benefits in thematic interviews and were not measured with standardized durable-skills instruments.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, critical evaluation, prompt engineering, and flexible thinking during AI-supported math story writing

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is math-centered, it directly focuses on creative writing with GenAI and reports that students used the system to draft, modify, and improve stories. The evidence is qualitative and perception-based, indicating that the tool supported writing creativity and narrative development, but it does not report standardized writing outcomes or quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived creative mathematical writing quality and story development

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter is a conceptual and technical survey of modern generative AI for information access, focusing on how large language models and related generative systems change the design of retrieval and generation pipelines. It contrasts traditional AI/IR approaches with generative AI, and organizes the discussion around two broad paradigms: information generation (directly producing answers or content) and information synthesis (grounding outputs in retrieved or external evidence).

The paper reviews foundational model architecture topics such as Transformers, scaling laws, training objectives, fine-tuning stages, prompt optimization, and multimodal applications. It then moves to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), modular RAG, retrieval planning, generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling, arguing that generative AI can improve both user-facing response generation and system-level information synthesis. The chapter does not report an empirical study, does not evaluate an educational intervention, and contains no K-12 classroom evidence or student engagement outcomes.

Because the paper is a broad review/chapter rather than a study of teachers or schools using AI tools, it does not match the requested K-12 teacher-facing AI evidence scope. There are no direct measurements of student engagement, attention, participation, on-task behavior, classroom behavior, or instructional responsiveness in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to a set of science-education prompts and what those responses might imply for educators and researchers. The author asks ChatGPT about effective science teaching, the choice between chalk-and-talk and student-centred pedagogies, how to support a student failing science, and how to generate a Year 7 unit, rubric, and quiz on renewable and non-renewable energy sources.

The study uses a self-study methodology with the author interacting directly with ChatGPT in January 2023 and then critically comparing the outputs to relevant science education literature. The paper is not a student outcome study; rather, it evaluates the perceived usefulness, limitations, and risks of ChatGPT as a pedagogical and research support tool. The author concludes that ChatGPT can be helpful for idea generation, unit/rubric/quiz drafting, and editing, but its outputs require careful verification because they can be generic, lack evidence, and may misrepresent or overstate educational claims.

The context is science education, especially Year 7 curriculum design, but the paper’s main contribution is conceptual and reflective rather than empirical. It argues that AI tools may support early-career teachers and pre-service teachers as a starting point for planning, while emphasizing that teacher expertise, contextual judgment, and critical evaluation remain essential. The paper also raises ethical concerns about bias, environmental cost, copyright, and research transparency when using large language models.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT produced science-education responses that were often broadly aligned with established themes in the literature, but the paper emphasizes that these outputs lacked evidence grounding and could overstate certainty. The study is an exploratory self-study with no student sample, no causal test, and no quantitative effect size; findings are based on qualitative comparison of ChatGPT-generated text to cited science education research.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of ChatGPT responses to science education literature and prompt outputs

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT generated a Year 7 science unit on renewable and non-renewable energy sources, a rubric, and a multiple-choice quiz that the author judged useful as starting points for classroom resource design. The paper reports that these outputs were functional but generic and required teacher refinement and contextual adaptation; no student learning outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Generated instructional materials: 5E unit plan, rubric, and quiz for Year 7 renewable/non-renewable energy

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may help reduce writer’s block and support teachers as a learning scaffold and drafting aid, which could lower effort barriers and support confidence in early-stage planning. This is a perceived benefit from the author’s self-study; it was not tested with users, so no causal or correlational estimate is available.
finding.measure: Author reflection on perceived usefulness for overcoming writer’s block and supporting idea generation

finding.finding_summary: The author argues ChatGPT can support critical thinking and planning by helping educators generate drafts that they must then evaluate, edit, and adapt to context. At the same time, the paper warns that users must scrutinize outputs for evidence quality, bias, and fit, so the tool’s value is contingent on human judgment rather than automatic correctness.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflection on critical evaluation, context adaptation, and prompt-based drafting

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT was useful for editing, rewriting sentences, and helping generate classroom resources, which the author suggests could save time in lesson planning and improve flow and clarity. However, the paper also notes added verification and refinement burden because outputs were sometimes generic, misleading, or insufficiently contextualized; no workload measurement was collected.
finding.measure: Perceived editing assistance and resource-generation utility for teaching and research writing

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of AI in education centered on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It argues that the rapid adoption of tools like ChatGPT creates both opportunities and risks: personalization, support for diverse learners, and efficiency gains on one hand, and hallucinations, misuse, and overreliance on AI on the other.

The paper uses a case study from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences (Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich) combined with a narrative literature review. The institutional case focuses on how the university developed internal AI guidelines for student work, emphasizing transparency, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and restrictions against copy-pasting generated text. The paper then broadens to practical recommendations for building an AI culture in schools and universities, including workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, paid expert roles, and AI literacy courses.

The article does not report original causal or correlational empirical results and does not benchmark AI tools against non-AI supports in a measured way. Its claims are primarily conceptual and normative, based on informal discussions and literature synthesis rather than a controlled study. It concludes that AI should be used as a sparring partner rather than a substitute for student thinking, and that institutions need training, guidelines, and critical reflection to use AI responsibly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can improve efficiency in curriculum creation, lesson planning, and other classroom preparation tasks, but also notes substantial implementation burden. In particular, it states that prompting a model to produce high-quality case studies or to be useful as a curriculum-planning assistant can take considerable time, and that in some cases doing the task oneself may be more effective.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher productivity and planning efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI use should foster, not replace, critical thinking, and that prompt engineering and AI literacy help students evaluate outputs more carefully. The paper argues that asking students to compare model outputs, critique them, and verify them against literature can strengthen critical thinking, but it does not report quantitative learning gains or follow-up data.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and prompt-engineering competence (conceptual/perceived)

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes the introduction of institutional AI guidelines at a Swiss university as a governance response to student use of ChatGPT and similar tools. The guidelines require transparency about model use, purpose, critical review, and manuscript location, but the article presents this as a descriptive policy case rather than an evaluated intervention with measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy / guidelines implementation

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Parental Involvement, Parental Support and Family Education on Pupil Achievements and Adjustment: A Literature Review
paper_profiles.venue: Research Report RR433, Department for Education and Skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report reviews English-language research on how parental involvement, parental support, and family education relate to pupil achievement and adjustment. The review distinguishes between studies of spontaneous parental involvement (for example, home learning activities, parent-child discussion, and school communication) and studies of interventions designed to increase involvement (such as parent training, home-school link initiatives, and community/family education).

The paper argues that high-quality observational studies consistently show a positive relationship between at-home parenting practices and pupil outcomes, even after controlling for social class and other background factors. By contrast, the intervention literature is extensive but methodologically weak, so the review concludes that there is insufficient reliable evidence to estimate the causal impact of specific programs on achievement. Overall, it suggests that parental involvement matters, but the evidence base for interventions to increase it was too weak at the time to support strong causal claims.

Because this is a review focused on children and families rather than a teacher-facing AI tool study, it does not benchmark AI against non-AI tools or human-only supports. Its relevance to the requested sub-question is only indirect, as it provides a model for evaluating correlational versus intervention evidence and highlights the importance of implementation quality and measurement when judging impact.
