finding.finding_summary: Across reviewed studies, parental involvement in the form of at-home reading, discussion, and learning support was associated with higher literacy achievement. For example, the review reports that in the British cohort study, parental involvement was positively related to reading test performance after background factors were controlled, and in the EPPE studies a stronger home learning environment predicted better cognitive development and later attainment.
finding.measure: standardised reading tests; home learning environment indicators

finding.finding_summary: Parental involvement was also associated with stronger mathematics achievement in large cohort analyses. The review notes that in the National Educational Longitudinal Study, home discussion had a significant unique association with academic achievement, including mathematics, after family background was controlled, and that this pattern was consistent with broader findings linking home support to school performance.
finding.measure: standardised mathematics tests

finding.finding_summary: The review cites evidence that parental involvement has a positive association with science-related outcomes, especially through parent-child discussion and support for science-related experiences. For instance, one NELS-based study found that parental involvement influenced science attitudes, which in turn were linked to better science achievement.
finding.measure: science attitudes; science achievement

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is children’s adjustment, resilience, and related non-cognitive outcomes. The review reports that higher home learning environments were associated with better cooperation, conformity, peer sociability, confidence, and lower anti-social or worried/upset behaviour, while parental involvement also predicted better personal adjustment in cohort studies.
finding.measure: British Social Adjustment Guide; behaviour/adjustment indicators; cooperation, conformity, peer sociability, confidence, anti-social behaviour

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly links parental involvement with self-concept as a learner, aspirations, and persistence-related outcomes such as staying on in education and selecting more challenging courses. These effects were most evident when parents expressed high expectations and encouraged learning opportunities at home.
finding.measure: student aspirations; self-concept; staying-on rates; course selection

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a substantial discussion of interventions to enhance parental involvement, including parent training, home-school links, and community/family education, but concludes that the evaluation literature was too technically weak to estimate their effect on pupil achievement reliably. It therefore finds strong demand and appreciation for these initiatives, but insufficient evidence to quantify institutional impact.
finding.measure: evaluation quality and implementation evidence for parent-training, home-school link, and family/community education interventions

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence in education (AIED) is changing teaching and learning in the post-pandemic context, with a particular focus on what teachers need to know and be able to do in order to use AI effectively. Rather than testing an intervention, it is a conceptual review and framework paper that synthesizes prior research and policy documents to identify opportunities and challenges of AI in education, especially around online and blended teaching.

The authors argue that AI can reduce workload, support personalization, improve feedback and assessment, and enhance instructional decision-making, but only if teachers have sufficient AI digital competencies. They adapt and integrate the DigCompEdu framework, TPACK-related ideas, and P21 twenty-first century skills to propose a broader framework for teacher AI competency that includes professional engagement, instructional design, content choices across disciplines, and student learning competencies.

The paper is written for educators and school leaders, but it does not report a primary empirical study, sample, or causal comparison. Its main contribution is theoretical: it reframes AI competency as both technical and non-technical, emphasizing ethical use, collaboration, communication, creativity, and lifelong learning alongside AI tool use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-driven tools can reduce teachers’ workload by automating repetitive administrative and instructional tasks such as grading, generating assessments, feedback, and paperwork, and by supporting learning analytics and decision-making. However, these claims are not based on a primary comparison study in this paper; they are synthesized from cited literature and presented as a conceptual conclusion, not a measured effect.
finding.measure: teacher workload, administrative task automation, grading/feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The framework discussion claims AI can support student motivation, self-regulation, and engagement through personalized guidance, immediate feedback, and adaptive learning environments. These are literature-based claims rather than direct findings from a study conducted in this paper, and no effect sizes or follow-up data are reported.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the cultivation of durable skills such as collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, and metacognition as part of AI competency. The authors synthesize prior frameworks and examples to argue these skills should be embedded in teacher AI competency and student AI learning, but they do not empirically test whether an AI tool improves these outcomes in this study.
finding.measure: collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes framework-level implications for teacher education, digital upskilling, curriculum design, and educational policy around AI competency. It argues that DigCompEdu and P21 should be revised to accommodate AI, and that institutions should provide professional development and standards for AI use, but these are recommendations rather than outcomes measured in an empirical study.
finding.measure: framework/policy alignment and competency standards

paper_profiles.title: Challenges and Future Directions of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no primary study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position/review article that surveys the current state of big data and artificial intelligence (AI) in education and argues for future directions across research, policy, and industry. The authors frame AI and learning analytics as increasingly important for assessment, individualized learning, precision education, teaching support, and administrative decision-making, while emphasizing that adoption should be guided by educational psychology, theory, and caution about bias, privacy, and overreliance on automation.

The article is not an empirical intervention study. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and conference discussions to outline major challenges: designing valid machine-generated data and algorithms, balancing human and machine assistance, addressing algorithmic bias and digital inequality, preparing teachers through professional development, and establishing privacy-protective policy frameworks. It also discusses commercialization and academia-industry collaboration, suggesting that AI tools may help teachers identify student learning trajectories, plan lessons, and reduce routine work, but should not replace the human role in schooling.

Because the paper is a broad conceptual review/position paper, it does not evaluate a specific teacher-facing AI tool against a non-AI comparator, nor does it report causal effects, effect sizes, or follow-up outcomes. Its main contribution is interpretive and agenda-setting rather than empirical.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI and learning analytics may support teachers by identifying learning trajectories, developing lesson plans, refining teaching strategies, and freeing them from monotonous routine tasks. At the same time, it cautions that overreliance on technology can create bias, workflow disruption, and risks of underestimating the human role in education; no empirical effect sizes or comparative workload data are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher support, planning, instructional decision-making, and routine task reduction (conceptual, not directly measured)

finding.finding_summary: The article argues for system-level changes in policy, teacher education, privacy protection, and academia-industry collaboration to enable responsible adoption of big data and AI in education. It emphasizes the need for legislation, regulatory safeguards, and teacher professional development, but presents no empirical evaluation of these institutional changes.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy protection, and institutional adoption of AI in education (conceptual synthesis)

paper_profiles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on learner–instructor interaction in online learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and instructors perceive the impact of AI systems on learner–instructor interaction in online learning. Rather than testing a deployed AI tool, the authors use a design-research approach to probe reactions to hypothetical AI scenarios, asking where AI might improve communication, support, and presence and where it might become invasive.

The study uses Speed Dating with storyboards: 12 university students and 11 instructors reviewed 11 storyboarded AI use cases such as an AI teaching assistant, grading assistant, analytics dashboard, intelligent suggestions, adaptive quizzes, virtual avatars, breakout-room matching, and facial analytics. Participants discussed perceived benefits and concerns in semi-structured Zoom interviews, which were then thematically analyzed.

Participants generally thought AI could improve the quantity and quality of communication, provide just-in-time personalized support, and enhance feelings of connection in large online classes. At the same time, they raised substantial concerns about unreliable answers and responsibility, over-standardizing learning and reducing student agency, and surveillance or privacy harms from monitoring facial expressions or eye movements. The paper concludes that explainability, human-in-the-loop design, and transparent data practices are essential for acceptable AI use in online learning.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived AI teaching assistants, grading assistance, and analytics tools as reducing routine work and speeding up communication, which would free instructors to focus on more meaningful interactions. This was a qualitative perception study with 12 students and 11 instructors; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived instructor workload, turnaround time for questions/feedback, and time saved from routine tasks

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed AI could increase engagement, confidence, and willingness to ask questions by reducing self-consciousness and enabling just-in-time support, but also feared anxiety, reduced autonomy, and lower motivation if AI over-guided learning. Findings are based on qualitative interviews with n=23 participants and no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived engagement, confidence, anxiety, and self-regulation/agency in online learning

finding.finding_summary: AI was seen as potentially supporting collaboration and problem solving in group projects and helping students reflect on gaps in understanding, but participants worried that AI could over-standardize work, reduce creativity, and weaken independent learning. The evidence is qualitative perceptions from n=23 participants; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived collaboration quality, creativity, independent learning, and metacognitive support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI in online learning raises institutional concerns about explainability, responsibility, surveillance, privacy, and acceptable data governance. Participants’ responses suggested that adoption would require clear data norms, human-in-the-loop decision making, and transparent justification of AI outputs; no quantitative effect was measured.
finding.measure: Perceived governance, responsibility, privacy, and institutional acceptability of AI use

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory comparative study asks how K-12 math educators evaluate lesson plans produced by generative AI versus human curriculum designers. The authors compare three sources of lesson plans: a customized GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human-authored lesson plans retrieved from open educational resources. Educators judge the plans using pairwise comparisons across four lesson-plan components: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality.

The study uses 20 experienced K-12 math educators (elementary, middle, and high school teachers) who each completed 20 pairwise evaluations over several weeks. Quantitative results show that human-authored plans are generally preferred overall, especially for elementary instruction and for warm-up and main-task components. AI-generated plans were more competitive for cool-down sections, and the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b performed relatively well in high-school contexts. Qualitative comments suggest educators value human plans for differentiation, student discourse, and contextualization, while AI plans are appreciated for structure and adaptability.

The main conclusion is not that GenAI replaces human lesson design, but that it can act as an assistive planning tool, especially for structured portions of lessons. The paper emphasizes a human-AI collaborative workflow in which AI may reduce planning burden while teachers retain responsibility for pedagogical judgment and contextual adaptation. However, the study measures perceived preference rather than student outcomes or actual time savings, so the evidence speaks to educator judgment about tool quality and usefulness rather than causal impact on classroom learning.

finding.finding_summary: Educators perceived GenAI lesson-plan tools as potentially helpful for reducing planning burden and producing structured lesson components, but they still preferred human-authored plans overall. The study measured perceived usefulness and preference in 529 lesson-plan pair evaluations (2,116 total judgments) rather than actual time savings, so the evidence suggests possible efficiency gains without demonstrating them causally.
finding.measure: Pairwise educator preference ratings for lesson-plan usefulness/quality; qualitative comments about workflow and planning burden

paper_profiles.title: How Can Video Generative AI Transform K-12 Education? Examining Teachers’ Perspectives through TPACK and TAM
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (mostly Elementary; one High School; one former Elementary teacher/data analyst)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how K-12 teachers perceive and evaluate video generative AI (Video GenAI) for educational use. The authors frame the work with TPACK and TAM to understand teachers’ initial impressions, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and willingness to adopt a new AI video-generation tool in classroom practice.

The researchers conducted semi-structured online interviews with 10 teachers who first received an educational guide and hands-on access to Luma Dream Machine, a public video-generation platform. Participants were purposefully selected because they already had above-average experience and interest in AI tools. The study is therefore not a test of student learning or a comparison against non-AI alternatives; rather, it is a qualitative exploration of educators’ perceptions after experimentation with the tool.

Teachers saw Video GenAI as promising for creating supplementary instructional materials, visualizing abstract or hard-to-film content, supporting project-based learning, and enabling student creativity and AI literacy. They also believed it might reduce preparation time for some teaching materials and broaden assessment formats. At the same time, they identified major barriers including rendering delays, short and inconsistent outputs, language limitations, safety risks, weak monitoring features, unclear legal/policy guidance, and implementation burdens such as parental consent, infrastructure needs, and subscription costs. Overall, the paper concludes that Video GenAI has clear pedagogical promise, but meaningful classroom use depends on stronger technical reliability, safety, institutional support, and policy guidance.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived Video GenAI as potentially reducing preparation time for instructional materials and making it easier to create supplemental videos for lessons. However, they also reported workflow burdens from long rendering times, need for heavy editing/verification, language issues, and the lack of classroom-oriented communication/monitoring features, so the net efficiency gain was viewed as conditional rather than established causally.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of preparation time, ease of creating instructional materials, and workflow burden

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed Video GenAI could strengthen subject learning in non-core areas such as science, history, Korean language arts, and social studies by generating visualizations, reenactments, and personalized explanatory videos. The evidence is purely perceived and qualitative, based on interviews after hands-on use of Luma Dream Machine, with no student outcome data or follow-up period reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of instructional usefulness for subject-specific video creation and comprehension support

finding.finding_summary: Participants thought Video GenAI could increase student engagement and motivation by supporting creative expression and making learning activities more interesting. Teachers described possible benefits for curiosity, imagination, and willingness to participate, but these were anticipated effects rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement, interest, and motivation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Video GenAI might foster creative expression, divergent thinking, and sentence formulation by prompting students to translate ideas into detailed prompts and visual outputs. They also believed it could support project-based learning and more varied assessment practices, but these claims were based on teacher judgment only and were not tested with student performance measures.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of creativity, divergent thinking, prompt-writing, and project-based learning support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified both enabling conditions and institutional barriers for Video GenAI adoption. They said adoption would require policy changes, professional development, stronger safety filters, clearer copyright and age policies, parental consent processes, better school infrastructure, and teacher-monitoring functions; they also warned that current administrative burdens and costs could impede implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of policy, governance, infrastructure, and institutional support needs

paper_profiles.title: Tailoring Education with GenAI: A New Horizon in Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and Undergraduate (mixed; preschool, secondary school, university were tested)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a generative-AI-based lesson-planning assistant designed to help educators create customized lesson plans through an interactive, multi-turn prompting workflow. The authors frame the tool as a digital assistant for teachers that can gather classroom context (target audience, topic, goals, format, duration, examples) and iteratively refine outputs to better fit instructional needs.

The paper evaluates the approach across multiple large language models (ChatGPT, Llama, and Google Bard) and across English and Greek learning-scenario prompts. Evaluation combined quantitative ratings from experts, qualitative feedback from teachers/educational experts, and linguistic analysis (spaCy tokenization and LDA topic modeling). The main reported finding is that newer models, especially ChatGPT 4 and Llama 2 70B, produced more relevant, coherent, and personalized lesson-plan outputs than older/smaller models, though some model outputs were criticized for inaccuracy or fabricated resources.

The testing context included preschool, secondary school, and university scenarios, but the paper is primarily a tool-evaluation study rather than a learner-outcome study. The authors report that educators found the GenAI-generated lesson plans effective and time-saving, while also emphasizing the need for human oversight, ethical caution, and additional rigorous testing such as RCTs before broad adoption. There is no direct benchmark against a non-AI planning intervention such as protected planning time, coaching, substitute coverage, or standard productivity tools, and no causal evidence on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that educators found the GenAI-generated lesson plans to be a significant time-saver in lesson preparation and helpful for producing customized plans. The evaluation was based on expert ratings, qualitative feedback, and response-time measures across multiple LLMs, but no controlled comparison against human-only planning or standard digital tools was conducted.
finding.measure: Perceived lesson-planning time savings; response time; expert/teacher evaluations of usability and practical value

finding.finding_summary: The tool was intended to support personalized lesson design, critical thinking, and iterative refinement of plans, and evaluators rated outputs on relevance, coherence, personalization, and operationality. However, these are proxy outcomes for teacher-facing planning quality rather than direct measurements of educator durable skills.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of relevance, coherence, personalization, and operationality in generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Model-Powered Chatbots for Internationalizing Student Support in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and pilot evaluation of a large language model (LLM)-powered chatbot intended to support international and exchange students at Al Akhawayn University (AUI). The authors frame the problem as improving access to institutional information, student engagement, and support during higher education internationalization, especially for students navigating administrative, academic, and cultural questions.

The intervention combines GPT-3.5-Turbo for initial response generation with GPT-4-Turbo as a verifier/fact-checker, plus LangChain memory and a Chroma vector store containing manually curated AUI website content. The system was tested on several internal test sets and evaluated via an anonymous student survey focused on general response quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness. The survey sample was small (11 final evaluators; 79 ratings per metric), and the reported results are descriptive bootstrapped confidence intervals rather than causal comparisons.

The main conclusion is that students rated the chatbot highly on the evaluated dimensions, with 95% confidence intervals around means near 4/5 for all five metrics. The authors argue that the chatbot is a relatively low-cost and relatively simple-to-implement way for universities to improve international student information access and support. However, the paper also notes limitations, including small sample size, lack of a large benchmark dataset, and the need for future evaluation of translation performance, response time, and broader deployment outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The chatbot was perceived as efficient and useful for student support, with students rating its response quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness highly on a 5-point Likert scale. The final survey set included 11 evaluators (79 ratings per metric), and bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for the mean were Quality [4.06–4.43], Relevance [4.02–4.41], Correctness [4.18–4.47], Formality [4.24–4.54], and Human-Like [3.87–4.32].
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of chatbot response quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness; bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals of mean Likert scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the chatbot could support higher education internationalization by improving access to official institutional information and student support services. This is a descriptive, prototype-level claim based on student ratings and internal testing, not a causal institutional outcome study.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for international student support and institutional information access

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a safety and governance problem in generative AI for medicine: large multimodal language models can produce recommendations for medical products that go beyond FDA-approved indications, thereby risking harmful off-label promotion. The authors argue that because these models are trained on broad internet-scale data with limited human oversight, they may learn and reproduce unvetted product–indication associations that are unsafe or illegal to market.

The paper proposes a post-hoc detection pipeline to identify off-label promotion in model outputs. The method standardizes user input, uses biomedical named entity recognition to detect drugs and diseases in responses, matches those entities to FDA labeling data, and then zero-shot prompts a T5 model to decide whether a detected drug–condition association constitutes a recommendation. The authors demonstrate the approach on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style medical product question-answering setting, generating 14,300 synthetic queries across 35 pharmaceuticals with known off-label uses.

In the experiment, 15.4% of model responses were flagged as containing off-label indications, and the detection system achieved 85.75% precision, 80.47% recall, and 83.02% F1 on a 2,000-sample human-annotated evaluation. The paper’s main conclusion is that generalist GenAI systems can surface off-label medical product uses at scale, and that guardrails or monitoring layers may be needed to filter such outputs before users see them. This is a proof-of-concept study focused on detection and policy implications rather than clinical effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a post-hoc detection pipeline for off-label promotion in MLLM outputs, showing that automated guardrails can identify problematic recommendations at scale. On a 2,000-sample human-annotated evaluation, the detector achieved precision=85.75%, recall=80.47%, and F1=83.02% for flagging off-label indications, suggesting the workflow could reduce manual review burden in safety monitoring. Study size for the main generation experiment was 14,300 synthetic queries over 35 pharmaceuticals, but the paper does not compare this system against human-only review time or other non-AI tools.
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and F1 for off-label promotion detection; proportion of responses flagged as off-label
finding.study_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; n=2000 annotated sample

finding.finding_summary: The central contribution is a governance/safety detection framework intended to keep generative medical systems aligned with FDA labeling and reduce illegal or harmful off-label promotion. In the Claude 3 Sonnet experiment, 15.4% of responses were identified as containing off-label indications, and the authors argue this demonstrates the need for post-hoc guardrails before deployment. No causal institutional outcome was measured, but the paper directly addresses regulatory compliance and model oversight.
finding.measure: Off-label promotion rate in model outputs; detection performance against human annotations

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can help teachers create personalized mathematics tasks, and whether keeping the teacher “in-the-loop” is efficient or effective. The central question is not a traditional learning intervention comparison, but rather how middle school math teachers use ChatGPT/GPT-4o to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so they align with students’ popular-culture interests, while preserving mathematical realism and readability.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated. After a 2-hour training, they used ChatGPT in recorded Zoom sessions to personalize 143 problems from two curriculum units (Unit 4 on proportional relationships and percentages; Unit 6 on expressions, equations, and inequalities) for 521 students in ASSISTments. The study analyzed teacher prompts, teacher time spent, and student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests, along with open-ended feedback. The design is observational and descriptive rather than causal: there was no control group, random assignment, or direct comparison against non-AI teacher planning conditions.

The main finding is that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization did not appear time-efficient. Teachers spent an average of about 4 minutes per problem (246 seconds; SD=165.7), and time increased rather than decreased from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (204 vs. 286 seconds per problem). Teachers averaged 3.2 prompts per problem overall, and 3–5 prompts was associated with slightly higher student ratings of interestingness and closeness (about +0.24 on a 5-point scale). However, even with growing experience, teachers did not become clearly faster; instead, they often needed extra prompts to fix realism, quantities, age-appropriateness, and other issues.

Students generally preferred specific, fine-grained popular-culture references, but also wanted problems to match their own interests more closely than a teacher-managed approach could typically provide. Student ratings were modest overall (means around 2.3–2.7 on a 5-point scale), and Unit 6 problems were rated somewhat higher than Unit 4 problems after reflection and iteration. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and quality control, but it is labor-intensive and may not scale well to highly individualized personalization.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies middle school mathematics problem personalization, but it does not measure student achievement or learning gains directly. The math-specific finding is that teachers had to repeatedly revise mathematical realism, numbers, and clarity in generated problems (e.g., 76 prompts about realism of numbers/quantities; 16 about math difficulty/clarity), suggesting GPT-4o could support drafting but often required human correction.
finding.measure: Teacher prompt coding of math-related revisions; student judgments of problem closeness/interestingness for math tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded positively to personalized tasks when the prompt matched their interests, but overall ratings were modest. On a 5-point scale, mean interestingness was 2.46 and mean closeness was 2.53 across rated problems; Unit 6 rated higher than Unit 4 by about 0.33 points (p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students (ratings collected for 52-53 problems; 454/449/446 open-ended responses across items)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the teacher-in-the-loop process supported teacher learning, prompting skill, and iterative refinement. Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem overall, and using 3–5 prompts was associated with higher student ratings by approximately 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073), suggesting more effective prompting within a narrow range.
finding.measure: Teacher prompt counts and mixed-effects regression relating prompts to student ratings

finding.finding_summary: This is the paper’s central outcome. Teachers spent an average of 246 seconds per personalized problem (SD=165.7), with no evidence that efficiency improved over time; in fact, Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4 by 70.4 seconds per problem (p=0.0189) and used 1.26 more prompts per problem (p=0.0025). The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization was time-consuming and did not become clearly more efficient with experience.
finding.measure: Time to create each personalized problem; number of prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: The study has implications for classroom workflow and teacher professional learning, but it does not evaluate policy or institution-level outcomes directly. The authors argue that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI may support professional learning and quality control, yet the implementation burden is substantial enough that scalability is limited without additional tools or multi-agent support.
finding.measure: Qualitative interpretation of workflow burden, teacher reflection, and implementation feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Learning and Motivational Impact of Game-Based Learning: Comparing Face-To-Face and Online Formats on Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher-authored educational video games are effective for computer science learning and motivation, and whether their effectiveness differs when the same game is delivered face-to-face versus online. The motivation for the study is the need for engaging instructional approaches in computer science education, especially in online settings where dropout risk is higher, and the practical challenge for teachers of finding or creating games aligned with course objectives.

The intervention is a teacher-authored educational video game created with the SGAME authoring tool and embedded learning objects made with ViSH Editor. The game was used in a software engineering fundamentals course at the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid during two academic years, with 217 students in a face-to-face group and 104 students in an online group. Students completed a pre-test, played for about 50 minutes, completed a post-test, and then answered a questionnaire about usability, motivation, fun, and preferences.

Results from the quasi-experiment show significant learning gains in both formats, with paired-sample t-tests indicating medium-to-large effects within each group (face-to-face d=0.71; online d=0.79). Between-group comparisons found no statistically significant difference in learning gains (d=0.05), suggesting similar knowledge acquisition in both modalities. Questionnaire results indicate that students viewed the experience positively in both settings, but perceived the face-to-face version as somewhat more fun and more favorable overall. The authors conclude that teacher-authored educational video games can be used effectively in either face-to-face or online formats, though some motivational aspects may be stronger in person.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed significant knowledge gains after playing the teacher-authored educational video game in both formats. In the face-to-face group (n=217), pre-test to post-test improvement was significant with Cohen's d=0.71; in the online group (n=104), the improvement was also significant with Cohen's d=0.79. The post-test assessed understanding of basic principles of software design, and between-group differences in gain were negligible (d=0.05).
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on 10 multiple-choice questions about basic principles of software design
finding.effect_size: d=0.71 (face-to-face within-group); d=0.79 (online within-group); d=0.05 (between-group gain difference)
finding.std_deviation: Face-to-face pre-test SD=1.77, post-test SD=1.66; online pre-test SD=1.57, post-test SD=1.68

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high motivation, enjoyment, and positive overall perceptions of the game in both formats. Questionnaire ratings were high in both groups, with statistically significant face-to-face advantages for overall opinion (d=0.36), perceived learning help (d=0.25), fun (d=0.20), future use (d=0.29), and preference over traditional materials (d=0.39), while motivation itself did not differ significantly between formats.
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire on opinion, motivation, fun, future use, and preference for game-based learning versus traditional materials
finding.effect_size: d=0.36, 0.25, 0.20, 0.29, 0.39 for selected perception items; motivation item not significant (d=0.16)
finding.std_deviation: Item-level SDs reported in Table IV; e.g., overall opinion SD=0.58 (face-to-face) and 0.94 (online)

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides limited evidence relevant to implementation burden and usability rather than direct productivity outcomes. Students rated the game as easy to use in both formats (item 3: M=4.76 face-to-face, 4.69 online) and reported little need for help (item 4: M=1.76 face-to-face, 1.68 online), with no statistically significant differences, suggesting the tool was workable without substantial workflow disruption.
finding.measure: Questionnaire items on ease of use, need for help, and integration with the virtual platform
finding.effect_size: d=0.11 for ease of use; d=0.06 for needed help; d=0.06 for platform integration
finding.std_deviation: Ease of use SD=0.55 face-to-face, 0.73 online; help needed SD=1.30 face-to-face, 1.35 online; platform integration SD=0.63 face-to-face, 0.77 online

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-based Applications over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint presents the Generative AI Toolkit, an open-source framework intended to automate development, testing, deployment, and monitoring workflows for LLM-based applications across their full lifecycle. The paper argues that current LLM application development is too manual, slow, and error-prone, and proposes a toolkit that supports prompt/model permutation testing, custom metrics, CI/CD integration, tracing, and production monitoring.

The paper is not an education study and does not focus on K-12 students or teachers. Instead, it uses representative software use cases—a text-to-SQL agent, a restaurant RAG agent, an in-vehicle voice assistant, and a model-comparison scenario—to illustrate how the toolkit can improve quality and reduce cycle time. The evidence is largely descriptive and demonstration-based, with no controlled comparison against human-only supports or standard digital productivity tools and no educational population or setting reported.

The authors report that automation can reduce manual work, shorten development cycles, and improve testing coverage and observability, but they also note that generic quantitative claims are difficult to make from the presented use cases. The paper mainly offers a framework and implementation examples rather than a rigorous causal evaluation of outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the toolkit improves operational efficiency by automating evaluation, CI/CD integration, deployment, logging, and monitoring for LLM-based applications. The authors state that it can significantly reduce cycle time and manual work, but they do not report a controlled study, effect size, or sample size for these claims.
finding.measure: Development cycle time, manual work, and automated testing/monitoring workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is framed as an institutional workflow framework for building, testing, deploying, and monitoring LLM systems across their lifecycle, including CI/CD and audit-proof logging. However, the paper provides no quantitative institutional outcome measures and no causal evidence of organizational impact beyond illustrative use cases.
finding.measure: Adoption of lifecycle workflow automation, CI/CD integration, and production monitoring capabilities

paper_profiles.title: ChatISA: A Prompt-Engineered, In-House Multi-Modal Generative AI Chatbot for Information Systems Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents ChatISA, an in-house, multi-modal generative AI chatbot developed for Information Systems and Analytics education in higher education. The authors frame the work as a response to the rapid growth of GenAI in professional settings, the uneven adoption of AI tools in business education, and concerns about access, privacy, and educational fit. The core question is how a domain-specific, institutionally managed chatbot can better support student learning than general-purpose tools.

ChatISA includes four modules: Coding Companion, Project Coach, Exam Ally, and Interview Mentor. The system is built with multiple LLMs, prompt engineering, Streamlit, and LangChain, and was designed around task-technology fit, usability, privacy, flexibility, and affordability. The paper emphasizes that ChatISA can be used across coding help, project support, exam preparation, and interview practice, with configurable model selection and PDF export of chats for instructional use.

The paper is primarily a design science artifact paper with illustrative use cases rather than a controlled evaluation. Evidence comes from demonstrations, author observations, and informal feedback from undergraduate ISA students in two courses. The authors report that students found the tool useful and engaging, that outputs were often reasonable, and that the system helped support learning at low marginal cost, but they do not provide rigorous causal evidence or comparative outcome data against non-AI or human-only supports.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatISA supported undergraduate Information Systems and Analytics coursework through coding help, project guidance, exam practice, and interview preparation. In two illustrative course examples, the authors state that the system generated reasonable answers and that students generally enjoyed using it, but no controlled performance metrics, effect sizes, or follow-up data are reported.
finding.measure: Informal student/faculty feedback and illustrative use-case outputs in ISA coursework

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe increased student interest, frequent usage, and positive feedback, especially for the interactive nature of Exam Ally. They also note that ChatISA appeared to increase engagement with studying and made AI-supported tasks more approachable, though these claims are based on informal observations rather than validated scales.
finding.measure: Informal engagement and enjoyment observations; mentions of student interest and usage patterns

finding.finding_summary: ChatISA was designed to support critical thinking, project scoping, reflection, and interview preparation through its Project Coach and Interview Mentor modules. The paper argues that these features help students structure tasks, anticipate risks, and practice responses, but the evidence is limited to demonstration and author interpretation rather than direct measurement of durable-skill gains.
finding.measure: Design-intended support for critical thinking, reflection, collaboration, and interview practice; no validated outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that ChatISA improves task efficiency by providing immediate, customizable academic support for coding, project work, exam preparation, and interview practice. The system is presented as reducing the need to switch between tools and as offering low-cost access to support, but the paper does not quantify time savings, workflow disruption, verification time, or workload changes relative to non-AI alternatives.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency, usability, and workflow support; no quantitative efficiency metric reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that an in-house GenAI system can improve access, privacy, affordability, and curricular integration for an academic department. It positions ChatISA as a way to reduce the AI divide and support institutional adoption of GenAI, but provides no policy evaluation, governance outcomes, or comparative institutional data.
finding.measure: Institutional design and implementation discussion; no formal policy or governance outcome measure reported

paper_profiles.title: "From Unseen Needs to Classroom Solutions": Exploring AI Literacy Challenges & Opportunities with Project-Based Learning Toolkit in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers understand AI literacy and how they would use a project-based learning (PBL) toolkit to teach AI concepts across subjects. The toolkit includes three teacher-configurable demo tools: an AI Art Lab, AI Music Studio, and AI Chatbot. The authors use interviews and co-design sessions to explore teachers’ current AI literacy, their classroom design ideas, and the perceived affordances and concerns of AI tools in education.

The study recruited 13 middle and high school teachers from North America and East Asia teaching a range of subjects, including general science, mathematics, Chinese, social studies, biology, English, media arts, and information technology. Teachers first watched a short demo video, then explored the toolkit and completed semi-structured interviews about AI literacy, prior teaching experiences, tool features, and lesson design. The paper reports that teachers generally viewed AI positively as a support for student self-study, creative work, and personalized exploration, but they also worried about accuracy, trustworthiness, copyright, and uneven AI skill levels among students and teachers.

The main conclusion is that a modular, adaptable PBL toolkit can help teachers imagine ways to integrate AI literacy into non-computer-science classes, especially by supporting independent student inquiry, concept reinforcement, and creative production. However, the paper does not benchmark the toolkit against non-AI alternatives or measure student learning outcomes causally; it is a formative qualitative study focused on perceptions, design ideas, and implementation barriers. The authors emphasize the need for stronger onboarding, scaffolding, and better support for diverse classroom contexts if AI literacy tools are to be scaled sustainably.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the AI Chatbot as a way to reduce direct instructional burden by letting students clarify misunderstandings and review notes independently before speaking with the teacher. In one example, a teacher suggested students spend 10 to 15 minutes reviewing notes with the AI assistant, and another teacher said AI could help review student work and save teachers time, but these are perceived benefits rather than measured workload effects.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of workload reduction and student self-support

paper_profiles.title: Experts’ View on Challenges and Needs for Fairness in Artificial Intelligence for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenges and needs that educational AI researchers and practitioners perceive when trying to design, evaluate, and govern fair AI systems for education. The authors focus on fairness across the AI development pipeline, including data collection, modeling, fairness assessment, auditing, transparency, and responsibility allocation.

The study uses an anonymous survey of 136 experts who had published at top educational conferences in 2021, followed by semi-structured interviews with 28 volunteers from that survey sample. Respondents discussed what fairness means in their work, where current practices fail, and what tools, standards, and organizational supports are needed to improve fairness-aware educational AI.

The main conclusions are that fairness in educational AI is highly context-dependent, cannot be reduced to model-level metrics alone, and requires continuous assessment, localized data practices, human-centered auditing, and clearer governance. The paper does not test an AI tool against a non-AI comparator; instead, it reports expert perceptions about design and governance needs, with repeated emphasis on tensions between accuracy, fairness, transparency, and workflow burden.

finding.finding_summary: Experts reported that fairness in educational AI requires organizational, procedural, and governance changes rather than only model-level fixes. Across a survey of 136 experts and interviews with 28 participants, they emphasized continuous fairness assessment, public scrutiny of data and source code, participatory checking, and clearer responsibility structures, but these were framed as needs and challenges rather than tested interventions.
finding.measure: expert survey and semi-structured interview responses about fairness challenges, governance, auditing, and responsibility

finding.finding_summary: Participants repeatedly noted that fairness auditing and stakeholder review can add substantial time and resource burden to development and deployment workflows. The paper reports expert concerns that non-expert stakeholders would need 'a lot of time and resources' to audit models, while some parts of evaluation could be automated; however, no empirical comparison of AI versus human-only or non-AI tools was conducted.
finding.measure: perceived workflow burden, auditing effort, and evaluation process demands

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities, limitations, and governance challenges of large language models—especially ChatGPT—for education. The authors discuss how LLMs might support student learning, teacher preparation, feedback, assessment, content generation, and inclusive or remote learning, while also warning about bias, privacy, hallucinations, overreliance, copyright, verification burden, and unequal access.

The paper is not an empirical study; it synthesizes early research and examples across learner and teacher use cases to argue for cautious, human-centered adoption. For teachers, it highlights possible workflow benefits such as lesson planning, personalized feedback, semi-automated grading, and generating exercises, but emphasizes that human oversight, fact-checking, and professional judgment remain necessary. The paper concludes that LLMs could be valuable educational tools if integrated with strong safeguards, training, and governance, but that more evidence-based research is needed before broad adoption.

Because this is a position paper rather than a study of a defined K-12 sample, it does not provide causal or correlational evidence on outcomes. It mainly offers conceptual claims about likely benefits and risks, with no reported intervention, comparator, follow-up duration, or effect sizes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher-facing large language models can reduce workload by supporting lesson planning, generating personalized materials, assisting with feedback, and semi-automating grading. It also notes that grading effort in one cited large-course context could be reduced by up to 85%, but this figure is reported from another study and not evaluated empirically in this position paper.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, lesson-planning efficiency, feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs can support critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, and inquiry by generating prompts, explanations, discussion structures, and scaffolds. However, it also warns that overreliance on model outputs may weaken students’ critical thinking and independent investigation if verification and human oversight are insufficient.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, inquiry/verification practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional issues such as privacy, security, fairness, copyright, sustainability, cost, and access, arguing that adoption of LLMs requires governance frameworks, training, and policy safeguards. It does not test these effects empirically, but it identifies them as central barriers and conditions for responsible system-level implementation.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, access, sustainability

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the concerns surrounding the use of chatbots in education, using ChatGPT as a representative case of an advanced generative AI tool. The authors ask what risks and limitations educators, students, and other stakeholders should consider when using chatbots in educational settings, especially given the rapid public enthusiasm around ChatGPT and the concurrent concerns about cheating, misinformation, privacy, and equity.

Methodologically, the study is a three-stage qualitative instrumental case study. First, the authors conducted a cross-sectional social network analysis and sentiment analysis of 2,330 tweets related to #ChatGPT and education. Second, they analyzed interviews with 19 early adopters who had publicly shared experiences using ChatGPT in education. Third, three experienced educators used ChatGPT for one week across ten educational scenarios to probe practical concerns such as cheating, response accuracy, fairness, quiz generation, emotional tone, privacy, and manipulation.

The study does not evaluate ChatGPT against a non-AI comparator in a causal way; instead, it reports perceived benefits and concerns. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is viewed as promising for lesson design, learning support, and reducing some teacher workload, but it also raises substantial concerns about inaccurate outputs, inconsistent responses, cheating, privacy risks, reduced critical thinking, and misleading or manipulative behavior. The authors argue that education systems should not simply ban chatbots, but should develop guidelines, teaching philosophies, and responsible-AI practices for safe and effective adoption.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived ChatGPT as potentially useful for reducing teacher instructional workload and helping with lesson planning, quiz creation, and resource generation, but also noted that inaccurate, inconsistent, or vague outputs could create extra verification and correction burden. The paper provides qualitative evidence from 19 interviews and 3 educators using ChatGPT over one week, but no causal comparison against non-AI supports or workflow-time measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher workload, lesson planning support, quiz/resource generation, and verification burden from interviews and hands-on scenarios
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators for one-week scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The study repeatedly highlights concerns that ChatGPT may weaken critical thinking, encourage overreliance, and enable cheating, while also being seen as a tool that can prompt learning when used carefully. Evidence is based on interview perceptions and scenario-based demonstrations rather than measured skill outcomes, so no causal effect on critical thinking was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived critical thinking, cheating, and prompt-quality competence

finding.finding_summary: Respondents described ChatGPT interactions as fun, exciting, and emotionally engaging, but also reported disappointment, reduced trust, and discomfort when the system produced inaccurate answers or failed to show genuine emotion. These are subjective perceptions from interviews and scenario use over one week, not measured changes in motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived enjoyment, emotional attachment, trust, and disappointment in interaction with ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT has implications for school policy, assessment design, privacy governance, and responsible AI adoption, especially because it can facilitate cheating, produce misleading information, and behave inconsistently across users. The evidence is qualitative and scenario-based, with no institutional outcome measure or follow-up beyond the one-week educator use period.
finding.measure: Perceived policy, assessment, privacy, and governance implications of ChatGPT in education

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective-style conceptual article examining the potential benefits and challenges of ChatGPT in higher education, framed through constructivist theory of learning. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors synthesize prior literature and present a set of propositions about how ChatGPT might support teaching, learning, feedback, research, administration, and assessment design.

The paper argues that ChatGPT could be useful for adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing support, automated administrative assistance, and innovative assessment development. At the same time, it highlights substantial concerns around academic integrity, bias, hallucinations, digital inequity, and the difficulty of assessing authentic learning outcomes when AI tools are used. The article concludes that higher education institutions should use ChatGPT cautiously, pair it with human judgment, and develop policies, training, and assessment approaches that preserve academic integrity and support constructive learning.

Although the paper discusses educational implications extensively, it does not present primary empirical data, an intervention study, or a direct comparison between ChatGPT and non-AI alternatives in K-12 settings. Its claims are argumentative and future-oriented rather than causal or correlational findings from a sample study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may reduce teacher and staff workload by automating parts of feedback, writing support, and administrative tasks, but these claims are conceptual rather than empirically tested. It suggests potential time and cost savings, especially for large student cohorts, yet provides no measured effect size, sample, or follow-up data.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of administrative support, feedback automation, and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT could support student engagement, motivation, and self-regulated learning through personalized feedback and adaptive interaction, but it also warns that overreliance may reduce active learning and human interaction. These are theoretical claims without empirical measurement.
finding.measure: Perceived engagement, motivation, and self-regulated learning

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that ChatGPT may support or undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and AI literacy. The article provides no empirical test; instead, it argues that benefits depend on how the tool is used and that superficial use may weaken these skills while guided use may strengthen them.
finding.measure: Theoretical discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and AI literacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses ChatGPT as a writing and language-support tool that may help generate drafts, improve grammar, and assist non-native English users, but it also warns about fabricated references and unreliable text. No primary data are reported, so this is a conceptual assessment of likely literacy-related effects.
finding.measure: Writing support, text generation, grammar/referencing assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional implications for policy, academic integrity, equitable access, assessment redesign, and AI literacy. It recommends training, policy development, and new assessment strategies, but offers no empirical evaluation of institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Policy, academic integrity, assessment design, and institutional AI adoption implications

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review of reviews that maps the state of artificial intelligence in higher education (AIHEd). The authors ask what kinds of evidence syntheses have been published, where they appear, who authors them, how they are conducted, and what the key findings and research gaps are. The review is not an intervention study; rather, it synthesizes 66 secondary studies published between 2018 and July 2023.

The review found that most AIHEd evidence syntheses were systematic reviews, followed by scoping reviews, with fewer meta-analyses and other review types. Reviews were most commonly focused on general AI applications, profiling/prediction, and adaptive systems/personalisation, while assessment/evaluation and intelligent tutoring systems were less common. The corpus was largely collaborative and mostly published in journals, but reporting quality was uneven: many reviews did not report screening reliability, exact extraction schemes, or quality appraisal procedures.

In terms of substantive conclusions, the field is dominated by research on adaptive systems, personalisation, chatbots/virtual assistants, recommender systems, and profiling/prediction, with many reviews emphasizing that the evidence base is still nascent and methodologically uneven. The paper argues for more rigorous, transparent, and ethically grounded research, and it highlights gaps around contextual detail, quality assurance, and interdisciplinary work. Because this is a review of higher education evidence syntheses, it does not directly benchmark teacher-facing AI tools against non-AI alternatives in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 66 higher-education AI evidence syntheses, the field shows growing publication volume but uneven methodological quality and limited reporting transparency. The review found that 45.5% of reviews did not conduct any quality assessment, 51.5% did not report a digital evidence-synthesis tool, and 34.8% did not reflect on limitations, indicating a mixed institutional picture of the research base rather than a demonstrated intervention effect.
finding.measure: Quality appraisal/reporting characteristics of secondary research corpus

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of AI in education centered on three skills the author argues are essential for the AI era: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It uses the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, informal discussions with students and staff, and a narrative literature review to develop a case-based account of how institutions can respond to the rapid spread of ChatGPT and similar large language models.

The paper focuses on higher education rather than K-12, though it suggests that some ideas may transfer to children’s schooling. It describes a Swiss institution’s internal AI guidelines for student use, then argues that guidelines alone are insufficient without workshops, ongoing training, dedicated budget, and staff support. The paper also surveys prompt-engineering approaches and proposes AI literacy coursework as a way to help students use AI responsibly and critically. The conclusions are normative and practice-oriented: AI should be treated as a sparring partner, not a tutor or ghostwriter, and institutions should build an AI culture that emphasizes transparency, critical evaluation, and ethical use.

The paper does not present a causal evaluation of an AI tool against non-AI alternatives or human-only supports. Instead, it offers descriptive observations and recommendations about implementation burdens, compliance problems, and the need for training and institutional support. Any claims about effectiveness are purely argued or perceived rather than empirically tested.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools may help with curriculum creation, case-study construction, and other teacher tasks, but it also emphasizes that prompting, checking outputs, and “indoctrinating” the model can take considerable time. In the author’s qualitative case discussion, AI is portrayed as potentially useful but often not more efficient than doing the work manually once implementation and verification burdens are considered; no effect size or formal comparison is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher workload, time spent prompting/verifying AI outputs, and ease of creating curricula/case materials

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI literacy and prompt engineering can foster critical thinking by requiring students to evaluate AI outputs, detect hallucinations, and reflect on how and why the tool was used. The paper cites prior studies and presents this as a pedagogical rationale rather than as a measured effect in the author’s own data; no sample size, effect size, or follow-up duration is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, AI literacy, and reflective evaluation of AI-generated outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on institutional policy and governance around AI use, using the Swiss university case to describe the development of formal AI guidelines, transparency requirements, and recommendations for workshops, budget, paid support roles, and regular updates. These are presented as practical solutions to governance and implementation problems, but they are not evaluated causally; the evidence is descriptive and normative.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, governance practices, and implementation recommendations

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a speculative, collective reflection on ChatGPT and generative AI in education rather than an empirical evaluation. The authors use fictional storytelling and a speculative methodology to imagine positive and negative future scenarios for AI in educational contexts, aiming to provoke critical thinking about how AI might reshape teaching, learning, assessment, and academic work.

The paper does not test an intervention, compare AI against non-AI tools, or report causal evidence. Instead, it synthesizes perspectives from a large, globally diverse group of education scholars and includes several fictional narratives about future uses of AI in higher education and other learning contexts. Across these narratives, the paper argues that generative AI could support personalization, accessibility, language support, and teacher efficiency, but also raises concerns about bias, privacy, academic integrity, dependence, and the dehumanization of education.

Because the piece is conceptual and speculative, it does not provide outcome data, follow-up periods, or measurable effect sizes. Its main conclusion is that AI in education is context-dependent and must be integrated carefully, ethically, and with human educators retaining a central role.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools may save educators time by assisting with routine tasks such as writing emails, summarizing concepts, creating test/quiz questions, drafting course outlines, and grading assignments. However, these claims are speculative and are not supported by empirical comparison against human-only supports or standard digital tools; implementation burden, verification time, and workflow disruption are discussed as potential limitations rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher workload / task efficiency in speculative narratives

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly suggests that generative AI can support writing by providing instant feedback, suggestions, translation, and text generation, and it presents fictional scenarios where students use AI for essays, stories, and language practice. These are narrative claims only; no controlled comparison, follow-up, or quantified writing outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived writing support, translation, and text generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can improve language skills by providing conversational practice, pronunciation support, real-time interpretation, and translated feedback, with fictional examples involving ESL and multilingual communication. These claims are presented as speculative possibilities rather than measured effects, so no effect size or causal estimate is available.
finding.measure: Perceived oral/written language practice and pronunciation support

finding.finding_summary: The narratives portray AI as potentially increasing motivation, confidence, and engagement by offering personalized support and encouragement, but also as potentially fostering frustration, dependence, or reduced trust in human interaction. These are purely speculative and subjective perceptions, not empirically measured social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived motivation, confidence, engagement, and frustration

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI may support collaboration, problem solving, and critical thinking through guided practice and alternative ideas, but it also warns that over-reliance could weaken creativity, agency, and critical thinking. No empirical benchmark against non-AI supports is reported, so this is best interpreted as a conceptual discussion of likely tradeoffs.
finding.measure: Perceived critical thinking, collaboration, and problem-solving support

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes broad institutional effects, including privacy, ethics, ownership, equity, academic integrity, policy, and the possible restructuring of teacher and student roles. It argues that AI could expand access and inclusion, but could also deepen inequity, amplify bias, and intensify surveillance; these are conceptual claims without empirical measurement.
finding.measure: Perceived institutional, policy, equity, and governance implications

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Model-Powered Chatbots for Internationalizing Student Support in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the design, implementation, and survey-based evaluation of a large language model (LLM) chatbot intended to support international and exchange students at Al Akhawayn University (AUI) in Morocco. The authors frame the chatbot as a student-support and internationalization tool that can answer questions about university information, academic regulations, and campus life using retrieved institutional documents and a two-stage GPT-3.5/GPT-4 Turbo prompt pipeline.

The system uses Python, LangChain, OpenAI embeddings, and Chroma vector storage to retrieve five relevant documents and generate answers constrained to official AUI data. A second GPT-4 Turbo “verifier” prompt fact-checks and edits the first response to reduce hallucinations and preserve the user’s language. The evaluation involved 11 final student raters (10 Moroccan, 1 international) who scored query-response pairs on five Likert-scale dimensions: quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness.

Results were reported as bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for the mean ratings, all centered around about 4/5, suggesting favorable perceptions of the chatbot’s answers. The paper concludes that the chatbot is promising for improving student support and information access in higher education internationalization contexts, but it also acknowledges limitations such as a small evaluation sample, limited data coverage, and the need for future work on larger-scale testing and expert evaluation of translation quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the chatbot improved the efficiency of student support by providing timely, relevant answers to international-student questions using a retrieval-augmented prompt pipeline. In the student survey, the chatbot scored well on quality, relevance, correctness, and formality (bootstrapped 95% CIs all around 4/5), which the authors interpret as evidence that the system can deliver support with relatively low implementation cost and reduced manual effort compared with conventional support workflows.
finding.measure: Student-rated chatbot response quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness on a 1-5 Likert scale; bootstrapped mean and 95% CI

finding.finding_summary: The study’s main institutional claim is that LLM chatbots can support higher-education internationalization by improving information access, multilingual assistance, and student support services. The paper presents the chatbot as scalable and cost-effective for university deployment, though these claims are based on a small single-institution evaluation rather than causal comparison with non-AI alternatives.
finding.measure: Survey-based evaluation of a university chatbot intended for international student support and institutional information access

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that AI literacy work should move beyond technical prompting skills and include metacognitive supports that help learners notice and mitigate cognitive biases when interacting with generative AI. The paper focuses on human biases such as anchoring, confirmation bias, and automation bias, and how these can interact with algorithmic and systemic biases in AI outputs.

The paper presents DeBiasMe, an illustrative metacognitive AIED concept for university students. The proposed system combines two friction-based interventions: a prompt refinement tool that flags potential bias before submission, and a bias visualization map that surfaces likely bias patterns in AI-generated responses after generation. These interventions are intended to slow down interaction, increase reflection, and support students in both input formulation and output interpretation.

The population discussed is university students, based on initial mixed-methods user research (surveys and interviews) and prototype development, but the paper is primarily a position/concept paper rather than a completed efficacy study. It does not report a controlled comparison against non-AI digital tools or human-only supports, nor does it provide outcome data such as effect sizes or follow-up duration. Its main conclusion is that deliberate friction and bidirectional bias support are promising directions for future AI literacy tool design and evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that metacognitive AI literacy interventions may improve critical thinking, bias awareness, and self-regulation during AI use, but this is presented as a design rationale rather than as empirical evidence. It reports that earlier prototype work with usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews suggested the interventions could make implicit human and AI biases explicit and actionable, but no effect sizes, sample sizes, or controlled outcome comparisons are provided.
finding.measure: bias awareness, critical thinking, metacognitive regulation during human-AI interaction

paper_profiles.title: Need of AI in Modern Education: in the Eyes of Explainable AI (xAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter argues for the importance of AI and explainable AI (xAI) in modern education, but the paper’s actual empirical work is not on K-12 instructional support tools. Instead, it uses the Adult Census Income dataset to study whether post-hoc explanation methods can reveal feature importance and bias in an XGBoost classifier that predicts whether an adult earns more than $50K, with the authors connecting parental income to downstream educational opportunity.

The chapter compares several explanation and auditing tools—Permutation Importance (ELI5), SHAP, LIME, global surrogate decision trees, and FairML—on the same trained model. It reports that LIME can be unstable across repeated runs, that a decision tree can approximate the XGBoost model reasonably well as a surrogate, and that FairML exposes sensitive-feature dependence on race, nationality, and sex that other methods may obscure. The paper concludes that xAI methods can improve transparency, but fairness audits are necessary because feature-importance tools alone may miss bias.

The work is essentially a methodological/illustrative analysis rather than an evaluation of an educational intervention, and it does not benchmark teacher-facing AI tools against non-AI alternatives such as human planning time, coaching, clerical help, substitute coverage, or standard productivity software. It also does not study K-12 students or teachers directly, nor does it provide causal evidence about educational outcomes. The paper is best understood as a conceptual and technical exposition of xAI applied to a non-education tabular dataset with a policy-oriented discussion of fairness in education.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that xAI can improve transparency and accountability in education-related decision systems, but also shows that bias can persist or be revealed differently depending on the audit tool. Using the Adult Census Income dataset, the authors report that FairML exposed strong dependence on race White, nac United-States, and sex Male, while SHAP and feature-importance methods sometimes did not reveal the same bias patterns.
