finding.measure: Bias/fairness audit outputs from FairML, SHAP, LIME, permutation importance, and surrogate models applied to an XGBoost classifier

paper_profiles.title: Urban Comfort Assessment in the Era of Digital Planning: A Multidimensional, Data-driven, and AI-assisted Framework
paper_profiles.venue: 19th International Conference on Computational Urban Planning and Urban Management (CUPUM 2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how urban comfort can be conceptualized and assessed in digital planning workflows, with an emphasis on combining multidimensional theory, data-driven modeling, and AI assistance. The authors argue that urban comfort should not be reduced to a single scalar index because it is subjective, context-dependent, and composed of multiple dimensions such as environmental comfort and social comfort.

The paper proposes a four-step assessment framework: conduct comfort surveys, build comfort models, scale predictions across the city, and validate the model using additional survey data. In the case study, the authors focus on thermal comfort in Singapore and use street view imagery, CNN-based feature extraction, deep neural networks, and linear regression to predict and interpret comfort at urban scale.

The study is not an evaluation of teacher-facing AI tools or K-12 educational interventions. It is a conceptual and applied urban-planning paper describing how AI can support digital planning by replacing some in-field comfort-survey work with street-view-image-based analysis and by enabling scalable prediction and mapping. The paper does not report a controlled comparison against human-only or non-AI educational supports, and it provides no K-12 population, grade band, or school setting.

paper_profiles.title: How Developers Interact with AI: A Taxonomy of Human-AI Collaboration in Software Engineering
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a taxonomy of how software developers interact with AI tools across the development lifecycle. Rather than evaluating a single tool, the authors synthesize prior work and examples to define eleven interaction types, including auto-complete suggestions, command-driven actions, conversational assistance, contextual recommendations, selection-based enhancements, explicit UI actions, comment-guided prompts, event-based triggers, shortcut-activated commands, file-aware suggestions, and automated API responses.

The paper’s main contribution is conceptual: it organizes the design space of human-AI collaboration in software engineering and uses that taxonomy to outline a research agenda. The agenda highlights open questions about effectiveness, trust, context-awareness, cognitive load, customization, ethics, privacy, and hallucination control. No K-12 population is studied, and the paper does not present an empirical comparison of AI tools against human-only or non-AI digital supports; it is primarily a taxonomy/research-agenda paper based on literature examples.

Because the paper is not an empirical study of educational settings, it does not provide evidence on teacher-facing AI tools, grade bands, school contexts, or follow-up outcomes. Its relevance to the retrieval question is therefore indirect only: it names interaction patterns that could matter for workload and workflow disruption in AI-assisted work, but it does not benchmark AI against protected planning time, coaching, clerical support, substitute coverage, or standard productivity tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses productivity, efficiency, and cognitive load as motivations for its taxonomy, but it does not empirically measure any efficiency outcome. Its claims are conceptual and illustrative only, with no study data, sample, or effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Predicted Composite Signed-Distance Fields for Real-Time Motion Planning in Dynamic Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses real-time motion planning for robots operating in dynamic environments with moving obstacles. The authors argue that standard signed-distance-field (SDF) approaches are too slow to update at the frequency needed for online replanning, especially when obstacle motion must be anticipated rather than merely reacted to.

To solve this, the paper introduces predicted signed-distance fields and a compositional update method that combines precomputed SDFs for static and moving objects. The method uses simple constant-velocity obstacle prediction and integrates these predicted SDFs into the GPMP2 motion planner, enabling time-indexed obstacle factors to be updated rapidly during execution.

The evaluation is conducted in robot simulation and on hardware using 7-DoF manipulators (WAM and Franka Emika Panda), not in an educational setting. The paper compares composite SDF prediction against full SDF recomputation and compares planning modes such as static planning, execute-and-update, and full prior knowledge. Results show substantial computation speedups for repeated SDF prediction after initialization, and better planning performance when obstacle trajectories are predicted, including smoother trajectories and fewer collisions. No K-12 education outcomes, teacher-facing tools, or instructional supports are studied.

paper_profiles.title: Meaningful human control: actionable properties for AI system development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual and engineering problem in responsible AI: how to translate the philosophical idea of “meaningful human control” into actionable design guidance for AI systems. The authors argue that existing discussions of tracking and tracing are too abstract for practitioners, and that developers need more concrete system-level properties to support human responsibility in AI-mediated decision-making.

Using an iterative abductive process that combines engineering, computer science, philosophy of technology, ethnography, and design perspectives, the paper proposes four actionable properties: an explicit moral operational design domain (moral ODD), mutually compatible human and AI representations, appropriate ability and authority for relevant human agents, and explicit links between AI actions and human decisions. These properties are illustrated through two non-K-12 case scenarios: automated vehicles and AI-based hiring. The paper does not report empirical testing; rather, it offers a conceptual framework and implementation considerations intended to guide design, development, and evaluation of AI systems in socio-technical contexts.

For education-relevant extraction, the paper does not study teachers, students, schools, or K-12 AI tools. It is a theoretical article about AI ethics and system design, with no benchmark comparison against non-AI educator supports, no outcome measures in education, and no causal or correlational evidence in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: BERT4beam: Large AI Model Enabled Generalized Beamforming Optimization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of using large language model–style architectures for wireless beamforming optimization in multi-user MISO systems. The authors argue that conventional optimization methods are computationally expensive and task-specific neural models do not generalize well across changes in user count, antenna count, and system utility.

They propose BERT4beam, a framework that reformulates beamforming as a token-level learning problem. Two model variants are developed: a single-task BERT-based model and a multi-task UBERT model with element-wise tokenization, antenna encoding, task embeddings, and supervised pre-training/fine-tuning. Both models are trained and evaluated in simulation on Rayleigh-fading wireless channels, with traditional convex optimization/SCA used to generate labels and serve as a baseline.

The paper reports that BERT and UBERT achieve near-optimal performance relative to SCA across sum-rate, min-rate, and energy-efficiency objectives, with BERT often within about 2% and UBERT within about 3% of SCA in pre-training tests. UBERT shows stronger generalization across tasks and configurations, while BERT can generalize well across user counts but is less adaptable to power-budget variation. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-inspired architectures can be effective and robust solvers for wireless beamforming, though the evidence is entirely simulation-based rather than a human-subject or K-12 education study.

paper_profiles.title: Seeing Multilingual Learners through Media and AI: Pre-Service Teachers’ Perceptions in an ESOL Course
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Interdisciplinary Research in Artificial Intelligence and Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory instrumental case study examines how pre-service teachers in an upper-level ESOL Foundations course made sense of media and AI influences on their views of multilingual learners, and how they translated those understandings into possible classroom practices. The paper is motivated by concern that teacher candidates encounter deficit-oriented media frames, algorithmically amplified content, and generative AI in ways that may shape beliefs about immigrant and multilingual communities.

The study focused on one course offering at a university in Southwest Florida during Spring 2024. Thirty-eight undergraduates volunteered after the semester ended; the analytic corpus consisted of two coursework artifacts from a teacher-attitudes module: a reading reflection paper and a written class discussion/activity response. The module included assigned readings on media representation, platform dynamics, and AI-generated content, plus a structured in-class activity using instructor-curated media examples, including an AI-generated image, to prompt credibility evaluation and reflection on implications for multilingual-learner teaching.

Findings from qualitative content analysis produced five themes: media as a curriculum for bias, uncertainty about distinguishing real versus AI-generated content, a perceived gap between basic technology use and critical evaluation, movement from diagnosis to instructional design, and equity-oriented teaching commitments. Participants generally saw media literacy and foundational AI literacy as important for noticing bias, evaluating credibility, and designing more equitable classroom routines, but the evidence is entirely self-reported and short-term, with no measure of student outcomes or observed instructional implementation beyond coursework artifacts.

finding.finding_summary: The course artifacts suggest that pre-service teachers developed stronger critical reflection about media framing, AI credibility, and how to translate those insights into teaching routines. Across 38 participants, qualitative themes indicated increased attention to analyzing bias, comparing perspectives, and questioning provenance, though the study did not measure gains with a standardized instrument or observe enacted practice.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of reading reflection papers and structured class discussion/activity responses about media framing, AI credibility, and classroom-facing instructional ideas

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews the educational chatbot literature to characterize how chatbots have been designed, deployed, and evaluated in education. The authors explicitly focus on seven dimensions: field of application, platform, educational role, interaction style, design principles, empirical evidence, and limitations.

The review screened 1,208 records and included 36 papers published between 2011 and 2021. Across the included studies, educational chatbots were most often web-based, frequently used in computer science and general education, and commonly framed as teaching agents or peer agents. The review also shows that most systems used chatbot-driven, flow-based or intent-based interaction patterns, with design principles such as personalized learning, experiential learning, social dialog, and collaborative learning.

For evidence, the review finds that the literature is largely short-term and pilot-like, with most studies relying on experiments, evaluation studies, questionnaires, or focus groups rather than long-duration or whole-school implementations. Reported outcomes were mainly improved learning, subjective satisfaction, interest, and engagement; one 8-week longitudinal English-learning study found declining interest in communicating with the chatbot. Overall, the paper concludes that the evidence base is promising but limited, with recurring challenges around dataset quality, usability heuristics, and incomplete validation.

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, several chatbot studies in language and writing contexts reported improved learning outcomes. For example, the authors summarize an experiment on writing support (n=55) where adaptive tutoring via chatbot improved the quality of students’ formal argumentation and produced better writing outcomes than the control condition.
finding.measure: Writing quality / formal argumentation quality

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that language-learning chatbots often improved learning or engagement, but evidence was not uniformly positive. In one 8-week longitudinal study teaching English (n=122), students’ interest in communicating with the chatbot significantly declined over time, indicating weaker sustained engagement despite short-term benefits in some other language studies.
finding.measure: English-language learning / interest in communicating with chatbot

finding.finding_summary: The review includes mathematics-focused chatbots and reports improved learning in at least one experiment. For example, a teachable-agent mathematics study (n=183) found statistically significant gains in learning compared with the control or baseline condition.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning / post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: A substantial share of the reviewed studies measured engagement, interest, subjective satisfaction, and motivation. Findings were generally positive in the short term, including improved engagement (e.g. n=56, p<0.0001) and improved subjective satisfaction (n=56, p=0.03), but one longitudinal study found no evidence for sustained engagement over 8 weeks.
finding.measure: Engagement, interest, subjective satisfaction, motivation
finding.study_size: Multiple studies; examples include n=56, n=122

finding.finding_summary: The review describes chatbot studies that targeted higher-order skills such as argumentation and collaborative discussion. One experiment found that adaptive tutoring through a chatbot improved formal argumentation quality in student writing, and other studies used chatbots to scaffold discussion or collaborative learning.
finding.measure: Argumentation quality; collaborative discussion
finding.study_size: Examples include n=55; other studies not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / no K-12 population studied
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an exploratory, demonstration-style account of early experiments with GPT-4, aiming to characterize its capabilities and limitations across a wide range of tasks. Rather than testing a school intervention or educational product, the authors use prompted examples, side-by-side comparisons with ChatGPT, and informal evaluations to argue that GPT-4 shows broad, human-like competence across language, coding, mathematics, vision, tool use, and social reasoning.

The paper is not a K-12 study and does not investigate classroom implementation, teacher adoption, training, or student outcomes. Its relevance to education is indirect: it includes a few prompts involving teacher-like evaluation and educationally adjacent tasks, but these are illustrative only. The main conclusion is that early GPT-4 appears substantially more capable than prior LLMs and may represent progress toward more general intelligence, while still exhibiting notable limitations such as hallucinations, weak planning, and other errors.

Because the paper is a qualitative, non-empirical demonstration without a school context or participant population, it offers no direct evidence on perceived usefulness, workload, morale, engagement, or institutional outcomes in K-12 settings. It should be treated as background/context on GPT-4 capabilities rather than implementation evidence for teacher-facing AI in schools.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 is demonstrated on a range of non-K-12 academic tasks, including coding, mathematics, medicine, and writing-style transformations, and the authors argue that it performs impressively on these tasks. For example, the paper reports that GPT-4 solved all three LeetCode interview rounds in about 10 minutes total and produced strong outputs on stylized proof-writing and code-generation prompts, but these are demonstration examples rather than controlled student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Illustrative task performance on coding, mathematics, and interdisciplinary writing prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims GPT-4 shows strong reasoning, planning, and problem-solving abilities across novel prompts, though the authors also emphasize that these capabilities are incomplete and sometimes inconsistent. The evidence is qualitative and example-based, not a controlled measure of critical thinking or metacognition in learners.
finding.measure: Qualitative performance on reasoning, planning, and novel problem-solving prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents examples suggesting GPT-4 can increase productivity in code generation and tool use, including passing simulated software-engineering interviews and generating usable code artifacts. However, these are not measured productivity outcomes in an educational implementation, and no teacher workload or school efficiency data are reported.
finding.measure: Informal task completion speed and code-generation usefulness

paper_profiles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on learner–instructor interaction in online learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and instructors perceive the impact of AI systems on learner–instructor interaction in online learning. The authors focus on three interaction dimensions from prior theory—communication, support, and presence—and ask where AI might improve online instruction and where it might become intrusive or harmful.

To study this, the authors created 11 storyboard scenarios representing plausible AI-enabled features for online courses, such as an AI teaching assistant, AI grading assistance, analytics, intelligent suggestions, adaptive quizzes, virtual avatars, breakout-room matching, and facial analytics. They then used a Speed Dating method with 12 undergraduate students and 11 instructors from a university context during the COVID-19 period; participants had at least three months of online learning/teaching experience and reacted to the scenarios in semi-structured Zoom interviews.

The study finds a consistent ambivalence: participants believed AI could improve the quantity and quality of communication, provide just-in-time personalized support, and enhance perceived connection in online learning. At the same time, they raised concerns about responsibility for incorrect AI outputs, loss of student agency from over-standardized support, and surveillance/privacy risks from tools that infer engagement or emotion from cameras, eye tracking, or facial analysis. The authors conclude that AI systems in online learning should be explainable, human-in-the-loop, and governed by clear data norms to avoid becoming invasive.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived AI as potentially improving student engagement, connection, and willingness to ask questions in online learning, but also as creating anxiety, self-consciousness, and discomfort around surveillance. The study is qualitative and reports counts of participants endorsing each view (e.g., 12/12 students said AI would nudge them to ask more questions; 10/12 students and 10/11 instructors raised concerns about surveillance/privacy), not effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived engagement, connection, willingness to ask questions, anxiety, and comfort in online learning scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines how AI affects student agency, autonomy, and collaboration-related learning in online courses. Participants thought AI-supported study tools and group-project helpers could improve learning efficiency, but they also worried that AI would over-standardize learning, reduce exploration and discovery, and do too much of the work for students.
finding.measure: Perceived agency, autonomy, exploration/discovery, and collaboration in AI-supported learning scenarios

finding.finding_summary: A major finding was that AI was perceived to improve instructional efficiency by handling repetitive questions, speeding feedback, and supporting just-in-time assistance. Instructors said this would let them focus on more meaningful communication and higher-value work; 10/11 instructors endorsed AI-based intelligent suggestions and adaptive quizzes, but the study does not report quantitative workload reduction effects.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher time savings, faster feedback loops, and reduced repetitive communication

finding.finding_summary: The study addresses institutional design implications for AI in online learning, especially explainability, human-in-the-loop decision-making, and data governance. Participants highlighted governance risks around responsibility, surveillance, and privacy, and the authors recommend clear data norms and consent processes, but the evidence is based on perceptions rather than causal institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived governance, responsibility, surveillance, and data-norm concerns for AI in online learning

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and large language models in academia: opportunities and challenges
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (academic and higher-education/general academia; discusses K-12 only as a subset in commentary)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial discusses the emergence of ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs) and considers their opportunities and risks for academic work. The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a specific educational intervention; instead, it synthesizes perspectives on how LLMs may be used for writing, editing, grant development, programming, and education, while emphasizing concerns about hallucinations, bias, plagiarism, access, and governance.

In the education section, the authors describe potential uses of LLMs across K-12, undergraduate, and graduate settings, including serving as a classroom aid, interactive study guide, content generator, lesson-planning support, and assessment tool. The discussion is framed as a conceptual/editorial argument rather than a study with participants, methods, or outcomes. The paper concludes that LLMs should be embraced carefully, with attention to bias, factual accuracy, and disclosure, but it provides no original data on teacher adoption, training, duration, frequency of use, autonomy over outputs, or student/teacher outcomes.

Because this is a commentary, it does not offer causal, correlational, or even systematic evidence on educational outcomes. It is useful mainly as background on perceived applications and risks of LLMs in academia and education, not as direct evidence for K-12 implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial argues that LLMs like ChatGPT could increase efficiency in academic work and should be embraced, but also highlights institutional concerns around bias, plagiarism, accuracy, access, and governance. No empirical evaluation is presented; the claims are conceptual and policy-oriented rather than data-driven.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Pilot Study on Teacher-Facing Real-Time Classroom Game Dashboards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a real-time teacher-facing dashboard for an educational game can help teachers monitor and facilitate student gameplay in K-12 classrooms. The motivation is that teachers often have to infer what students are doing by checking screens one at a time, which is inefficient and can make it hard to identify struggling or disengaged students during gameplay.

The authors used a participatory design process to co-develop a prototype dashboard for Lakeland, a classroom educational game used in grades 7-12. The work had two phases: a teacher workshop with 12 teachers and teaching mentors to elicit dashboard requirements, followed by a small pilot deployment in classrooms with four teachers, mostly online during COVID-related school closures. The pilot gathered post-session surveys, interviews, and design artifacts to assess co-design influence, feasibility, and usefulness of the tool.

The main findings were that teachers saw clear evidence of their input in the prototype and generally rated the tool favorably for ease of setup, usability, and facilitation support. Teachers reported that the dashboard helped them identify student progress, inactivity, and strategy use, although some bugs, data inaccuracies, and visualization issues limited the experience. The authors conclude that the participatory design approach produced a promising classroom dashboard, but the evidence is preliminary and explicitly framed as a short pilot rather than a longer-term classroom evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the dashboard was easy to set up and use, and that it helped them facilitate gameplay by quickly checking student progress and identifying who needed help. Survey ratings were high for setup and usability (e.g., setup of class code and student connection: 5/5; dashboard easy to use: 4/5), though some bugs and information overload reduced practicality in a few cases.
finding.measure: Teacher post-session survey and exit interviews on feasibility/usefulness of the dashboard for classroom facilitation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived that the dashboard helped them detect when students were disengaged, inactive, or frustrated, and some used it to identify students with technical issues or who were not progressing. One teacher noted it was useful to know students were 'actually making progress,' while another used the inactivity indicator to spot a student who had completed 0/6 tutorials.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement/disengagement and progress during gameplay

paper_profiles.title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short position pieces from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it asks how AI education should evolve across several themes: ethics in the curriculum, early introduction of AI in secondary school and early undergraduate settings, and interdisciplinary AI education for non-engineering fields.

Across the essays, contributors propose instructional ideas such as peer-learning seminars, project-based interdisciplinary work, Montessori-inspired student-centered discovery, more accessible hands-on AI activities for K-12 and early undergraduates, and explicit ethics instruction embedded throughout the curriculum. One section proposes a 12-week secondary-school AI course using the General Video Game AI framework, with students given videos, books, software, and instructor access, but no outcome data are reported. The paper’s main contribution is conceptual: it argues for more engaging, contextualized, and ethically grounded AI teaching, but it does not evaluate these ideas empirically.

Because the paper is a set of opinion/blue-sky responses, it provides no causal, correlational, or longitudinal evidence on teacher-facing AI tools in K-12 classrooms. It does not report implementation outcomes such as perceived usefulness, workload, teacher morale, or student engagement beyond speculative claims and proposed course designs. As a result, it is best understood as a qualitative, non-empirical discussion piece rather than direct evidence for synthesis.

paper_profiles.title: Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety (AAAI-Safe AI 2019)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to organize and compare the rapidly growing set of AI principles, ethics statements, codes, and governance guidelines issued by academic groups, non-profits, governments, and industry. Rather than proposing a new principle set, the authors build LAIP (Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles), a platform for semantically linking and analyzing 27 AI principles documents.

The approach combines manual keyword selection with word2vec-based semantic expansion to identify shared topics across principles. The authors define 10 high-level topics (e.g., humanity, fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, accountability) and use topic and keyword coverage to compare how different organizations emphasize different issues. They also represent the links in RDF/OWL and provide a public online service for keyword and paragraph search.

The paper is a descriptive text-analysis and knowledge-organization study of AI governance documents, not an evaluation of an educational intervention or AI tool used in schools. Its main conclusion is that AI principles differ in emphasis but share enough common vocabulary and themes to be linked into a comprehensive framework; the authors argue that this can support more robust future AI governance analysis. It also notes that different publisher types vary in how often they reference collaboration, security, privacy, and accountability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that LAIP can semantically link and compare 27 AI principle documents across 10 shared topics, making differences in organizational emphasis more visible. It concludes that no single AI principle set is complete and that integrating multiple principles into a comprehensive framework is useful for AI governance analysis.
finding.measure: Topic coverage and keyword coverage across 27 AI principle documents

paper_profiles.title: Probability Judgment in Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual/technical essay about probability judgment in artificial intelligence, contrasting Bayesian probability with belief functions (Dempster-Shafer theory). Shafer explains how each framework represents evidence, why belief functions can be useful when evidence is incomplete, and how these ideas matter for the design of expert systems.

The paper uses illustrative examples rather than an empirical study. It discusses cases involving a speaker's reliability, a thermometer, and dependent versus independent evidence to show when Bayesian and belief-function arguments differ. The main conclusion is that belief functions can be more modular and better suited to some AI expert-system settings, especially when evidence is incomplete or not naturally modeled as direct probabilities over answers, but the paper does not evaluate a K-12 educational intervention or any teacher-facing AI tool.

Because the article is theoretical and not an education study, it does not report population-specific implementation details such as grade band, school context, duration, training, access, guardrails, or user autonomy. It also does not present empirical outcomes like perceived usefulness, workload, morale, or student engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup as an Evaluation Domain for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-2019 Workshop on Games and Simulations for Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS), a complex single-player roguelike game, is a strong evaluation domain for artificial intelligence and cognitive systems research. The authors emphasize DCSS’s large state space, partial observability, stochastic dynamics, long-horizon planning demands, and rich natural-language descriptions as features that make it useful for studying AI planning, inference, reinforcement learning, explainability, knowledge extraction, and human-agent interaction.

The paper does not test an intervention or report an empirical study with human participants; instead, it describes the game domain, estimates its complexity, and outlines a proposed API for AI agents to interact with the game. The API would expose structured game-state objects, accept action commands, support multi-step actions, and enable custom scenarios, with the aim of facilitating future AI experiments and human-user studies. The main conclusion is that DCSS offers a highly complex yet manageable simulated environment for evaluating AI systems, especially because it avoids real-time reaction constraints while still requiring sophisticated decision making.

Although the paper mentions possible educational uses such as intelligent tutors and novice/expert interaction, it does not study K-12 classrooms, teacher-facing AI, or any educational outcomes. It is primarily a conceptual/domain paper about AI benchmarking in games, with no reported causal, correlational, or perceptual evidence about student engagement, workload, or learning.

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI Fall Symposium Series (AAAI FSS-21): Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review of certification and verification approaches for artificial intelligence and machine learning systems, with a focus on how to establish performance bounds, documentation, and operational safeguards for deployment. Rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention, it surveys standards and frameworks such as model cards, MAST, verification/validation methods, and safety certification practices drawn from defense, aviation, and software engineering.

The paper’s main contribution is a proposed certification-oriented way of thinking about AI/ML adoption: define intended use, characterize data and uncertainty, test performance under relevant operating conditions, and document limitations and warnings for users. It uses image fusion for automatic target recognition as a notional example to illustrate quantitative performance metrics and robustness bounds, showing how certifiable AI might be evaluated in a technical domain.

This is not a K-12 study and does not involve teachers, schools, students, or educational outcomes. It is best understood as a policy/engineering perspective on AI assurance and deployment, with no empirical evaluation of an AI system in educational practice.

paper_profiles.title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: A Survey.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of two closely related AI subfields: statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). Its central question is how learning and reasoning can be integrated, and it proposes seven shared dimensions for comparing systems across the two fields, including proof- vs model-theoretic inference, logic syntax, semantics, learning type, representations, paradigms, and task classes.

The paper does not report an empirical study, intervention, or K-12 implementation. Instead, it organizes prior work into a conceptual framework and illustrates the framework with representative systems such as ProbLog, Markov Logic Networks, DeepProbLog, Semantic Loss, SBR, and LTN. The discussion highlights how symbolic knowledge can be compiled into neural architectures or loss functions, and how different semantic choices affect scalability, control, and interpretability.

Because it is a survey, the paper is not specific to any learner population, school context, or educational setting, and it does not evaluate teacher-facing AI tools in classrooms. Its main conclusion is theoretical: the field can be better understood by mapping systems along common dimensions, which may help transfer methods between probabilistic logic and neurosymbolic learning.

paper_profiles.title: How Do Teachers Create Pedagogical Chatbots?: Current Practices and Challenges
paper_profiles.venue: CHI 2025 Workshop on Augmented Educators and AI
paper_profiles.population: Elementary and Middle School (K-12 teachers; some participants taught elementary and middle school students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers create, test, and deploy LLM-based pedagogical chatbots in practice, and what challenges emerge across the chatbot lifecycle. The authors position the work as a foundational study of teacher-created educational chatbots, with emphasis on the design, implementation, and classroom deployment process rather than on student learning effects.

The study uses hour-long semi-structured interviews with seven K-12 teachers in Korea. Three participants were experienced chatbot creators, while four were novice teachers who were asked to use the commercial platform Mizou to build a chatbot during the interview session. The interviews elicited teachers’ current workflows, prompt engineering practices, testing habits, deployment experiences, and concerns about safety, pedagogical fit, and classroom management.

The paper finds that teachers prefer narrowly scoped chatbots tailored to specific lessons and instructional roles rather than versatile general-purpose bots. Teachers rely on prompt templates, iterative debugging, and opportunistic testing, but these activities are time-intensive and often limited in coverage. During classroom deployment, teachers want visibility into student-bot interactions for real-time intervention and post-class review, yet current tools make monitoring and feedback difficult. The authors conclude that teacher-facing systems should better support contextualized design guidance, role separation between pedagogical and technical work, safer testing, and analysis of conversation data to reduce teacher workload while preserving teacher agency.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed chatbot creation as potentially useful for supporting lesson-specific tasks, but the process was highly time-consuming in practice. All teachers reported substantial effort in prompt engineering and debugging, and novices in particular said iterative refinement would be difficult to sustain during a semester. The study is qualitative (n=7) and reports perceived workload rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Perceived time burden and workload during prompt engineering, debugging, testing, and deployment review

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed pedagogical chatbots could make lessons more engaging and help sustain student participation, especially when aligned to specific activities such as book discussions or essay brainstorming. However, the paper does not measure student engagement directly; the finding is based on teachers’ perceptions and deployment reflections from interviews with seven teachers.
finding.measure: Perceived student engagement and motivation in chatbot-supported lessons

finding.finding_summary: Several teacher-created examples targeted writing support, including essay brainstorming and a writing assistant that suggested arguments and evidence. Teachers saw these chatbots as potentially helpful for helping students begin essays and complete writing tasks within limited class time, but the paper provides no student outcome data. The evidence is entirely interview-based and focused on intended literacy support rather than causal effects.
finding.measure: Teacher-described use cases for essay writing and writing support

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Conference paper (arXiv preprint of CHI-style manuscript)
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (including educators working with elementary through high school students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers value and design integrated AI curriculum when AI is embedded into core subjects rather than taught as a standalone computer science topic. The authors argue that, although AI education is increasingly important, many existing tools are difficult for non-CS teachers to adopt because they do not fit classroom contexts or subject-specific goals.

To explore this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from diverse grade bands and subject areas. Teachers received introductory presentations on AI concepts and tools, completed pre-work using tools such as Teachable Machine and Machine Learning for Kids, and then worked in small groups with researchers to draft integrated curricula for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The study is primarily qualitative and focuses on design needs and implementation considerations rather than student outcome measurement.

The main findings are that teachers want AI lessons to support evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that they value scaffolding for ethics and data discussions. Teachers were able to generate implementable lesson drafts and saw integration points through data, reflection, and ethics, but they also expressed the need for clearer guidance, more time, and more explicit tool support to make these lessons classroom-ready. The paper concludes that co-design with teachers can surface practical requirements for more accessible, integrated AI education, especially for non-CS classrooms and remote collaboration settings.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the workshop increased engagement-related thinking and reflected positively on the value of AI teaching, with some indicating the experience broadened their view of classroom possibilities. The evidence is based on teachers’ post-workshop reflections and ratings rather than student-level outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of engagement value and workshop helpfulness; post-workshop reflections

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that teachers wanted AI curricula to support collaboration, reflection, and evaluation, and they used co-design to create lesson drafts that integrated these skills with AI concepts. The paper reports qualitative evidence from 15 teachers that collaboration in small groups and reflective prompts were important for lesson design and implementation.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of workshop discussions and curriculum drafts; teacher reflections on collaboration and reflection

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified logistics and tool selection as key implementation issues and valued structured supports that would make AI lessons easier to run in classrooms. The study does not measure workload quantitatively, but it shows that teachers perceived the workshop and provided scaffolds as helpful for planning and implementation efficiency.
finding.measure: Teacher reports about lesson structure, tool choice, and implementation logistics

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating AI into core K-12 curricula could expand access beyond computing classrooms and improve institutional adoption of AI education. Evidence is qualitative and based on teacher co-design across multiple schools and subject areas, with the conclusion that teacher buy-in and contextualized design are necessary for broader implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher co-design outputs and discussion of adoption/accessibility across school contexts

paper_profiles.title: AI Instructional Agent Improves Student’s Perceived Learner Control and Learning Outcome: Empirical Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI instructional agent can improve students’ perceived learner control and academic performance compared with human-led lecture and MOOC-style video instruction. The authors argue that many AI learning tools provide limited instructional support, so they test a more integrated system that can deliver lecture content and answer questions in real time.

The study uses a randomized controlled trial with 140 undergraduate students from universities in Beijing (final analytic sample n=125) in a general education course on artificial intelligence. Students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: in-person human teacher, self-paced MOOC videos with chatbot support, or an AI instructional agent embedded in the MAIC platform that delivered the lecture and responded interactively in real time. The intervention covered two course modules with identical content across conditions, and the AI condition allowed pausing, interruption, and questions answered immediately by the agent.

Results show that the AI instructional agent significantly increased perceived learner control relative to both the human teacher and MOOC conditions, and also produced higher post-test scores. Students in the AI condition interacted more frequently with the system and completed the learning task in less time, suggesting more efficient self-paced learning. Regression analyses further indicated that perceived learner control was positively associated with post-test performance. The study is short-term and immediate-post-test only, with no evidence on longer-term retention or school-level implementation.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with 125 valid undergraduate participants (41 human teacher, 43 MOOC, 41 AI agent), the AI instructional agent condition produced significantly higher post-test performance than both comparison groups. Post-test scores differed by group, F(2,122)=7.673, p<.01; Tukey tests showed AI-human mean difference = 0.128 (p<.01) and AI-MOOC mean difference = 0.112 (p<.01).
finding.measure: Post-test score on a 16-item multiple-choice assessment of course content

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s primary outcome was perceived learner control, measured with a newly developed 4-item scale (Cronbach’s alpha=0.823). The AI instructional agent group reported significantly higher perceived learner control than the human teacher group (mean difference=0.732, p<.001) and the MOOC group (mean difference=0.416, p<.05), with an overall group effect of F(2,122)=12.155, p<.001.
finding.measure: Perceived learner control scale; learning engagement scale also assessed

finding.finding_summary: Perceived learner control was positively associated with academic performance and negatively associated with learning duration, indicating more self-directed time management. Across all participants, PLC correlated with post-test scores (r=0.23, p<.01) and with shorter learning duration (r=-0.30, p<.001); in regression, PLC remained a significant predictor of post-test performance (β=0.055, p<.05) controlling for gender, age, self-regulated learning, and pre-test score.
finding.measure: Correlation and regression analyses involving perceived learner control and learning duration

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent condition was more efficient than the human teacher condition, with significantly shorter learning durations and higher interaction frequency. Learning duration showed a strong group effect, F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001, and the AI condition was approximately 30 minutes shorter than the human teacher condition; interaction frequency was also higher in the AI group, F(2,122)=21.755, p<.001, with mean differences of 5.410 versus human and 7.015 versus MOOC.
finding.measure: Learning duration and number/frequency of student-initiated feedback/questions

finding.finding_summary: Although engagement was measured in cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions, only behavioral engagement showed a significant positive correlation with post-test performance. Group differences in cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement were not significant overall (F values reported as 1.092, 0.215, and 1.670 respectively), suggesting the intervention did not reliably change these engagement subscales at the group level.
finding.measure: Three-dimensional student engagement scale (cognitive, emotional, behavioral)

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Multi-Agent AI Supporting Teachers in Scaling Differentiated Learning for Diverse Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping teachers differentiate instruction in increasingly heterogeneous K–12 classrooms, where student differences in performance, motivation, language proficiency, and learning needs can make individualized planning time-intensive and difficult to sustain. The authors position existing AI tools as mostly student-facing and performance-centric, arguing that teacher-facing systems need to support broader differentiation while preserving educator control.

The paper introduces FACET, a teacher-facing multi-agent framework with four specialized agents: learner simulation, diagnostic assessment, material generation, and evaluation. Teachers define learner profiles, upload or select tasks, and retain full review/modify/reject control over outputs. The system is designed to support curriculum alignment, accessibility (including dyslexia-related formatting), and differentiated worksheet generation, with local/on-premise LLM hosting for data privacy.

Evaluation combined two stakeholder studies. First, two one-hour workshops with German school principals (N=30) elicited requirements around differentiation support, curriculum fit, accessibility, and teacher autonomy. Second, an online survey with 70 in-service K–12 teachers from the UK, US, Canada, and Australia rated five example worksheets generated for grade 7 mathematics profiles. Teachers generally rated scaffolded worksheets favorably on didactic structure and clarity, while enrichment materials for high-motivation learners were weaker and the dyslexia-adapted worksheet needed improvement in font readability and accessibility. The paper concludes that FACET appears promising for teacher-facing differentiated material generation, but it remains early-stage, with no classroom outcome evaluation yet; the authors explicitly frame future work as longitudinal deployment across schools.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests FACET may reduce teacher effort for differentiated material preparation, but this is based on perceived usefulness rather than measured time savings. School principals emphasized that the system could help with workload and differentiation at scale, and the design explicitly aims to reduce prompting and material-creation burden.
finding.measure: Perceived workload reduction, workflow integration, and usefulness in workshops/surveys

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ ratings indicate generally favorable perceived usability and suitability, especially for scaffolded worksheets, but more limited appeal for enrichment materials and mixed accessibility judgments for dyslexia-adapted outputs. The paper also reports high teacher openness to AI use for lesson preparation (91.43%) and existing AI use (70.0%), which are attitudes rather than learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of worksheet quality; teacher openness to AI use
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported for worksheet ratings, but no single overall effect size

finding.finding_summary: The evaluated example worksheets were based on a grade 7 mathematics area-calculation task, and teachers rated the generated materials as generally suitable, with stronger scores for scaffolded profiles than for enrichment-oriented profiles. Didactic structure and clarity were highest for low-motivation worksheets (structure M=4.41-4.50; clarity M=4.23-4.46 on a 6-point scale), while the high-performance/high-motivation worksheet received lower ratings (structure M=3.87; clarity M=3.57).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of grade-7 mathematics worksheet quality (area calculation)
finding.std_deviation: SDs vary by worksheet and criterion; e.g., structure SDs about 1.02-1.20

finding.finding_summary: Literacy-related accessibility was examined indirectly through the dyslexia-adapted worksheet, with teachers rating spacing/layout and language simplification above midpoint but font readability near midpoint. The paper therefore suggests partial success on text accessibility, but it does not test reading performance or literacy gains.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of dyslexia-adapted worksheet accessibility (font readability, language simplification, spacing/layout)
finding.std_deviation: Font readability SD=1.61; language simplification SD=1.40; spacing/layout SD=1.39

finding.finding_summary: School principals indicated that FACET could fit institutional needs if it preserves teacher control, aligns to curriculum, and supports accessibility and differentiation. The paper also reports prospective school partnerships across 10 German schools for a semester-long deployment, indicating institutional interest but not yet measured system-level outcomes.
finding.measure: Principal workshop feedback; school partnership/deployment plans
finding.study_size: n=30 principals; 10 schools planned for deployment

paper_profiles.title: NaMemo2: Facilitating Teacher-Student Interaction with Theory-Based Design and Student Autonomy Consideration
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of supporting teacher-student interaction (TSI) in large university classrooms, where teachers may struggle to remember many student names and students may have unexpressed preferences or willingness for interaction. The authors argue that existing TSI support tools largely emphasize teacher awareness while overlooking student autonomy, privacy, and consent.

To address this, they developed NaMemo2, an augmented-reality classroom system that uses facial recognition to identify students for the teacher and lets students indicate their willingness to interact. The paper also proposes STUDIER, a theory-based framework for designing and evaluating TSI support tools, integrating teacher-student interaction theory, behavioral theory, and ethics-aware design principles.

The evaluation was a four-week field deployment in four undergraduate classes at a university in China (two teachers, micro-controllers course). The study used a single-arm pre/post mixed-methods design with student and teacher surveys plus qualitative feedback. Results suggested improved perceived TSI, more positive student attitudes toward TSI and the system, and perceived benefits such as better attention, livelier classroom atmosphere, and easier teacher recall of names. The paper concludes that NaMemo2 is promising for university classroom interaction, but the evidence is short-term, small-scale, and largely perception-based; the authors explicitly note limitations in sample size, lecture diversity, and the need for more objective outcome measures and broader follow-up.

finding.finding_summary: Student attitudes toward teacher-student interaction improved significantly over the four-week deployment. Pre/post survey comparisons showed a statistically significant increase in attitudes to TSI (t(229) = -3.73, p < .001, d = 0.46) and willingness to engage in TSI (t(229) = -2.20, p = .029, d = 0.29), based on 105 pre-study and 126 post-study valid student responses.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of attitudes to TSI and willingness to TSI on 7-point Likert scales
finding.effect_size: d=0.46 for attitudes to TSI; d=0.29 for willingness to TSI

finding.finding_summary: The system was intended to reduce teacher cognitive load and make classroom interaction more fluent by helping teachers remember student names in real time. Teachers reported that they used NaMemo2 often during lectures and found it helpful for interacting with students, with qualitative feedback emphasizing easier name recall, improved flow, and reduced difficulty identifying students in a large class.
finding.measure: Teacher perceived helpfulness and qualitative feedback on classroom interaction workflow; student free-text reports of class fluency/attention

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the design, iterative prototyping, and classroom evaluation of Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses intended to support teachers in AI-supported K-12 classrooms. The central problem is how to help teachers interpret and act on AI tutor data in real time without distracting them from the classroom or overwhelming them with information.

The authors used participatory design methods with teachers who had prior experience using AI tutors, including field observations, storytelling, card-sorting, speed-dating exercises, and replay enactments. They then refined Lumilo through four pilot studies (14 teachers, 15 classrooms, 304 students) and followed with an in-the-wild randomized classroom study across 18 middle-school classrooms, 8 teachers, 4 schools/districts, and 286 analyzed students. Teachers used Lumilo during two class sessions with an AI tutor for linear equation solving, while comparison conditions included business-as-usual monitoring and a reduced glasses condition without analytics.

The main conclusion is that the full Lumilo system improved student learning relative to both controls, and the analytics feature added benefit beyond minimal monitoring support. The paper also reports process evidence that the tool shifted teacher attention toward lower-performing students and helped teachers give brief, targeted support, suggesting a complementary human–AI partnership rather than teacher replacement. Overall, the evidence is short-term and classroom-based, but it provides experimental support that real-time teacher-facing AI analytics can improve student outcomes in AI-enhanced math instruction.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized classroom study, students in the Glasses + Analytics condition showed higher pre/post gains on linear equation solving than students in the No Glasses business-as-usual condition, and also outperformed the reduced-Glasses condition without analytics. The intervention was tested with 286 analyzed middle-school students across 18 classrooms, and the authors report that the full Lumilo system improved learning on the posttest relative to both controls.
finding.measure: 15-minute pre-test and 15-minute post-test on linear equation solving
finding.study_size: n=286 analyzed students (343 enrolled; 57 excluded for absence)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Lumilo changed teachers’ time allocation and classroom attention patterns in ways consistent with more efficient prioritization of student support. Across the 286 analyzed students, teachers in the Glasses + Analytics condition spent more time with students entering with lower prior knowledge, and the authors estimate that teachers averaged about 24 seconds per student visit during class.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation / time spent with students during class

paper_profiles.title: AI in Pakistani Schools: Adoption, Usage, and Perceived Impact among Educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how AI is being adopted and used by K–12 educators in Pakistan, a context the authors describe as under-explored in the AI-in-education literature. The study asks what teachers know about AI, how often and for what purposes they use it, what support they have received, and how they perceive its impact on students, teaching workload, and equity.

The authors used a cross-sectional online survey distributed to in-service teachers across Pakistan in July 2025, yielding 125 responses. The questionnaire asked about demographics, familiarity with AI, frequency and modes of use, formal training, and perceived impacts on engagement, student performance, workload, teaching strategies, and access. Most respondents worked in public schools, and the sample was skewed toward larger institutions, suggesting the results reflect relatively resource-rich school contexts more than the full national distribution.

Findings show generally positive attitudes toward AI, with many teachers willing to adopt it if supported and trained. Reported uses were concentrated in lesson planning and content generation, while grading and tutoring were uncommon. Teachers perceived AI as improving student engagement, student performance, and workload efficiency, but they also expressed strong concerns about unequal access and students being left behind due to device/infrastructure gaps. The paper concludes that AI adoption in Pakistani schools is still early-stage and uneven, and that training and infrastructure are needed before broader implementation can be effective or equitable.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI improved student engagement. In the survey of n=125 educators, 67% agreed that using AI tools in the classroom had improved students' engagement levels, indicating a positive perceived effect rather than a measured causal impact.
finding.measure: Teacher survey item on perceived student engagement improvement

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived AI as reducing their workload and time spent on routine teaching tasks. Among n=125 educators, 73% agreed that AI tools reduced time spent on tasks such as grading and content creation, making workload reduction the strongest perceived benefit reported in the study.
finding.measure: Teacher survey item on perceived reduction in time spent on routine teaching tasks

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights both positive and negative institutional implications of AI adoption, especially around equity and access. Among n=125 educators, only 42% believed all students had equal access to AI-enhanced learning opportunities, while 73% were concerned that some students were left behind due to lack of devices, suggesting that infrastructure gaps may widen disparities even as AI use expands.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on equal access and concern about students being left behind

paper_profiles.title: A Pilot Study on Teacher-Facing Real-Time Classroom Game Dashboards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a real-time teacher-facing dashboard for an educational game can support classroom facilitation. The authors start from the problem that teachers often have to inspect students’ gameplay individually and may lack quick, interpretable access to student progress, strategy, or disengagement during game play.

Using a participatory design approach, the study first ran a two-day workshop with 12 teachers and teaching mentors to elicit desired dashboard features through prompt cards and mockup activities. The team then built a prototype dashboard for the game Lakeland, a real-time city-building/resource-management game used in grades 7-12, and pilot-tested it in authentic classroom settings. The classroom pilot involved 4 teachers, with 3 testing across multiple classes; sessions were mostly online due to COVID-19, with one face-to-face class, and class sizes were no more than 20 students per session.

The paper reports generally positive teacher feedback on co-design, feasibility, and usefulness. Teachers felt their input was reflected in the prototype, found the dashboard easy to use, and said it helped them identify student progress, inactivity, and strategy issues. However, the study was explicitly small-scale and short-term, with bugs, missing overview features, and unresolved visualization issues; the authors frame it as a pilot and note that longer-term, larger classroom evaluations remain future work.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported that the dashboard made classroom game facilitation easier and reduced the need to inspect each student screen individually. In the pilot survey, teachers rated setup and ease of use highly (setup a class code and connect students: 5/5; dashboard easy to use: 4/5), and they said the tool helped them monitor progress and watch the dashboard instead of having to continuously watch student screens. The study is small (4 teachers; multiple class sessions, with one teacher intending 12 sessions), so findings are pilot-level and based on perceptions rather than causal outcome measures.
finding.measure: Teacher survey and exit interview feedback on feasibility, ease of use, and facilitation usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was reported to help teachers notice student disengagement, inactivity, and frustration-like states during gameplay. Teachers described using the interface to identify students who were 'inactive' or who had 'zero out of six tutorials done,' which helped them intervene and support students; one teacher also said students enjoyed seeing their statistics on screen. These are perceived classroom-engagement effects from a pilot study, not measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement/inactivity during gameplay

paper_profiles.title: Implementation Considerations for Automated AI Grading of Student Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers implemented an AI-powered grading and feedback platform in real classroom settings, with a focus on what makes automated grading usable, trustworthy, and pedagogically meaningful. The core problem is whether AI can support formative assessment without undermining teacher judgment, especially in standards-based grading contexts where narrative feedback may matter more than numeric scores.

The study used a seven-week co-design pilot with 19 teachers from four public school districts and one independent school in the Puget Sound region of Washington state. Teachers implemented the platform across grades 8–12 in 33 classrooms and 58 logged assessments, using the system to generate rubrics, grade student work, and provide AI-generated feedback; they also completed weekly surveys, participated in discussions/interviews, and the researchers analyzed platform logs.

Findings suggest that teachers generally valued the speed and formative usefulness of AI-generated narrative feedback, especially for revision-oriented use, but distrusted automated scoring and routinely edited or overrode AI outputs. Students appreciated rapid feedback in some cases but also expressed skepticism about AI-only grading, confusion about low scores paired with positive comments, and usability challenges. The main conclusion is that AI grading tools in K–12 are best positioned as teacher-mediated formative supports rather than autonomous summative graders, and successful implementation depends on human oversight, editable outputs, clear interfaces, and alignment with teacher pedagogy.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students saw value in AI-generated narrative feedback for assessment tasks, especially when used formatively. In a pilot spanning 19 teachers, 33 classrooms, and 58 logged assessments, teachers reported that the feedback was often specific and actionable, even when they questioned the AI-generated scores.
finding.measure: Perceptions of rubric quality and feedback usefulness from teacher surveys, interviews, and platform logs
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers; 33 classrooms; 58 assessments; 936 student works

finding.finding_summary: Student responses to AI feedback were mixed: some students welcomed quick, revision-oriented feedback and felt more confident, while others were skeptical, confused, or overwhelmed by the volume and form of comments. The study relied on teacher reports and qualitative evidence rather than direct student outcome measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student reactions, engagement with revision, and confidence/confusion around feedback

finding.finding_summary: The strongest implementation finding was that the platform could reduce grading turnaround time and automate most scoring work, but only when teachers retained oversight. Logs showed a median AI grading coverage of 92.2% on submitted work, and teachers repeatedly described the tool as a time-saving first pass that still required human review before final grading.
finding.measure: Platform usage logs, teacher reports of time-saving, turnaround, and grading workflow
finding.std_deviation: SD=27.9% for mean submission rate; other effect metrics not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests possible support for revision, self-correction, and reflective iteration, but does not directly measure durable-skill outcomes. Evidence comes from observed resubmission behavior (mean 8.7%) and teacher reports that students used AI feedback to revise work, alongside concerns that some students ignored or misunderstood the feedback.
finding.measure: Resubmission behavior and qualitative reports of revision-oriented use

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school (middle school and high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI responsibly for learning, especially how to craft effective prompts when interacting with AI chatbots. The authors designed a web-based AI literacy module centered on prompting literacy, using scenario-based practice, direct interaction with an LLM chatbot, and immediate AI-generated feedback via an auto-grader.

The module was deployed in two classroom iterations across 11 authentic secondary education classrooms in East Asia. Study 1 (6 classrooms, 111 valid student participants) examined the accuracy of the AI auto-grader and students’ prompting performance, confidence, and perceptions of the learning experience. Study 2 reused the same instructional materials with a revised assessment format (true/false and open-ended questions) to improve measurement quality. Across both studies, the authors report that students improved most clearly in adding background/context to prompts and became more confident using AI for learning, while overall performance gains were limited by ceiling effects and the short, pilot-like nature of the intervention. The paper concludes that the approach is promising but needs broader and longer-term evaluation, and that assessment design matters for measuring prompting literacy accurately.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in using AI for learning after completing the module. In Study 1, self-reported confidence increased by 10.4% on average (SD = 0.92), and the Wilcoxon test indicated this gain was statistically significant (p < .001).
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-report item: 'I know how to use AI to help me learn' / confidence in using AI for future learning
finding.study_size: n=111 (Study 1 valid data); n=98 for pre-post confidence/test comparison

finding.finding_summary: The module improved students’ prompting literacy, especially their ability to embed background/context in prompts. McNemar tests showed a significant increase from Q1 to Q3 on the Background dimension (p = .039), while Relevance, Conciseness, and Purpose did not change significantly. Overall post-test scores showed a ceiling effect (Mean = 4.4/6, SD = 0.96), suggesting students had baseline knowledge but variable prompt-writing skill.
finding.measure: Prompt-quality rubric dimensions, six-question prompting literacy test, and practice prompts across three scenarios
finding.study_size: n=98 for pre/post test comparison; 483 unique student-written prompts in Study 1

finding.finding_summary: Students learned AI-related knowledge about how to use AI for learning and how to ask effective questions. In open-ended responses, 87% of learners reported learning AI-related knowledge, including not asking for direct answers, adding background/context, and understanding AI capabilities. The study frames this as growth in prompting literacy rather than improvement on a traditional academic subject test.
finding.measure: Open-ended reflection survey responses about what students learned; prompting literacy practice performance
finding.study_size: n=131 students completed reflection questions in Study 1

paper_profiles.title: Student Log-Data from a Randomized Evaluation of Educational Technology: A Causal Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper uses log data from a randomized evaluation of the Cognitive Tutor Algebra I (CTA1) curriculum to examine how implementation details relate to student outcomes. The core question is not whether the curriculum works overall—that was studied in the original RAND RCT—but how one specific implementation feature, hint usage inside the tutor, may help explain or moderate the program’s effects.

The authors analyze high school students in the second year of the CTA1 trial, focusing on students in the treatment group and using computerized log files that record hint requests, errors, timestamps, and worked problems. They compare three analytic approaches for implementation data: an observational study within the experiment using propensity score matching, a causal mediation analysis, and a principal stratification model. The paper is methodological and uses standardized Algebra I posttest scores as the main outcome.

The main substantive finding is that frequent hint use is associated with lower posttest performance in the matched observational analysis (roughly -0.12 to -0.18 SD depending on weighting), with a sensitivity analysis suggesting the negative effect is not easily explained away by confounding of similar magnitude to observed ethnicity indicators. The mediation analysis estimates a small negative indirect effect of hints (about -0.04 SD) alongside a positive direct effect of CTA1 through other channels (about 0.14 to 0.18 SD). The principal stratification discussion is framed as a way to study heterogeneity in treatment effects by latent hint-use propensity, but the paper’s central empirical takeaway is that the overall CTA1 benefit does not appear to come from hint use itself.

finding.finding_summary: In the observational analysis within the treatment arm, being a high hint user was associated with lower Algebra I posttest performance. The estimated effect was about -0.12 SD (ATE, 95% CI [-0.23, -0.02]) to -0.18 SD (OLS, 95% CI [-0.25, -0.10]), with similar results for the TOT (-0.14 SD, 95% CI [-0.25, -0.03]) among n=2,108 treated students.
finding.measure: Standardized Algebra I posttest score
finding.study_size: n=2,108 treatment students for hint-usage analyses; n=5,026 total in the original trial context

finding.finding_summary: The paper also uses the hint-request analysis to infer a behavioral implementation pattern: students who requested hints more often tended to perform worse, suggesting less effective problem-solving or metacognitive engagement during Algebra I work. This is not a direct test of a durable-skill outcome, but the authors explicitly interpret hint requesting as an implementation behavior tied to problem-solving strategy and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Hint-request frequency / propensity to request hints during algebra problem solving
finding.effect_size: -0.14 (TOT as the effect of high hint use on posttest)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses hint use as a proxy for students' persistence and self-regulated help-seeking while working through Cognitive Tutor problems, but it does not directly measure engagement or motivation with a survey. The substantive empirical result is that greater hint use was associated with lower posttest scores, which the authors interpret as suggesting that the way students used hints may have been less productive.
finding.measure: Hint-request behavior; indirect proxy for engagement/help-seeking

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Student Behaviors and Motivations when using AI Teaching Assistants with Optional Guardrails
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how undergraduate students use an AI-powered teaching assistant (AI TA) with optional guardrails in a large introductory programming course. The central question is whether students choose to disable pedagogical guardrails in order to access direct solutions, and how that choice relates to performance and timing of work. The authors are motivated by concerns that unconstrained GenAI tools can enable over-reliance or academic misconduct, while overly restrictive tools may frustrate students and prompt them to seek alternative help.

The intervention was a web-based tool, Edugator, deployed in one weekly lab of a 12-week programming course at a large public research university in the Australasian region. Students completed three C programming tasks (one code-writing and two debugging problems) and could interact with an LLM-based chatbot that was prompted not to reveal code. A separate “See Solution” feature allowed students to deactivate the guardrails and receive a verbatim solution from OpenAI’s 4o model. The study analyzed log data from 885 students and open-ended reflections from 839 students.

Results showed that 50% of participating students used the solution feature at least once, and 14% used it on all three problems. Lower-performing students were more likely to use the solution feature, and usage was associated with working closer to the deadline, though the decision to use the feature itself was not significantly related to when students started the lab. Qualitative responses suggested students used the feature for problem-solving assistance, verification, time pressure, lack of self-regulation, and curiosity, while others avoided it because they valued independent learning or considered it unethical. The authors conclude that students’ motivations are mixed and that more longitudinal evidence is needed to understand whether optional-solution AI TAs help learning or encourage dependence.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported both constructive and problematic motivations for using the optional solution feature. In open-ended responses (n=839), themes included time pressure, lack of self-regulation, curiosity, and problem-solving assistance; many non-users emphasized learning value and self-directed problem solving.
finding.measure: Open-ended reflections on why students used or avoided the 'See Solution' feature; feature-use logs

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined metacognitive and help-seeking behavior in programming tasks. Students used the solution feature to verify work, get unstuck, and compare approaches, but lower-performing students were more likely to use it repeatedly (14% used it on all three tasks), suggesting differing levels of self-regulation and problem-solving persistence.
finding.measure: Help-seeking behavior, solution-feature use, course performance quartiles, and thematic analysis of reflections

finding.finding_summary: Students frequently used the solution feature as a time-saving strategy, especially when under deadline pressure.
