The tool enabled rapid access to direct solutions in a one-week lab setting, and qualitative comments indicated that some students used it to avoid spending too much time on debugging or boundary-check issues.
finding.measure: Self-reported rationale for using the 'See Solution' feature and interaction logs

paper_profiles.title: DrawSim-PD: Simulating Student Science Drawings to Support NGSS-Aligned Teacher Diagnostic Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a teacher professional development problem in K–12 science education: teachers need practice interpreting student drawings to diagnose scientific understanding and misconceptions, but authentic student work is difficult to collect and share at scale because of privacy constraints. The authors propose DrawSim-PD, a generative AI framework that synthesizes student-like science drawings, first-person reasoning narratives, and teacher-facing diagnostic concept maps aligned to NGSS performance expectations.

The system uses capability profiles to control what a simulated student can and cannot yet demonstrate, enabling outputs at four performance levels across K–12 grade bands. The paper describes corpus construction over 100 NGSS topics and 10,000 artifacts, then reports an expert feasibility study with six K–12 science educators who reviewed 480 generated artifacts online over one week. Educators rated the outputs as largely NGSS-aligned, developmentally plausible, and useful for diagnostic reasoning, though they noted weaknesses at grade-band extremes (K–2 and 9–12) and called for more transparency about how performance levels are determined.

Overall, the paper is an implementation and feasibility study rather than an outcome study of teacher learning. It provides early evidence that synthetic drawings plus diagnostic scaffolds may be a promising PD resource for calibration and misconception analysis, but it does not test whether use of DrawSim-PD improves teacher accuracy, workload, or student outcomes over time. The contribution is therefore mainly technical and formative: it demonstrates a privacy-preserving approach for generating teacher-facing AI supports and characterizes perceived utility and plausibility in a small, short-term expert review.

finding.finding_summary: Six K–12 science educators judged the generated artifacts to be aligned with NGSS expectations and useful for interpreting student thinking in an expert feasibility study (N=6 educators; 480 artifact evaluations). Core alignment items were high: topic–PE alignment 89.6%, DCI representation 84.2%, drawing–prompt coherence 86.7%, capability-statement match 75.0%, and performance-level match 73.8%.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of NGSS alignment, performance-level matching, and diagnostic usefulness for student science drawings and concept maps

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on teacher diagnostic reasoning, a metacognitive/interpretive skill, and experts reported that the multimodal outputs supported calibration and interpretation of student thinking. Qualitative feedback indicated that the drawings, narratives, and concept maps helped teachers compare levels of understanding, though participants wanted more explanation of why a drawing was classified at a given performance level.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of teacher comments about diagnostic reasoning and calibration utility

finding.finding_summary: The system is framed as a scalable way to overcome privacy barriers and reduce the difficulty of collecting enough student work for teacher PD and research. Educators perceived the corpus as useful infrastructure for calibration exercises and misconception libraries, but the study did not measure actual time savings, workload reduction, or productivity gains.
finding.measure: Perceived utility for scalable calibration and professional-development infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Human-Generative AI Collaborative Problem Solving Who Leads and How Students Perceive the Interactions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students collaborate with ChatGPT during a collaborative maze design and solving task, focusing on who leads the interaction, how students perceive the interaction, and how these perceptions relate to collaborative problem-solving and sense of agency. The authors frame the study around broader questions in human-AI collaboration in education, especially whether generative AI helps students maintain agency or instead encourages reliance and overreliance.

The study was conducted with 79 undergraduate students enrolled in an interdisciplinary digital literacy course at an autonomous university in Singapore. In a two-hour class activity, students worked in small groups with ChatGPT in a 3D Maze environment and then completed surveys plus written reflections about contribution balance, interaction experience, collaborative problem-solving, and sense of positive/negative agency. Students could choose when and how to use ChatGPT, and the study coded their reflections into collaboration types (human leads, even contribution, AI leads) and interaction experience categories (positive, mixed, negative).

Results showed that most students perceived themselves as leading or sharing the work evenly with ChatGPT (77.21%), while 15.19% reported that AI led. Interaction experiences were often positive or mixed, but 30.38% were negative. In correlational and regression analyses, only sense of negative agency significantly predicted worse collaborative problem-solving; collaboration type and interaction experience did not. The paper concludes that, in this short, pilot-like context, students’ perceived loss of control may matter more than whether ChatGPT was seen as leading or whether the experience felt positive, and it calls for better curriculum and tool design to reduce overreliance and support agency.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaborative problem-solving as a durable skill in a ChatGPT-supported maze task. In the regression model (n=72 observations), collaboration type and interaction experience were not significant predictors, but sense of negative agency was associated with lower collaborative problem-solving scores (b=-0.34, p=.006), and the model explained 10.8% of the variance (adjusted R2=.108).
finding.measure: Self-reported collaborative problem-solving scale adapted from the TEAM Collaboration Questionnaire: Integration subscale
finding.confidence_interval: b=-0.34, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.10] for negative agency predictor

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines students’ interaction experience with ChatGPT and sense of agency. More positive interaction experiences were positively correlated with sense of positive agency (r=0.26), while sense of negative agency was negatively related to collaborative problem-solving and inversely related to positive agency (r=-0.41).
finding.measure: Interaction experience scale coded from reflections; sense of positive agency and sense of negative agency survey subscales
finding.std_deviation: SoPA SD=0.71; SoNA SD=0.75; InterExp SD=0.76

finding.finding_summary: The task was a maze design-and-solving activity in 3D Maze with ChatGPT, but the paper does not report objective academic achievement or performance outcomes. It does show that 44.30% of students perceived themselves as human-leading the collaboration, 32.91% as equal contribution, and 15.19% as AI-leading, suggesting that students often used ChatGPT as a support tool rather than ceding control.
finding.measure: Perceived human-generative AI collaboration type during maze design and solving

paper_profiles.title: “AI+建筑学”模块化融合设计课教学探索：以浙江大学建筑设计Ⅲ/Ⅳ课程为例
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a teaching experiment integrating AI into Zhejiang University’s third-year undergraduate architectural design studio (建筑设计Ⅲ/Ⅳ) during the 2024–2025 academic year. The authors frame the work as a modular curriculum reform that adds a 20-hour AI skills component plus in-class AI ethics discussions while preserving the original design-studio structure.

The AI module introduced a range of tools and methods, including deep learning models, large language models, generative image tools, LoRA fine-tuning, and ComfyUI workflows, supported by a dedicated technical instructor and cloud/platform infrastructure. The intervention was phased across four design tasks, moving from design-concept support to rendering and finally site-research applications, with AI ethics topics covering privacy, copyright, human-AI responsibility, stylistic bias, and model bias.

Evidence comes primarily from descriptive course implementation and a post-course questionnaire completed by 70 students. Students reported generally positive experiences: 95.7% said they benefited from the course, 82.8% expressed willingness to use AI in future design work, and perceived usefulness was strongest for information organization and logical analysis. Use was uneven across stages and tools, with large language models strongest in early research and more complex custom workflows gaining importance later. The paper concludes that modular AI integration is feasible in a high-intensity design studio when a technical specialist, platform support, and incremental pedagogy are in place, but it also notes persistent limitations in students’ ability to use AI for deeper design reasoning and concerns about bias, authorship, and aesthetic homogenization.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived AI as most helpful for organizing information and supporting analysis, and the authors report that AI improved efficiency in research, concept development, and rendering workflows. In the post-course survey (n=70), 84.1% rated AI as strong for information organization (M=4.28, SD=0.84) and 67.1% for logical analysis (M=3.86, SD=0.94), while 95.7% reported some benefit from the course overall.
finding.measure: Post-course student questionnaire on AI tool usefulness, including information organization and logical analysis items; reported course benefit

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports generally positive student attitudes and engagement with the AI-enhanced studio. In the questionnaire (n=70), 95.7% reported gaining something from the course, 82.8% expressed positive future use intentions, and 30.0% said they applied AI in actual design work, suggesting substantial acceptance and engagement with the intervention.
finding.measure: Student self-reported course benefit, future AI-use intention, and level of participation/application

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the module strengthened students’ strategic cognition, digital adaptability, and critical judgment in AI-mediated design. Survey items showed moderate-to-strong perceived gains in logical analysis (M=3.86, SD=0.94) and lower but still positive ratings for innovation and design expression (both 44.3% rating 4–5), while the authors emphasize improved human-AI collaboration awareness and critical reflection on bias, authorship, and responsibility.
finding.measure: Student ratings of AI tool capabilities and qualitative feedback on strategy, critical thinking, and ethics

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents the course as evidence that modular AI integration can be embedded into a core studio without changing the overall curriculum structure, helped by a dedicated technical instructor and platform support. The authors report that the model was implemented across a full academic year and was recognized as a provincial-level teaching case, suggesting institutional feasibility and scalability rather than a causal student-outcome evaluation.
finding.measure: Course implementation model, institutional support structures, and recognition as a teaching case

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence research in higher education has developed, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical concerns are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied. The authors conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed English- and Spanish-language journal articles indexed in EBSCO Education Source, Web of Science, and Scopus, identifying 146 included studies from 2007 to November 2018.

The review organizes AI applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalization. Most studies were quantitative, often machine-learning based, and focused on undergraduate settings; relatively few papers came from education-affiliated authors, and only a tiny minority explicitly defined AI or critically reflected on ethical issues such as privacy and cost.

The paper concludes that AI research in higher education is dominated by technical and administrative applications, with comparatively little teacher-centered or pedagogical grounding. The authors argue that more work is needed on the educational, ethical, and critical dimensions of AI, especially in relation to supporting teachers and learning processes rather than only prediction, automation, and institutional efficiency.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that many AI applications were designed to reduce workload and automate tasks such as admissions decisions, course scheduling, grading, feedback, and plagiarism detection. Across the included studies, these systems were generally reported as accurate and efficient, although the paper does not aggregate a single effect size; the review is based on 146 articles and notes that AI could relieve administrative and teaching staff by automating routine processes.
finding.measure: Accuracy/efficiency of AI systems for admissions, scheduling, grading, feedback, plagiarism detection, and related administrative tasks
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in the review; individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature used AI for institutional and administrative services such as monitoring attrition, supporting admissions, course planning, counseling, and alignment with industry needs. The review reports that 48 studies (32.8%) focused on administrative/institutional services and that these applications were typically quantitative prediction or decision-support systems rather than pedagogical interventions.
finding.measure: Institutional and administrative AI applications (e.g., admissions, retention, course scheduling, student monitoring, competency matching)
finding.study_size: n=48 studies focused on institutional/administrative services

finding.finding_summary: Some studies in the review targeted student engagement, motivation, and self-regulation, particularly through predictive analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, and adaptive systems. For example, one included study used machine learning on virtual learning environment data to predict student engagement, but the review does not synthesize a common effect size across studies and largely reports feasibility and preliminary positive findings.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and self-regulation as measured in individual primary studies

finding.finding_summary: The review includes some AI applications supporting collaboration, problem solving, and metacognitive or self-regulatory processes, especially within intelligent tutoring systems and collaborative learning tools. These studies generally reported promising or positive preliminary results, but the paper provides no pooled quantitative estimate and notes that the evidence base is limited and short-term.
finding.measure: Collaboration, problem solving, and self-regulatory/metacognitive processes in AI-supported learning tools

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT in the digital era: Perspectives on chatbot implementation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators and students perceive the use of ChatGPT in education in the digital era. The authors focus on perceived benefits and challenges rather than testing an intervention, asking whether ChatGPT is seen as useful for supporting learning, reducing educator workload, and providing immediate feedback.

The study used a qualitative design with in-depth interviews and purposive sampling. Twenty-five participants from higher education institutions in Krabi, Thailand were interviewed: ten educators and fifteen students. The data were analyzed using content analysis with NVivo. Participants generally viewed ChatGPT positively as a tool for answering routine questions, supporting students outside class, and freeing educators to focus on higher-order tasks. At the same time, they raised concerns about information accuracy, loss of personal interaction, and data privacy/security.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT may be a valuable educational support tool, but its use should be balanced with human interaction and guided by ethical safeguards. They recommend improving information accuracy, maintaining educator-student relationships, and strengthening privacy protections. The paper is exploratory and perception-based, offering contextual insights rather than causal evidence of learning or wellbeing effects.

finding.finding_summary: Educators perceived ChatGPT as helpful for reducing workload by answering routine questions and freeing time for more complex tasks. The study is based on qualitative interviews with n=25 participants (10 educators, 15 students); no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived educator workload and task efficiency from in-depth interviews

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT’s immediate feedback and easy access to support could increase student motivation, engagement, and confidence in learning. This finding comes from qualitative interview data with n=25 participants, and no effect size or validated scale was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived student motivation, engagement, and confidence from interviews

finding.finding_summary: Participants saw ChatGPT as useful for supporting independent learning and providing quick answers, but they also emphasized the need for critical evaluation of chatbot output. The paper discusses these durable-skill implications qualitatively (n=25) rather than measuring them with a validated instrument.
finding.measure: Perceived independent learning and critical evaluation/cognitive judgment from interviews

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of literature reviews on artificial intelligence in education (AIED): a roadmap to a future research agenda
paper_profiles.population: Not specific to a single K-12 level; synthesis of AIED literature reviews across educational levels, with notable coverage of higher education and some K-12
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper does not evaluate a single AI intervention. Instead, it conducts a systematic review of literature reviews on artificial intelligence in education (AIED) to map the field, identify trends, and surface gaps and future research directions. The authors followed PRISMA and analyzed 143 eligible review articles published across a wide range of contexts, stakeholders, educational levels, and subject areas.

The study asks what the AIED review literature says about who is being studied, what outcomes are being targeted, which AI techniques are most common, and what benefits and challenges are repeatedly reported. The synthesis shows that most reviews focus on students and teachers, with much more attention to higher education than K-12, and that teaching/learning support is the dominant objective. Machine learning, large language models/generative AI, intelligent tutoring systems, and chatbots are the most frequently discussed technologies.

The paper concludes that AIED is widely viewed as promising for personalization, assessment support, and improved teaching/learning quality, but that important challenges remain around privacy, equity, reliability, lack of humanity, and insufficient teacher training. For K-12 specifically, the review suggests that the field still lacks enough focused evidence, especially on teacher-facing uses and on outcomes beyond general support and efficiency.

finding.finding_summary: Across the synthesized review literature, AIED is most often framed as improving teaching and learning support, including reducing teacher workload through automation of manual tasks, chatbots, AI tutors, and support for assessment and monitoring. The paper does not report a single pooled effect size because it is a review of reviews, but it identifies workload reduction and assessment/support efficiency as recurring benefits in the literature.
finding.measure: Reported themes from literature reviews on teaching/learning support, workload reduction, assessment automation, and monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports that AIED is frequently associated with increased student cognitive engagement and motivation, and occasionally emotional support. These claims are drawn from the included reviews rather than a single effect study, so no pooled effect size is reported, but engagement/motivation appears as a recurring positive outcome in the literature base.
finding.measure: Reported themes from literature reviews on engagement, motivation, and emotional support

finding.finding_summary: The review literature summarized in this paper links AIED to improved critical thinking and creativity, especially through personalized learning, adaptive systems, and AI-supported instructional designs. Because this paper synthesizes prior reviews rather than primary studies, it does not provide a quantitative effect estimate, but durable-skill gains are repeatedly described as a benefit in the reviewed literature.
finding.measure: Reported themes from literature reviews on critical thinking and creativity

paper_profiles.title: Facilitators and barriers to AI adoption in nursing practice: a qualitative study of registered nurses’ perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines registered nurses’ perspectives on the facilitators and barriers to adopting artificial intelligence (AI) in nursing practice in Saudi Arabia. The paper asks what factors support or impede AI adoption and uses those findings to propose an extended Technology Acceptance Model for AI in Nursing (TAM-AIN).

The authors conducted eight focus groups with 48 registered nurses from four hospitals in Al-Kharj, Saudi Arabia, using a semi-structured interview guide informed by the Technology Acceptance Model. Analysis was thematic, with triangulation across transcripts, field notes, and demographic data. The study highlights nurses’ cautious optimism about AI, especially when it is perceived to improve patient care, but also identifies key concerns including technical infrastructure limits, privacy and ethical risks, fear of job displacement or deskilling, and resistance to change.

Facilitators of adoption included perceived patient-care benefits, organizational leadership support, ease of use, and training. The paper concludes that successful AI implementation in nursing requires a nurse-centered approach that combines technical readiness, ethical safeguards, professional development, and strong institutional support. It argues that the proposed TAM-AIN framework better captures the organizational and professional factors shaping AI adoption than traditional acceptance models alone.

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally believed AI could improve workflow efficiency by automating routine tasks, speeding data analysis, and supporting decision-making, which they felt could reduce workload and help identify deteriorating patients earlier. However, they also reported that poorly designed systems, outdated IT infrastructure, and workflow disruptions could increase burden and hinder adoption. This was a qualitative finding based on eight focus groups (n=48), with no effect size reported.
finding.measure: Perceived workflow efficiency, workload reduction, and ease of integration into nursing practice from focus group discussions

finding.finding_summary: The study found that organizational support, leadership commitment, technical infrastructure, ethical governance, and training systems were central to AI adoption in nursing. Participants emphasized that institutional readiness and policy-like supports such as data privacy protections and phased implementation would shape whether AI could be successfully integrated across facilities. Findings come from focus groups with registered nurses (n=48); no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived organizational readiness, leadership support, governance, and institutional conditions for AI adoption

paper_profiles.title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual reflection paper; studies summarized span K-12 through higher education and beyond)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This reflection paper examines current claims about the effects of AI on learning and argues for a more evidence-based, theory-driven approach. The authors focus on the growing use of generative AI and large language models in education, criticizing publication trends that emphasize novelty and potential benefits while often relying on weak measures, limited comparison conditions, or overinterpreted performance outcomes.

The paper does not test a single intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior empirical and theoretical work to propose the ISAR model, which distinguishes inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition effects of AI in education. The authors argue that AI can sometimes support learning by substituting for routine instructional functions, augmenting feedback and scaffolding, or enabling redesigned learning tasks, but that poorly designed AI use can also reduce cognitive engagement and learning through inversion effects.

The paper also identifies conditions for successful AI integration, including student and teacher prerequisites such as AI literacy, as well as contextual factors like infrastructure and governance. Although the discussion is broad and includes examples from K-12, higher education, and teacher education, its main contribution is conceptual rather than empirical: it calls for rigorous research designs, better outcome measurement, and careful comparison conditions before strong claims about AI’s educational value are made.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can reduce teacher workload and improve efficiency by substituting for routine instructional functions such as content generation, feedback delivery, question generation, and answering clarification questions. However, these claims are presented as a conceptual synthesis rather than a single empirical estimate, and the authors stress that quality control and teacher oversight remain necessary.
finding.measure: Teacher workload; efficiency of instructional support tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally discusses critical thinking, metacognition, problem-solving, collaboration, and communication as key learning outcomes affected by AI. It highlights evidence that overreliance on ChatGPT can reduce cognitive processing depth and metacognitive engagement, while other AI-supported instructional designs may foster deeper learning, but the paper does not present a single aggregated effect size.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive processing, problem-solving, collaboration, communication

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses writing and reading-related AI uses, including ChatGPT-supported writing revision, AI-generated instructional videos/podcasts, quiz questions, and intelligent textbooks. It reports that ChatGPT improved task performance during supported writing revisions but did not improve posttest knowledge gain or transfer, and it emphasizes that better performance during support does not necessarily indicate lasting learning.
finding.measure: Writing task performance; posttest knowledge gain; knowledge transfer

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Quality of Responses Generated by ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how final-year teacher-education students understand and evaluate ChatGPT for educational use. The authors are motivated by the rapid spread of generative AI and the need for future primary school teachers to develop competencies for critically using AI tools rather than relying on them uncritically.

The study used a researcher-developed questionnaire with both closed and open-ended items, plus a five-item attitude scale, administered to 55 fourth-year students at the University of Belgrade Faculty of Education. Students were asked whether they knew ChatGPT, whether they had used it, whether they preferred it to search engines for professional preparation, whether they could distinguish human-written from AI-generated methodological answers, and whether ChatGPT could help them improve their own responses to teaching-related tasks. The scale assessing attitudes toward ChatGPT-generated responses had acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s alpha > 0.81).

Results suggested limited prior, institutional experience with ChatGPT: most respondents had heard of it through friends or social media, only a small share learned about it through education, and fewer than half had personally used it. Most students preferred search engines over ChatGPT for professional preparation. However, many were able to distinguish human from AI-generated responses, and students’ own responses improved numerically when they used ChatGPT-assisted text as support. Overall attitudes toward the quality of ChatGPT-generated responses were moderately positive (M=3.71 on a 5-point scale), especially regarding clarity and meaningfulness, but students still viewed the tool as something to be used critically and as a support rather than a replacement for teachers.

finding.finding_summary: Students were able to better identify human-written versus AI-generated methodological responses and to critically evaluate the quality of ChatGPT outputs. In the recognition task, 60% of participants correctly identified at least four of the six answers, suggesting moderate competence in discriminating AI-generated text from human work (n=55).
finding.measure: Accuracy in recognizing whether methodological responses were written by a human or generated by ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: Students’ responses to teaching-method tasks showed a numerical increase when they used ChatGPT-generated text as support. Mean scores rose from 1.81 to 1.87 for Task 1 vs. Task 2 and from 1.85 to 1.95 for Task 3 vs. Task 4, indicating that ChatGPT-assisted prompting helped them produce more meaningful and higher-quality answers (n=55).
finding.measure: Quality scores for lesson-planning and conflict-resolution responses with and without ChatGPT assistance
finding.std_deviation: Task 1 SD=1.00; Task 2 SD=1.26; Task 3 SD=0.85; Task 4 SD=1.30

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that teacher-education programs need to strengthen institutional preparation for AI use, since only 5.5% of respondents learned about ChatGPT through education and most had not used it for planned professional development. The study frames this as evidence that institutional curricula should be updated to build competencies for responsible AI integration.
finding.measure: Students’ reported sources of ChatGPT knowledge and their stated need for institutional preparation

paper_profiles.title: Challenges and opportunities for classroom-based formative assessment and AI: a perspective article
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may reshape classroom-based formative assessment, with a particular focus on teachers’ work. The paper asks what longstanding challenges in formative assessment—such as providing timely individualized feedback, managing large classes, supporting peer and self-assessment, and handling workload—might be eased by AI, and what new challenges may arise from AI use.

Rather than reporting an original empirical study, the authors synthesize prior literature and professional examples to argue that AI tools could automate or augment aspects of scoring, feedback generation, assessment scheduling, learner profiling, and analysis of process data. The article also highlights risks around bias, validity, interpretability, ethics, and the possibility that AI increases teachers’ professional learning burden if they lack AI/data literacy. The authors conclude that AI should augment, not replace, teachers, and that self-regulated learning, critical thinking, ethical use, and teacher guidance are central to effective AI-enhanced formative assessment.

The paper is framed around K-12 classroom assessment contexts and is primarily relevant to educators. Its claims are conceptual and literature-based, not based on a new dataset or experimental evaluation. As such, it offers a forward-looking argument about how AI could support formative assessment at scale while emphasizing careful design, validation, and co-design with teachers and students.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI can reduce teacher workload by automating or partly automating scoring, feedback generation, assessment scheduling, and analysis of assessment data, which could make formative assessment more feasible at scale. At the same time, it emphasizes that AI may also add burden through the need for professional development, critical review of model outputs, and ongoing validation, so the net efficiency effect is presented as mixed rather than purely positive.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time burden, and efficiency of formative assessment processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-supported formative assessment can strengthen student self-regulation by providing timely, individualized feedback and by supporting goal-setting, monitoring, and adjustment of strategies. It also notes that AI-enabled peer assessment and feedback can foster learner agency and self-regulated learning, although these claims are drawn from prior literature rather than new empirical data.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, motivation, engagement, and related non-scholastic learner attributes

finding.finding_summary: A central argument of the paper is that AI-enhanced formative assessment should be paired with critical thinking and self-regulated learning, and that these skills become even more important in AI-driven classrooms. The article does not report a new effect estimate, but it repeatedly frames AI as potentially supporting students’ metacognition, reflective judgment, and critical engagement with feedback and evidence.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulated learning, and reflective judgment

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses broader institutional effects of AI adoption in assessment, including implications for policy, teacher professional development, accountability structures, data privacy, and governance of AI use in schools. It argues that AI can support more scalable assessment systems, but that implementation quality will depend on trust, context, ethics, and institutional support, so the overall institutional impact is mixed.
finding.measure: Policy, accountability, professional development, privacy, and assessment system implementation

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of a comprehensive framework for understanding how artificial intelligence is being applied in educational leadership. The author asks how AI applications in educational leadership can be systematically categorized to support understanding and implementation, especially amid rapid growth in AI tools and fragmented adoption practices.

To answer this, the paper uses a systematic literature review and general inductive analysis of peer-reviewed publications from 2017 to 2024, screened from databases including IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ERIC, and Scopus. From 1,247 initial records, 314 publications were reviewed in detail and synthesized into ten domains: administrative efficiency, personalized learning, enhancing teaching practices, decision-making and policy formulation, student support services, organizational leadership and strategic planning, governance and compliance, community engagement and communication, ethical AI leadership, and diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.

The study is focused on higher education leadership contexts rather than a single intervention or outcome study. It concludes that AI has broad potential to improve institutional efficiency, decision-making, and support services, while also raising important ethical, governance, privacy, and equity concerns. The taxonomy is intended as a practical framework for educational leaders, policymakers, researchers, and institutions to assess and plan AI adoption, and the paper calls for further longitudinal, cross-cultural, and ethics-focused research.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that AI can improve administrative and operational processes in educational leadership, including scheduling, enrollment management, and decision support. Reported examples include advanced scheduling systems reducing administrative workload by up to 40% and AI-powered enrollment models predicting enrollment patterns with accuracy above 85%, but these figures are drawn from cited studies rather than a new empirical test in this paper.
finding.measure: Administrative workload, scheduling efficiency, enrollment prediction accuracy, resource utilization

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a taxonomy for institutional AI adoption in higher education, showing how AI applications cluster across governance, policy, leadership, compliance, communication, and DEI functions. The main finding is conceptual rather than experimental: AI is framed as having broad institutional benefits when implemented through structured governance and ethical frameworks, but the paper does not report a single aggregate effect size.
finding.measure: Taxonomy/domain synthesis of AI applications in educational leadership

paper_profiles.title: Utilization of Writing Assistance Tools in Research in Selected Higher Learning Institutions in the Philippines: A Text Mining Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how faculty researchers in selected higher learning institutions in the Philippines use AI-powered writing assistance tools in their research writing. The study asks what faculty perceive as the usefulness, positive and negative implications, and concerns associated with these tools, using text mining and sentiment analysis on open-ended survey responses.

The researchers collected responses from 327 faculty members across 11 public and private higher education institutions in the Philippines. Participants reported using or intending to use tools such as Grammarly, Quillbot, ChatGPT, and other grammar-checking or generative writing systems. The analysis used unigram tokenization, k-means clustering, and sentiment analysis to identify recurring themes in the corpus.

Findings indicate that respondents generally view writing assistance tools positively because they help with grammar, clarity, proofreading, paraphrasing, translation, formatting, and speeding up research writing. At the same time, participants expressed concerns about overreliance, reduced critical thinking and creativity, plagiarism, and poor contextual or cultural fit for Filipino academic writing. The paper concludes that these tools can improve efficiency and writing quality, but they should be used responsibly and with institutional guidance to avoid academic integrity problems and skill erosion.

finding.finding_summary: Faculty respondents overwhelmingly described AI writing tools as helpful for improving writing quality, including grammar, clarity, proofreading, paraphrasing, and formatting. However, they also noted risks such as incorrect suggestions, plagiarism, and reduced originality; the study is qualitative/text-mining based and reports counts of positive vs negative sentiments (77 positive, 61 negative) rather than effect sizes.
finding.measure: Faculty perceptions of writing quality, grammar, clarity, proofreading, paraphrasing, and plagiarism-related concerns from open-ended survey responses analyzed with text mining and sentiment analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly identifies critical thinking, creativity, and independent writing skill development as central concerns and benefits of writing assistance tools. Respondents valued tools for reducing writing burden and improving output, but worried that overreliance could hinder critical thinking and the development of writing skills.
finding.measure: Faculty-reported concerns and perceived effects on critical thinking, creativity, and independent writing skill development

finding.finding_summary: Respondents said AI writing assistance tools expedite research writing, automate proofreading/formatting, and save time and effort, allowing more focus on higher-level tasks. The paper reports that positive sentiment (77) exceeded negative sentiment (61) for the implications of using these tools in research, but does not provide inferential effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency, speed, and workload reduction in research writing tasks from open-ended responses and sentiment analysis

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that institutions should create clear guidelines and strict plagiarism policies for responsible AI use in research and education. Respondents also raised concerns about academic integrity, ethical use, and the need for detection/prevention measures, indicating institutional relevance rather than a directly measured institutional effect.
finding.measure: Faculty concerns and recommendations about institutional policy, academic integrity, and ethical governance of AI writing tools

paper_profiles.title: A Scoping Survey of ChatGPT in Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a scoping survey of the emerging literature on ChatGPT in mathematics education, asking what benefits and challenges teachers’ and students’ interactions with ChatGPT create for teaching and learning mathematics. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the authors searched Google Scholar, Web of Science, arXiv, HAL, and conference/book sources for work published from November 2022 to May 2024, screened about 200 records, and synthesized 50 relevant papers using thematic synthesis.

The review organizes the literature into seven themes: mathematics content use cases, teacher interaction and lesson planning, assessment and task design, student interaction and personalized learning, critical thinking challenges, collaborative learning, and attitudes/student outcomes. Across the literature, ChatGPT is portrayed as useful for generating explanations, lesson plans, feedback, and practice tasks, and for supporting self-regulated learning and collaboration. At the same time, the authors emphasize recurring limitations including inaccuracies, hallucinations, weak conceptual understanding, bias, ethical concerns, and the risk of over-reliance on AI.

Because the paper is a scoping review, it does not report a single pooled effect or a validated outcome measurement. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT has promise as a supplementary tool in mathematics education, including for teachers’ planning and assessment work, but it requires human oversight and careful prompt design. The review also argues that future research should more directly examine ethical, pedagogical, and practical implications as the technology evolves.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT sometimes supported mathematical problem solving, explanations, and feedback, but performance depended heavily on task type and difficulty. The review highlights studies reporting strong results on basic arithmetic/algebra or undergraduate-level tasks, alongside failures on more complex or graduate-level mathematics, so the overall picture is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Mathematical problem-solving accuracy, correctness on arithmetic/algebra/logic tasks, and performance on mathematics examinations and reasoning tasks

finding.finding_summary: Several studies summarized in the review reported that using ChatGPT was associated with higher motivation, more positive attitudes, and improved engagement-related outcomes. For example, one undergraduate programming study (n=45) found significantly higher motivation in the ChatGPT group than in the control group, and a statistics study reported more positive attitudes toward statistics in the experimental group.
finding.measure: Motivation toward the lesson, attitudes toward statistics, and related engagement/self-belief measures
finding.study_size: n=45 in one included experimental study; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly identifies durable-skill effects, especially on computational thinking, reasoning, proof quality, and critical thinking. One included experimental study with 45 undergraduate students found significantly higher computational thinking skills in the ChatGPT group, while other studies reported improved reasoning support and proof feedback but also warned that heavy reliance on ChatGPT could reduce critical thinking.
finding.measure: Computational thinking scale scores, reasoning/proof quality, and related critical thinking outcomes
finding.study_size: n=45 in one included experimental study; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing uses of ChatGPT were consistently framed as saving time and reducing workload by helping with lesson planning, curriculum development, assessment design, feedback generation, and task adaptation. The review reports multiple studies in which ChatGPT produced lesson plans or assessment materials similar in structure to human-authored ones and could automate or semi-automate parts of teacher work, though with quality caveats.
finding.measure: Lesson plan generation quality, assessment/scoring support, feedback generation, and teacher planning efficiency/workload

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence on programming education and related computer-science tasks, especially one experimental study where ChatGPT supported weekly programming lab work. That study found higher computational thinking, programming self-efficacy, and motivation in the experimental group, suggesting benefits for this non-core mathematics-adjacent academic area.
finding.measure: Programming self-efficacy and performance in programming education

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students, and what that design choice means for personalization quality, teacher effort, and student reactions. The authors frame the work around three dimensions of personalization design: depth (realism and mathematical fit of the context), grain size (how specific the interest match is), and ownership (how much control the teacher versus the LLM has over the final task).

In the study, seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers at six U.S. schools used ChatGPT/GPT-4o to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems from Unit 4 and Unit 6 into interest-based personalized versions. Across 143 problems given to 521 students, the researchers logged teacher prompts and time, coded teacher prompting strategies, and analyzed student closed- and open-ended feedback on interest and closeness to their interests. The design is descriptive and correlational rather than experimental: it examines how prompting choices and iteration relate to teacher efficiency and student ratings, without a control group.

The main findings were that teachers most often asked the LLM to add or swap popular-culture references, but they also spent substantial effort correcting realism and age appropriateness. Students tended to prefer narrower, more specific references, and they rarely commented on deeper realism issues. Teachers took about 4 minutes per personalized problem on average, and using 3–5 prompts was associated with the most favorable student ratings; however, teachers did not become clearly more efficient over time. From Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers actually used more prompts and more time per problem, while student ratings of interest and closeness increased modestly. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and monitoring of quality, but it is time-intensive and may not deliver the fine-grained personalization many students want.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main academic outcome is students’ ratings of personalized mathematics problems, not test performance. Across 143 personalized problems given to 521 7th-grade students, student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests were modest overall (mean interestingness 2.46/5, closeness 2.53/5), and ratings were higher when teachers used 3–5 prompts to create a problem (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073). The authors did not measure learning gains or standardized math achievement.
finding.measure: Student ratings of the interestingness and closeness of personalized mathematics problems; no direct achievement measure

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined student interest as an affective outcome. Students generally rated the personalized tasks as only moderately interesting (mean 2.46/5), but ratings were higher for Unit 6 than Unit 4 (interestingness 2.27 to 2.56; closeness 2.28 to 2.66), and the unit effect on combined student ratings was statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012). Student open-ended responses showed stronger reactions to specific popular-culture references than to broader contexts.
finding.measure: Student self-reported interestingness and closeness to interests on 1-5 scales; open-ended feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454/449/446 open-ended responses across items

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports indirect evidence about teacher and student problem-posing/feedback skills, including how teachers refined prompts and how students suggested improvements, but it does not use validated durable-skills instruments. Teachers improved their ability to craft personalized problems over time, yet student feedback indicated a preference for finer-grained specificity and revealed limited attention to deeper realism issues.
finding.measure: Prompting behavior, revisions, and qualitative feedback on problem improvement

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency was a central outcome. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6), and each problem took about 246 seconds on average (SD=165.7), or roughly 4 minutes. Efficiency did not improve over time; Unit 6 actually took more prompts and more time than Unit 4 (prompts: B=1.26, SE=0.41, p=0.0025; time: B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher prompts per problem and time spent creating each personalized problem
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 (prompts increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=70.4 seconds (time increase)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses implications for teacher professional learning, curriculum design, and the feasibility of teacher-in-the-loop GenAI workflows, but these are not measured as institutional outcomes. The authors argue that teacher-in-the-loop personalization may preserve teacher knowledge and oversight, yet the time burden suggests limits for scalable adoption in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: Qualitative implications drawn from teacher prompting, time, and student feedback

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school curriculum content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, overly reliant on multiple-choice formats, and not representative of real educational tasks, so they build a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, including arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The approach is not an instructional intervention for students or teachers; instead, it is an evaluation study of AI model capabilities on school-like tasks. The benchmark includes questions that require visual reasoning, subject knowledge, basic calculation, OCR-like reading, and in some cases adversarial questions designed to be unanswerable from the image alone. Thirteen open-weight VLMs were tested using automated judging with multiple LLM evaluators. The paper finds that even the strongest models achieve under 45% overall accuracy, with particularly weak performance on music, math, and adversarial items, and that performance on public benchmarks such as MMMU does not reliably predict performance on this German, school-grounded dataset.

Overall, the paper concludes that middle-school-level visual and knowledge-based tasks are still challenging for current VLMs, especially in German and when open-ended responses are required. It also shows that models often fail to say 'I don't know' on adversarial questions, and that scaling up model size helps only modestly beyond the medium-size range. The work is primarily a benchmark contribution for AI evaluation rather than a study of student or teacher outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a benchmark evaluation of VLMs on German middle-school subject content, not a study of learner outcomes. It reports that the best model reached only 43.26% overall accuracy (Qwen2.5VL 32B) across 2,038 questions on 486 images, with subject-level best scores ranging from roughly 31% in music and math to about 54% in history and religion.
finding.measure: Open-ended benchmark accuracy on subject-specific image-question tasks

finding.finding_summary: Math performance was one of the weakest areas on the benchmark, indicating that current VLMs struggle with middle-school numeracy when visual interpretation and background knowledge must be combined. Best reported math accuracy was about 34.09% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while some models were far lower (e.g. 9.09% for Ovis2 4B).
finding.measure: Accuracy on math questions involving area, circumference, geometry, and simple calculations

finding.finding_summary: The physics and biology items required diagram interpretation, explanation, and term-label matching, and the authors report substantial model difficulty on these tasks. Best physics performance was 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and biology performance reached 48.53% at best, with many failures on explanation-based questions and part-label identification.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics and biology visual reasoning questions
finding.study_size: n=13 models; 234 physics questions; 169 biology questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly assess speaking or listening fluency, but it does evaluate German-language comprehension in open-ended question answering. The authors report that models often failed more on German, free-text, and context-dependent prompts than on benchmark-style tasks, suggesting language-processing limitations, but no dedicated fluency metric was used.
finding.measure: Open-ended German question answering accuracy

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Workshop on Generative AI and Law (co-located with ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines market concentration and platform power in the generative AI ecosystem from an antitrust-law perspective. Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention or educational technology outcome, it analyzes how a small number of large technology firms may dominate the data, talent, infrastructure, funding, and model-development layers underlying generative AI systems.

The authors argue that incumbent firms such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon benefit from vertical integration across the generative AI stack, which may create barriers to entry for new competitors and reinforce existing market structures. The paper discusses legal and economic implications of this concentration, including concerns about proprietary models, reliance on large-scale infrastructure, and the role of the EU AI Act and digital platform regulation. Its main conclusion is that competition policy and legal oversight may shape who controls generative AI, but it does not present empirical education research or any teacher/wellbeing measures.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is becoming concentrated among a few major firms because they control key inputs such as data, compute, talent, infrastructure, and research funding. It suggests this vertical integration may strengthen incumbent power and make meaningful competition difficult, but it is an analytic/legal argument rather than an empirical institutional outcome study.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a safety and regulatory problem in generative AI: large multimodal models can recommend medical products for uses that are not approved by regulators, potentially exposing users to unsafe or ineffective off-label promotion. The author argues that because these models are trained on broad internet-scale data with limited oversight, they may internalize and reproduce unvetted product–indication relationships.

To investigate this issue, the paper proposes a post-hoc detection pipeline for identifying off-label promotion in model outputs. The method standardizes user input, applies biomedical named entity recognition, matches products and indications against the FDA FDALabel database, and then uses a zero-shot prompt to determine whether a product–indication pair constitutes a recommendation. The approach is demonstrated on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style medical product question-answering scenario, where the user provides a product label image and asks about the product.

For evaluation, the author generated 14,300 synthetic queries across 35 pharmaceuticals with known off-label uses. The model outputs contained off-label indications in 15.4% of responses, and the detection method achieved 85.75% precision, 80.47% recall, and 83.02% F1 on a 2,000-sample human-annotated set. The paper concludes that generative AI systems can produce potentially harmful off-label medical recommendations and that automated guardrails may help filter such responses before they are shown to users.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a post-hoc detection pipeline that can automatically identify off-label medical product promotion in MLLM outputs, which is directly relevant to automated safety filtering and moderation workflows. On a human-annotated sample of n=2,000 responses, the method achieved precision=85.75%, recall=80.47%, and F1=83.02%, indicating reasonably strong detection performance for reducing manual review burden.
finding.measure: Off-label promotion detection performance (precision, recall, F1)

paper_profiles.title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of making relational databases accessible to non-technical users who do not know SQL. It argues that existing natural-language-to-SQL approaches often fail to validate generated queries, handle domain-specific business rules, or return user-friendly answers.

The paper proposes a generative-AI-based natural language assistant that scans database schemas, stores schema metadata and business rules in a vector database, retrieves relevant context for a user query, generates SQL with an LLM, validates the SQL syntactically and semantically, and then produces a natural-language response. The prototype was built with IBM watsonx.data, watsonx.ai, Milvus, Python, and Streamlit.

Evaluation was conducted on the BIRD-SQL benchmark, which tests natural-language querying of relational databases. The paper reports that over 50% of queries were correctly translated on the first attempt, with better performance on simple queries, and that natural-language responses were judged positively by a small set of nontechnical users. However, the study is an engineering prototype paper rather than a K-12 education study, and it does not examine teacher wellbeing or validated wellbeing instruments.

finding.finding_summary: The prototype is designed to improve user productivity by letting non-technical users query relational databases in natural language instead of writing SQL. On BIRD-SQL, the system reportedly translated over 50% of queries correctly on the first attempt, with more than 58% for simple queries, and iterative refinement further improved success rates; however, no formal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: SQL translation accuracy; natural-language response quality

paper_profiles.title: Enterprise AI Canvas: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Business
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the “Enterprise AI Canvas,” a structured framework for planning and integrating AI systems into business operations. The paper addresses the practical problem that organizations often separate business planning from data science planning, which can lead to misaligned projects, weak operational fit, and overlooked organizational change needs.

The approach is presented as a two-part canvas. Part 1 focuses on the business view—value, success metrics, decision optimization, organizational change, sponsorship, and domain expertise—while Part 2 focuses on the model and data view—prediction and action, features, data sources and processing, data quality, constraints, and evaluation/monitoring. The paper is conceptual and draws on a supermarket replenishment example to illustrate how the canvas could support AI project planning, but it does not evaluate the framework empirically.

Because the paper is a framework/proposal rather than an empirical study, it does not measure outcomes in a K-12 educational setting or report validated instrument data. Its main conclusion is that successful AI adoption requires joint discussion between business stakeholders and data scientists across both organizational and technical dimensions, with attention to decision-making, change management, and operational metrics.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Wine Industry: AI-Driven Management in Viticulture, Wine Production and Enotourism
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence could support sustainability and efficiency in the Polish wine industry. The authors ask two main questions: what winemakers in Poland currently do to support environmental, economic, and social sustainability, and what AI applications could plausibly enhance those efforts in viticulture, wine production, and enotourism.

The study uses an electronic questionnaire distributed to all officially registered vineyards in Poland, supplemented by a literature- and market-based review of AI tools relevant to the wine sector. Seventy-five vineyards responded. The paper reports descriptive findings on winemakers’ sustainability practices, such as environmental management, support for local economies, and enotourism offerings, then maps these practices to possible AI use cases like drone monitoring, irrigation optimization, supply-chain tools, chatbots, recommendation systems, and virtual tastings.

The main conclusion is that Polish winemakers already show substantial engagement with sustainability, especially in local economic and social relations, and that AI could further improve resource management, marketing, and tourism operations. However, the paper is primarily prospective and conceptual regarding AI: it does not evaluate an AI intervention or measure outcomes of AI use. The authors conclude that AI adoption may help the sector maintain sustainability under future pressures such as climate change and possible scale-up, but implementation should be tailored to local vineyard conditions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that Polish winemakers generally report strong sustainability-oriented practices and views that align with local economic, social, and environmental development. In a survey of 75 vineyards, 77% said they consider environmental issues in production, 96% reported contributing to local development, and 83% of respondents indicated openness to visitors, suggesting a sector-level orientation toward sustainable and tourism-based institutional practices.
finding.measure: Survey responses on environmental practices, local development actions, and enotourism openness

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how YouTube content creators use generative AI tools across the video production workflow. The authors ask what specific use cases of GenAI appear in how-to videos and how these uses map onto planning, production, editing, and uploading tasks. The study is motivated by the rapid adoption of tools such as ChatGPT, MidJourney, Leonardo.AI, and similar systems in creator workflows, alongside limited understanding of their concrete roles in practice.

The authors collected 3,854 YouTube videos with a search query focused on AI content creation, filtered them to 1,046 videos, and then manually reviewed them to identify 274 relevant how-to videos. They used thematic analysis on 2,829 transcript clips to develop a conceptual framework of GenAI use cases. The paper documents that creators use GenAI for scripting, topic ideation, prompt refinement, image/video generation, animation, avatars, stock-footage selection, voiceover generation, music/sound effects, lip-syncing, restyling, upscaling, clipping, visual effects, filling images, translation, speech correction, subtitles, and title generation.

The main conclusion is that GenAI is being used to streamline many labor-intensive parts of video creation and to reduce creative labor, while also raising concerns about originality, authenticity, visibility, transparency, and the need for better prompt-support tools. The paper is primarily descriptive and design-oriented rather than evaluative: it does not test an intervention or measure outcomes for learners or teachers, but instead provides a conceptual map of creator practices and future HCI directions. Although it mentions possible support for creators with disabilities and people facing anxiety or depression, it does not empirically study wellbeing or K-12 teacher outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Making Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly: Considering Fabrication Constraints, Sustainability, Time, Functionality and Accessibility
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how 3D generative AI can be paired with physical fabrication methods to produce real-world objects more effectively. The authors argue that existing work has focused too narrowly on making AI-generated meshes more printable, and instead propose a broader framework for evaluating fabrication processes along five dimensions: fabrication constraints, time, sustainability, functionality, and accessibility.

As a case study, the paper presents a system that converts speech into AI-generated 3D models and then fabricates them using discrete robotic assembly with a UR10 robotic arm. The system voxelizes AI-generated geometry into modular components, applies checks for overhangs, connectivity, and robot reachability, and assembles objects from 40 reusable parts. The paper reports that the approach can handle variable AI outputs, produce large objects in under five minutes on average, and support sustainable reuse of components to create seven distinct objects; however, accessibility remains limited by hardware cost, and some assembled objects lacked sufficient structural integrity for intended use.

The paper is primarily a technical workshop contribution and case study, not an educational study. It does not investigate K-12 teachers, students, or validated wellbeing instruments. Its main conclusion is that discrete robotic assembly is a promising fabrication companion to generative AI for on-demand physical making, but future work is needed to improve object functionality and lower cost barriers.

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the moderating effects of social good and confidence on teachers’ intention to prepare school students for artificial intelligence education
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (lower and upper secondary)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines psychological factors related to teachers’ intention to prepare K-12 students for artificial intelligence (AI) education. The authors focus on AI anxiety, perceived usefulness, attitude toward AI, AI relevance, AI readiness, and behavioral intention, and they extend the planned behavior/TAM-based model with two moderators: AI for social good and confidence in teaching AI.

The study used a quantitative survey of 320 in-service teachers from government-owned lower and upper secondary schools in southwest Nigeria, mostly STEM teachers. Teachers responded to validated/adapted self-report measures, and the authors analyzed the data using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The paper reports acceptable reliability and validity for the measures and finds that most hypothesized relationships were supported, except the path from AI readiness to behavioral intention.

Main results indicate that perceived usefulness, attitude toward AI, and AI relevance all positively predict teachers’ behavioral intention to teach AI, while AI anxiety negatively predicts perceived usefulness. AI for social good and confidence in teaching AI moderated several model paths, suggesting that teachers’ beliefs about AI’s societal value and their confidence in teaching AI shape how other perceptions translate into intention. The authors conclude that professional development should address AI’s benefits, risks, ethics, and practical teaching examples to strengthen teachers’ willingness to teach AI.

finding.finding_summary: The study shows teachers’ AI-related attitudes, anxiety, relevance perceptions, and confidence are associated with their behavioral intention to teach AI, but it does not measure wellbeing or social-emotional outcomes directly. In the structural model, attitude toward AI (β=0.389), perceived usefulness (β=0.134), and AI relevance (β=0.435) positively predicted behavioral intention, while AI anxiety negatively predicted perceived usefulness (β=-0.272) among 320 in-service secondary teachers.
finding.measure: Self-report survey scales for AI anxiety, attitude toward AI, perceived usefulness, AI relevance, AI readiness, AI for social good, confidence in teaching AI, and behavioral intention to teach AI

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies teachers’ intention to prepare students for AI education and identifies institutional-level moderators that shape that intention. Behavioral intention was positively predicted by attitude toward AI, perceived usefulness, and AI relevance, and the authors argue that professional development and school support are important for AI implementation; AI readiness did not significantly predict intention (β=-0.028, p=0.451).
finding.measure: Behavioral intention to teach AI; moderation by AI for social good and confidence in teaching AI

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education learners and teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the emerging role of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT and GPT-3, in education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early research and presents a conceptual analysis of opportunities, risks, and mitigation strategies for educational use by students and teachers.

The paper discusses a wide range of potential applications, including automated quiz generation, tutoring support, feedback on student work, lesson planning, assessment support, and professional development for teachers. It also reviews then-available research on LLMs in education and argues that these tools could improve productivity, personalization, and engagement, while also supporting learning tasks across subjects and settings.

Because the article is primarily a position paper, its emphasis is on challenges and governance rather than empirical evaluation. It highlights concerns about bias, plagiarism, privacy, cost, overreliance, and the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated from human-generated text, and recommends human oversight, careful curriculum integration, and ethical safeguards. The paper concludes that LLMs hold promise for education, but that robust policies, transparency, and further empirical research are needed before widespread adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can reduce teacher workload by supporting lesson planning, personalized feedback, grading, and generation of teaching materials. However, this is a conceptual claim rather than a tested empirical result; no sample size, effect size, or validated outcome measure is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / task efficiency (conceptual, not empirically measured)

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional issues such as governance, privacy, copyright, fairness, sustainability, and policy responses to LLM adoption in education. It does not present empirical estimates; instead, it synthesizes risks and proposes mitigation strategies for responsible deployment at the system level.
finding.measure: policy, governance, privacy, fairness, and adoption considerations (conceptual synthesis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may support critical thinking and problem-solving through prompts, explanations, and personalized scaffolds, but also warns that overreliance could undermine those same skills. No empirical study was conducted, so there are no measured effects, sample sizes, or statistics reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking / problem-solving (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLM-based tools may improve student engagement, participation, and curiosity, particularly in dialog and question-asking contexts. These are presented as anticipated benefits and summaries of prior work rather than findings from a single empirical study, so no effect sizes or validated instruments are reported.
finding.measure: engagement, participation, curiosity (conceptual and literature-synthesized)

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines concerns about using chatbots in education, using ChatGPT as a representative case of an advanced AI chatbot. The authors ask what concerns arise when ChatGPT is used in educational settings and investigate those concerns through a three-stage instrumental case study.

The study combines three qualitative components: social network analysis and sentiment analysis of 2,330 tweets (from 1,530 Twitter users), content analysis of interviews with 19 self-described early adopters who had posted about using ChatGPT in education, and hands-on user experience testing by three experienced educators over one week. The paper focuses on how educators, students, and other stakeholders perceive ChatGPT’s educational value, risks, and limitations.

Across the three stages, the paper finds broadly positive sentiment and perceived usefulness, but also substantial concerns about cheating, inaccurate or misleading outputs, fairness and inconsistency across users, privacy risks, manipulation, lack of emotional understanding, and ethical issues such as plagiarism and reduced critical thinking. The main conclusion is not that ChatGPT should be banned, but that education systems need better guidance, policies, and responsible design principles to support safe and effective adoption. The authors argue that teachers need new teaching philosophies and students need new competencies for working with AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: Participants frequently described ChatGPT as useful for reducing teacher workload and speeding up instructional tasks such as preparing teaching materials, generating quizzes, and producing outlines. However, the paper also documents that outputs could be inconsistent, inaccurate, or poorly structured, which sometimes made teachers’ duties more complicated rather than easier.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview responses and user-experience observations about teacher workload, resource creation, and task efficiency
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators in user-experience testing

finding.finding_summary: A central concern was that ChatGPT could weaken critical thinking by encouraging reliance on easy answers, plagiarism, cheating, and reduced effort. At the same time, some participants said it could support higher-level thinking if users developed stronger prompt skills and evaluated outputs critically. The study does not report quantitative effect sizes; the evidence is based on interviews, tweets, and scenario-based observation.
finding.measure: Perceived effects on critical thinking, prompt skill, and reliance on AI-generated answers

finding.finding_summary: Users often found interacting with ChatGPT enjoyable, exciting, and fun, and some described emotional attachment because it felt like a patient tutor. However, participants also reported disappointment when ChatGPT failed to provide genuine empathy or emotional value, and scenario testing showed it could not meaningfully reveal emotions or student reflection. Findings are qualitative and do not include validated instrument scores.
finding.measure: Perceived enjoyment, attachment, disappointment, and emotional response during interaction with ChatGPT
