finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators in user-experience testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may substantially affect school policy, assessment practices, privacy governance, and the broader organization of teaching. It documents concerns about cheating policies, privacy and data storage, fairness across users, and the need for new rules and responsible-AI guidance, while also suggesting that banning the tool alone is insufficient.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional concerns identified through tweets, interviews, and scenario testing

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to prompts related to science education and what educators might do with its outputs. The author asks three questions: how ChatGPT answers science-education questions, how educators could use it to support pedagogy, and how the tool functions as a research aid in the study itself. The study uses a self-study methodology, with prompts entered into ChatGPT in January 2023 and the generated text compared against themes in the science education literature.

The paper is not an intervention study with students; rather, it is a qualitative examination of the usefulness, limitations, and risks of generative AI for science teaching and research. The author finds that ChatGPT often aligns with established science education themes such as inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, differentiation, collaboration, and assessment. It also produces potentially useful drafts for lesson units, rubrics, and quizzes, but these outputs are often generic and require substantial educator judgment and refinement.

A central conclusion is that ChatGPT may be helpful as a brainstorming, drafting, and editing tool for educators and researchers, but its outputs should not be treated as authoritative because they may lack evidence, context sensitivity, and reliable citations. The paper also emphasizes ethical and practical concerns, including bias, false references, environmental costs, copyright issues, and the need for clear expectations around AI use in teaching and assessment. Overall, the study argues for critical, responsible, and context-aware use of generative AI in education.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s responses often aligned with established science-education themes such as inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, and assessment, but the author argues that the outputs are not sufficiently grounded in evidence and can present a single truth without qualifications. The paper is an exploratory self-study, so it does not report student outcome data, effect sizes, or experimental comparisons.
finding.measure: Alignment of ChatGPT-generated science education responses with research themes; qualitative critique of evidence base and pedagogical appropriateness

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames ChatGPT as supporting critical thinking, reflection, and the generation of pedagogical ideas, while also warning that users may accept outputs uncritically. The author suggests that educators and students need to evaluate AI output carefully, consider context, and detect bias, but these claims are conceptual rather than based on measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation of ChatGPT outputs; reflections on critical thinking, context awareness, and bias detection

finding.finding_summary: The author reports that ChatGPT was useful for editing sentences, clarifying phrasing, and generating starting points for science units, rubrics, and quizzes. No formal productivity metrics were measured, but the paper provides concrete examples of reduced drafting effort and faster idea generation in a self-study context.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for editing, drafting lesson materials, rubric design, and quiz generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses broader institutional issues around AI in education, including authorship, transparency, assessment policy, ethics, bias, environmental impact, and copyright. It argues that schools and journals will need clearer guidelines for AI use, but it does not evaluate policy implementation or institutional outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of AI governance, assessment integrity, disclosure norms, and ethical considerations

paper_profiles.title: Predicting teacher resilience by using artificial neural networks: influence of burnout and stress by COVID-19
paper_profiles.venue: Anales de Psicología / Annals of Psychology
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (K-12 educators) in southeastern Spain
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether teacher resilience can be predicted from burnout dimensions, COVID-19-related stress, and socio-demographic characteristics using artificial neural networks. The authors frame the work around the idea that resilience helps teachers cope with occupational adversity and that the COVID-19 context may have intensified stress and burnout among teachers.

The sample consisted of 401 secondary school teachers from southeastern Spain (70.6% women). Participants completed three validated instruments: the Brief Resilient Coping Scale, the Maslach Burnout Inventory-General Survey, and a COVID-19 stress questionnaire. The study compared women and men on resilience, burnout, and COVID-19 stress, then built three multilayer perceptron ANN models: one for the full sample and one gender-specific model for women and men.

Results showed no meaningful gender difference in resilience, but women reported higher emotional exhaustion/professional efficacy and higher COVID-19 stress than men, while cynicism did not differ significantly. In the ANN models, professional efficacy was the strongest predictor of resilience in all models, with marital status, experience, cynicism, and COVID-19 stress contributing to varying degrees depending on gender. The authors conclude that artificial neural networks can be useful for educational research and that resilience and burnout-related interventions should be tailored with attention to gender differences.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher resilience was the central outcome and was measured with the Brief Resilient Coping Scale (BRCS) in 401 secondary school teachers. The ANN models indicated that resilience could be predicted from burnout and COVID-19 stress variables, with professional efficacy the strongest predictor across models; however, the raw gender comparison showed essentially no difference in mean resilience between women and men (women M=15.63, men M=15.59).
finding.measure: Brief Resilient Coping Scale (BRCS) resilience score

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined burnout dimensions and their relationship to resilience, focusing on emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and professional efficacy among secondary teachers. Professional efficacy was the strongest predictor of resilience in the ANN models, while exhaustion and cynicism also contributed to prediction; women reported higher exhaustion (M=3.20 vs 2.71) and higher professional efficacy (M=4.63 vs 4.47) than men, suggesting that burnout-related work functioning is closely tied to resilience.
finding.measure: Maslach Burnout Inventory-General Survey (emotional exhaustion, cynicism, professional efficacy)
finding.std_deviation: Women exhaustion SD=1.606; Men exhaustion SD=1.598; Women efficiency SD=.725; Men efficiency SD=.814; Women cynicism SD=1.423; Men cynicism SD=1.516

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses artificial neural networks to model teacher resilience and argues that such AI methods can support educational decision-making and more tailored intervention programs. The findings suggest that gender-specific modeling may improve understanding of resilience-related risk factors in teacher populations, but the study does not test any institutional policy or system-level intervention effects.
finding.measure: Artificial neural network predictive modeling of resilience using burnout, stress, and demographic variables

paper_profiles.title: Development of an artificial intelligence curriculum design for children in Taiwan and its impact on learning outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study addresses the lack of systematic AI education resources for children in Taiwan and asks how an AI curriculum can be designed for ages 9–12 and what effects it has on students’ learning outcomes and attitudes toward AI. The authors position the work within the growing interest in AI literacy for K–12 learners and emphasize both conceptual understanding and hands-on use of generative AI tools.

The intervention was a five-day, 30-hour AI curriculum delivered to 30 elementary school students in grades 3–4 in Taiwan. The curriculum covered AI basics, machine learning, generative AI applications, and social/ethical issues, and used tools such as Artbreeder, ChatGPT, Boomy, and cutout.pro for creative tasks including drawing, storytelling, music creation, and animation. The study used a single-group pretest/posttest design with AI knowledge tests, AI knowledge self-assessments, a pupils’ attitude toward technology questionnaire, expert assessments of student projects, and semi-structured interviews.

Results showed significant gains in objective AI knowledge scores and in self-reported AI knowledge, AI skills, and AI attitudes from pre to post. Expert ratings also indicated strong student project creativity, aesthetic appeal, and technical quality. Interview data suggested that students enjoyed the course, were more interested in AI, and recognized both the opportunities and ethical concerns associated with AI. Overall, the paper concludes that the curriculum was effective for improving elementary students’ AI literacy and positive attitudes toward AI, while also supporting creative project work.

finding.finding_summary: Students in grades 3–4 showed significant improvement in AI knowledge after the 5-day curriculum. On the objective AI knowledge test, mean scores increased from 45.16 (SD=19.67) to 73.50 (SD=13.07) out of 100, n=30, with a paired-samples t-test showing p<0.001 (t=-6.58, df=29).
finding.measure: AI knowledge score test (pre/post quiz)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported significantly more positive attitudes toward AI technology after the course, including stronger technological career aspirations and greater interest in technology. On the adapted PATT-related questionnaire, all six subscales were significantly above the neutral midpoint of 4, with mean scores ranging from 5.45 to 5.84 (n=30, all p<0.001), indicating increased motivation and engagement toward AI learning.
finding.measure: Pupils’ attitude toward technology questionnaire
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for subscales reported as lower=1.30 to 2.02, upper=1.61 to 2.11; exact mapping unclear in paper table

finding.finding_summary: The course improved students’ self-assessed AI skills, which included using AI-based systems, approaching real-world problems with AI, and operating generative AI systems. Mean self-assessment for skills rose from 3.92 (SD=1.08) to 5.81 (SD=0.47), n=30, with a significant pre/post difference (p<0.001; t=-8.13, df=29).
finding.measure: AI knowledge self-assessment questionnaire — AI skills subscale

finding.finding_summary: Students also improved in self-reported AI knowledge and AI attitudes, suggesting gains in understanding and critical orientation toward AI. AI knowledge self-assessment increased from 3.63 (SD=0.85) to 5.45 (SD=0.42), and AI attitude from 3.85 (SD=1.06) to 5.82 (SD=0.48), both with p<0.001 (n=30).
finding.measure: AI knowledge self-assessment questionnaire — knowledge and attitude subscales
finding.std_deviation: Knowledge: pre SD=0.85, post SD=0.42; Attitude: pre SD=1.06, post SD=0.48

finding.finding_summary: Expert reviewers rated the students’ final AI-created projects above the neutral midpoint on creativity, aesthetic appeal, and technical advantages. Mean ratings were 5.82 for creativity, 5.22 for aesthetic appeal, and 5.57 for technical advantages on a 7-point scale, all significantly above 4 (n=30, all p<0.001), indicating strong creative product outcomes.
finding.measure: Expert consensual assessment of student projects
finding.confidence_interval: Creativity 1.64–2.00; Aesthetic appeal 1.07–1.37; Technical advantages 1.63–2.11 (reported as CI around difference from neutral)
finding.std_deviation: Creativity SD=0.89; Aesthetic appeal SD=0.74; Technical advantages SD=0.11

paper_profiles.title: Validating an Instrument for Teachers’ Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of well-validated instruments for measuring teachers’ acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) in education. The authors argue that existing teacher-AI acceptance measures often have limited psychometric evidence and may be undermined by respondents’ unfamiliarity with AI, so they develop and validate a new instrument for teachers’ acceptance of AI (TAAI).

The approach combines instrument development and psychometric validation. The authors define TAAI through five dimensions drawn from technology acceptance theory and prior literature: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, self-efficacy, and anxiety. They create an initial 32-item survey with a reading stimulus about AI and its educational applications, then refine it through expert review and think-aloud interviews with five pre-service teachers. The revised instrument is field-tested with 274 pre-service teachers from a Chinese four-year university, spanning STEM and non-STEM majors and both undergraduate and graduate levels.

Using item discrimination tests, Cronbach’s alpha, and confirmatory factor analysis, the authors reduce the scale to 27 items across five factors. The final model shows strong fit and reliability (overall alpha = 0.92; CFA fit indices RMSEA = 0.061, CFI = 0.981, TLI = 0.979, SRMSR = 0.051), and the dimensions also show good convergent and discriminant validity. The paper concludes that the TAAI instrument is a robust measure for future research on teachers’ acceptance of AI in education and can support studies on teacher professional development and adoption of AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: The instrument measures teachers’ acceptance of AI partly through perceived usefulness items tied to saving time and improving teaching performance. In validation with 274 pre-service teachers, the scale showed strong psychometric performance overall (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.92; factor loadings for the usefulness dimension ranged from 0.70 to 0.94), indicating respondents consistently endorsed the AI-usefulness/timesaving construct.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of AI for teaching efficiency and performance; item discrimination, Cronbach’s alpha, and CFA factor loadings

finding.finding_summary: The scale includes an anxiety dimension, capturing negative feelings and concerns about using AI in teaching. The final anxiety subscale showed acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.77) and factor loadings ranging from 0.60 to 0.81, but the paper reports this as a measurement-validation result rather than a change in wellbeing; thus it provides evidence that teacher AI anxiety is measurable, not that it was reduced or increased.
finding.measure: AI-related anxiety in teaching practice; reliability and CFA factor loadings

finding.finding_summary: The validated instrument assesses behavioral intention and self-efficacy related to using AI in teaching, both of which are relevant to teachers’ confidence and planned use of new technologies. In the final model, these subscales showed strong internal consistency (alpha = 0.91 for both) and high standardized loadings (behavioral intention: 0.75–0.95; self-efficacy: 0.81–0.92), supporting measurement of these teacher capacity-related constructs.
finding.measure: Behavioral intention to use AI and self-efficacy for using AI in teaching; reliability and CFA factor loadings

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The central question is not whether AI can personalize problems, but how teachers actually use ChatGPT to adapt existing middle school math problems, how long the process takes, and how students respond to the resulting tasks.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated. After training, they used GPT-4o/ChatGPT to personalize Illustrative Mathematics problems for units on proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities. The study analyzed 143 personalized problems, teacher prompt logs and talk-aloud/video recordings, student closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests, and open-ended student feedback. The paper finds that teachers primarily prompted for broad or specific popular-culture references, but also spent substantial effort fixing realism, age appropriateness, and numerical plausibility. Students tended to prefer finer-grained personalized references, and teacher personalization was time-consuming: roughly 4 minutes per problem and about 3.2 prompts per problem on average.

The study also compares Unit 4 and Unit 6 to look for growth over time. Teachers used more prompts and spent more time in Unit 6, likely because they were responding to student feedback and trying to improve the problems. Student ratings of interestingness and closeness increased in Unit 6, but the study is exploratory and correlational rather than causal. Overall, the paper argues that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and oversight, but it is not clearly time-efficient and may not achieve the fine-grained personalization students want.

finding.finding_summary: The study centered on middle school mathematics task personalization, but it did not measure math achievement or learning outcomes directly. Teachers personalized 143 problems in proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities, and the authors note that the work was exploratory and focused on student ratings and task design rather than performance; thus any impact on mathematical numeracy remains unmeasured.
finding.measure: personalized middle school mathematics problem design; no direct math achievement measure reported

finding.finding_summary: Students generally rated the personalized problems at low-to-moderate levels of interestingness and closeness to their interests, and ratings improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6 after teacher reflection and iteration. Average interestingness increased from 2.27 (SD=1.17) to 2.56 (SD=1.26), and average closeness increased from 2.28 (SD=1.20) to 2.66 (SD=1.29); the unit effect on combined ratings was significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: student self-reported interestingness and closeness-to-interests ratings on 1-5 scales
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings on 52-53 problems depending on measure
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.17 to 1.29 (unit-level averages); SD=1.24 and 1.28 overall on the two closed-ended items

finding.finding_summary: Personalizing math problems with ChatGPT was time-consuming for teachers and did not become clearly more efficient over time. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems (3.2 prompts/problem) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7); in Unit 6, teachers actually used more prompts and more time than in Unit 4 (prompt increase B=1.26, SE=0.41, p=0.0025; time increase B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: teacher prompt counts and time spent creating each personalized problem
finding.effect_size: B=1.26; B=70.4 seconds; 3-5 prompts associated with +0.24 student-rating points
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; Unit 4 SD=153 seconds, Unit 6 SD=169 seconds

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that teachers developed skill in using ChatGPT and reflected more deeply on task design over time, though this was not measured with a validated durable-skills instrument. Teachers adjusted prompts to improve realism, age fit, and mathematical clarity, and the authors interpret this as evidence of growth in problem-posing and prompting practice; however, the main quantitative outcomes were prompt counts, time, and student ratings rather than direct measures of metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: teacher prompting practices and iterative revisions during problem posing

paper_profiles.title: How Can Video Generative AI Transform K-12 Education? Examining Teachers’ Perspectives through TPACK and TAM
paper_profiles.population: K-12 Teachers (mostly Elementary, plus High School)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how K-12 teachers perceive and evaluate video generative AI (Video GenAI) as an instructional tool. The paper asks what teachers think their first experiences with Video GenAI are, what educational uses they see for it, and what limitations and future improvements they identify. The authors frame the analysis using TPACK and TAM to understand both pedagogical fit and technology acceptance.

Ten participants took part: eight elementary teachers, one high school English teacher, and one former elementary teacher working as a data analyst. Each teacher used Luma Dream Machine, supported by an educational guide and semi-structured interview protocol, and then discussed impressions, ease of use, usefulness, and willingness to adopt the tool. The study does not test student outcomes experimentally; instead it uses interview coding to identify themes about instructional potential and barriers.

Teachers saw promise in Video GenAI for visualizing abstract concepts, supporting project-based learning, encouraging creativity, and diversifying assessment. They also believed it could reduce preparation time and support AI literacy, but they raised concerns about rendering quality, hallucinations, Korean language limitations, safety, age restrictions, copyright, and lack of monitoring features. Overall, the paper concludes that Video GenAI may be useful in K-12 settings, but successful adoption depends on stronger technical performance, clearer policies, and more teacher training and institutional support.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived Video GenAI as potentially useful for reducing preparation time and creating supplementary instructional materials more quickly than conventional video production. They reported that the tool could streamline the creation of visuals for class materials, although this was based on interview perceptions rather than a measured time-saving outcome.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of preparation time and material-creation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed Video GenAI could help students understand scientific phenomena by visualizing experiments and simulating outcomes that are hard to observe directly. This was described as a potential instructional use for science learning, but the paper did not report student achievement data or validated science outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of science concept visualization and comprehension

finding.finding_summary: Teachers saw Video GenAI as useful for history, language arts, and other non-math/non-science subjects, especially for reenactments, text-to-video adaptations, and subject-specific visual supports. The finding is thematic and qualitative, based on teachers’ descriptions of likely classroom uses rather than direct student outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of interdisciplinary instructional applications

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly described Video GenAI as a tool that could increase student engagement, motivation, and creative expression. They expected it to help students express ideas, explore imaginative scenarios, and become more invested in project-based tasks, but these claims were not validated with student survey instruments or behavioral measures.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of student engagement, motivation, and creative expression

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed Video GenAI could support divergent thinking, composition skills, and AI literacy, and that prompt-writing activities might improve students’ ability to articulate ideas more precisely. The study also suggests possible benefits for critical thinking in project-based learning, but these were inferred from teacher perspectives rather than measured with validated instruments.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of divergent thinking, composition, and AI literacy

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified both enabling and constraining institutional factors: they wanted better safety filters, teacher monitoring functions, national-level guidelines, professional development, infrastructure, and funding support, but they also cited age restrictions, parental consent burdens, copyright uncertainty, and access inequities as barriers. The paper is primarily qualitative and does not quantify policy effects, but it strongly centers institutional adoption conditions.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, infrastructure, and institutional support

paper_profiles.title: Games for Artificial Intelligence Research: A Review and Perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of publicly available games and game-based platforms used for artificial intelligence research. It reviews how games can serve as controlled, cost-effective testbeds for studying AI capabilities such as learning, planning, generalization, multi-agent coordination, and game design, and it organizes the literature by game type, platform, number of agents, and observability.

The paper focuses on both game-playing and game-design environments, spanning tabletop games, grid-based and pixel-based video games, 3D environments, social games, and text-based games. It also discusses which platforms are suitable for different AI research goals, such as reinforcement learning, planning, procedural content generation, and balancing/tuning game parameters. The main contribution is taxonomic and methodological rather than empirical: it provides a roadmap for researchers selecting benchmark environments and highlights major challenges in game AI research.

Because this is a review, it does not study a K-12 educational intervention, teacher-facing AI tool, or teacher wellbeing outcome. Its educational relevance is indirect, limited to the paper’s discussion of games and platforms as research and education resources for AI researchers and students.

paper_profiles.title: The impacts of artificial intelligence on environmental sustainability and human well-being
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the existing literature says about AI’s impacts on environmental sustainability and human well-being, and how those impacts are being studied. The authors conducted a systematic review of 1,291 studies published between 2010 and 2024, drawn from 6,655 records across Scopus, arXiv, and NBER Working Papers, and coded them by impact type, analytical scale, method, and sentiment.

The review finds a sharply uneven evidence base. Environmental studies are mostly quantitative, micro-level, and focused on energy use and CO2 emissions, with 83% portraying AI’s environmental impacts as positive and systemic effects largely neglected. Human well-being studies are more conceptual and macro-oriented, with only limited empirical work; they cover social cohesion, inequality, employment, health, income, subjective well-being, and cognition, and overall sentiment is nearly split between positive and negative. The authors conclude that both literatures are too narrow: environmental research should broaden beyond carbon to water, materials, biodiversity, and rebound effects, while social/well-being research needs more empirical studies, especially on upstream supply-chain impacts and subjective dimensions of well-being. The paper also proposes a unified framework for mapping AI’s environmental and well-being impacts across computing-related, application-level, and systemic categories.

finding.finding_summary: This is a systematic literature review, not an intervention study, so it does not estimate a causal effect size. Its main finding is that AI’s systemic impacts are widely discussed in the literature but remain underexplored empirically: 11% of environmental studies and 44% of well-being studies address systemic effects, with much of the evidence being conceptual rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Proportion of reviewed studies addressing systemic impacts; review-based sentiment and evidence mapping

paper_profiles.title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short position statements from participants in the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program. The contributions respond to three broad “blue sky” questions in AI education: how to incorporate ethics into AI curricula, how to teach AI at early undergraduate or secondary-school levels, and how to make AI education more interdisciplinary for non-engineering fields.

Across the essays, authors propose pedagogical ideas such as peer-learning across disciplines, student-centric discovery, experiential and game-based learning, and using real-world problems to teach AI concepts. Several pieces also argue that ethics should be threaded throughout AI education and institutional practice, including codes of ethics, risk assessment, and explicit consideration of consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics.

The paper does not report an empirical study or evaluate any intervention with outcome measures. Instead, it offers expert perspectives and speculative recommendations intended to motivate future discussion and curriculum design for university and secondary-school AI education.

paper_profiles.title: Probability Judgment in Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines two approaches to probability judgment in artificial intelligence: Bayesian probability and belief functions (Dempster-Shafer theory). Shafer argues that these approaches differ not just technically but also philosophically, especially in how they handle incomplete evidence and how probability models are designed for practical inference. The paper’s central question is when a belief-function approach is more appropriate than a Bayesian one for AI reasoning tasks.

To illustrate the distinction, the paper walks through several toy examples involving testimony, thermometer evidence, and combinations of independent or dependent evidence. These examples show how belief functions can represent reasoned support based on partial or indirect evidence, and how Dempster’s rule combines independent sources of evidence. The paper also contrasts this with Bayesian designs that require more explicit prior and conditional probability judgments, which may be difficult to justify when evidence is incomplete.

The final section applies these ideas to expert systems such as PROSPECTOR and MYCIN, arguing that belief functions offered greater modularity for rule-based AI systems of the time. The paper concludes that both Bayesian and belief-function designs have niches, but that the deeper challenge for AI is improving the ability to design probability arguments flexibly, rather than treating any single probability language as normative.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Programming Task Creation of Primary School Teachers in Training
paper_profiles.population: Adult (preservice primary school teachers in training)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how primary school teachers in training create Scratch programming tasks and whether a static analysis tool, LitterBox, can support that process. The motivation is that teachers often have limited programming subject knowledge, which can lead to poor example code in classroom materials and potentially harmful misconceptions for students. The authors ask how teachers proceed when creating tasks, how tool support affects the resulting task text and code, and how teachers perceive the tool.

The study combined a pre-study (n=26) and a main A/B study with 59 teachers in training at the University of Passau, Germany. In the main study, one group created tasks without support and the other group used LitterBox at least twice while constructing a Scratch task for primary school children; participants then completed surveys, and the researchers analyzed task texts, Scratch programs, and open-ended responses. The analysis found that teachers often began with brainstorming and programming before writing the task text, and that tool-supported participants produced tasks with more hints in the text and Scratch programs with fewer bug patterns and smells.

Overall, participants viewed LitterBox positively, especially for detecting code patterns, providing suggestions, and saving time, though they also noted limitations such as false positives, lack of semantic understanding, and the absence of automatic refactoring. The paper concludes that automated analysis tools like LitterBox can support teacher task creation by improving code quality and scaffolding task texts, and suggests that teacher education should include both task-design pedagogy and automated code analysis tools.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers in training using LitterBox produced Scratch programs with fewer bug patterns and smells than the control group, suggesting the tool improved the efficiency/quality of task creation. Group Trmt inserted significantly fewer bug patterns (0.72 vs 1.26; p=0.034, ˆA12=0.66) and fewer smells (2.28 vs 3.19; p=0.022, ˆA12=0.68), and participants also reported that the tool saved time and provided timely feedback during creation.
finding.measure: Scratch program code quality during task creation; counts of bug patterns and smells, plus self-reported usefulness/time-saving comments
finding.study_size: n=56 analyzed programs (53 solution programs, 3 starter programs); n=59 main study participants

finding.finding_summary: Teachers in training reported affective benefits from the tool, including motivation and reduced difficulty when creating tasks. The paper notes that participants valued receiving positive feedback on code perfumes and described the tool as motivating and helpful for inexperienced teachers, although this was based on survey responses rather than a validated wellbeing instrument.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on positive/negative aspects of LitterBox and Likert-rated usefulness
finding.study_size: n=59 main study participants; pre-study comparison also discussed (n=26)

paper_profiles.title: Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety (AAAI-Safe AI 2019)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the landscape of published Artificial Intelligence (AI) principles and governance documents and asks how different principles overlap, differ, and can be semantically linked. Rather than studying an educational intervention, the authors build a platform called LAIP (Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles) to organize, compare, and search 27 AI principle proposals from academia, non-profits, governments, and industry.

The approach combines manual keyword selection with word2vec-based semantic expansion to identify common topics across principles, including humanity, collaboration, fairness, transparency, privacy, security, safety, accountability, and AGI/ASI. The paper then analyzes topic coverage and keyword coverage across proposals and compares patterns by publisher type. The authors conclude that AI principles are complementary rather than mutually substitutable and argue for a comprehensive framework that integrates multiple principles instead of adopting any single one in isolation.

The paper is best understood as a conceptual and descriptive analysis of AI governance texts, supported by text mining and semantic web representation (RDF/OWL). It does not study teachers, students, or classroom use of AI, and it reports no experimental or outcome data about education or wellbeing. Its main contribution is the LAIP framework and a synthesis of themes in AI ethics/policy documents.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that AI principles from different organizations vary in topic coverage and emphasize different governance concerns, but together they are complementary rather than complete on their own. Based on analysis of 27 principle documents, the authors argue for linking multiple AI principles into a comprehensive framework rather than adopting a single proposal.
finding.measure: Topic and keyword coverage of 27 AI principle proposals; comparative analysis across publisher types

paper_profiles.title: Modular Belief Updates and Confusion about Measures of Certainty in Artificial Intelligence Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines conceptual confusion in AI and expert-systems research about the difference between absolute belief and belief updates under uncertainty. The authors define a property they call modularity for belief updates, show how modular updates can be derived from probabilistic reasoning (especially likelihood ratios), and argue that this distinction had been misunderstood in the AI literature.

The paper uses two influential medical expert systems, MYCIN and INTERNIST-I, as illustrative cases. It argues that both systems implicitly treated elicited certainty-like measures as modular updates even though the quantities were closer to absolute beliefs or posterior probabilities, leading to theoretical inconsistencies. The paper is primarily a conceptual and historical analysis rather than an empirical study of educational or wellbeing outcomes.

Because the paper is about uncertainty reasoning in artificial intelligence and medical expert systems, not K-12 teaching or student outcomes, it does not report empirical findings relevant to teacher wellbeing, student learning, or validated instruments. Its main contribution is to clarify terminology and methodological assumptions in AI reasoning under uncertainty.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Economic Theories
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may alter foundational concepts in economics and economic theory. Rather than testing a specific intervention empirically, it provides a conceptual review of how AI interacts with theories such as demand and supply, pricing, rational choice, rational expectations, bounded rationality, asymmetric information, game theory, mechanism design, portfolio theory, prospect theory, efficient markets, counterfactual reasoning, and causality.

The central approach is theoretical and illustrative: the authors argue that AI, machine learning, multi-agent systems, optimization, and big data can make markets more individualized, improve prediction and decision-making, and reduce information asymmetries. The paper discusses examples from stock trading, pricing, and market simulation to suggest that AI can enhance efficiency and consistency in economic decisions.

The paper does not study a K-12 population, teachers, or educational outcomes, and it reports no empirical evaluation of AI tools in schools. Its conclusions are primarily speculative and descriptive, claiming that AI will reshape economic decision-making and market behavior by improving prediction, optimization, and rationality in economic systems.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education has developed, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical issues are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied. The authors conduct a systematic review of peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2007 through November 2018, screening 2,656 records and including 146 articles for synthesis.

The review maps AI applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. Across the sample, most articles were quantitative, most were authored by computer science researchers, and most focused on undergraduate contexts. The review finds that AI applications are often used for prediction, feedback, and automation, but that explicit definitions of AI and critical discussion of ethics, privacy, and risks are rare.

Overall, the paper concludes that research in this field is technically oriented and often lacks pedagogical grounding and reflection on consequences for educators and learners. The authors argue for more educator involvement, more attention to ethical and educational implications, and more research on how AI can meaningfully support teaching and learning in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education AI studies, teacher-facing and administrative AI applications were primarily justified as tools to reduce workload, automate assessment and feedback, and streamline student services. The review reports that many AI systems were designed to relieve staff from routine tasks such as admission decisions, grading, feedback generation, and student monitoring, but it does not provide a single pooled effect size because this was a narrative systematic review.
finding.measure: Workload reduction, task automation, administrative efficiency, assessment/feedback automation

finding.finding_summary: The review shows substantial use of AI for institutional and administrative functions such as admissions, drop-out prediction, course scheduling, institutional policy support, and alignment of students to programs or labor-market needs. These applications were discussed as enabling earlier intervention and more informed institutional decision-making, though the paper did not synthesize quantitative impacts across studies.
finding.measure: Institutional decision support, admissions, retention/attrition prediction, policy and planning support

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies addressed student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and related learner behaviors, often through predictive analytics or adaptive tutoring systems. The review notes that some systems were intended to identify low-engaged students and support intervention, but the overall evidence is mixed and largely preliminary rather than based on pooled causal estimates.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, participation, at-risk identification

finding.finding_summary: A smaller set of studies focused on collaboration, problem solving, and metacognitive support, especially in intelligent tutoring systems and collaborative learning tools. The review describes systems that facilitated collaborative writing, peer dialogue, and socially productive talk, generally reporting promising preliminary results, but without sufficient longitudinal evidence or pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Collaboration, problem solving, metacognitive/self-regulatory support, collaborative writing/discussion

finding.finding_summary: Literacy-related applications appear mainly in automated essay scoring, writing feedback, and reading comprehension tutoring. The review reports generally high agreement for some automated grading systems and promising feedback uses, but also notes concerns about feedback quality and appropriateness for some learners, so the overall pattern is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Essay scoring, writing feedback, reading comprehension support

finding.finding_summary: Some intelligent tutoring and adaptive system studies targeted mathematics and related quantitative subjects, including tutoring in mathematics and differential equations. The review characterizes these systems as generally showing positive preliminary results for content learning and feedback, but again does not provide pooled effect sizes or a causal synthesis.
finding.measure: Mathematics and quantitative course performance, tutoring outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A subset of the reviewed ITS and adaptive learning studies were situated in STEM, including computer science, engineering, medicine, and virtual laboratories. These studies were mostly reported as promising for supporting domain learning, diagnosis of errors, and adaptive feedback, but the review does not isolate a single scientific-reasoning effect estimate.
finding.measure: STEM/technical course learning, diagnostic feedback, virtual lab performance

finding.finding_summary: The review includes diverse subject areas beyond literacy and math, such as business, statistics, accounting, languages, psychology, and medicine. Across these contexts, AI applications were typically described as promising for tutoring, personalization, assessment, and feedback, though the evidence base was heterogeneous and mostly short-term.
finding.measure: Course learning outcomes across non-literacy/non-math subjects

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how ChatGPT should be understood in the context of higher education, especially its implications for learning, teaching, and assessment. Rather than evaluating a specific classroom intervention, the authors provide an early review and conceptual analysis of ChatGPT, situating it within the broader history of educational technology and artificial intelligence in education (AIEd).

The paper combines a desktop literature review with the authors’ own exploratory use of ChatGPT. They describe what ChatGPT can do, where it performs well (for example, generating short explanatory text and basic problem-solving explanations), and where it performs poorly (for example, higher-order analytical writing, accurate referencing, and some non-English writing). The discussion then maps ChatGPT onto Baker and Smith’s student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing AIEd framework, emphasizing that the tool resembles other AI writing assistants but with broader generative capabilities.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is likely to disrupt conventional assessment practices, particularly take-home essays, but that the response should not be simple prohibition. The authors argue for adapting assessment and teaching practices, using ChatGPT as a prompt for innovation in assessment design, feedback, and student-centered learning, while also recognizing risks around plagiarism, misinformation, and the commercialization of AI systems.

finding.finding_summary: In the authors’ exploratory use of ChatGPT, the system could generate short essays and explanations quickly, but the output was often generic, shallow, and sometimes inaccurate or poorly referenced. It performed better on basic explanatory writing than on higher-order academic writing tasks that require critical analysis, structure, and evidence.
finding.measure: Quality of generated writing and essay composition tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT is weak at supporting higher-order thinking demands such as critical and analytical reasoning. In the authors’ trials, it produced plausible but largely descriptive text and struggled when tasks required deeper synthesis or judgment.
finding.measure: Performance on tasks requiring critical/analytical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can increase efficiency by rapidly generating draft explanations, essays, and other text, potentially saving time for both students and teachers. The authors also note broader teacher-facing AI uses such as automating feedback and reducing workload, although these are discussed conceptually rather than tested empirically.
finding.measure: Speed and ease of text generation; potential teacher workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper concludes that ChatGPT may force institutions to rethink assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and instructional design. It highlights both the threat to traditional essay-based assessment and the opportunity for institutions to redesign assessment and support appropriate AI use.
finding.measure: Implications for assessment policy and institutional practice

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how AI should be integrated into education, with a primary focus on higher education. It argues that the rapid adoption of ChatGPT and other large language models creates both opportunities and risks, especially around student misuse, hallucinations, unclear academic integrity expectations, and uneven educator preparedness. The paper is organized around a Swiss University of Applied Sciences case study, informal discussions with students and staff, and a narrative literature review.

The author proposes that responsible AI use in education requires three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper describes institutional “AI guidelines” that allow AI use but require transparency, critical evaluation, and documentation of how AI was used in student work. It also suggests practical steps such as workshops, dedicated budgets, AI literacy courses, and broader institutional support to build an AI-friendly culture.

The paper further outlines ways AI can be used in classrooms, including student AI experiments, AI-assisted case study construction, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies. However, these are presented as illustrative use cases and recommendations rather than evaluated interventions. The paper does not report a controlled study of classroom engagement or learning outcomes; its contribution is mainly conceptual and policy-oriented.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that prompt engineering, AI literacy, and critical thinking are essential student skills for working with AI responsibly. It does not report a quantitative effect estimate, but it repeatedly claims that structured prompting and critical evaluation can help students think more critically and better recognize AI limitations and hallucinations.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, prompt engineering, and AI literacy; no formal outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a university case study showing the development of institutional AI guidelines, documentation requirements, and proposed supports such as workshops, budgeting, and dedicated staff roles. The main finding is that schools need governance structures and training systems to manage AI use rather than relying only on prohibitions or unrestricted access.
finding.measure: Institutional policy and implementation practices at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences; no quantitative outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can help educators create curricula, generate case studies, and support classroom activities more efficiently, but it also notes that prompting high-quality outputs can take time and may sometimes be less efficient than doing the task manually. Overall, the operational benefit is presented as promising but contingent on skillful use.
finding.measure: Illustrative use cases for curriculum creation, case study construction, and classroom support; no formal efficiency metric reported

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty‑first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper examines what digital competencies teachers need to effectively use artificial intelligence (AI) in education in the post-pandemic context. The authors frame the problem as a mismatch between the rapid adoption of AI-driven tools in teaching and the limited preparedness of many teachers to use these tools pedagogically, ethically, and efficiently.

Rather than testing an intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research and examples to identify opportunities and challenges associated with AI in teaching, learning, and assessment. It then adapts and revises two existing competency frameworks—DigCompEdu and the P21 framework for twenty-first century learning—to propose a broader view of teachers’ AI digital competency, including professional engagement, digital resources, teaching and learning, assessment, learner empowerment, and facilitating students’ AI competency.

The paper is aimed at educators and school leaders, with a broad focus on teaching practice across educational levels, though it does not report a primary empirical study or specific K-12 sample. Its main conclusion is that AI competency for teachers should go beyond technical know-how to include pedagogical, ethical, collaborative, and life/career skills, and that professional development and standards are needed to support effective AI use in classrooms.

paper_profiles.title: The Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL): a Theoretical Research-Based Model of Learning in Immersive Virtual Reality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL), a theoretical framework intended to explain how learning occurs in immersive virtual reality (IVR). The authors respond to a growing body of IVR education research and argue that the field lacks an integrated theory that connects technology features, learner psychology, and learning outcomes.

Rather than reporting a new primary experiment, the paper synthesizes prior empirical work on immersive learning, multimedia learning, educational psychology, and virtual reality. It proposes that IVR learning is shaped by two core affordances—presence and agency—which are in turn influenced by immersion, control factors, and representational fidelity.

The model further argues that presence and agency affect situational interest, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, and self-regulation, which then influence factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge as well as transfer. The paper concludes that IVR can be powerful, but only when instructional design supports learning goals and manages cognitive load; it calls for more empirical tests of the model, especially studies that compare media while holding instructional method constant.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior IVR studies showing that immersive lessons often increase situational interest, enjoyment, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and presence, but can also increase extraneous cognitive load and undermine self-regulated learning when reflection/scaffolding is absent. Across the cited empirical studies, outcomes vary by design: for example, IVR has been associated with higher intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy in some comparisons, but also with poorer self-regulation and learning when the environment is overly engaging.
finding.measure: Situational interest, intrinsic motivation/enjoyment, self-efficacy, and self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on durable skills insofar as it discusses embodiment, self-regulation, and transfer-oriented generative learning strategies such as summarization, enactment, and teaching. The synthesis argues these strategies can improve deeper processing and transfer in IVR, but only when instructional design supports reflection and reduces cognitive overload; otherwise, high immersion may distract from metacognitive processing.
finding.measure: Embodiment, self-regulation, generative learning strategies, and transfer

finding.finding_summary: The paper reviews evidence on IVR effects on factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge across subject areas, concluding that IVR is not uniformly superior to less immersive media. It highlights cases where IVR improved procedural knowledge and transfer, but also cases where video or desktop formats produced equal or better factual/declarative learning; for example, Parong and Mayer (2018) found IVR less effective than PowerPoint for factual knowledge, while other studies reported gains in procedural learning and transfer under specific instructional conditions.
finding.measure: Factual/declarative knowledge, conceptual knowledge, procedural knowledge, and transfer

finding.finding_summary: Scientific content is used as the main illustrative domain for the CAMIL, especially biology and laboratory/science simulations. The paper synthesizes findings that IVR can support procedural and conceptual learning in science contexts, but may also impose extraneous cognitive load that reduces factual learning; no single consistent advantage of IVR is reported across the science studies discussed.
finding.measure: Science learning outcomes in biology, biochemistry, and laboratory simulation contexts

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (K-12, higher education, and adult learners across reviewed studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on educational chatbots to understand how they are designed, what roles they play, how learners interact with them, and what evidence exists for their effectiveness. The authors explicitly note a gap in prior reviews: most had focused on learning outcomes or general benefits, but had not examined interaction styles, design principles, and empirical evidence in a more structured way.

Using a search across ACM Digital Library, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink, the authors screened 1,208 records and retained 36 studies published between 2011 and 2021. The reviewed chatbots span multiple educational fields, with the largest share in computer science and general education, and are most often web-based and designed as teaching agents or peer agents. Most chatbots used chatbot-driven interaction, typically flow-based or intent-based, while a smaller subset used user-driven conversations.

Across the reviewed literature, the paper concludes that educational chatbots are generally associated with improved learning, engagement, satisfaction, or interest, especially when paired with personalized learning, experiential learning, collaboration, affective feedback, or scaffolding. However, the authors also highlight limitations such as weak dataset training, limited usability heuristics, and in some cases no sustained engagement gains. The review does not evaluate a single intervention directly; rather, it synthesizes evidence across chatbot studies and identifies future research directions for chatbot design and evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, educational chatbots were often associated with improved engagement, interest in learning, and subjective satisfaction, but not uniformly. For example, experiments reported improved engagement (e.g., Ruan et al., 2021, n=56, p<0.0001) and improved subjective satisfaction (Tegos et al., 2020, n=56, p=0.03), while one longitudinal study found no evidence for sustained engagement (Fryer et al., 2017, n=122, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, sustained engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review reports multiple studies in which chatbots improved literacy-related outcomes, especially writing and language learning. For instance, Wambsganss et al. (2021, n=55, p<0.05) found improved learning in a writing task, and Ruan et al. (2021, n=56, p<0.0001) reported improved engagement in foreign-language learning; the review also cites improved learning for text- and audio-based suggestions in a formative assessment context (Hayashi, 2013, n=58, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Writing quality, language learning outcomes, formative assessment performance

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics-focused chatbot studies in the review generally reported improved learning. The review highlights a teachable-agent mathematics study by Matsuda et al. (2013, n=183, p<0.001) that found improved learning, and describes chatbot use for solving equations and other mathematical tasks as part of the evidence base.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning / problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, chatbots were associated with improved learning in several non-literacy, non-math domains, especially computer science and general education. Examples include improved learning in programming and tutoring contexts such as Rodrigo et al. (2012, n=126, p=0.65 reported as non-significant on the table but discussed as improved learning in the review), Wambsganss et al. (2020, n=182, p<0.001), and Mellado-Silva et al. (2020, n=50, p=0.04418).
finding.measure: Learning outcomes across computer science, general education, and other subject-specific tasks

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies targeted durable skills such as collaborative learning, critical thinking, and argumentation. The review reports that collaborative-learning chatbot designs and open-ended discussion scaffolds were used to support these skills, and one experiment found improved formal argumentation quality in writing (Wambsganss et al., 2021, n=55, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Formal argumentation quality, collaboration, critical thinking/argumentation processes

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a German-language benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on middle-school-level questions grounded in real curricular content. The central problem is that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and sometimes solvable from text alone; the authors argue these properties overestimate real-world visual reasoning. To address this, they build a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, including math, history, biology, geography, arts, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The paper does not study a classroom intervention or student outcome; instead, it evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs on their ability to answer these benchmark questions. The evaluation includes both standard questions and deliberately adversarial questions that refer to absent but semantically related concepts, with model answers scored using a panel-of-LLMs judging scheme. The best model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, and performance is especially weak on adversarial questions, showing that current VLMs often struggle to combine image understanding with subject knowledge and to abstain when the answer is not visible.

The dataset is designed around German middle school materials and uses native-speaker-authored questions and answers rather than machine translation. The authors conclude that middle-school tasks provide a useful stress test for VLMs and that benchmark performance on popular public datasets does not reliably predict performance on this more realistic, language-specific benchmark. They also report substantial variation by subject, with comparatively better results in history and religion and poorer results in music and math.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that even strong VLMs struggle on middle-school math tasks that require visual interpretation plus arithmetic or geometric reasoning. The best overall model reached only 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), and the weaker models were much lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%), indicating substantial limitations in this area.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=308 math questions (486 images total; 13 models evaluated)

finding.finding_summary: Models showed limited ability to answer science-related image questions that required integrating diagrams with background knowledge, especially in physics and biology. Performance was modest at best, with physics accuracy ranging up to 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and biology up to 48.53% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), but many models performed substantially below that, and explanatory questions were often answered incorrectly.
finding.measure: Accuracy on biology and physics benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=403 science questions total (biology n=169; physics n=234)

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds broad limitations across non-math, non-science school subjects, including arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports. Best-model accuracies remained modest overall, such as 54.36% in history and 52.92% in religion, while music was especially difficult (best 31.03%), and adversarial questions sharply reduced performance across domains.
finding.measure: Accuracy on subject-specific benchmark questions across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: n=1,123 questions across arts (286), geography (251), history (264), music (166), religion (206), sports (154)

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark targets reasoning behaviors such as combining visual cues with background knowledge, handling adversarial prompts, and recognizing when an image does not support an answer. Results show that models often failed at these reasoning demands, especially on adversarial questions where the best overall score was only 32.83% and many models hallucinated rather than saying the question was unanswerable.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions requiring refusal / contextual reasoning
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; adversarial subset reported across domains (e.g. overall adversarial evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: The study also evaluates a mixed set of middle-school curricular tasks beyond core STEM, and performance differs substantially by subject and model family. This includes arts, religion, sports, and geography/map interpretation, with strong evidence that current VLMs do not generalize reliably to authentic school subject material in German.
finding.measure: Accuracy across mixed curricular domains and model families

paper_profiles.title: AI Instructional Agent Improves Student’s Perceived Learner Control and Learning Outcome: Empirical Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an AI instructional agent can improve students’ perceived learner control and academic performance relative to a human teacher and a MOOC-style self-paced video format with chatbot support. The motivation is that many AI tools in education support content management or reactive chat, but fewer systems combine real-time lecture delivery with interactive questioning in a pedagogically coherent way.

The study was conducted in a university general education course in Beijing with 140 undergraduate students, of whom 125 were retained for analysis. Students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: live human instruction, MOOC-style videos plus chatbot support, or an AI instructional agent in the MAIC platform that delivered lectures and answered questions in real time. The content, slides, and scripts were held constant across conditions to isolate the delivery mode.

Results showed that the AI instructional agent group reported significantly higher perceived learner control than both comparison groups, interacted more frequently with the system, and completed the task more efficiently. The AI group also achieved higher post-test scores than both the human-teacher and MOOC groups. Regression analyses further indicated that perceived learner control positively predicted post-test performance, suggesting that the subjective sense of control was associated with better learning outcomes in this setting.

finding.finding_summary: In this undergraduate general education course RCT (final valid n=125), students in the AI instructional agent group scored significantly higher on the post-test than those in the human teacher group (mean difference = 0.128, p < .01) and the MOOC group (mean difference = 0.112, p < .01). Academic performance was measured with a 16-item post-test derived from an initial 22 multiple-choice items; the reported ANOVA for post-test scores was F(2,122)=7.673, p<.01.
finding.measure: Post-test scores on a 16-item multiple-choice assessment

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent significantly increased students’ perceived learner control relative to both the human teacher and MOOC conditions (F(2,122)=12.155, p<.001). Post-hoc comparisons showed higher perceived learner control in the AI group versus human teacher (mean difference = 0.732, p<.001) and versus MOOC (mean difference = 0.416, p<.05). Perceived learner control was measured with a newly developed 4-item scale (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.823).
finding.measure: Perceived learner control scale (4 items; self-report)

finding.finding_summary: The AI condition produced more control-related behaviors, including higher interaction frequency and shorter learning duration, suggesting greater self-management of learning. Interaction frequency differed significantly across groups (F(2,122)=21.755, p<.001), with the AI group exceeding the human teacher group by 5.410 and the MOOC group by 7.015; learning duration also differed strongly (F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001), with the AI and MOOC groups completing the task in about 30 minutes less than the human teacher group. These behavioral indicators were used as evidence of time management and self-directed learning behavior.
finding.measure: Learning duration and feedback/interactions initiated by students

finding.finding_summary: Students in the AI instructional agent condition completed the learning task more efficiently than those taught by the human teacher. Learning duration showed a very large group effect (F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001), and the AI group was reported to finish in approximately 30 minutes less than the human teacher group. The paper interprets this as more efficient time use in a self-paced, equivalent-content environment.
finding.measure: Learning duration (time to complete the learning task)

paper_profiles.title: DMP_AI: An AI-Aided K-12 System for Teaching and Learning in Diverse Schools
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 (conference venue not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents DMP_AI, an AI-aided educational system designed for K-12 schools that integrates data mining, natural language processing, machine learning, and learning analytics. The system aims to support teaching and learning through five functions: student academic performance prediction, behavior prediction, an early warning system, analytics for individualized education plans (IEPs), gifted/talented student identification, and cross-school elective recommendation.

The paper addresses a practical problem in deploying AI across diverse real-world schools, especially where data are heterogeneous and privacy constraints limit centralized sharing. The authors describe the system architecture and report pilot deployment in eight local schools (three primary and five secondary) beginning in March 2023, with feedback from 33 users. The evaluation focuses on user experience and perceived usefulness rather than causal effects on student outcomes. Results indicate generally positive perceptions of the interface and helpfulness of the modules, but lower ratings for helping users understand AI and notable challenges around training, data heterogeneity, and acceptance of AI-based talent identification.

Overall, the paper concludes that a cohesive AI-aided K-12 platform is feasible in real school settings and may support educators with predictive analytics and personalized recommendations. At the same time, the authors emphasize that sustained training, explanation, and ethical development are necessary for long-term adoption and effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot deployment suggests the system was perceived as helpful for educators and usable in practice, with a generally positive user experience across four AI modules. In a survey of 33 users, the overall average ratings were above 3.0/5 for most questions, and the 'installed module is helpful' item averaged 3.54/5, indicating modest perceived utility for school workflows rather than measured productivity gains.
finding.measure: User experience survey ratings on perceived helpfulness, interface experience, usability, and willingness to continue using the modules

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates the feasibility of implementing a cross-school AI platform in real K-12 schools, emphasizing privacy-preserving data integration, heterogeneity handling, and institutional deployment. The authors report successful installation of four AI modules in eight schools and conclude that the system can serve as a resource for supporting effective and inclusive K-12 education, although sustainability, training, and ethics remain open challenges.
finding.measure: Successful pilot implementation across eight schools and participant feedback on real-world applicability

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how students with different baseline dispositions perceive and prefer different AI roles during mathematical modelling, and whether design thinking (DT), computational thinking (CT), and mathematical modelling self-efficacy (MMSE) are related. The authors frame mathematical modelling as a key higher-order competency that is difficult for many learners because it requires abstraction, representation, and iterative reasoning.

To examine this, the researchers ran a within-subjects randomized controlled trial with 26 university students who had not taken university-level mathematics courses, using modelling tasks at about a high-school level. Each participant completed one baseline task without AI and five comparable tasks with GPT-based AI agents playing five roles: Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer Student, Struggling Student, and Excellent Student. Participants also completed pre-task questionnaires on CT, DT, and MMSE, plus post-task ratings and open-ended feedback about each role.

The study found that DT and CT were both significant positive predictors of MMSE, with DT showing a particularly strong association (β=0.730, p<.001; CT β=0.300, p<.001; R²=0.808). Students preferred competent AI roles over the Struggling Student role across preference, confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction, but did not meaningfully differentiate among the Tutor, TA, Peer, and Excellent Student roles. A small but statistically significant exception was that students with higher DT scores preferred the TA role more than those with lower DT scores. Overall, the paper suggests that AI support for mathematical modelling should be competence-oriented and adaptable to learner profiles, with different AI personas potentially useful for different students.

finding.finding_summary: Students completed mathematical modelling tasks with five AI role personas, and their baseline competencies were positively related to mathematical modelling self-efficacy. Design thinking and computational thinking were both significant positive predictors of MMSE (DT β=0.730, p<.001; CT β=0.300, p<.001; R²=0.808) in the PLS-SEM model (N=26).
finding.measure: Mathematical modelling self-efficacy (MMSE) scale; mathematical modelling task performance and role preference ratings

finding.finding_summary: AI role significantly affected task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction across the within-subjects experiment (N=26). Competent roles (Tutor, TA, Peer, Excellent Student) were rated much higher than the Struggling Student role, which received the lowest confidence (M=1.88), helpfulness (M=1.92), and ease-of-interaction ratings (M=1.81).
finding.measure: Post-task questionnaire ratings of task confidence, AI helpfulness, and ease of interaction; overall role preference ranking
finding.effect_size: Friedman χ2(4)=24.85 for confidence; χ2(4)=32.63 for helpfulness; χ2(4)=36.43 for ease of interaction; Struggling Student vs others r=0.57-0.85 in pairwise tests
finding.std_deviation: Task confidence SDs: 1.19, 1.16, 1.39, 1.14, 1.24; helpfulness SDs: 0.91, 1.04, 1.25, 1.39, 1.23; ease of interaction SDs: 0.93, 0.98, 1.12, 1.36, 1.17 (role order as reported)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined computational thinking and design thinking as learner traits in relation to mathematical modelling self-efficacy. Both constructs were positively associated with MMSE, with several subdimensions significantly correlated; however, only design thinking differentiated AI-role preferences, and only for the TA persona (high DT group ranked TA more favorably, p=.049).
finding.measure: Computational Thinking Scale; Design Thinking Scale; Pearson correlations; PLS-SEM; group comparisons of AI role rankings
finding.effect_size: DT→MMSE β=0.730; CT→MMSE β=0.300; significant TA group difference p=.049

paper_profiles.title: Quantum Computing as a High School Module
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a one-week instructional module on quantum computing for motivated high school students ages 15–18. The module is designed to bridge the gap between popular-science introductions and advanced undergraduate texts by making foundational quantum concepts more accessible without requiring programming experience. The content focuses on core ideas such as superposition, measurement, qubits, beam splitters, Stern-Gerlach experiments, quantum cryptography, quantum gates, entanglement, teleportation, and quantum algorithms.

The paper is primarily a curriculum description rather than an empirical evaluation of a classroom intervention. It outlines prerequisites, learning objectives, example explanations, and a set of activities and worksheets intended to reinforce conceptual understanding through simulations and problem sets. The module appears intended for use after AP exams, in extracurricular settings, or as an independent project resource.

Because the paper does not report a study with measured outcomes, control conditions, or statistical analysis, it does not provide evidence about student achievement, engagement, or other educational impacts. Its main contribution is pedagogical: it offers a structured, accessible high-school-level introduction to quantum computing concepts and suggests how teachers or students might use the materials in practice.
