paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This participatory design study asks how middle school students perceive an AI peer in collaborative mathematical problem solving and what features, behaviors, and controls they want from such a system. The authors argue that most prior AI-in-education work has framed AI as a tutor or teacher aide, whereas collaborative classroom mathematics requires an AI that can function as a peer teammate inside group work.

The study was run as a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students at a U.S. public university. Students first experienced human-only collaborative math problem solving and then worked with two AI peers in a web-based technology probe using text chat and stage-based collaboration logic; they also completed participatory design activities, surveys, interviews, and artifact creation. The design intentionally compared human-only CPS with AI-involved CPS, but it was not a full efficacy trial of learning outcomes.

Findings show a consistent preference for an AI peer that is scaffold-first, deferential, and controllable: students wanted hints, checks, error detection, and concept refreshers before direct answers, along with control over when the AI speaks, how much it says, and what kind of help it gives. Quantitatively, AI peers reduced perceived temporal demand (M=5.67 vs. 9.62, d=1.15) but increased physical demand (M=8.48 vs. 4.90, d=1.14) and lowered social cohesion/coordination (ATGS M=5.21 vs. 6.50, d=0.94; GIT M=4.76 vs. 5.54, d=0.81) relative to human-only collaboration. Qualitatively, students rejected overly teacher-like, repetitive, or emotionally unresponsive AI behavior and preferred a peer-like expert tone with minimal persona embellishment and strong emotional attunement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on middle-school mathematics collaborative problem solving and shows that students preferred an AI peer that provided mathematics scaffolds such as hints, checks, error detection, and concept refreshers rather than direct answers. However, the study does not report learning gains on math achievement; instead, it reports design preferences and interactional reactions to math problem-solving support.
finding.measure: Math collaborative problem-solving tasks; student design preferences for math-help behaviors

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower social cohesion when working with AI peers than in human-only groups, with lower Attractions to Group-Social scores (M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs. 6.50, SD=2.05; d=0.94). Qualitatively, students also emphasized the need for encouragement, emotional attunement, and an AI that does not intensify frustration or self-blame during struggle.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (ATGS) and interview/reflection themes about emotional support
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey analyses; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines collaboration, co-agency, turn-taking, and joint problem solving. Students valued AI peers that negotiated methods, listened, and worked with them rather than doing the task for them; they criticized repetitive or dominating behavior as breaking collaboration. Quantitatively, perceived task coordination was lower with AI peers (GIT M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. 5.54, SD=1.52; d=0.81).
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (GIT) and qualitative analysis of collaborative interaction
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey analyses; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: AI peers reduced perceived time pressure during collaborative math work, with significantly lower NASA-TLX temporal demand scores (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. 9.62, SD=4.13; d=1.15). At the same time, students experienced higher physical/interactional load because the text-based interface required typing, navigation, and managing AI output, increasing NASA-TLX physical demand (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs. 4.90, SD=2.41; d=1.14).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand subscales
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 (AI peer), 4.13 (human-only); Physical demand SD=4.65 (AI peer), 2.41 (human-only)

finding.finding_summary: The study includes students’ attitudes toward math and task completion in a summer-camp context, but it does not evaluate a non-mathematics academic domain. Any broader academic effects beyond mathematics are not substantively tested in the paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four perceived learning factors—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—relate to one another in AI-mediated classroom learning, and whether those relationships differ between middle school and high school students. The authors argue that much of the existing AI-in-education literature focuses on older learners and on isolated perceptions rather than on the structure of perceptions as interconnected dimensions.

The study was conducted in authentic extracurricular computer science settings, where students encountered AI as part of programming learning activities. A total of 53 students participated: 25 middle school students (ages 10–13) and 28 high school students (ages 15–20). Middle school students used Teachable Machine in an introductory AI course, while high school students used LLMs such as Gemini and Claude for Python/vibe-coding activities; data were collected through a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale and open-ended items, plus text mining of student reflections.

Results showed generally positive perceptions in both groups, but with markedly different correlation structures. Middle school students exhibited strong positive correlations across the learning dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluation pattern in which a positive view in one area tended to generalize to others. High school students showed weaker and more differentiated relationships, indicating that they assessed clarity, comfort, motivation, and experience more independently. The paper concludes that AI integration strategies should be developmentally responsive, emphasizing clarity and scaffolding for younger learners and more targeted support for motivation and usability for older learners.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive experiences with AI tools, including comfort, motivation, and willingness to use AI again. The paper found one statistically significant between-group difference on ease of use (Q3; Mann-Whitney U=192.00, p=0.0013), with high school students rating the tool as easier to use than middle school students (67.9% vs 24.0% selecting the top category).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of experience, ease of use, comfort, motivation, and future AI use from a 17-item questionnaire
finding.std_deviation: Middle school SDs ranged from 0.62 to 1.15 across items; high school SDs ranged from 0.44 to 0.94 across items

finding.finding_summary: Open-ended responses suggest that students perceived the AI tool as supporting understanding and reasoning, but the paper does not directly measure durable skills with a formal instrument. High school students’ reflections emphasized explanation, code, and thinking, whereas middle school students emphasized general understanding and learning support, indicating differentiated but mostly positive cognitive engagement.
finding.measure: Text-mined open-ended responses to the question about how AI influenced learning (Q7), including word frequency and co-occurrence patterns

paper_profiles.title: How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how much AI assistance changes the speed of completing a complex software development task. The authors position the study as a randomized controlled trial designed to estimate whether AI-enhanced coding tools shorten time on task in an enterprise setting, and whether developer- and task-level characteristics moderate that effect.

The intervention consisted of three production AI features embedded in Google’s internal IDE: AI Code Completion, Smart Paste, and Natural Language to Code. Ninety-six full-time Google software engineers were recruited, trained on the tools, and then randomly assigned to either use the AI features or complete the same standardized coding task without them. The task required modifying a pre-existing changelist to implement a new logging service, including code changes, build updates, data structure work, and testing until all tests passed.

The main outcome was time spent on task. The authors report that participants using AI completed the task faster than controls: about 96 minutes versus 114 minutes, with a statistically significant difference in the primary t-test. In adjusted models, the estimated AI effect remained negative and directionally consistent, corresponding to roughly a 21% shorter time on task in the best-fit model, though the confidence interval was wide and the adjusted effect was not statistically significant at p < .05. The study also found that more hours spent coding per day and higher seniority were associated with faster task completion, while interaction effects suggested—but did not conclusively prove—that heavier coders may benefit more from AI.

finding.finding_summary: Using AI shortened time spent completing the enterprise-grade coding task. In the primary analysis, developers in the AI condition finished in 96 minutes (N=47) versus 114 minutes (N=46) in the no-AI condition; the log-time t-test was significant, t(83.6)=2.11, p=.038. In the adjusted model, the best estimate suggested about a 21% reduction in time on task (β=-0.24; 95% CI [-0.51, 0.03]), although this adjusted effect was not statistically significant at p<.05.
finding.measure: Time spent on task / logged time on task in IDE during completion of a standardized coding task
finding.effect_size: about 21% shorter time on task; β=-0.24

paper_profiles.title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether peer reviewers anchor to their initial scores when they are later shown additional information that corrects an error in the reviewed paper. The authors frame the problem around rebuttal/response stages in conference peer review, where reviewers often have an opportunity to revise scores after reading new evidence from authors, but it is unclear whether those revised scores fully reflect the new information or remain biased toward the original score.

To test this, the authors ran a randomized controlled trial with 108 researchers who had recently published in computer science-related fields and were currently PhD students or PhDs. Participants acted as reviewers for the same mock conference paper in a simulated review setting. The control group saw the correct version of the paper, which included an animated GIF showing strong results; the experimental group initially saw a flawed frozen frame showing much weaker results, then after review was told this was a technical error and was shown the corrected animated version, after which they could revise their scores.

The main outcome was whether revised scores in the experimental group differed from the control group’s scores, which would indicate anchoring. The manipulation successfully lowered initial scores relative to control scores, especially on the Evaluation category, showing that participants perceived the two versions differently. However, the revised scores did not differ significantly from the control scores on Overall or Evaluation ratings, so the study found no evidence of reviewer anchoring in this peer-review rebuttal-like context. The authors conclude that muted score changes in rebuttal stages may arise from factors other than anchoring, such as limited participation or weak rebuttals, and note limitations related to realism, domain specificity, and statistical power.

finding.finding_summary: The study tested whether a rebuttal-like revision process in conference peer review produces anchoring in reviewers’ final judgments. In a randomized controlled trial with n=108 researchers, revised scores did not differ significantly from control scores on either Overall ratings (Vargha-Delaney A=0.5048, adjusted p=0.6064) or Evaluation scores (A=0.4863, adjusted p=0.6064), so the authors found no evidence that the review process induced anchoring bias.
finding.measure: Peer-review score revision in a simulated conference review setting (Overall score and Evaluation category score)

paper_profiles.title: Are Educational Escape Rooms More Effective Than Traditional Lectures for Teaching Software Engineering? A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a virtual educational escape room is more effective than a traditional lecture for teaching software modeling in software engineering. The study was motivated by a broader lack of robust empirical evidence on the learning effectiveness of educational escape rooms, especially compared with conventional teaching methods.

The authors conducted a cluster randomized controlled trial in a second-year undergraduate software engineering fundamentals course at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid. A total of 326 students participated: 164 in the experimental group learned UML software modeling concepts through a face-to-face, team-based virtual escape room delivered via the Escapp platform, while 162 control-group students received a traditional lecture covering the same content for the same duration. Learning was measured with identical pre- and post-tests, and experimental-group perceptions were collected via questionnaire.

Results showed statistically significant learning gains in both groups, but the escape room group outperformed the lecture group on post-test knowledge acquisition after controlling for pretest scores. The effect favoring the escape room was small to medium (r = 0.25). Students also reported very positive perceptions of the activity, including high enjoyment, engagement, and strong preference for the escape room over traditional instruction. The authors conclude that educational escape rooms can be more effective than lectures for this topic, while also noting that further research is needed to test generalizability to other topics and longer-term outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students who learned software modeling through the educational escape room significantly outperformed those who learned via traditional lecture on the post-test, after controlling for pretest scores. The difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001) with a small-to-medium effect (r = 0.25) in favor of the escape room group.
finding.measure: Software modeling knowledge test (10-item multiple-choice pretest/post-test; UML use case, class, sequence, activity, and state machine diagrams)

finding.finding_summary: The experimental-group questionnaire results indicated very positive perceptions of the escape room, including strong enjoyment, immersion, acceptance, and preference for the activity over traditional lecture. Students also reported that the activity was motivating and that it improved their perceived learning.
finding.measure: Perceptions questionnaire with Likert items and closed-ended acceptance/opinion items

finding.finding_summary: The escape room was designed and implemented in teams of 4–6 students, and the authors report that the activity was well received in this collaborative format. However, collaboration itself was not directly measured as an outcome, so this assignment reflects only the paper’s substantive emphasis on team-based participation and related soft-skill practice.
finding.measure: Team-based participation / reported perceptions of the activity

paper_profiles.title: The Hands-Up Problem and How to Deal With It: Secondary School Teachers’ Experiences of Debugging in the Classroom
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers teaching lower secondary computing (ages 11–14)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines secondary school computing teachers’ experiences of teaching debugging in text-based programming classrooms, a topic the authors argue is under-studied relative to student perspectives. The central research questions ask what teachers experience and observe when students debug, what barriers make debugging difficult, and what teaching strategies teachers use to support debugging in class.

The study uses semi-structured interviews with nine teachers from England and two other countries, all teaching lower secondary computing and Python (with some also teaching Swift). Using codebook thematic analysis, the authors identify six themes: barriers to successful debugging, the emotional nature of debugging, reliance on the teacher, varying levels of scaffolding, improving students’ debugging ability, and promoting a positive error culture. A major contribution is the concept of the “hands-up problem,” describing the classroom difficulty created when many students simultaneously request teacher help while debugging.

The paper concludes that debugging support is often constrained by limited lesson time, syntax barriers in text-based languages, unclear error messages, and students’ low resilience or motivation. Teachers who are more experienced or confident report using counters to the hands-up problem, such as insisting on independent attempts first, encouraging peer help, modelling debugging, teaching students to interpret error messages, and cultivating a classroom culture where errors are normal. The authors argue that debugging-specific professional development and a clearer conception of debugging pedagogical content knowledge could help less confident teachers support students more effectively.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that student debugging is shaped by both negative and positive socio-emotional responses. Negative emotions such as frustration, disappointment, anxiety, and disengagement were most common, while successful debugging could produce intense joy and pride; however, the paper does not report quantitative effect sizes. The study is based on nine semi-structured interviews (n=9) with secondary computing teachers describing observed student experiences rather than directly measuring student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported observations of student motivation, frustration, resilience, disengagement, and emotional reactions during debugging

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described instruction intended to improve students’ independent problem-solving, resilience, and metacognitive debugging behaviours, such as testing after small changes, asking students to explain their thinking, and modelling debugging strategies. Reported student improvements were qualitative rather than measured with a standardized outcome; no effect size is provided. Evidence comes from nine teacher interviews (n=9).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported changes in students’ debugging independence, resilience, and problem-solving strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly emphasizes that debugging places substantial workload pressure on teachers, especially when many students simultaneously raise their hands for help. Teachers described lessons as busy or chaotic and reported that helping every student is unrealistic; this is a qualitative finding from nine interviews (n=9), with no quantitative workload metric or effect size reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, lesson busyness, and feasibility of providing individual debugging support

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education published between 2007 and 2018. The authors ask how the literature has developed over time, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical challenges are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied in higher education.

The review screened 2,656 records and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles for synthesis. The corpus was heavily concentrated in computer science and STEM, with most studies using quantitative methods and focusing on four application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. The review shows that AI in higher education is mostly studied as learner-facing or institutional tooling rather than as teacher-facing support, and that explicit definitions of AI are rare.

The paper is not an intervention study itself; rather, it maps the field and synthesizes patterns of use and reported effects. The main conclusions are that AI applications in higher education are often presented positively, but critical reflection on ethics, privacy, and broader pedagogical implications is limited. The authors argue that educators have been largely absent from the literature and call for more educationally grounded, ethically informed research on AI in teaching and learning.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education literature, AI applications were commonly reported to improve prediction, personalization, assessment, or tutoring performance relative to conventional baselines. For example, the review notes that machine-learning classifiers often outperformed logistic regression in prediction tasks, and that automated systems could reach high agreement or accuracy in tasks such as admission prediction and grading.
finding.measure: Prediction/classification accuracy; grading agreement; task performance in AI applications

finding.finding_summary: A substantial subset of the reviewed studies examined student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and related behavioral outcomes. The review reports that AI systems were used to identify low-engaged students, model motivation, and support intervention, but findings were not uniformly positive; one ITS study produced negative results because its support was poorly matched to more advanced learners.
finding.measure: Student engagement, academic motivation, and related behavioral indicators

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed applications targeted durable skills such as collaboration, problem solving, and metacognitive/self-regulatory processes. The review highlights systems that facilitated collaborative learning, provided productive talk moves, or supported self-regulation through tutor-like scaffolds, generally reporting positive preliminary results.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning quality; self-regulatory process measures; problem-solving support

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that teacher-facing and administrative AI can reduce workload and improve efficiency by automating tasks such as assessment, feedback, admission prediction, and detection of at-risk students. The authors describe these systems as often achieving high accuracy and efficiency, though they note that the review literature rarely reports long-term implementation evidence.
finding.measure: Task automation, workload reduction, efficiency of assessment/administrative processes

finding.finding_summary: The review found many studies using AI for institutional and administrative functions, including admission decisions, retention, student profiling, course scheduling, and aligning student capabilities with institutional or labor-market needs. Overall, these applications were presented as supporting institutional decision-making and service delivery, though ethical and governance issues were seldom discussed in depth.
finding.measure: Institutional decision support, retention prediction, admissions and scheduling systems, alignment with institutional needs

paper_profiles.title: The Use of Cronbach’s Alpha When Developing and Reporting Research Instruments in Science Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (paper analyzes published science education research instruments; not a participant study itself)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a methodological critique of how Cronbach’s alpha is used and reported in science education research. Rather than evaluating an intervention, it examines whether authors appropriately interpret alpha as evidence of reliability or internal consistency and whether high alpha values are being overused to claim instrument quality, unidimensionality, or validity.

To address this question, the author surveyed papers published in four leading science education journals in 2015 and identified 69 explicit references to Cronbach’s alpha. The paper reviews examples from studies of affective measures and knowledge tests, showing that alpha is often reported with little explanation, with highly variable qualitative labels, and sometimes used in ways that are not statistically justified. The main conclusion is that alpha has limited value as a stand-alone indicator of instrument quality; it should be interpreted cautiously and alongside other evidence such as factor analysis and construct validity, especially when instruments measure multiple constructs.

The paper’s context is science education research across K-12 and higher education, but it does not study a learner population directly. Its audience is primarily researchers, reviewers, and editors who develop, use, or evaluate measurement instruments. The author recommends clearer reporting and more careful interpretation of alpha, especially avoiding the assumption that values above 0.70 are automatically sufficient or that very high values necessarily indicate a better instrument.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that better reporting and interpretation of Cronbach’s alpha would improve research practice in science education. It finds, based on a survey of 69 explicit alpha references across four journals, that authors often use the statistic inconsistently or without explanation, and it recommends clearer standards for authors, reviewers, and editors.
finding.measure: Survey of published science education papers reporting Cronbach’s alpha; analysis of reporting practices
finding.study_size: n=69 articles with explicit references to Cronbach’s alpha

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The authors focus on the tension between two goals: keeping teacher expertise and oversight in the personalization process versus achieving the smaller-grain, more individually tailored adjustments that students may prefer. The study asks what kinds of prompts teachers use with ChatGPT, what students think about the resulting personalized problems, and how efficient the process is for teachers.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools collaborated with GPT-4o/ChatGPT to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems in Units 4 and 6 into versions personalized to students’ popular-culture interests. In total, 521 students received 143 personalized problems, with subsets providing closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback. The analysis combines prompt logs, teacher video/audio transcripts, student survey responses, and mixed-effects regression models examining prompt patterns, time spent, student ratings, and change over time.

The main findings are that teachers frequently used ChatGPT to personalize at broad grain sizes first, then refined prompts to add specific references, improve realism, and address age, location, readability, and mathematical clarity. Students generally preferred specific, small-grain references over broad categories, but they rarely commented on deeper realism issues. Personalizing one problem took about four minutes on average, and this did not clearly become faster over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and spent more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4, though student ratings also improved in Unit 6. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports professional learning and oversight, but it is time-intensive and may not easily deliver the fine-grained personalization many students want.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students worked on personalized 7th-grade mathematics word problems (n=143 problems assigned to 521 students). The study did not measure achievement or learning outcomes, but it found that student ratings of personalized math problems were modestly higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts to create a problem, and ratings increased from Unit 4 to Unit 6.
finding.measure: Student-rated interestingness and closeness of personalized mathematics problems; prompt counts and time spent creating problems
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs. other prompt counts; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs. Unit 4 on student ratings
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; interestingness SD=1.24; closeness SD=1.28

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied student interest/engagement responses to personalized math problems. Across 454 open-ended responses and closed-ended ratings from 52-53 problems, students generally preferred problems with specific popular-culture references, and their average ratings of interestingness and closeness were moderate-to-low (mean interestingness=2.46/5; mean closeness=2.53/5). Ratings improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (interestingness 2.27 to 2.56; closeness 2.28 to 2.66).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback about interest
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 responses to interestingness item; 449 responses to improvement item; 446 responses to accuracy item; ratings available for 52-53 problems
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs. other prompt counts; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs. Unit 4
finding.std_deviation: interestingness SD=1.24; closeness SD=1.28; Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20; Unit 6 closeness SD=1.29

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret teacher prompting as evidence of problem-posing, iterative refinement, and monitoring of realism and mathematical clarity. Teachers used ChatGPT not just to generate text but to brainstorm, check realism, and improve problem structure, showing a clear role for professional judgment and iterative refinement. The study does not measure durable skills directly in students, but it substantively analyzes teachers’ iterative prompting behavior as a form of metacognitive and problem-solving work.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting patterns, iterative revision behavior, and categories of prompt use
finding.study_size: n=7 teachers; 558 total prompts across 143 problems

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined whether teacher-facing AI made personalization time-efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem and about 246 seconds (roughly 4 minutes) per problem. Efficiency did not improve over time; in fact, Unit 6 required more prompts and more time than Unit 4 (4.6 vs. 3.2 prompts/problem; 286 vs. 204 seconds/problem), indicating that the process remained time-intensive.
finding.measure: Teacher time spent creating each personalized problem; number of prompts per problem
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 more prompts/problem in Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds more/problem in Unit 6
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; Unit 4 time SD=153; Unit 6 time SD=169

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI could influence how schools and curriculum systems implement personalization, but it does not test institutional policy or governance outcomes directly. Its main institutional implication is that teacher-facing AI may support professional learning and oversight, yet its time cost and limited personalization granularity may constrain scale-up in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: Discussion-based implications for curriculum design, teacher professional learning, and feasibility of scaling teacher-in-the-loop GenAI

paper_profiles.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Schools: Unveiling Factors Influencing Teachers’ Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference of Artificial Intelligence in Education 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses why AI-based adaptive learning platforms, despite evidence of positive learning effects in controlled studies, are adopted slowly in real schools. The authors argue that adoption depends not only on platform features or individual teacher attitudes, but also on broader school-level conditions such as workload, teacher ownership, support, governance, and ethical concerns.

To investigate this, the authors developed and validated a survey instrument on factors influencing adoption of adaptive learning platforms in schools. They first conducted a semi-systematic literature review, expert discussions with platform creators, and pilot testing with teachers, then administered the resulting instrument to 792 public school teachers from Grades 5-12 in a country-level sample. Exploratory factor analysis identified seven factors: workload, teacher ownership, perceived support, perceived knowledge and confidence, classroom orchestration, product quality, and ethics.

The study then correlated survey responses with teachers’ real-world engagement on the platform, measured using platform log data for the first half of the 2022-2023 academic year. The strongest positive correlations with engagement were tied to useful professional development, belief in the platform’s success, satisfaction, helpful feedback, and trust. A predictive model using the survey data explained about 24% of the variance in engagement (R2 = 0.244), suggesting that holistic school-level and teacher-level factors can meaningfully predict whether teachers actually use adaptive learning platforms. The authors conclude that reducing workload, strengthening teacher ownership and support, improving orchestration, and minimizing privacy concerns may improve adoption in practice.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ engagement was associated with workload-related perceptions, but the workload factor itself had only a neutral mean (3.09/5), suggesting the platform neither clearly increased nor decreased workload on average. The paper emphasizes that teachers prefer adaptive platforms that do not add extra work, but it does not report a direct causal effect on workload outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses on workload-related items; real-world engagement with the adaptive learning platform
finding.study_size: n=792 (survey); engagement correlations analyzed on the surveyed teacher sample
finding.effect_size: R2=0.244 for the predictive model; item-level Pearson correlations up to r=0.246

finding.finding_summary: Teachers who reported greater ownership, support, knowledge/confidence, and satisfaction with the adaptive platform were more engaged in real-world use. The strongest association was with helpful professional development (r=0.246), followed by belief in success (r=0.226) and satisfaction with the platform (r=0.200), indicating that teacher attitudes and engagement-related dispositions were meaningfully linked to usage.
finding.measure: Teacher engagement with the adaptive learning platform (log-based active days) and survey measures of ownership, support, confidence, and satisfaction
finding.effect_size: r=0.246 (highest reported correlation); R2=0.244 predictive model

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that school-level and system-level factors such as governance, support structures, teacher community, and ethics are relevant to predicting adoption. The predictive model explained 24.4% of variance in teachers’ real-world engagement, and the authors argue that institutional supports may matter more than individual teacher knowledge alone for scaling adoption of AI platforms in schools.
finding.measure: Survey-derived school-level adoption factors; predictive model of teachers’ engagement with platform log data

paper_profiles.title: Multimodal Engagement Analysis from Facial Videos in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student engagement can be automatically estimated from classroom video in a real secondary-school setting, and whether personalization improves such models. The authors position the work within affective computing and classroom analytics, arguing that prior studies were limited by small samples, computer-based settings, or weak engagement measures.

Using audio-visual recordings from 47 classes over about one and a half months in a German secondary school, the authors manually annotated continuous student engagement for a subsample of 15 students in Grades 8 and 12. They extracted two feature streams from face videos: attention-related features from a head-pose model and affect-related features from a facial-expression model, then trained several classifiers (SVM, random forest, MLP, LSTM) to predict 3-level engagement. The best models achieved AUROC values up to 0.719 (Grade 12, attention features), and personalization with about 60 seconds of student-specific labeled data improved AUROC by an average of 0.084, with larger gains for affect features.

The main conclusion is that classroom engagement can be predicted from facial video with moderate performance, especially using attention-related features, and that a small amount of personalized data can materially improve model performance. The study also concludes that continuous, observer-based engagement labels are feasible in authentic classrooms, though performance is constrained by class imbalance, limited sample size, and the difficulty of observing disengagement from facial video alone. The paper is primarily a methods paper for classroom analytics and teacher-facing monitoring rather than an evaluation of an educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that engagement could be predicted from classroom facial videos with moderate accuracy, indicating that observable behavioral and affective cues are meaningfully associated with student engagement. In person-independent models, the best AUROC reached 0.719 (Grade 12, Attention-Net + LSTM), and personalization with 60 seconds of student-specific data improved AUROC by an average of 0.084, with gains up to 0.124.
finding.measure: Continuous observer-rated student engagement, discretized into low/medium/high engagement; model performance measured by weighted AUROC
finding.study_size: n=15 students (Grade 8 n=7; Grade 12 n=8), 75 labeled samples total

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and their teachers perceive a generative AI-supported activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors ask what educational benefits and challenges arise when 5th-grade students use a GenAI-powered platform to read, represent, and transform math story problems into their own culturally relevant mathematical stories.

The intervention was implemented in six classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 fifth-grade students and six teachers. Students worked through a three-step process: asking questions about provided math stories, representing their understanding with visual tools, and transforming their ideas into original stories using GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. The study then used semi-structured student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended student survey responses, and classroom observations, analyzed through thematic analysis.

The main findings were entirely perceptual and qualitative. Participants reported benefits in creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. At the same time, they identified challenges including weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent stories, AI being 'too perfect,' limited formative feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and lack of multiple communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support K-12 mathematical creative writing, but only when carefully designed to preserve learning opportunities, human interaction, and pedagogical feedback.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity as supporting writing-related skills, including generating, expanding, revising, and making stories more original. The study is qualitative and does not report standardized writing scores, but interview evidence from 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers suggests the tool helped students produce more detailed and coherent math stories.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of creative mathematical writing quality and originality

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the activity helped students understand fraction-related math ideas, represent mathematical thinking visually, and identify misconceptions. The study was conducted with 79 5th-grade students in fraction division and fraction multiplication units, but it provides thematic evidence rather than quantified achievement effects.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, representation, and problem comprehension

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI activity as increasing interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. The qualitative findings from focus groups, interviews, and observations indicate that working with AI made math feel more engaging and motivating, though no numerical engagement measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the activity promoted prompt engineering, flexible/divergent thinking, convergent thinking, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses, all of which map to durable skills such as critical thinking and metacognition. However, it also found challenges: some students struggled to critically evaluate AI output and to formulate coherent stories, suggesting uneven skill development.
finding.measure: Perceived critical thinking, metacognition, and prompt engineering in AI-supported writing

finding.finding_summary: The study also frames the activity as supporting creative writing in a mathematics context, including culturally relevant storytelling and use of images. This is substantively about creative writing as a cross-disciplinary academic activity, although the paper does not provide objective writing performance measures.
finding.measure: Perceived creative writing and storytelling quality in math tasks

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school students want generative AI to function as a peer during collaborative mathematics problem solving, rather than as a tutor or teacher aide. The authors argue that most K-12 AI research has focused on individualized tutoring, leaving an important gap in understanding how AI might support group-based classroom work where students are expected to co-construct solutions, negotiate strategies, and share responsibility.

To study this question, the authors ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 students in grades 6-8. Students experienced both human-only collaborative math tasks and interactions with two text-based AI peers embedded in a technology probe, then reflected on the differences and co-designed their ideal AI peers through posters, dialogue-writing, surveys, interviews, and group discussion. The design emphasized middle-school mathematics CPS tasks aligned to state standards and used both quantitative measures (NASA-TLX, GEQ) and qualitative analysis of reflections, artifacts, and interviews.

The main finding is that students did not want an AI peer that simply optimized correctness or followed a rigid instructional script. Instead, they preferred a scaffold-first peer that offers hints, checks, and concept refreshers under clear student control, uses a friendly but competent peer tone, and supports co-agency rather than doing the work for them. Quantitatively, AI peer sessions reduced temporal demand but increased physical demand and lowered some group climate scores; qualitatively, students criticized overly directive, repetitive, or emotionally unresponsive AI behaviors as 'teachery,' rude, or not collaborative. The paper concludes with design recommendations for building AI peers that better fit middle-school norms of collaboration, pacing, and emotional attunement.

finding.finding_summary: The study centered on middle-school mathematics collaborative problem solving tasks aligned to grades 6-8 standards. Students reported that AI peers could help them move through math tasks faster and provide useful hints/explanations, but they also criticized rigid or overly direct mathematical help that did not support co-agency. The findings suggest AI peers can scaffold math problem solving, but only when help is adjustable and student-controlled.
finding.measure: Collaborative mathematics problem-solving task performance and student perceptions of math help

finding.finding_summary: Students valued encouragement, emotional recognition, and support during moments of confusion or frustration, and they reacted negatively when AI peers failed to acknowledge these states. In qualitative accounts, emotionally unresponsive AI sometimes increased self-blame or made the interaction feel less trustworthy, while human peers were described as offering better emotional scaffolding. The paper shows emotional attunement was central to whether students accepted the AI peer as supportive.
finding.measure: Interview and reflection themes on frustration, encouragement, trust, and emotional support; GEQ social climate indicators
finding.study_size: n=24 (interviews from n=18; whole-class reflections in 5 sessions)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examined collaboration, co-agency, negotiation of methods, and group coordination in mathematics CPS. Students wanted AI peers that would ask questions, negotiate strategies, and work with them rather than take over or repeat themselves; when AI behavior was rigid or redundant, students saw it as breaking collaboration. Quantitatively, perceived task coordination decreased in AI peer sessions (GIT: M=4.76, SD=1.58) compared with human-only CPS (M=5.54, SD=1.52), indicating weaker collaborative functioning.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (Group Integration-Task, Attractions to Group-Social) and qualitative reflections/interviews about collaboration
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative analyses; qualitative n=24
finding.std_deviation: GIT SDs=1.58 vs 1.52; ATGS SDs=1.81 vs 2.05

finding.finding_summary: AI peers reduced the sense of time pressure during collaborative math work, but they also increased physical/operational effort because students had to manage text input, navigation, and interpreting AI outputs. On NASA-TLX, temporal demand was lower with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than with human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), but physical demand was higher (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41). This indicates a tradeoff between efficiency gains and interaction overhead.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX subscales (temporal demand, physical demand)
finding.effect_size: Temporal Demand d=1.15; Physical Demand d=1.14
finding.std_deviation: Temporal Demand SDs=4.38 vs 4.13; Physical Demand SDs=4.65 vs 2.41

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Programming Task Creation of Primary School Teachers in Training
paper_profiles.population: Adult (teachers in training; primarily preservice primary school teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how preservice primary school teachers create Scratch programming tasks for primary school students, and whether support from an automated static analysis tool, LitterBox, changes the quality of the tasks they produce. The motivation is that teachers in primary school often have limited programming knowledge, which can lead to poor example code and potentially negative learning consequences for students.

The authors ran a pre-study and a main A/B study with teachers in training at the University of Passau. In the main study, 59 participants created their own Scratch task; 30 were instructed to use LitterBox at least twice, while 29 served as controls. Participants submitted task texts and Scratch programs and also answered surveys about their process and their evaluation of the tool. The study used thematic analysis for open responses and nonparametric statistical comparisons for the task artifacts.

The paper finds that teachers in training usually begin task creation by brainstorming ideas and then often start with programming before writing the task text. Tool support changed the artifacts: the LitterBox group wrote more hints in task texts and produced fewer bug patterns and smells in their Scratch programs, while also reporting fewer programming difficulties. Participants generally viewed the tool positively, especially for detecting patterns and giving suggestions, though they wanted features such as automatic refactoring and noted some comprehension/usability limitations. Overall, the paper concludes that automated code analysis can help preservice teachers create more scaffolded and higher-quality programming tasks, and that teacher education should explicitly include such tools.

finding.finding_summary: In the main study, preservice primary school teachers using LitterBox created task artifacts with better programming-code quality than controls. Across 56 analyzed programs, the tool group inserted significantly fewer bug patterns (group Ctrl 1.26 vs. Trmt 0.72; p=0.034, A12=0.66) and fewer smells (Ctrl 3.19 vs. Trmt 2.28; p=0.022, A12=0.68), with lower bug and smell density as well.
finding.measure: Scratch code quality metrics: number of bug patterns, smells, and densities in created programs
finding.study_size: n=56 analyzed programs (59 teachers in training total; 29 control, 30 treatment)
finding.effect_size: A12=0.66 for bug patterns; A12=0.68 for smells

finding.finding_summary: The tool support was perceived as helping teachers in training work more efficiently and with less difficulty, although the paper does not report a direct time-saving effect. Participants in the treatment group reported significantly fewer programming difficulties (p=0.038, A12=0.66), and several survey responses indicated that LitterBox helped detect bugs without long searching and provided timely feedback during task creation.
finding.measure: Self-reported programming difficulties and perceived usefulness/time help from survey responses
finding.effect_size: A12=0.66 for fewer reported programming difficulties

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that LitterBox encouraged more scaffolded task design, which is a task-creation practice related to planning and metacognitive decision-making. Treatment participants included significantly more hints in their task texts than controls (Ctrl 1.28 vs. Trmt 1.90; p=0.01, A12=0.33), indicating more deliberate scaffolding of the learner task.
finding.measure: Number of hints included in task texts; qualitative reports about task-creation process

paper_profiles.title: Investigating High School and Pre-High School Teachers’ Perceptions and Experiences Introducing Quantum Concepts: A Survey of QuanTime and other Quantum-related Activities
paper_profiles.population: Pre-high school (grades 4-8) and High School (grades 9-12) teachers in K-12 settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-high school and high school teachers perceive and experience the use of QuanTime and other quantum-related activities for introducing foundational quantum concepts in K-12 classrooms. The central question is whether these packaged, ready-to-use activities are practical, engaging, and supportive for educators who may have limited prior background in quantum physics.

The intervention/approach studied is not a controlled treatment but a survey-based evaluation of teacher experiences with QuanTime activities such as Wave-Particle Duality, Electron Transitions, and Art & Polarization, as well as other teacher-selected quantum activities. The study surveyed 36 educators (12 pre-high school and 23 high school teachers, plus one outreach coordinator) using 12 Likert-scale items and open-ended responses about curriculum fit, confidence, student engagement, preparation time, administrative support, and willingness to use the activities again. Teachers were self-selected from a National Q-12 partnership mailing list.

Findings indicate that teachers generally perceived the activities positively. Most respondents agreed that the activities fit their curriculum, were manageable to implement, and engaged students; teachers also reported limited need for additional preparation time or support. Open-ended responses emphasized that the activities were visually engaging, easy to integrate, and useful for sparking student curiosity about quantum concepts. The authors conclude that QuanTime and related activities are promising tools for early quantum literacy in K-12 settings, though the evidence is based on self-reported teacher perceptions rather than direct student outcome measures.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported broadly positive student reactions to QuanTime and other quantum-related activities. On a 7-point Likert scale, mean ratings for student enjoyment (5.8 overall) and engagement (5.7 overall) were above neutral, with high school teachers reporting somewhat higher scores than pre-high school teachers. Open-ended comments described students as excited, curious, and interested in the activities.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings of student enjoyment and engagement; open-ended teacher feedback
finding.study_size: n=36 teachers (12 pre-high school, 23 high school, 1 outreach coordinator)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers indicated that the activities supported student curiosity, questioning, and group-based sensemaking. Several open-ended responses described students asking conceptual questions, working in groups, and using visuals to solidify understanding, suggesting gains in collaborative problem solving and critical thinking rather than direct measured skill growth.
finding.measure: Teacher open-ended responses about student questions, collaboration, and sensemaking

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on teachers’ experiences introducing foundational quantum concepts, with reported alignment to topics such as wave-particle duality, electron transitions, entanglement, and light properties. Teachers generally agreed that the activities helped students learn quantum concepts, with an overall mean of 5.7 for the item on student learning/engagement with quantum concepts, but no direct student assessment data were collected.
finding.measure: Teacher Likert-scale ratings of student learning about quantum concepts and open-ended descriptions of concept understanding

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally found the activities easy to implement and not overly demanding in terms of preparation or support. The mean rating for needing more preparation time was 4.0 and for needing more support was 3.6, indicating that most respondents did not feel substantial additional workload was required. Open-ended feedback also emphasized minimal preparation and ease of integration into existing curricula.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings of preparation time, support needs, and curriculum fit; open-ended feedback on usability

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported supportive school contexts and strong willingness to reuse the activities, suggesting potential for broader institutional adoption. Mean ratings were positive for administrator support (5.6 overall) and for wanting to do the activities again next year (6.2 overall), and some teachers indicated sharing the materials with colleagues or planning future use. However, these are perceptions and intentions rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of administrative support and intention to reuse/share activities

paper_profiles.title: Towards an optimised evaluation of teachers’ discourse: The case of engaging messages
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (Grades 9-12), with classroom transcripts from secondary students in Spain
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical measurement problem in educational research: how to efficiently evaluate teachers’ discourse, specifically engaging messages, without relying on slow manual transcript coding. The authors argue that teacher discourse is important for student motivation and outcomes, but that existing approaches are too labor-intensive to scale. They propose a semi-automated workflow combining automatic speech transcription with fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) to detect engaging messages in classroom transcripts and then classify them as gain-framed or loss-framed.

The study has two parts. In Study 1, the authors trained and tested two GPT-3 Ada models using real transcripts from secondary school lessons in Spain across two academic years: one model identified engaging messages, and the other classified them by framing. The identification model achieved sensitivity of 84.31% and specificity of 97.69% on a testing set of 80 engaging messages and 1,576 non-engaging sentences; the framing model achieved sensitivity of 91.11% and specificity of 86.36% on a testing set of 45 gain-framed and 44 loss-framed messages. In Study 2, they applied the models to 719 lesson recordings from a third academic year, reducing 303,418 transcript sentences to 202 verified engaging messages after manual review, and found that 67.33% were gain-framed and 32.67% were loss-framed.

The context is public secondary schools in Spain, involving 74 teachers in Study 1 and 19 teachers in Study 2 across grades 9-12. The main conclusions are methodological rather than causal: fine-tuned LLMs can substantially reduce the labor needed to analyze teacher discourse while retaining acceptable accuracy, making large-scale transcript-based study more feasible. Substantively, the descriptive results suggest teachers use more gain-framed than loss-framed engaging messages overall, with use declining in Grade 12 and toward the end of the academic year. The paper suggests this approach could support future feedback-based interventions aimed at improving discourse and student outcomes, but it does not test such an intervention directly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that fine-tuned LLMs can dramatically reduce the workload of transcript coding for teacher discourse analysis. In Study 2, 719 audio transcripts containing 303,418 sentences were reduced to 1,828 candidate sentences, later refined to 202 verified engaging messages, and the identification/classification steps were completed within seconds once the models were trained. Study 1 also reports model performance that supports this efficiency approach: sensitivity 84.31% and specificity 97.69% for identification, and sensitivity 91.11% and specificity 86.36% for framing classification.
finding.measure: Transcript coding efficiency, model-based identification and classification of engaging messages, processing time, and classification performance metrics
finding.study_size: Study 1: n=74 teachers, 2,516 audio files; testing set n=80 engaging messages and n=1,576 non-engaging sentences for identification, and n=45 gain-framed and n=44 loss-framed messages for classification. Study 2: n=19 teachers, 719 audio files, 303,418 transcript sentences

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on engaging messages as a discourse feature linked in prior literature to student motivation, vitality, and performance, and it describes the actual prevalence of gain- versus loss-framed messages in teachers’ speech. In Study 2, 67.33% of the 202 verified engaging messages were gain-framed and 32.67% were loss-framed; the authors interpret gain-framed messages as more supportive of motivation and engagement, while loss-framed messages are associated with anxiety and poorer outcomes, though these outcomes were not directly measured in this paper.
finding.measure: Frequency and framing of teacher engaging messages (gain-framed vs loss-framed) in lesson transcripts
finding.study_size: Study 2: n=19 teachers; 202 verified engaging messages extracted from 719 audio files

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that scalable AI-based discourse analysis could support teacher evaluation, professional development, and future feedback interventions at the institutional level. Its main institutional contribution is methodological: it offers a more efficient way to analyze classroom discourse that could enable larger-scale monitoring and feedback systems, especially for teacher professional development. However, the paper does not evaluate policy or institutional outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Feasibility of scalable discourse analysis for teacher evaluation and professional development
finding.study_size: Study 1 and Study 2 combined; n=74 teachers in Study 1 and n=19 teachers in Study 2

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how in-service secondary school physical education (PE) teachers in South Korea perceive the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI into K-12 PE. The authors focus on a context that is underexplored in AIED: PE classes, where teachers face unique demands related to large open spaces, safety, heterogeneous student abilities, individualized feedback, and assessment workload.

The study used participatory, focus-group ideation workshops with 17 PE teachers. After a brief AI literacy lecture, teachers discussed classroom challenges, sketched AI ideas, developed storyboards, and role-played scenarios. The process elicited four envisioned AI roles in PE: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. Teachers imagined AI helping with class management, personalized movement feedback, balanced team formation, and automated multidimensional assessment.

The paper’s main contribution is a teacher-centered account of where AI might realistically add value in PE and what barriers could limit adoption. Teachers generally viewed AI as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for educators, but they also raised concerns about infrastructure, teacher readiness, alignment with PE goals, overreliance on AI, and student privacy/data security. The study concludes that successful AI design for PE should be grounded in teachers’ lived classroom needs and careful attention to institutional and ethical constraints.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently described AI as a way to reduce workload in PE classes by supporting class management, environment setup, student monitoring, safety warnings, and data handling. In the qualitative workshop with 17 teachers, participants emphasized that these functions could free time for more meaningful instruction and feedback, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, class management burden, and time-saving potential in ideation workshops

finding.finding_summary: Teachers raised institutional and infrastructural barriers to AI adoption, including low subject priority for PE, lack of space, weak IT infrastructure, device fragility, and limited support for implementation and maintenance. The paper shows strong concern that adoption depends on broader school and policy conditions, but it does not test institutional interventions or quantify institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of institutional support, infrastructure, and implementation barriers

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Perspectives and Experiences After Deployment of AI Literacy Curriculum in Middle-School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school teachers experienced implementing the MIT RAICA (Responsible AI for Computational Action) AI literacy curriculum. The study asks how teachers adapted the modules to their classrooms, how their beliefs about AI and teaching changed over the course of implementation, and what supports or materials would improve future deployments.

The intervention consisted of three project-based RAICA modules taught by seven teachers with interdisciplinary backgrounds in art, business, and computer science. Teachers received ongoing professional development, participated in weekly debriefs with researchers, and later took part in semi-structured interviews. The modules asked students to build an interactive art installation, create a chatbot, or design an app for their school/community, with an emphasis on AI concepts, ethical thinking, and computational action.

Using thematic analysis of eight interviews, the authors found that teachers generally became more confident in understanding AI and more able to connect it to real-world applications, biases, and ethical concerns. Teachers reported using creative, interdisciplinary, and student-centered strategies to increase engagement, but they also encountered technical hurdles, time constraints, vague guidance, and uneven student readiness. Overall, the paper concludes that flexible curriculum design, stronger teacher support, more concrete implementation resources, and accommodations for diverse learners are important for successful K-12 AI literacy instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the RAICA curriculum increased student engagement, playful learning, and interest in AI-related careers, while also helping students feel comfortable expressing ideas in multiple modalities. Because this was a qualitative interview study, no effect size was reported; the finding is based on teachers’ descriptions of student enthusiasm, curiosity, and comfort during module implementation (n=7 teachers, 8 interviews).
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of student engagement, interest, and comfort participating in AI lessons

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum was used to foster critical thinking, ethical reasoning, collaboration, and design thinking. Teachers described students brainstorming, peer feedback, group prototyping, and repeated reflection on stakeholders, intended and unintended impacts, and bias in AI systems; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of student critical thinking, collaboration, reflection, and ethical reasoning during project work

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported both benefits and burdens to implementation efficiency. On one hand, tools like the kanban board, checklists, and structured materials supported planning and assessment; on the other, teachers said the workbook was too long, the guidance too vague, the content time-consuming, and technical issues and preparation demands sometimes forced them to drop AI components.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of workload, preparation demands, and usefulness of curriculum materials/tools

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that implementing AI literacy curricula can inform future curriculum design, professional development, and school-level integration of AI into existing programs. Teachers advocated for broader AI integration, more inclusive access, and stronger institutional supports such as technical assistance, clearer guides, and accommodations for students with diverse learning needs.
finding.measure: Teacher recommendations and reflections on curriculum adoption, support needs, and integration into school curricula

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-to-classroom assignment and student achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student achievement can be improved by changing which teachers are assigned to which classrooms, without changing the teacher workforce. The authors focus on within-school and within-district teacher-to-classroom reassignment policies and estimate average reallocation effects (AREs) using data from the Measures of Effective Teaching (MET) project.

The empirical strategy uses experimentally generated teacher assignment variation from MET, but the realized data include teacher non-compliance, student movement, and classroom peer changes. To address this, the paper develops a semiparametric instrumental-variables framework that uses assigned teacher and peer characteristics as instruments for realized ones. The main assignment variables are teachers’ observational Framework for Teaching (FFT) scores and students’ baseline achievement levels, discretized into categories.

The study sample includes elementary and middle school students in grades 4–8 from six large urban U.S. districts, with about 8,500 math students and 9,600 ELA students. The paper finds that alternative teacher-to-classroom assignments could raise average achievement by up to 0.04 standard deviations relative to the status quo, and about 0.02 standard deviations relative to the random-assignment baseline in MET schools. The authors conclude that teacher assignment policies are resource-neutral and potentially meaningful, though they emphasize limits to external validity and note that classroom-composition changes are not studied.

finding.finding_summary: Alternative teacher-to-classroom assignments based on teacher FFT and student baseline achievement are estimated to improve average student test performance. The paper reports that changing within-district teacher assignments could raise average classroom achievement by as much as 0.04 standard deviations, and that moving from the MET status quo to the optimal assignment yields about a 0.02 standard deviation gain.
finding.measure: End-of-year standardized state test scores in mathematics and English language arts (ELA), reported as district-standardized z-scores
finding.study_size: math: n=about 8,500 students and 614 teachers; ELA: n=about 9,600 students and 649 teachers
finding.effect_size: 0.04 SD (maximal reallocation effect); 0.02 SD (status quo to optimal in MET schools)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the proposed teacher reassignment policy is resource neutral because it improves outcomes by redeploying existing teachers rather than hiring new ones or reducing class size. This is a policy/operational finding rather than a direct workload measure, but it is central to the paper’s contribution.
finding.measure: Feasibility and resource-neutrally of alternative teacher-to-classroom assignment policies

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that teacher-to-classroom assignment policies can meaningfully affect student achievement and therefore have policy relevance for districts and schools. It also reports that the optimal and worst feasible assignments differ enough to produce nontrivial aggregate achievement differences, suggesting institutional assignment rules matter.
finding.measure: Difference in aggregate student achievement under alternative teacher assignment policies

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '24 (The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve math learning processes for middle school students, particularly those from low-income backgrounds. The authors argue that AI-supported tutoring may help address persistent access and equity gaps by combining adaptive math software with human tutor support, especially during the school day when high-quality tutoring is often unavailable.

Across three quasi-experimental studies in urban middle schools in Pennsylvania and California, students used different math platforms (IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia) and received varying forms of human support. Site 1 compared math software alone to software plus a math teacher and then software plus a math teacher plus remote tutoring; Site 2 compared i-Ready use before and during a brief tutoring period; Site 3 examined changes in a dashboard-supported tutoring implementation as tutor-to-student ratios improved. The samples were 125 students in Site 1, 385 in Site 2, and 75 in Site 3, all in low-income settings, with Site 3 serving Black male students exclusively.

The study finds that adding human support to AI software increased engagement and learning-process measures such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, and lessons/workspaces completed. Effects were strongest for students with lower prior achievement, while higher-achieving students benefited less and in some cases may have been interrupted by round-robin tutoring. The authors conclude that hybrid human-AI tutoring shows promise as a scalable and lower-cost way to improve student engagement and may work best when human attention is better targeted, potentially with dashboard guidance.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental studies, hybrid human-AI tutoring was associated with improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software alone or earlier less-intensive tutoring conditions. In Site 1 (n=125), adding a math teacher and then remote tutoring increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient; for time spent, the tutoring increment was significant (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]). In Site 2 (n=385), weekly i-Ready usage increased from 24 to 33 minutes and lesson passing increased during the tutoring period; in Site 3 (n=75), students completed 0.36 more MATHia workspaces per hour after tutor-to-student ratios improved from about 1:8 to 1:4.
finding.measure: Math software engagement and progress measures: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly reports increased student engagement with math software under hybrid human-AI tutoring, which the authors treat as a key intermediate outcome. In Site 1, tutoring significantly increased time spent on IXL (β=0.202, p=0.006) and questions answered, and the authors interpret this as improved engagement; in Site 2, average time on task rose from 24 to 33 minutes per week during tutoring. Effects were stronger for lower-pretest students, indicating the intervention especially improved participation among students with greater need.
finding.measure: Engagement / time on task / participation in math software

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved students' productivity with the software, suggesting more efficient use of tutoring time and learning opportunities. In Site 3, when tutor-to-student ratios improved from approximately 1:8 to 1:4, students completed an additional 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]), and in Site 2 students completed more lessons per week during tutoring than before treatment (β=0.2437, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381]). The authors also argue that dashboard-guided tutoring could reduce inefficient round-robin interruptions and better target tutor effort.
finding.measure: Workspaces completed per hour; lessons passed per week; time spent on task

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report describes a seven-week classroom pilot of Colleague AI Classroom, a generative-AI platform co-designed with 21 in-service teachers across five Washington State school settings. The study asks how teachers design and implement AI-assisted classroom tools, how teacher judgment and prior AI competency shape student-AI interactions and instructional outcomes, and what supports are needed for effective AI integration.

The pilot introduced four teacher-facing and student-facing features: Teaching Aide (structured student-AI conversation), Assessment & AI Grading (rubric generation, automated feedback and grading), AI Tutor (open-ended student support), and Student Growth Insights (teacher-facing summaries of interaction patterns). More than 600 students in grades 6-12 used the platform in class at teacher direction, with teachers planning parallel AI and non-AI versions of activities and providing weekly reflections, surveys, interviews, and usage logs.

Across features, the report concludes that AI was most useful when teachers framed it clearly, aligned it to instructional goals, and retained final authority over evaluation. Teachers generally valued narrative feedback, individualized scaffolds, and workload reduction more than automated scores, while student engagement and learning varied by grade band, subject area, and implementation frequency. The study’s core claim is that generative AI can function as a helpful “third agent” in classrooms, but only when supported by teacher expertise, careful design, and strong pedagogical framing.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported conversations and feedback helped students with writing-related tasks, especially in English/ELA and Spanish. The report notes that high school English teachers used AI for prewriting and brainstorming, which improved essay quality, and Spanish teachers used AI for ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback; however, these conclusions are qualitative and no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported quality of writing/prewriting, essay quality, and language-feedback usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described AI conversations as helping multilingual learners participate more confidently in discussion and practice language use. The report states that students who previously hesitated in whole-class talk found their voice through AI conversations and that Spanish teachers used the tool for real-time proficiency feedback, but no formal language fluency measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of student oral participation and proficiency feedback in AI conversations

finding.finding_summary: Math implementations were more variable than humanities or some science uses.
