The report says middle school math conversations sometimes produced thoughtful engagement, but math also showed challenges with accurate diagrams, Socratic-style prompting, and flexible non-linear reasoning; similarly, AI grading trust was lower in math because of scale drift and off-rubric deductions. No quantitative achievement outcome was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement and utility in math conversations and math assessment feedback

finding.finding_summary: Science classrooms generally showed favorable results for AI-assisted conversation and feedback. Teachers reported that AI-facilitated conversations supported inquiry, expanded culturally relevant content, and sometimes helped students learn, though math and earth science were more mixed because of technical and diagram-related limitations. No standardized science test or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student learning, inquiry, and engagement in science AI conversations

finding.finding_summary: Across non-core subjects and interdisciplinary courses, teachers reported useful AI support for tasks such as brainstorming, individualized skill development, and concept building. The report highlights stronger high-school outcomes in 'Other' subjects like Spanish, engineering, and interdisciplinary STEM, but findings are descriptive rather than based on formal achievement measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement and learning in non-ELA/non-math/non-science subjects

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly reports increased student engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate when AI activities were well scaffolded. Teachers said students were more engaged when prompts were clear, when activities were tied to graded work, and when AI provided a low-pressure environment for revision and participation; no standardized engagement scale or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated engagement, participation, confidence, and buy-in

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI supported deeper thinking, inquiry, revision, and evidence-based reasoning when teachers framed tasks well. Teachers described AI as helping students generate drafts, reflect on feedback, and revise their work, and the report emphasizes benefits for inquiry and problem-solving, though these are qualitative observations rather than measured gains in critical thinking or metacognition.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of inquiry, revision, reflection, and reasoning during AI-supported activities

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency was a central focus of the report, and teachers reported substantial workload benefits. Platform logs showed median AI grading coverage of 92.2% across submitted work and 58 classroom assessment records, while teachers said SGI saved hours of scanning, AI grading reduced feedback burden, and narrative feedback sped turnaround; no formal time-on-task effect size was reported.
finding.measure: AI grading coverage, teacher-reported time savings, and reduced feedback workload
finding.study_size: n=58 classroom-level assessment records; n=21 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that effective AI adoption depends on teacher AI competency, co-design, school-district partnership, and institutional support such as MOU-based implementation and privacy policies. These are implementation and governance findings rather than outcome effects, and no quantitative institutional impact metric was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher implementation patterns, district partnership structures, and co-design process
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; five Washington State school settings

gaps: The sweep is heavily skewed toward general AI-in-education or student-use papers; it does not yet adequately cover the 'teacher morale' component of the thread, especially studies linking AI tools to teacher morale, wellbeing, job satisfaction, burnout, or engagement.

K-12 coverage is present, but it is patchy and mostly secondary/high school or mixed teacher samples; there is little explicit elementary/primary teacher or student evidence tied to classroom engagement outcomes.

The current results are dominated by descriptive surveys/case studies about AI tools and perceptions, with little evidence of intervention, experimental, or longitudinal studies on classroom engagement or morale.

The AI tool-type angle is under-specified: results mention ChatGPT/AI broadly, but not distinct tool categories such as tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, monitoring systems, generative AI, or teacher augmentation tools as they relate to engagement and morale.

Geographic/contextual coverage is limited and may not generalize well; the sweep includes a few non-US contexts, but not enough to confidently characterize K-12 study populations and settings across regions.
Coverage is still skewed toward broad or tangential AI-in-education papers rather than the thread’s core framing questions.
Teacher morale is not yet directly covered; no study on teacher morale, well-being, job satisfaction, burnout, or attitudes toward AI tools in K-12 classrooms is evident.
Classroom engagement is only indirectly represented; missing are studies that explicitly measure student engagement, participation, attention, or behavioral engagement with AI-supported instruction.

AI tool types are under-specified; current results include general AI, ChatGPT, adaptive learning, monitoring platforms, and curriculum papers, but not a clear mapping of tool categories such as generative AI, tutoring systems, analytics dashboards, automated feedback, or classroom management tools.

K-12 study populations and contexts remain incomplete; there is some coverage of elementary, middle, and high school students/teachers, but not enough on teachers as the primary population across diverse K-12 settings, nor on cross-country/contextual variation.
One visible result is higher education, which does not help the K-12 thread and suggests the sweep needs tighter population filtering.

The sweep currently surfaces broad K-12 AI review/literacy papers, but not the core target of the thread: studies that evaluate AI tools in K-12 with an explicit baseline, pre-AI condition, or comparator/control group.

Comparator-specific evidence is missing: no clear randomized trials, quasi-experiments, matched controls, pretest-posttest designs, or within-classroom before/after studies of AI interventions in K-12.

The findings appear skewed toward conceptual/systematic review literature rather than empirical evaluation studies, so they do not yet establish what suitable comparators or pre-AI benchmarks have been used in practice.

No clear coverage is shown for specific K-12 tool categories relevant to the thread (e.g., tutoring/chatbots, automated feedback, grading/assessment, writing support) where comparator design would matter most.

The sweep is heavily weighted toward reviews/search-method papers and AI literacy, but it does not yet surface studies that explicitly establish baseline/pre-AI classroom conditions in K-12, which are needed to evaluate change attributable to AI tools.

Comparator designs are under-covered: I do not see trials or quasi-experimental studies comparing an AI tool against non-AI baselines (business-as-usual, teacher-led instruction, rule-based software, or alternative edtech) in K-12 settings.

The current results skew toward broad K-12 AI applications and teacher perceptions, but miss distinct student populations and subject areas where comparator choice matters (e.g., math, writing, science, special education, early literacy).
There is little evidence of studies discussing methodological guidance for counterfactuals, pre/post baselines, or control groups specific to K-12 AI interventions.

The sweep also appears to miss implementation/evaluation papers that report pre-intervention performance or routine practice metrics, which are essential for defining 'baseline supports' in this thread.

The sweep is dominated by a broad adoption-focused review/article and search failures; it does not yet surface enough empirical K-12 studies on concrete implementation mechanisms (how teachers actually use AI tools in lesson planning, feedback, assessment, differentiation, admin work).
There is little direct coverage of teacher morale, job satisfaction, stress, burnout, or workload outcomes tied to AI tool use in daily teaching work.
Classroom engagement is mentioned only indirectly; missing are studies on student engagement, participation, interaction quality, and classroom dynamics after AI adoption in K-12 settings.
K-12 specificity is weak: the current result explicitly notes that K-12 integration studies are scarce, but no strong elementary/middle/high-school empirical papers are yet identified.

Pathways affecting implementation are underdeveloped: missing are barriers/enablers such as training, school leadership, policy, privacy concerns, infrastructure, and professional development in K-12 contexts.

The sweep is heavily weighted toward higher education, generic educational technology, and teacher wellbeing, but the research thread is specifically about daily K-12 teaching work and AI tool implementation mechanisms.

There is little direct evidence on K-12 classroom practice: lesson planning, grading, feedback, differentiation, communication with parents, behavior management, or administrative workload reduction using AI.

The morale/classroom engagement angle is underdeveloped; few results examine how AI adoption affects teacher motivation, professional identity, stress, autonomy, or student engagement in K-12 settings.

No clear studies focus on implementation pathways, school-level rollout models, training/coaching, leadership support, policy constraints, or adoption barriers/enablers specifically for K-12 teachers.
A key missing study type is practitioner or design-based research in schools (pilot interventions, case studies, mixed-methods implementation studies), rather than broad reviews or bibliometrics.

No empirical comparative evidence yet on whether AI tools improve teacher morale, burnout, job satisfaction, or retention in K-12 settings; current hits are mostly reviews, conceptual pieces, or AI literacy/curriculum studies.
No direct evidence on classroom engagement outcomes attributable to teacher-facing AI tools in K-12 schools (e.g., engagement compared with non-AI instruction or pre/post adoption).
No randomized, quasi-experimental, or matched comparative studies surfaced; the sweep is missing the study designs needed to answer 'improves' causally.
Heterogeneity is not addressed: missing subgroup evidence by grade level, subject, teacher experience, school context, or implementation intensity.
Risks/adverse effects are only lightly covered; missing empirical evidence on workload increase, surveillance concerns, bias, privacy, equity, or teacher autonomy impacts.

The sweep is heavily weighted toward higher education, dissertations, and broad reviews; it does not yet surface empirical K-12 studies directly measuring teacher morale, job satisfaction, burnout, or classroom engagement outcomes.
There is little or no comparative evidence (e.g., AI tool vs. non-AI control/comparison, pre/post, or quasi-experimental designs) in K-12 settings, which is central to the research thread.

Heterogeneity is only weakly covered; the current results do not clearly distinguish effects by AI use case (lesson planning, grading, tutoring/chatbots, feedback systems), teacher role, grade level, subject area, or school context.

Risks/downsides are mentioned abstractly, but the sweep does not capture K-12 evidence on unintended consequences such as surveillance concerns, workload shifting, reduced teacher autonomy, inequities, or impacts on student interaction/classroom climate.

No clear studies focused on teacher morale/classroom engagement outcomes in K-12 schools are identified; the current set mostly concerns student satisfaction, generic workload, or institutional responses.
